The most recent documented statement of this housing practice is dated January 2021, with no later instance documented. The GLAAD ALERT Desk documented more than 1,000 anti-LGBTQ incidents nationwide in 2025, of which California recorded 198, the highest of any state. That ranking is by raw count only with no population or per-capita denominator, so it does not establish higher individual risk than a smaller state. A separate analysis of the same 2025 data reports a dramatic increase in anti-LGBTQ hate-crime reports in Los Angeles in law-enforcement data covering the same period as Governor Gavin Newsom's platforming of anti-trans figures. A July 2026 analysis places California in the Safest States band with a score of 4.1 and 1.9 recorded incidents, arguing even the most protective floors do not eliminate recorded hostility.

name: New Jersey
text: Federal passports and visas apply. The national record for United States covers the federal layer in detail. New Jersey's Law Against Discrimination, amended in 1991 to cover affectional or sexual orientation and in 2006 to cover gender identity and expression, bars denial of goods, services, facilities and lodging on those grounds in places of public accommodation, described as including hotels, restaurants, stores and transportation, as well as in housing and employment. A trans visitor refused service or lodging can complain to the Division on Civil Rights, which investigates and can grant relief. Bias-motivated crimes carry enhanced penalties where bias rests on gender identity or expression, with sensitivity training available as a sentencing condition. A bill extending bias and intimidation protections to gender identity passed the lower house 71-0 in March 2021. A July 2022 police licensing system carries gender-identity protections, and state-run hospital patient records are required to protect sexual orientation and gender identity data. State identity documents are comparatively open. Since 1 February 2019 a transgender person may obtain an amended birth certificate with corrected name and sex without surgery or any medical procedure, under three laws signed in June 2018; those laws also created an X marker on official documents and put transgender and intersex people on death certificates. Since February 2020 no doctor's note is required to change the M or F marker on a driver licence or state ID, and since April 2021 the X, M and F markers are all available. A November 2022 executive order provides privacy and confidentiality in legal name changes. An April 2023 executive order directs state agencies to protect and defend gender-affirming healthcare within New Jersey's borders, including access by people travelling in from other states. The state has recognised and performed marriages of same-sex couples since 21 October 2013, following a 27 September 2013 court decision whose appeal was rejected on 19 October 2013; the legislature codified the position in December 2021 and the governor signed it on 10 January 2022, effective immediately. A trans visitor whose relationship would be read as same-sex under birth-sex status can marry and have that marriage recognised here. A January 2020 law bars the gay and transgender panic defence, providing that provocation is not objectively reasonable when based on actual or perceived gender identity or expression, including an unwanted non-forcible romantic or sexual advance. The bill passed both chambers 73-0 and 39-0. A July 2026 legal-risk ranking built from a rubric over thousands of tracked anti-trans bills places New Jersey in the fifteen-state Most Protective tier, alongside California, Colorado, Connecticut, Hawaii, Illinois, Massachusetts, Maryland, Minnesota, New Mexico, New York, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont and Washington.

name: Connecticut
text: Connecticut sits in the fifteen-state 'Most Protective' tier of a July 2026 national legal-risk ranking; the national record for United States covers the federal layer in detail. A 2022 shield law protects patients and providers from civil or criminal charges when care that is lawful in Connecticut was banned in the patient's home state, directly relevant to a visitor arriving from a state that has criminalised gender-affirming care. State law bans discrimination on the basis of gender identity or expression in public places, in public and private employment, in governmental services and in the receipt of goods and services; gender identity and expression were added to the statute in 2011. The state hate-crime law covers gender identity or expression and carries additional penalties, consolidated and strengthened by legislation signed in June 2026 and effective 1 October 2026. Identity documents are comparatively open. Since 1 October 2015, under H.B. No. 7006, a birth-certificate sex marker can be changed without surgery on a notarised affidavit from the applicant plus a notarised affidavit from a licensed physician, advanced practice registered nurse or psychologist stating that the person has received appropriate clinical treatment such as hormone therapy. That change replaced an earlier surgery requirement, which the Senate voted 32-3 to remove on 1 June 2015. Driver's licences and state identification can be changed on request, and birth certificates, IDs and licences offer M, F and X options. Since 1 July 2018, people in Connecticut custody are treated consistent with their gender identity, including in strip searches and in access to clothing, commissary items and educational materials, and in housing based on recognised gender. The state anti-bullying law prohibits bullying on the basis of gender identity and expression, explicitly covering cyberbullying and harassment, and applies to all school premises. In April 2021 a federal judge dismissed the lawsuits seeking to block transgender female athletes from competing in Connecticut girls' high-school sports, leaving their eligibility intact. Conversion therapy on minors was banned with immediate effect after signing in May 2017, following House passage 141-8 on 2 May and Senate passage 36-0 on 10 May. The gay panic defence was repealed after unanimous passage in June 2019, signed by Governor Ned Lamont and effective 1 October 2019. Consensual same-sex sexual activity was decriminalised with effect from 1971, and the age of consent is 16 regardless of gender or sexual orientation, having been lowered to 15 in 1975.

name: Illinois
text: See the national record for United States covers the federal layer in detail. Illinois is in fifteen-state Most Protective tier in July 2026 ranking over thousands anti-trans bills. Gender identity bias in employment, housing, credit and public accommodations banned since 1 June 2006 via sexual orientation covering gender-related identity. Under 15 employees exemption removed signed August 2019 effective 1 July 2020 after 2018 veto, jury-selection bias banned effective 1 January 2020. HB 3930 added gender identity to hate crime passed unanimously 16 April and 20 May 2015 signed Governor Bruce Rauner 20 July 2015 effective 1 January 2016, prior only perceived sexual orientation with enhanced penalties for actual or perceived sexual orientation since 1991. SB1761 repealed gay and trans panic passed unanimously June 2017 signed 25 August 2017 effective 1 January 2018. Care protected signed 13 January 2023 effective immediately including travellers, shield bars civil and criminal charges where Illinois-lawful care is banned in home state. Conversion therapy on under 18 banned under Youth Mental Health Protection Act since 1 January 2016, pastors suit dismissed 15 February 2017 as private religious counselling is not trade or commerce. Birth certificate change without surgery passed 31 May 2017 63-43 House and 32-22 Senate signed 25 August 2017 effective 1 January 2018, X since July 2020 and self-attestation passed January and February 2023 effective 1 July. Since 1 July 2024 out-of-Illinois births can change Illinois certificate sex, licences and ID use Gender Designation Change Form with X from 2024. Single-occupancy restrooms gender-neutral passed 109-5 House and 53-0 Senate signed July 2019 effective 1 January 2020. Chicago Human Rights Ordinance as amended in 2016 lets each person determine gender identity with no proof beyond expression for bathroom access, all Chicago public schools have had all-gender bathrooms by signage since December 2021. May 2023 multi-occupancy bill consistent with gender identity passed both chambers but had not been signed or vetoed. Marriage equality signed Governor Pat Quinn 20 November 2013 effective 1 June 2014 after 61-54 House and 32-21 Senate superseding 1996 ban, gender-neutral certificates under July 2021 law and 2023 repeal of out-of-jurisdiction null-and-void provisions took effect in 2024. Civil unions since 1 June 2011 signed 31 January 2011 with out-of-state same-sex marriages recognised as civil unions. Illinois Domestic Violence Act gender-neutral covering partners sharing or having shared dwelling or dating relationship. Consensual same-sex activity lawful since 1 January 1962 when new criminal code eliminated sodomy law making Illinois first state to do so. Age of consent 17 raised from 16 effective 1 January 2012.

name: Massachusetts
text: Federal framework applies alongside state law, the national record for United States covers the federal layer in detail. Massachusetts bans gender identity/expression discrimination in credit, public/private employment, union practices and housing under legislation enacted on 23 November 2011 and in force from 1 July 2012, after executive order of 17 February 2011 for state government, contractors and transgender employees. Public accommodation added by Senate vote of 33-4 on 12 May 2016 and House vote of 117-36 on 7 July 2016, signed by Governor Charlie Baker effective 1 October 2016, retained at ballot on 6 November 2018 by 67. 8 per cent to 32. 2 per cent, for hotels, restaurants, shops and transport. Gender identity in hate-crime statute from 1 July 2012 as criminal act with overt actions motivated at least in part by prejudice, including gender/sexual orientation, incidents collected, summarised and reported via Crime Reporting Unit created by 1990 Hate Crimes Reporting Act with State Police, Attorney General and legislative committees, plus Governor's Task Force on Hate Crimes established in 1991. Birth certificates amendable to gender identity without sex reassignment surgery. X on licences/IDs since November 2019 under Registry of Motor Vehicles regulation. X birth certificates and gender amendment on marriage certificates by law signed on 29 July 2024 in FY25 budget. Boston marriage licence forms with no gender/sex field since August 2023. Confidential name changes without public notice under An Act Protecting Personal Security, signed on 25 November 2025. Shield law since 2022 protects patients/providers from civil/criminal charges where Massachusetts-lawful care banned in home state. July 2022 gender-affirming healthcare bill effective immediately under emergency clause not after usual 90-day period. Conversion therapy on minors banned by 147-8 House vote 13 March 2019 and 34-0 Senate vote 28 March 2019, enacted 4 April 2019, signed 8 April 2019 with immediate effect. Same-sex marriage open per Supreme Judicial Court ruling 18 November 2003, licences from 17 May 2004 after 180-day window, amendment attempts failed, ended 2007. 1913 non-resident marriage bar repealed 31 July 2008, so travelling couples can marry, and 2012 rulings equate out-of-jurisdiction civil unions and California registered domestic partnerships to marriage. Unrepealed section 34 criminalising abominable and detestable crime against nature and section 35 covering any unnatural and lascivious act remain, but private consensual adult conduct exempt since 1974 Commonwealth v. Balthazar, unenforceable there. Repeal stalled, including 2018 session removing abortion, adultery and fornication laws but leaving sodomy, anal-sex and oral-sex provisions, Senate passed repeal unanimously January 2024, House advanced June 2025, Senate committee set floor consideration 24 July 2025. Trans visitor read as same-sex under birth-sex status nominally within wording, not enforced privately. July 2026 rubric on thousands of anti-trans bills puts Massachusetts in fifteen-state Most Protective tier.

name: New Mexico
text: See the national record for United States covers the federal layer in detail. Law effective 1 July 2003 bans gender-identity discrimination in employment, housing, credit, public accommodations and union membership, including restaurants, hotels, shops and other public places. The 15-or-more-employees exemption was repealed effective 1 July 2019, 2023 legislation extended coverage to local entities, counties, schools, universities and government-run agencies under emergency clause, and Albuquerque amended its Human Rights Ordinance in May 2024. Since 1 November 2019 gender change needs no surgery under law passed 26-13 in the House and 33-14 in the Senate signed by Governor Michelle Lujan Grisham, repealing the 1984 surgery requirement for male, female and X neutral designations on birth certificates, driver's licences and state IDs via birth-certificate form with fees and parental consent for minors or Motor Vehicles Division form, replacing perjury statement plus certified name-change order. Since 1 July 2019 single-occupancy restrooms must be gender-neutral for any person regardless of gender identity or sex under law passed 54-12 in the House and 23-15 in the Senate. No law bars transgender girls sports with eligibility by birth certificate original or amended and no further New Mexico Activities Association guidance. March 2023 House Bill 7 protects gender-affirming care and sex-reassignment surgery for adults on request without restrictions including interstate travellers as refuge for transgender youths, with shield law or 2023 executive order protecting patients and providers from civil or criminal charges where care is legal in New Mexico but banned in the patient's home state. In 2026 the state health care authority announced use of state funds to maintain Medicaid coverage for gender-affirming care after a federal rule moved to exclude it. Since 2003 hate-crime law has covered violence based on actual or perceived gender identity, and in February 2022 the Legislature passed omnibus crime bill HB68 repealing the gay and trans panic defence signed 9 March 2022. March 2019 school-bullying legislation protects students based on gender identity and requires districts to adopt prohibition, reporting, investigation, disciplinary, prevention and staff-training policies effective 1 July 2019. Same-sex marriage has been equal since the 19 December 2013 state Supreme Court ruling making New Mexico the 17th state to recognise same-sex marriage, codified 62-0 in the House and 39-0 in the Senate in March 2019 effective 1 July 2019, so a trans visitor in a relationship read as same-sex under birth-sex status has that relationship recognised here.

name: Oregon
text: Federal rules apply nationwide, and the national record for United States covers the federal layer in detail. Oregon sits in the fifteen-jurisdiction "Most Protective" tier of a July 2026 ranking covering thousands of tracked anti-trans bills including youth care bans, bathroom bans, birth-certificate and driver's licence restrictions, and measures removing legal recognition, described as going beyond baseline safeguarding of trans rights. The Oregon Equality Act, signed 9 May 2007 as Senate Bill 2 and in force since 1 January 2008, prohibits discrimination on gender identity in employment, housing, public accommodation, public education and public services. Sexual orientation is defined to include gender identity regardless of whether identity, appearance, expression or behaviour differs from that traditionally associated with sex assigned at birth. Protections apply uniformly statewide and do not depend on locality, with exemption for religious employers, organisations and institutions. State hate-crime statutes add punishment for crimes committed because of the victim's gender identity. SB704, passed and signed in May 2021 and effective 1 January 2022, abolishes gay panic and trans panic defences in murder, manslaughter and hate-crime cases. The driver-licensing agency has offered X for neutral or non-binary identity on licences and state IDs since 1 July 2017, with X also on birth certificates. Sex reassignment surgery has not been required to change the gender marker on a birth certificate by request since 2014. Legislation in May 2017 abolished the 1991 requirement to publish names in newspapers before a legal change of sex. A circuit court ruling on 10 June 2016 allowed a resident to change gender to non-binary, believed by the Transgender Law Center to be the first ruling of its kind in the country. An October 2019 executive order added gender identity to a 1987 policy barring state agencies from unlawful discrimination and required a third gender option X, and legislation signed in June 2021 updated the 2008 definition of gender identity. Oregon's shield law, signed by Governor Tina Kotek on 13 July 2023, protects patients and providers from civil or criminal charges or investigation when care legal in Oregon was prohibited in the patient's home state, after House passage in May 2023 and Senate passage with amendments after a Republican boycott. Federal district judge Michael McShane struck down the 2004 constitutional amendment banning marriage for same-sex couples on 19 May 2014, marriages of same-sex couples performed elsewhere have been recognised since 16 October 2013, and gender-neutral marriage was codified effective 1 January 2016. Domestic partnerships have been available since 4 February 2008.

name: Rhode Island
text: A July 2026 map lists Rhode Island among its 'Most Protective' states for gender-identity nondiscrimination. Federal conditions vary, and the national record for United States covers the federal layer in detail. Discrimination based on gender identity or expression has been unlawful since 2001 in employment, credit, housing and public accommodations under R.I. Gen. Laws §§ 28-5-3, 28-5-7, 34-37-4, 34-37-4.3 and 11-24-2. A bill signed in June 2023 added explicit bans covering patient care, nursing and related healthcare, and the housing exemption for dwellings with three occupants or fewer was repealed with effect from 1 January 2023. Hate-crime law provides penalty enhancements for crimes motivated by actual or perceived gender identity or expression under R.I. Gen. Laws § 42-28-46. The gay and trans panic defense was repealed in June 2018 by votes of 68-2 in the House and 27-0 in the Senate, signed by Governor Gina Raimondo the following month and effective immediately. Identity documents are changeable on a self-declaration-plus-clinical-confirmation basis rather than a surgical one. Since 23 October 2014 a birth certificate gender change has required a Birth Certificate Request Form with an affidavit from a physician, certified nurse practitioner or physician's assistant confirming transgender status. The Division of Motor Vehicles issues a corrected driver's licence on a Gender Designation Form signed by the applicant. A third marker X was announced for driver's licences and birth certificates in August 2019 with availability from July 2020, and a June 2018 law requires transgender people to be recorded correctly on death certificates. Single-occupancy toilets may be designated gender-neutral with effect from 1 January 2022 under a bill signed in July 2021. Rhode Island appears on the transgender healthcare equality map among jurisdictions covered by shield laws or executive orders from the 2023 and 2024 batches enforceable against out-of-state action. In March 2025 the Rhode Island Interscholastic League revised its transgender athletes policy. Transgender athletes remain able to compete, but member schools now carry responsibility for ensuring compliance with all applicable state and federal law when determining gender-based eligibility, replacing the prior rule allowing participation consistent with gender identity.

name: Vermont
text: Federal rules also apply; the national record for United States covers the federal layer in detail. As of July 2026 Vermont is listed among the most protective states on gender-identity nondiscrimination. Law bans gender-identity discrimination in employment, public accommodations, education, housing, credit, insurance and union practices, after a 2006 veto, passed again in 2007, signed by Jim Douglas on 22 May 2007, effective 1 July 2007. Hotels, restaurants, shops and service providers fall under it. Hate-crime law adds penalties for gender-identity motive, added in 1999 to a 1990 statute covering sexual orientation. The gay and trans panic defence was repealed after House 144-1 in March 2021 and Senate 29-0 in April 2021, signed by Phil Scott on 5 May 2021, effective 1 July 2021. Single-user bathrooms must be gender-neutral since 1 July 2018, under a bill signed in May 2018. Shield laws of 2023 and 2024 are enforceable against out-of-state action and protect transgender and non-binary people travelling in for gender-affirming healthcare, the 2023 measure effective immediately by emergency clause. Civil unions began in July 2000 as the first state status identical to marriage after a 1999 Vermont Supreme Court ruling on equal marriage benefits, and same-sex marriage has been legal since 1 September 2009, first adopted through legislature and governor rather than court decision.

name: Washington
text: Washington operates under the United States federal framework on passports, entry screening and federal custody; the national record for United States covers the federal layer in detail. State law governs health care, insurance, the state prison system and ballot measures. A July 2026 legal-risk assessment places Washington among the most protective states, but flags two ballot initiatives, I-001 and I-638, due for a November vote, as targeting transgender residents; whether they pass decides whether that protective posture holds. Washington has shield laws or executive orders from the 2023 and 2024 batches enforceable against out-of-state action, listed among covered states by a nationwide tracker. For a trans visitor travelling for gender-affirming care, these measures bear on whether another state's action can reach care provided in Washington. State correctional practice carries a documented reversal: since October 2023, under court order, Washington state prisons must provide gender-affirming healthcare and, where indicated, sex-reassignment surgery. In July 2024 a transgender woman prisoner was transferred from a women's prison back to a men's prison as punishment for consensual sex with a cisgender inmate, so housing assigned by birth sex functioned as the disciplinary sanction.

name: Monaco
text: The national record for Monaco covers the federal layer in detail. Same-sex intimacy has been lawful since the 18th century, with age of consent 15 for same-sex and opposite-sex relationships. Hate crime and hate speech on sexual orientation are criminalised, but discrimination on sexual orientation and gender identity is not banned and reported discrimination is rare. One travel guide says such discrimination is illegal only in certain contexts, conflicting with country overviews reporting no general prohibition. Loi n° 1.299 of 15 July 2005 on public freedom of expression bans hate speech and incitement to hatred and violence based on sexual orientation. Article 234-2, amended by Loi n° 1.435 of 8 November 2016, punishes threats based on sexual orientation with 2 to 5 years' imprisonment and related offences with 6 months to 3 years. Law n° 1.478 of 12 November 2019 added sexual orientation to articles 238-1, 239 and 421, covering violent acts not causing total incapacity (6 months to 1 year), attacks on a partner or co-resident (10 years), and unprovoked attacks on a person or group (5 years). None cites gender identity, so a trans visitor has no equivalent statutory protection. In July 2010 a Monegasque court jailed a man for five days and fined him €5,000 for openly homophobic rhetoric against a gay man. Legal gender recognition is unavailable and transgender people cannot alter legal gender, with ILGA-Europe's 2019 ranking placing Monaco 45th of 49 European countries. A trans visitor's documents correspond to no Monegasque procedure because none exists. Monaco does not recognise same-sex marriage and same-sex couples have no right to adopt. Since 27 June 2020 same-sex couples may sign a contrat de vie commune before a notary and deposit it at a public registry. Cohabiting couples are treated like siblings for inheritance tax rather than married couples, and the arrangement is also open to siblings and to parents and children. Same-sex partners have no equal succession rights, survivor pensions or parental leave, so none produces spousal recognition where a relationship would be read as same-sex. The 2011 bill's article 44 would have required a school programme in every year of primary and secondary cycles against racism and other article 1 discriminations including sexual orientation. The Council of Government did not approve it, and the replacement of 18 December 2012 dropped sexual-orientation provisions. Roughly ten people are openly out and visibility is limited. Most Monegasques affiliate with the Catholic Church, which regards homosexuality and transgender identity as immoral, and Council of Europe rapporteur Béatrice Fresko-Rolfo called it the sad record of Monaco. There is no Pride and no official gay bars, clubs or events, with visitors going to France or Italy for Pride and nearest scenes in Marseille, Nice and Lyon. Some gay-friendly establishments operate with community support. The US State Department's 2023 report recorded no significant changes and no reports of torture, arbitrary detention or other abuses, with significant issues only libel and lèse-majesté laws described as not enforced.

name: Cabo Delgado

name: Aruba
text: Aruba is a constituent territory within the Kingdom of the Netherlands and stands under that framework; the island's own Criminal Code (Wetboek van Strafrecht / Kódigo Penal), enacted in 2012, carries the anti-discrimination provisions in force here. Article 1:221 defines discrimination as any form of discrimination, exclusion, restriction or preference that has the purpose or effect of affecting the recognition, enjoyment or exercise of human rights and fundamental liberties in political, economic, social or cultural fields or in other areas of social life, and Articles 2:61 and 2:62 set penalties ranging from fines to one year of imprisonment. The enumerated grounds cover heterosexual or homosexual orientation only. Gender identity and gender expression are not addressed, and no transgender-specific provision is cited in the sources. Same-sex sexual activity is legal for both male and female forms, and the age of consent is 16, equal for heterosexual and homosexual intercourse. This is the only youth-specific legal threshold in the record; no findings on education, schools, or minors' access to services or documentation appear in the sources. Partner recognition is established at two levels. On 8 September 2016 the Aruban Parliament voted 11 to 5, with four abstentions per the Associated Press account of 9 September 2016, to extend civil-code marriage articles to registered partnerships open to both opposite-sex and same-sex couples, granting spousal pension and emergency medical decision rights. Same-sex marriage has been legal since 12 July 2024, when the Supreme Court of the Netherlands upheld the Appeals Court decision barring discrimination based on sexual orientation in the ruling that made same-sex marriage legal in Aruba. Since the Dutch Supreme Court ruling of 13 April 2007, Aruba must recognize same-sex marriages registered in the Netherlands and in Bonaire, Sint Eustatius and Saba. A same-sex marriage bill introduced in June 2022 was rejected after tied parliamentary votes in May and June 2024, immediately before the July 2024 ruling. A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship is dealing with a regime whose protections are written in terms of sexual orientation alone. On 22 April 2015 representatives of all Kingdom governments endorsed prompt equal rights for LGBT persons expressly including transgender persons on Aruba, Curaçao and Sint Maarten. Aruba's own representation at that meeting acknowledged that strict conservative norms made coming out difficult for LGBT youth on the island, who were stigmatized as disordered. Harassment has been documented. Charlene and Esther Oduber-Lamer reported frequent harassment and having rocks thrown at them during their court challenge (2004–2007) that forced Aruba and the other Dutch Caribbean islands to recognize same-sex marriage. The Aruban government was particularly vocal in opposing same-sex marriage during that court challenge, and the Roman Catholic Church, the island's largest denomination, contributed to mainstream societal opposition to LGBT rights. The most recent documented incident of anti-LGBT harassment in this record is from that 2004–2007 period; no later instance is documented. Several specific gay bars and clubs operate in the capital city of Oranjestad, and various venues, hotels and restaurants cater to or advertise as 'LGBT-friendly'. Numerous LGBT associations operate, including Equality Aruba (Igualdad Aruba), Equal Rights Aruba and Alternative Lifestyle Federation Aruba. The last is quoted: 'Aruba has always been accepting, as long as it's not in their face. People are out, but discreetly out. There has never been anything official.'

Since the Dutch Supreme Court ruling of 13 April 2007, Aruba must recognize same-sex marriages registered in the Netherlands and in Bonaire, Sint Eustatius and Saba. A same-sex marriage bill introduced in June 2022 was rejected after tied parliamentary votes in May and June 2024, immediately before the July 2024 ruling. A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship is dealing with a regime whose protections are written in terms of sexual orientation alone. On 22 April 2015 representatives of all Kingdom governments endorsed prompt equal rights for LGBT persons expressly including transgender persons on Aruba, Curaçao and Sint Maarten. Aruba's own representation acknowledged strict conservative norms made coming out difficult for LGBT youth, stigmatized as disordered. Charlene and Esther Oduber-Lamer reported frequent harassment and having rocks thrown at them during their court challenge (2004–2007) that forced Aruba and the other Dutch Caribbean islands to recognize same-sex marriage. The Aruban government was particularly vocal in opposing same-sex marriage during that challenge, and the Roman Catholic Church, the island's largest denomination, contributed to mainstream societal opposition. The most recent documented harassment in this record is from that 2004–2007 period, with no later instance documented. Several gay bars and clubs operate in Oranjestad, and various venues, hotels and restaurants cater to or advertise as 'LGBT-friendly'. Numerous LGBT associations operate, including Equality Aruba (Igualdad Aruba), Equal Rights Aruba and Alternative Lifestyle Federation Aruba, which stated: 'Aruba has always been accepting, as long as it's not in their face. People are out, but discreetly out. There has never been anything official.'.

name: Anguilla
text: Visitors are governed by local Anguilla law, with United Kingdom law applying only where extended by Order in Council. The national record for United Kingdom covers the federal layer in detail. Private consensual same-sex conduct was decriminalised by Privy Council order on 5 January 2001 covering Anguilla with the Cayman Islands, the British Virgin Islands, Montserrat and the Turks and Caicos Islands. The order was issued unilaterally after local legislatures refused repeal and drew protest from religious leaders. Anguilla had never carried the prohibition in exactly the same statutory form as those other territories. Anguillian law provides no protection against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity. The Constitution's anti-discrimination clause covers race, political opinions, colour, creed, sex and place of origin only, leaving gender identity outside protected categories and a trans visitor without statutory non-discrimination footing. The age of consent is 18 for same-sex conduct and 16 for different-sex conduct, so a trans visitor in a locally classed same-sex relationship carries legal exposure a different-sex couple does not face. The Marriage Act defines marriage as the union of a man and a woman as husband and wife. Same-sex marriage and civil unions are not legal, and Anguilla has not legislated for civil partnerships. A commercial wedding service states same-sex marriage is not recognised under Anguillan law, so a trans visitor in a locally classed same-sex relationship has access only to a symbolic non-legal ceremony. Such non-legal ceremonies have taken place. Public LGBT life is highly constrained, with a subdued and subtle climate of homophobia pushing local LGBT people toward secrecy. The island has no pride events, gay organisations, venues, bars or clubs and no community infrastructure, attributed to a population of about 15,000. The only recorded public event is a small protest on 17 May 2011 in The Valley marking the International Day Against Homophobia, Transphobia and Biphobia. Visiting same-sex couples have described the island as gay-friendly and reported nobody was discriminatory in any way, though the same source cautions local people may differ. A 2023 first-person account by a queer family found same-sex conduct legal under the British order but the scene muted rather than openly visible, an outcome that account attributes to externally imposed decriminalisation rather than local initiative.

name: Bonaire Sint Eustatius and Saba
text: The national record for Netherlands covers the federal layer in detail. No island marriage or discrimination legislation operates here. No source describes a provision addressing trans visitors directly. Protection rests on marriage registration and anti-discrimination law, not text naming gender identity, gender markers or facilities. Saba Census Office registered the Caribbean Netherlands' first same-sex union on 4 December 2012: Aruban Cedeno Xiomar Gonzalez (26) wed Venezuelan Israel Ernesto Ruiz Pinto (27), both visiting residents. Same-sex unions have been registrable since 2012, with one performed for visitors, the only dated union event documented with no later instance. For a trans visitor read as same-sex, that registration evidences a working route rather than a paper right. Saba civil ceremonies run through the registry, with the Court Room in the Administrative Building as simplest efficient venue and registrar Julieta Woods flexible about couples' wishes. Destination-wedding suppliers including caterers, florists and accommodation operate there.

name: Saint Barthélemy
text: Saint Barthélemy follows French national law; the national record for France covers the federal layer in detail. The island covers about 8 square miles and holds roughly 10,000 residents, with limited healthcare access as the single red flag in an aggregate travel-safety rating. Prescriptions and ongoing gender-affirming treatment cannot be assumed available locally, so carry supplies and confirm provision before arrival. The same index rates Saint Barthélemy 7.7 out of 10, counting nine positive rights against the one healthcare red flag. The island is discreet, with no LGBTQ venues, no Pride events and no visible scene; same-sex couples attract no attention, crime is low, and sources record no hostility toward gay or trans visitors. The luxury-yacht economy has long welcomed gay couples, and staff are described as trained for a diverse clientele. Saint Barthélemy's joint deputy with Saint Martin was among 11 overseas deputies who voted against the 2013 law opening marriage to same-sex couples.

name: Bermuda
text: Bermuda applies its own local legislation. See the national record for United Kingdom covers the federal layer in detail. Bermuda has no legal recognition of transgender people. The Human Rights Act has prohibited discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation since 2013, when the Senate passed the Human Rights Amendment Act, which also banned age discrimination. Gender identity is not a protected ground, so trans people have no statutory protection against discrimination. Proposals to extend that protection failed or were dropped in 2004–2006 and again in 2009. The sources identify no Bermuda-specific provisions on identity documents or gender markers, border or airport screening, restroom and facility access, custody, healthcare, penalties or protection machinery for transgender people. Expression of gender identity is described as often difficult. One instance of official interference is documented: in 2006 the Government attempted to bar Mark Anderson, the drag performer known as the Queen of Bermuda Sybil, from participating in a parade, stating that he contradicted local mores and sensitivities. No later instance is documented. Same-sex marriage has been unavailable since 2022. The Supreme Court legalised it in May 2017 in the Godwin and DeRoche case. The Domestic Partnership Act 2017, given royal assent 7 February 2018 and effective 1 June 2018, replaced marriage with domestic partnerships for both same-sex and heterosexual couples, making Bermuda the first jurisdiction to revoke marriage equality. The Supreme Court restored marriage on 6 June 2018 and the Court of Appeal on 23 November 2018, but the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council banned it again on 14 March 2022, with July 2022 laws retrospectively backdating prior legality. A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship should expect no marital recognition. Consensual sex between adult men was decriminalised in 1994 when the House of Assembly voted 22–16 to remove two Criminal Code sections, replacing prior liability of up to ten years imprisonment for anal and oral sex. Lesbian activity was never illegal. As of 2022 the age of consent stands unequal at 18 for consensual anal intercourse under the law effective 1 November 2019 against 16 for other sexual activity, and the gross indecency provision between men was repealed in 2019. Organised religious hostility toward visible same-sex couples is documented: Bermuda's AME and other churches protested a gay cruise, the Norwegian Dawn, New York–Bermuda, 12 July, as incompatible with the word of God and the Christian moral fibre. Such hostility is aimed at couples read locally as same-sex, which would reach a trans visitor whose relationship is read that way.

name: Cook Islands
text: See the national record for New Zealand covers the federal layer in detail. Crimes Amendment Bill decriminalised sex between men, passed 14 April 2023, effective 1 June 2023. It repealed Crimes Act 1969 sections 154 and 155 on sex between men and indecent acts with or upon another male, where consent was no defence. Accounts differ on maxima: 2017 reports up to seven years for sex between men and five years for an indecent act, but repeal coverage cites up to ten years for indecent acts between males. No prosecution in living memory is recorded and the bill note cited growing acceptance of LGBT people in the Cook Islands. The same bill added protections for sexual abuse and assault victims. Marriage was unchanged: the Marriage Amendment Act 2000 defines marriage as between a man and a woman. A trans visitor in a locally classed same-sex relationship has no spousal standing, and such foreign marriage is not recognised locally.

name: Curaçao
text: Curaçao is autonomous within the Kingdom of the Netherlands except for defence, foreign affairs and Supreme Court matters, the national record for Netherlands covers the federal layer in detail. Both male and female same-sex sexual activity is legal with equal age of consent of 16 for heterosexual and homosexual intercourse. A trans visitor in a relationship read locally as same-sex faces no conduct offence on that basis. Same-sex marriage has been legal since 12 July 2024, when the Supreme Court of the Netherlands upheld an Appeals Court decision barring discrimination based on sexual orientation. Before that ruling Curaçao recognised as valid same-sex marriages registered in the Netherlands and in Bonaire, Sint Eustatius and Saba, but offered no in-island marriage, civil union or other recognition. Recognition arrived by court order rather than by statute. A limited-rights proposal was put to the Estates of Curaçao in 2017, and a marriage bill submitted on 4 June 2019 was withdrawn in September 2020 for lack of support. In April 2015 all Kingdom governments agreed LGBT people on Aruba, Curaçao and Sint Maarten should receive equal rights quickly, and the August 2015 Oliari and Others v. Italy judgment of the European Court of Human Rights, applicable to Curaçao, required legal recognition. The Criminal Code enacted in 2011 prohibits unfair discrimination and incitement to hatred and violence on grounds including heterosexual or homosexual orientation. Article 1:221 defines discrimination as any distinction affecting recognition, enjoyment or exercise of human rights in political, economic, social, cultural or other social life, and Articles 2:61 and 2:62 set penalties from fines to one year of imprisonment. The protected grounds named do not include gender identity, and no Curaçao-specific authority on gender-identity coverage was identified. Official rhetoric has not consistently governed practice. In April 2015 commissioner Marvelyne Wiels of Pueblo Soberano backed equal rights for everyone, while colleague Winifred Raveneau opposed the push and used a last-minute, exceptionally strict permit requirement to force Curaçao's 2013 Gay Pride to a hotel premises. Public LGBT assembly can be obstructed through administrative permitting at short notice. The Pink House LGBT centre opened in 2010, and with Aruba and Sint Maarten Curaçao has driven equal-rights moves across the Kingdom. Frank Holtslag cites an IGLTA award naming the island the most gay welcoming in the region, and a rights wishes-package was delivered to ministers in The Hague. Gender markers in locally issued documents, entry screening triggered by gender presentation, access to gender-affirming care, and designation of facilities are unassessed rather than cleared, with no Curaçao-specific sourcing found.

name: Western Sahara
text: Western Sahara is a disputed territory with no single legal order running through it. Morocco controls most of the ground, while the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic claims sovereignty through exile institutions and refugee camps in Algeria; which framework a visitor stands under depends on where they are. The national record for Morocco covers the federal layer in detail. Moroccan jurisdiction reaches into the territory in practice. On 9 December 2005 Human Rights Watch reported the trial of seven human-rights defenders from Moroccan-controlled Western Sahara on charges of fomenting illegal protests, called the charges dubious and demanded a fair trial. The case shows Moroccan courts and detention operating on Sahrawi political cases, not only on paper. Same-sex intimacy is criminalised under both frameworks. Moroccan law carries six months to three years of imprisonment. For the SADR, the Council for Global Equality, Equaldex and ILGA record same-sex sexual activity as illegal for both men and women, punishable by up to three years, and a July 2017 PinkNews roundup listed the SADR among jurisdictions where homosexuality is illegal for men and women and had been for decades. A trans visitor in a relationship that local law would read as same-sex under birth-sex status therefore stands inside a criminal prohibition in either part of the territory. The SADR's own position is contested. In 2010 Ahmed Mulay Alli, the SADR's diplomatic representative in Mexico, said the Constitution 'does not refer to homosexuality or any other sexual practice... it does not punish it'. The Spanish Commission for Refugee Aid (CEAR) reads the same silence as leaving LGBTQ people with no legal protection against discrimination or violence. Constitutional silence is not decriminalisation, and no statute in the inventory decriminalises anything. The only documented account of the Sahrawi authorities applying such charges comes from a 2009 USCRI report: officials running the refugee camps in Algeria said they were holding some prisoners on 'homosexuality' charges while alleging facts that would more fittingly describe rape. The charge sits in the hands of camp administration rather than a court. Social exposure is high. Most residents are Muslim, and relationships between people of the same sex are widely read as a foreign phenomenon. No source in the inventory records a trans-specific statute, a protection mechanism, or a documented case of a trans visitor being processed under either framework.

name: Faroe Islands
text: The anti-discrimination provision in force since 1 January 2007 makes anyone who publicly makes a statement threatening, insulting or degrading a group on account of race, colour, national or ethnic origin, religion or sexual orientation liable to a fine or up to two years' imprisonment. Gender identity is not among the listed grounds. On the sourced account this made the Faroe Islands the last Northern European jurisdiction to prohibit discrimination and harassment on grounds of sexual orientation. Before that provision took effect, homophobic conduct was legally unaddressed. In 2006 the openly gay singer, songwriter and radio host Rasmus Rasmussen was severely beaten by five men in Tórshavn and hospitalised shortly after coming out; he and his family then received threatening telephone calls, and police refused to handle the case because no Faroese law banned discrimination against sexual minorities at the time. He was later moved to a psychiatric hospital with severe depression exacerbated by the beating, never recovered, and died by suicide in 2012. The most recent documented assault in this record is that 2006 attack; no later instance is documented. A second documented attack dates from 2005, when the Norwegian drag group Great Garlic Girls had to run from a gang of young men intent on physically assaulting them in Tórshavn; the group was not attacked anywhere else on its tour. Hostility from elected office is documented across a decade. In September 2010 Centre Party leader Jenis av Rana refused to attend a state banquet for the visiting Icelandic prime minister and her partner, citing his religion. In June 2015 Løgting Speaker Jógvan á Lakjuni published a letter attacking the national broadcaster Kringvarp Føroya for the space it gave LGBT Føroyar and condemning a drag show at the Nordic House as 'non-culture', asking whether 'these people do not feel any shame'. The same year av Rana demanded that Pride be banned and repeatedly compared LGBT Føroyar to Sea Shepherd whale-hunting protesters, and his party remains formally opposed to homosexuality. Singer Eivor Pálsdóttir publicly urged people to ignore him, documenting organised public pushback alongside the hostility. Public expression has been contested since the first gay pride march in 2005, which provoked substantial controversy; in 2015 av Rana also suggested the Tórshavn pride parade be moved out of the city centre. Partner recognition is unresolved in this record. In 2006 LGBT activists gathered around 20,000 online signatures demanding an end to sexual-orientation discrimination and a registered-partnership law aligned with the rest of the Nordics; at that point the Faroe Islands, with a population of about 47,000, had neither protection nor partnership recognition. No later sourced statement establishes the current status of partnership or marriage registration here.

name: Faroe Islands
text: The national record for Denmark covers the federal layer in detail. Since 1 January 2007 a Faroese provision punishes public threatening, insulting or degrading statements against a group on race, colour, national or ethnic origin, religion or sexual orientation with a fine or up to two years' imprisonment. Gender identity is not listed. This made the Faroe Islands the last Northern European jurisdiction to prohibit sexual-orientation discrimination and harassment, before which homophobic conduct was legally unaddressed. In 2006 singer, songwriter and radio host Rasmus Rasmussen was severely beaten by five men in Torshavn and hospitalised shortly after coming out. He and his family received threatening telephone calls, and police refused the case because no Faroese law then banned sexual-minority discrimination. He entered a psychiatric hospital with severe depression exacerbated by the beating, never recovered, and died by suicide in 2012. No assault later than that 2006 attack is documented. In 2005 Norwegian drag group Great Garlic Girls fled a gang of young men intent on assault in Torshavn, the only tour stop where they were attacked. In September 2010 Centre Party leader Jenis av Rana refused a state banquet for the visiting Icelandic prime minister and her partner, citing religion. That year av Rana demanded Pride be banned, compared LGBT Foroyar to Sea Shepherd protesters, and his party remains formally opposed to homosexuality, while singer Eivor Palsdottir urged the public to ignore him. The first pride march in 2005 provoked substantial controversy, and in 2015 av Rana suggested moving the Torshavn parade from the city centre. Partnership status is unresolved. In 2006 activists gathered around 20,000 online signatures for anti-discrimination and registered-partnership law aligned with the Nordics, when the Faroe Islands with about 47,000 people had neither protection nor partnership recognition. No later sourced statement establishes current partnership or marriage registration here.

name: Guernsey
text: Guernsey is a self-governing Crown Dependency with its own parliament, the States of Guernsey, and its own statute book. United Kingdom measures including the Equality Act 2010 reach Guernsey only by Order in Council, and the national record for United Kingdom covers the federal layer in detail. Same-sex sexual activity is lawful for men and women. Decriminalisation preceded 1983, when the age of consent was set at 21. The male same-sex age of consent fell to 18 in 2000 and was equalised at 16 by legislation approved in 2011 that took effect on 5 November 2012. Guernsey nonetheless retains specific male homosexual offences in its criminal law, including a ban on homosexual sexual acts not conducted in private. Transgender people have been able to legally change their gender since 2007, including obtaining a new birth certificate. Guernsey law only allows a new birth certificate to be issued and does not amend or remove records from existing birth certificates. Guernsey is the only part of the British Isles never to have enacted civil partnership legislation, though United Kingdom civil partnerships were recognised for succession purposes from 2 April 2012. The States of Guernsey approved same-sex marriage on 10 December 2015 by a vote of 37 to 7, rejecting both a civil-partnership-only option and a single 'Union Civile' alternative, with implementing legislation separate and not expected before 2017. A 2004 law enabled the States of Guernsey to pass Ordinances banning discrimination, and the Sex Discrimination (Employment) (Guernsey) Ordinance, 2005 banned discrimination based on gender identity. As of 2020 no equivalent Ordinance had specifically outlawed discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation. Anti-discrimination protections covering sexual orientation and gender identity existed in child welfare proceedings in Guernsey and Alderney since 2008 and in Sark since 2016. In September 2022 the States of Guernsey passed a comprehensive anti-discrimination bill unanimously (33-0) explicitly including sexual orientation, rejecting all amendments proposing exemptions for small businesses of five employees or fewer and for religious affiliations, and it takes effect from 1 October 2023. Guernsey's only prison, Les Nicolles, opened in 1989 and holds male, female and vulnerable prisoners of juvenile and adult ages, has 11 wings, capacity 139, is operated by the States of Guernsey, and held about 99 prisoners in November 2024. No rule on housing prisoners by birth sex versus gender identity, no separate unit for trans prisoners, and no solitary or segregation practice for them is recorded. The States of Guernsey repealed the 50-year Adoption Law's ban on unmarried couples adopting on 24 June 2015, agreeing that same-sex couples may adopt, with civil partnerships recognised and equal parental responsibility for both partners. The Billet d'État of 24 June 2015 records the review of Adoption Law at p.1170. Guernsey adopted relaxed blood-donor rules on 23 September 2011, making gay and bisexual men eligible after a 12-month deferral, targeted to around 7 November 2011, ending the local 1980s HIV-era ban, with other donation restrictions unchanged.

name: Gibraltar
text: Gibraltar is a self-governing British Overseas Territory with its own Parliament and Supreme Court; the national record for United Kingdom covers the federal layer in detail. The principal legal gap facing a trans visitor is gender recognition: no process exists in Gibraltar for changing a legal gender marker, and transgender persons are not permitted to change legal gender. A trans visitor therefore travels on a document whose marker cannot be altered by any local route, and can expect to be read at the border and in public under that marker. Statutory discrimination protection covering gender reassignment has been in place since the Equal Opportunities Act 2006 took effect on 1 March 2007. The Act prohibits discrimination in employment and in the provision of goods and services on the ground of gender reassignment, defined as a process for the purpose of reassigning a person's sex by changing physiological or other attributes of sex. Sexual orientation is a protected ground under the same Act. Hate-crime coverage extends to trans people. Parliament amended the Crimes Act 2011 in September 2013 to criminalise hatred and harassment on grounds of sexual orientation, with approval on 19 September, royal assent on 25 September and effect from 10 October 2013. In July 2026 Parliament passed a bill amending hate crime and hate speech legislation to include protections for transgender identity. In July 2021 the Ministry for Justice and Equality said it would urgently consider legislation to tackle what the Chief Minister, Fabian Picardo, called "disgusting lurking homophobia" on social media during Pride month, following an incident of anti-gay abuse. The proposal at that stage concerned sexual orientation; the trans-inclusive amendment came in July 2026. In July 2026 Parliament also passed a bill making it an offence to offer or practise conversion therapy; the sourced excerpt states the offence generally without specifying whether its scope covers sexual orientation, transgender identity, or both. Partner recognition is established locally. Civil partnerships have been available since March 2014, and same-sex marriage since 15 December 2016, after the Civil Marriage Amendment Act passed unanimously on 26 October 2016, received royal assent on 1 November and took effect on 15 December, with the first marriage the following day. A deputy registrar may opt out, requiring assignment of an alternative registrar. Because no gender-recognition route exists, a trans visitor's legal sex for marriage purposes remains that recorded at birth; a relationship locally read as same-sex can be registered. Adoption is open to same-sex couples. The Supreme Court ruled on 10 April 2013 that section 5(2) of the Adoption Act 1951 violated the Gibraltar Constitution, and the Adoption Act 2023 took full effect on 18 April 2024, expressly allowing same-sex couples to adopt without discrimination. The age of consent is 16 for all sexual activity regardless of sexuality or gender. The Supreme Court ruled on 8 April 2011 that the previous age of 18 for gay sex was unconstitutional, and the gender-neutral Crimes Act 2011, approved in August 2011, set the equal age of 16 with effect from 23 November 2012.

name: Guadeloupe
text: Guadeloupe is a French overseas department. Criminal law, identity-document rules, custodial conditions and the national preventive mechanism are set at the national level and carried by the parent record; this assessment covers what is specific to the island. Guadeloupe's first LGBT+ centre, the Maison des Diversités et de l'Inclusion, opened on 24 April 2024, run by a federation of Guadeloupean associations. It offers reception, support and orientation for people of diverse identity, sexual, bodily and gender diversities. The opening was attended by the visiting national minister Aurore Bergé, who announced measures to strengthen the fight against gender-based violence and discrimination in Guadeloupe, with structures adapted for the overseas territories. The centre's opening was presented as a concrete step toward inclusion and safety. Community organisations Secret's Out, Queer Gang and Lovo Nova partnered on a year of LGBT-friendly social events across Guadeloupe in 2025, described locally as a potential 'annus mirabilis' for the island's community. A September 2023 interview with Leïla of Secret's Out reported that community members increasingly reconcile their lives with their orientation, and described activism on the island as advancing after neighbouring Martinique; the interview also featured Prisca Melyon-Reinette of Amalgame Humani's.

name: French Guiana
text: French Guiana is an overseas department of France with no gender-identity legislation of its own; the national record for France covers the federal layer in detail. Detention carries the most serious documented risk. No local protocol governs the custody of transgender detainees, so placement in French Guiana's facilities follows the national practice: assignment to a men's or women's wing is based on the detainee's legal gender and decided case by case, without a consistent protective standard. Specialist gender-affirming care is not provided locally on the same basis as in metropolitan France. Patients travel to the mainland for surgery and specialist assessment, and the journey adds cost and delay to every medical step, including any undertaken during a stay in the department. Transphobia and cultural taboos discourage visibility in the department, and abuse is less likely to be reported, including to the police. Under-reporting is a feature of the local situation rather than evidence that abuse is rare.

name: Isle of Man
text: The Isle of Man is a self-legislating Crown Dependency of the United Kingdom. Tynwald enacts its own statutes on gender recognition, equality and criminal law, and United Kingdom legislation reaches the island only when extended by Order in Council rather than automatically. The Gender Recognition Act 2009 (c.11) allows transgender people to change their legal gender and to have the new gender recognised. The Equality Act 2017, granted royal assent on 18 July 2017 and largely in force from 1 January 2019, lists gender reassignment as a protected characteristic and as a ground on which discrimination is prohibited. A ban on conversion therapy covering sexual orientation and gender identity was passed in 2020 as an amendment to the sexual offences bill in the Legislative Council and took effect in 2024. In 2024 the Isle of Man became the first British territory, and the first part of the British Isles, to prohibit the practice. In July 2022 community consultation progressed on a hate crime bill that would explicitly include gender reassignment alongside sexual orientation and marital or civil partnership status. The bill's status after that consultation is not sourced. Sexual offences law applies gender-neutrally. Private consensual male homosexual acts were decriminalised in September 1992 with an age of consent of twenty-one, lowered to eighteen by the Criminal Justice Act 2001 (c.4), then lowered to sixteen and made gender-neutral for all sexual conduct regardless of gender and sexual orientation by the Sexual Offences (Amendment) Act 2006 (c.3). Until 2021, Section 9 of the Sexual Offences Act 1992 retained offences of buggery and gross indecency between men if under sixteen or committed elsewhere than in private; in 2021 the more-than-two-persons specification was deleted and language on indecent exposure and sexual activity in a public place was made gender-neutral under the Sexual Offences and Obscene Publications Act 2021, which received royal assent in July 2021 and took effect on 1 July 2022 by proclamation. On partner recognition, same-sex couples have held civil partnerships since 6 April 2011 under the Civil Partnership Act 2011 (c.2), and marriage has been available since 22 July 2016 following royal assent on 19 July 2016. Existing civil partnerships could be converted without a second ceremony, and the first conversion was completed within days of entry into force. A trans visitor in a relationship that would be locally classed as same-sex enters a jurisdiction that recognises the union. Family law has not kept pace with that recognition. Under the Civil Partnership Act 2011, same-sex couples have had equal access to full joint or stepchild adoption since 6 April 2011 and lesbian couples have access to artificial insemination, but as of an August 2023 consultation same-sex couples are not recognised as parents on birth certificates in cases of IVF and surrogacy, and no law on the island acknowledges surrogacy.
