name: Montserrat
text: Montserrat is a British Overseas Territory standing under the United Kingdom's framework, including the European Convention on Human Rights. The national record for United Kingdom covers the federal layer in detail. Same-sex sexual activity between consenting adults in private has been lawful since 2001, when the prohibitions were swept away retrospectively by an Order in Council under Sections 3(1) and 3(7) of the Caribbean Territories (Criminal Law) Order, 2000. Lesbian conduct was never an offence. Group sex and sex in public remain criminal offences for all persons. The age of consent is 18 for homosexual activity and 16 for heterosexual activity. A trans visitor whose relationship would be read locally as same-sex therefore falls under the higher threshold of 18. Same-sex marriage and civil unions are not legal. Article 10(1) of the Constitution protects only opposite-sex marriage, providing that every man and woman of marriageable age has the right to marry a person of the opposite sex and to found a family. A trans visitor's partner would not be recognised as a spouse or civil partner. Article 16 of the Montserrat Constitution and Article 79 of the Labour Code prohibit discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation, defining 'discriminatory' as affording different treatment on grounds such as sex, sexual orientation, race, colour, language, religion or other status. Neither provision names gender identity among the enumerated grounds, which end with an open-ended 'other status'. There are no gay bars, nightclubs or other dedicated venues on the island. Several hotels welcome gay tourists and operate non-discrimination policies, which is the main documented point of entry for a visitor seeking a welcoming environment.

name: Martinique
text: Martinique is an overseas department of France under Article 73, so identity documents, criminal law and the marriage regime are national law operating locally. The national record for France covers the federal layer in detail. Same-sex conduct has been lawful in Martinique since 1815. The 2013 marriage-equality law applies in the department, discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation has been prohibited in goods and services since Law No. 2001-1066 (Penal Code articles 225-1 and 225-2) and in employment since 2008 (Labour Code article L1132-1), and gender-identity discrimination has been prohibited since Article 4 of the 2012 sexual-harassment law, with the term "sexual identity" replaced by "gender identity" in 2016. Community infrastructure operates on the island. JM Concept 972 runs information, meetings and services for Martinique's LGBT community, and LGBTQ organisations listed for the overseas departments include AIDES Territoire Martinique, KAP Caraïbe, Tjenbé Rèd Prévention and SAFE SXM.

name: Mayotte
text: Mayotte is a French overseas department applying French national law. The national record for France covers the federal layer in detail. Trans detainees in Mayotte's establishments are held according to the gender shown on their identity document under Article D248 of the French criminal procedure code, which in practice places trans women in all-male facilities where other detainees threaten them. Placement follows the document marker rather than anatomy. The national detention-places opinion extends to Mayotte's local jails as French establishments. Formal entitlement and lived experience diverge. A teacher at the university centre of Mayotte and his Malagasy partner married at Sada town hall in 2023, after what reporting described as a long and complicated path, on a predominantly Muslim island where the written law is not the whole of what a couple faces. Same-sex marriage has been legal here since Mayotte voted to remain part of France in 1975. Legal representation is thinly available locally. A French-language directory of LGBT-friendly lawyers returns no referenced practitioner for Mayotte's towns, including Mamoudzou, Koungou, Dzaoudzi and Sada, while listing a Paris-based lawyer admitted to the Conseil d'État and Cour de cassation, including persons and family law, as available.

name: New Caledonia
text: New Caledonia is a French collectivity under French penal and civil-status law, and the national record for France covers the federal layer in detail. Same-sex marriage has been available in New Caledonia since France's 2013 marriage-equality law, signed 18 May 2013, under which a trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship can marry here. The inventory records no New Caledonia-specific law, enforcement action, incident, institution or statistic bearing on trans visitors, and no local ordinance narrowing the national protections. No region-specific signal was identified beyond the extension of the French framework, and the national assessment for France applies.

name: Pitcairn Islands
text: The national record for United Kingdom covers the federal layer in detail. Same-sex sexual activity has been legal since 2001 with no criminalisation exposure under local law. The Pitcairn Constitution Order 2010 has prohibited discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation since 2010. It is constitutional rather than an offence provision, with no express protection on gender-identity grounds. The Same Sex Marriage and Civil Partnerships Ordinance 2015 made same-sex marriage legal on 14 May 2015 and defines marriage as the union of two people regardless of sex, sexual orientation or gender identity. That definition is the only express reference to gender identity in the territory's legislation recorded in these sources. Approved unanimously by the Island Council on 1 April 2015, signed by Governor Jonathan Sinclair on 5 May 2015 and published on 13 May 2015. It recognises civil partnerships performed outside the Pitcairn Islands as recognised locally. No incident of violence targeting a trans person is documented, and no dated case appears in the record.

name: French Polynesia
text: French law governs justice and civil status in the territory while territorial institutions in Papeete regulate much of daily life; the national record for France covers the federal layer in detail. Gender-diverse healthcare in the territory is limited by the small number of specialists available locally. Under Vice-President Eliane Tevahitua, the territorial government tabled a social-security bill that would have fully reimbursed hormonal treatment with progesterone and testosterone, matching mainland France; after heated debate in the Territorial Assembly the bill did not obtain sufficient support and lapsed. For a trans visitor staying any length of time, the gap between the law on paper and the care actually reachable in the archipelago is the most concrete material constraint. The mahu role, a traditional Polynesian recognition of gender diversity in which individuals embody both male and female qualities and hold recognised standing, predates colonisation, and mahu and rae-rae are visible across the islands in daily life. Reporting from OutTraveler in July 2025 described this openness as ingrained in the culture rather than secured by law, noting that a visiting gay couple checked online whether the destination was safe before travelling and found mainstream inclusivity and acceptance operating without pride flags or organised protest. The 118-island territory has no Pride movement to speak of, which visitors read either as reassurance or as evidence that visibility is tolerated rather than defended.

name: Réunion
text: Réunion is a department of France and stands under French national law without local variation. The national record for France covers the federal layer in detail. No Réunion-specific signal on transgender visitors was identified in the source inventory: the criminal law, identity-document rules, anti-discrimination statute, marriage regime and custodial-placement rules that govern the island are the French national rules, and the national assessment applies here unchanged.

name: Saint Helena
text: Saint Helena applies its own ordinances, with United Kingdom law applying only where extended; the national record for United Kingdom covers the federal layer in detail. No transgender-specific criminal, documentation, screening, facilities, custody, care, violence, penalty, marriage or adoption provision is documented in territory law. Consensual same-sex activity has been lawful since 2001, with the age of consent equalised at 16 across Saint Helena, Ascension Island and Tristan da Cunha. The St Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha Constitution Order 2009 bans discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation and has been in force since 2009. It defines discriminatory as affording different treatment to different persons on grounds such as sex, sexual orientation, race, colour, language, religion, political or other opinion, national or social origin, association with a national minority, property, age, disability, birth or other status. The enumerated grounds do not include gender reassignment, and no extension to gender reassignment is documented. The Commission for Equality and Human Rights Ordinance 2015 defines gender reassignment as an intended, current or past process, or part of such a process, for reassigning sex by changing physiological or other attributes of sex, or the state of mind whereby a person psychologically identifies with a gender inconsistent with, or not culturally associated with, their assigned sex at birth. It defines sexual orientation as orientation towards persons of the same sex, the opposite sex, or either sex. The Equality and Human Rights Commission in Saint Helena monitors human rights laws, promotes understanding of equality, and works towards elimination of unlawful discrimination. It may conduct inquiries and investigations into unlawful discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender reassignment. Same-sex marriage is legal on Ascension Island under the Marriage (Ascension) Ordinance 2016, approved 31 May 2016 by 5 votes to 0, signed and gazetted 20 June 2016, and commenced 1 January 2017. It has been legal on Tristan da Cunha since 4 August 2017 under the Marriages (Tristan da Cunha) Ordinance 2017, which defines marriage as the union of two persons regardless of sex with equal eligibility, formalities, rights and recognition. It has been legal on Saint Helena since 20 December 2017 under the Marriage Ordinance 2017, with the first same-sex marriage on 31 December 2018. Adoption by same-sex couples has been permitted since 2017. Under the Saint Helena Welfare of Children Ordinance 2010, covering Saint Helena and Tristan da Cunha, and the Ascension Island Child Welfare Ordinance 2011, single and married people may adopt regardless of sexual orientation.

name: Turks and Caicos Islands
text: The Turks and Caicos Islands is a British Overseas Territory standing under the United Kingdom framework; the national record for United Kingdom covers the federal layer in detail. Its own ordinances and courts govern immigration status, family recognition and non-discrimination. Same-sex sexual activity has been legal there since 2001, and the constitution prohibits discrimination on the ground of sexual orientation. In a Court of Appeal ruling, the Director of Immigration was ordered to issue a residence permit to Timothy Haymon as the spouse of Richard Sankar. The court read "spouse" in the Immigration Ordinance to include a spouse lawfully married in another jurisdiction, and held that refusing the permit on sexual-orientation grounds contravened the constitution's equality, non-discrimination and private-and-family-life guarantees. The statutory definition of marriage was left untouched, so the decision creates no local right to marry. A trans visitor whose relationship local law would read as same-sex under birth-sex status can rely on a marriage lawfully entered elsewhere to support residence in the territory, in the same way as the spouses of residents. Document handling for trans people runs through United Kingdom channels. The HM Passport Office knowledge-base profile for the Turks and Caicos Islands, official operational guidance published in 2025, states that transgender citizens are recognised in the territory and that the passport office processes gender-recognised documents for this jurisdiction. A visitor presenting a United Kingdom passport with a changed gender marker can expect it to be treated as valid in the territory. No local statute or instrument giving effect to that recognition is identified in the available sources. Visibility is low. A resident account published in 2009 described virtually no information about gay life in the territory and no visible social scene, with privacy as the everyday norm; the account attributed this partly to a population in which roughly two-thirds of residents are not originally from the islands, leaving full-citizen Belongers a demographic minority. That account is dated and impressionistic, and does not establish anything about current violence risk.

name: Holy See
text: The national record for Vatican City covers the federal layer in detail. No Vatican City criminal provision reaches consensual same-sex sexual activity between adults in private and non-commercial. The code derives from the Italian Zanardelli Code of 1889 with no such offence since 1890, including through the sovereign state's founding in 1929. Nothing in criminal law addresses being transgender. The age of consent is 18 for all regardless of gender, except 14 within a marriage valid under Catholic Church and Vatican City law. No gender-marker change, anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation or gender identity, single-sex facility rule for trans visitors, or document-amendment route exists. It has no prison system, only a few pre-trial cells, with sentences served in Italian prisons at Vatican expense. No trans-specific placement policy or documented trans prisoner case exists. Its 2019 Congregation for Catholic Education document 'Male and Female He Created Them' frames 'gender theory' as denying man-woman difference and reciprocity and eliminating the family's anthropological basis. It instructs Catholic institutions and does not bind visitors. A 2023 Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith declaration allowed spontaneous same-sex couple blessings while forbidding marriage-like rites, reaffirmed by a January 2024 press release as never extending to the unions themselves. It rejects civil same-sex unions, same-sex marriage, and same-sex couple adoption. Pope Francis in 2023 supported same-sex civil unions outside the Church while holding marriage is between a man and a woman as instituted by God. In 2021 foreign minister Archbishop Paul Richard Gallagher wrote to the Italian ambassador opposing an Italian bill protecting LGBTQ Italians from violence and discrimination. He called its ban on incitement of hatred based on sexual orientation and gender identity a violation of speech and religious freedom and sought reformulation. On 13 January 1998 activist Alfredo Ormando self-immolated on St. Peter's Square under Vatican jurisdiction protesting Catholic refusal of homosexuality and died days later in hospital from severe burns.

name: British Virgin Islands
text: The British Virgin Islands stands under the United Kingdom's constitutional framework; measures of the United Kingdom's Parliament extend to it only when brought into force by Order in Council. The national record for United Kingdom covers the federal layer in detail. Same-sex intimacy has not been a criminal offence here since January 2001, when the Privy Council ordered repeal of the sodomy laws after the local legislature declined to act; legislator Orlando Smith said "there is nothing we can do." United Kingdom protections such as the Equality Act 2010 do not apply by default; trace any protection to local legislation or a specific extension order. Recognition of same-sex marriages contracted elsewhere remains contested: the case testing the United Kingdom marriage of Kinisha Forbes and Kirsten Lettsome was still running when, on 29 July 2022, the BVI Christian Council lost its bid to appeal Justice Adrian Jack's case-management orders (BVI News) — a procedural step, not a ruling on recognition. No criminalisation of trans people and no trans-specific protection machinery appears in the sources.

name: Wallis and Futuna Islands
text: French civil and criminal law applies in Wallis and Futuna unless locally overridden. The national record for Wallis and Futuna covers the federal layer in detail. Gender-identity discrimination has been banned since 2012 by extension to Wallis and Futuna of employment, housing and services law, with terminology changing from sexual identity to gender identity in article 225-1 in 2016. Same-sex marriage has been legal in all French overseas departments and territories since 2013. Locally, the collectivity has a population of about 11,000, and its isolation and dominant Catholic and Polynesian norms leave practical barriers to healthcare and social acceptance. Roles comparable to fakafafine coexist with stigma and concealment.

name: Centro
text: Centro stands under Italy's national framework on legal gender recognition, discrimination and asylum; the national record for Italy covers the federal layer in detail. Progetto Gionata's region-by-region study of anti-LGBT hate-motivated violence, covering 2012 to 2025, ranks six Italian regions at the top by victim count. Lazio and Toscana, both within Centro, are two of the six, alongside Lombardia and Piemonte in the north-west and Campania and Puglia in the south. The ranking is by raw victim counts, which track population, and the study supplies no per-capita denominator, so it does not establish that any one of these regions carries a higher rate of violence than another. In Rome, the municipal administration announced on 30 August 2025 that the Consiglio di Stato, the country's highest administrative court, had upheld the city's 2022 removal of Pro Vita & Famiglia posters attacking "gender" ideology in schools. The court found the images discriminatory, one of them showing a boy being handed a red hairbow, and held that public spaces may not be used for messages that generate alarmism, fear or serious disturbance, particularly where minors are concerned. The campaign behind the posters had collected 105,000 online signatures. The outcome confirms that anti-trans public messaging can be restricted in the region's largest city. In Perugia, the Court of Cassation confirmed on 5 March 2026 the appeal acquittal of a trans woman, Pinheiro Reis Duarte Hudson, known as Patrizia, over the death of Samuele De Paoli on 27 April 2021. The court held that the death resulted from cardiac arrhythmia caused by accidental compression during a scuffle that De Paoli started, making the acquittal on the homicide charge final. The case was a national anti-trans media flashpoint, and the definitive judicial outcome favoured the trans defendant in the region's main university city.

name: Nord-Ovest
text: Nord-Ovest stands under Italy's national framework. The national record for Italy covers the federal layer in detail. Milan operates Italy's first gender registry, the registro di genere, allowing transgender people to use their chosen name on civic and municipal documents. LifeGate calls it a milestone for transgender rights tied to a 2022 council motion by the country's first elected transgender councillor. Turin runs parallel Identita Alias at municipal offices and libraries. Both are city-level with no region-wide equivalent documented. Progetto Gionata's 2012–2025 breakdown of anti-LGBT aggressions by region and city places two constituent regions among Italy's six highest-victim regions for anti-LGBT hate-motivated violence. Ranking is by raw victim count with no population denominator, so it does not measure per-capita risk nor show a larger population is more dangerous than a smaller one.

name: Nord-Est
text: Visitors to Nord-Est stand under the national framework of Italy. Entry rules, identity documents, legal gender recognition, criminal law and the national protection and health-care layers are set by Italy and are recorded in the country's own dossier. The material identified at region level concerns Veneto and, in narrower form, Emilia-Romagna. The Veneto Regional Council passed motion n.340 at its 178th public session in Venice on 3 July. Deliberation n.92 of 14 October 2014 approved that motion, committing the regional government to a mandatory 'Natural Family Day' observance on the last school day before Christmas and rejecting the aims of gender-awareness content in schools. The official regional government bulletin carries the primary-source text of the deliberation. The most recent documented instance of this instrument in this record is 14 October 2014; no later amendment, repeal or successor measure is documented here. The Veneto measure operates through the school calendar and regional policy statements. It creates no criminal offence, no penalty and no restriction on entry, documents or movement, and it does not alter the national rules on legal gender recognition or anti-discrimination protection.

name: Nord-Est
text: National rules apply, and the national record for Italy covers the federal layer in detail. Local material concerns Veneto and, in narrower form, Emilia-Romagna. Veneto Regional Council passed motion n.340 at its 178th public session in Venice on 3 July. Deliberation n.92 of 14 October 2014 approved that motion, committing the regional government to mandatory 'Natural Family Day' observance on the last school day before Christmas and rejecting aims of gender-awareness content in schools. Regional government bulletin carries the primary-source text of the deliberation, last documented here on 14 October 2014 with no later amendment, repeal or successor measure documented here. It operates through the school calendar and policy statements, creating no criminal offence, penalty or restriction on entry, documents or movement and not altering national rules on legal gender recognition or anti-discrimination protection.

name: Sud
text: Sud stands under Italy's national framework; the national record for Italy covers the federal layer in detail. No regional statute, court ruling or administrative measure specific to Sud addressing gender identity or sexual orientation was identified in this inventory, so the assessment rests on documented incidents within the region. In March 2025 a young man was assaulted by attackers on a scooter in Scampia, a neighbourhood of Naples. On 13 October 2025 a 63-year-old man was arrested in Torre Annunziata, in the province of Naples, after making stabbing threats against a young LGBTQIA+ activist; Il Gazzettino described it as a grave homophobic episode in the Naples area. Trans detainees remain within the ordinary men's and women's prison circuit, including in this region.

name: Isole
text: Isole is a region of Italy and stands under the Italian national framework; no region-specific legal regime governing gender identity or sexual orientation was identified in the sources, and the national assessment applies. The national record for Italy covers the federal layer in detail. On 26 April 2025 three young men were beaten at a fast-food restaurant in Catania because they were gay. The Procura etnea, the Catania prosecutor's office, reconstructed a sequence of insults and threats that preceded the physical assault, and video of the attack circulated publicly. A Catania outlet's follow-up of 5 June 2026, titled "Omofobia in Sicilia, continuano le violenze", catalogues continuing assaults and suicide cases across Sicilian towns, indicating that the pattern of attacks recorded in 2025 has not stopped.

name: Alberta
text: Alberta's trans-specific lawmaking is a package of three statutes that passed final legislative stage on 4 December 2024. The Education Amendment Act, 2024 introduced parental opt-in for classroom instruction on sexuality and rules governing students' preferred names and pronouns and their participation in school sport. The Health Statutes Amendment Act, 2024 bars certain gender-affirming care for minors. The Fairness and Safety in Sport Act bars trans women from women's sport. Bill 9, the Protecting Alberta's Children Statutes Amendment Act, passed at the tail of the fall sitting and invokes the Charter's notwithstanding clause to shield the three trans-youth laws from legal challenge for years. Egale Canada, the Skipping Stone Foundation and five families announced constitutional litigation, calling the package discriminatory, and state that their court challenge continues regardless; the laws are in force with constitutional litigation pending. Premier Danielle Smith's 12 February 2024 announcement of the package stated the bans would not include a ban on women's shelters, women's prisons or women's changing rooms, and Alberta's statutory trans package deliberately excluded jail and prison settings. No provincial placement-by-birth-sex rule for trans prisoners was enacted, and no Alberta-specific trans-prisoner placement, special unit or segregation case is documented in this record. Provincial correctional policies vary and no Alberta-specific rule is documented. Federal corrections operations inside Alberta accommodate offenders based on gender identity rather than sex assigned at birth: since 2018 the Correctional Service of Canada permits gender-diverse offenders to request placement or transfer to a men's or women's institution aligned with their gender identity or expression, regardless of anatomy or the sex/gender marker on identity documents, with requests refused only where CSC finds unresolvable overriding health or safety concerns. As of 2025 CSC reported 90 self-identified transgender women in federal institutions, 73 housed in men's institutions and 17 in women's. The Office of the Correctional Investigator called CSC's 2022 gender-diversity policy an important change but flagged the lack of clear parameters for what counts as an overriding health or safety concern and the absence of a dedicated mechanism for gender-diverse prisoners to report abuse. Alberta's Human Rights Commission handles discrimination complaints in areas of provincial responsibility, and gender identity and gender expression are prohibited grounds in employment, housing and public and private accommodations across Canadian jurisdictions as of 2017. Section 15 of the Charter applies to all laws and government institutions including law enforcement authorities, and Supreme Court jurisprudence has interpreted sex and physical disability in section 15 to include transsexuality. Transgender people are able to change their legal gender in Alberta under provincial vital statistics rules governing identity documents such as birth certificates. Since 2022 the Criminal Code statutorily bans conversion therapy nationwide for both minors and adults, making it a crime to subject anyone to it as defined by statutory law. Same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since 20 July 2005 under the federal Civil Marriage Act; Alberta's 2000 Marriage Act defining marriage as between a man and a woman and invoking the notwithstanding clause was invalid because capacity to marry is exclusive federal jurisdiction and its five-year exemption expired in 2005. In a poll commissioned for the Privy Council Office reported for 2020, 87.6% of those surveyed said they would be comfortable if a neighbour was a transgender person. This figure is a general-population attitude finding from 2020, not a measure of current risk or of violence.

name: Alberta
text: Federal equality, criminal and corrections rules also apply in Alberta. The national record for Canada covers the federal layer in detail. Alberta's trans-specific lawmaking is a package of three statutes that passed final legislative stage on 4 December 2024. The Education Amendment Act, 2024 introduced parental opt-in for classroom instruction on sexuality and rules governing students' preferred names and pronouns and their participation in school sport. The Health Statutes Amendment Act, 2024 bars certain gender-affirming care for minors. The Fairness and Safety in Sport Act bars trans women from women's sport.
