name: Saskatchewan
text: Federal protections also apply, and the national record for Canada covers the federal layer in detail. Saskatchewan's human rights legislation lists gender identity and gender expression as prohibited grounds in employment, housing, and public and private accommodations, with a provincial complaints route. Change of legal gender is a provincial function available in Saskatchewan under the province's own rules. On 22 August 2023 the education ministry announced parental inclusion and consent policies requiring parent or guardian permission to change preferred name and pronouns for students under 16, parent notice on sexual-health curriculum, and a pause to third-party school programs. That release initiated the court challenge. The Education (Parents' Bill of Rights) Amendment Act, 2023 passed with the province invoking the notwithstanding clause, a five-year override of the Charter, requiring parental consent for students under 16 requesting use of gender-related preferred name or gender identity. Human rights groups called for repeal, and the clause may prevent legal action succeeding on Charter grounds. On 11 August 2025 the Court of Appeal for Saskatchewan (2025 SKCA 74) set aside the 2023 chambers decision, so the pronoun-notice policy stands. It held Charter breaches under sections 1 and 15 cannot be tested where section 33 was invoked, while reporting states the appeal was granted in part, a judge has jurisdiction to decide whether the law limits Charter rights, and UR Pride's litigation may continue in the Court of King's Bench. Amnesty International Canada intervened and welcomed the 11 August 2025 decision as a meaningful victory for human rights in Canada, arguing courts can still decide Charter violation and issue a declaration despite the shield, and use must align with Canada's international-law obligation to provide an effective remedy. Egale Canada co-counsel Bennett Jensen said UR Pride will continue litigation, noting students had lived under the law for two years. On 6 November 2025 the Supreme Court of Canada said it will hear appeals in the school pronoun law challenge. Both the province and UR Pride appealed and sought expedition alongside Quebec's Bill 21 challenge. No merits ruling has changed the policy, and the shielded consent rule is now before Canada's highest court.

name: New Brunswick
text: The national record for Canada covers the federal layer in detail. Policy 713 of the Department of Education and Early Childhood Development in force since 17 August 2020 was revised on 1 July 2023, 23 August 2023 and 1 January 2025. Effective 1 January 2025, students of any age may choose names and pronouns in informal settings with parental consent encouraged but not required, while formal records for students under 16 still require parental consent. That revision went further than child advocate Kelly Lamrock's recommendations. It applies in the school environment to all students, school personnel, contract and casual employees, visiting professionals, student teachers, parents, volunteers and visitors. From 1 July 2023 until the January 2025 revision, teachers were barred from using a chosen name and pronouns for a student under 16 without parental consent, reversing a three-year-old rule requiring student informed consent before discussing names and pronouns with parents. The 1 July 2023 change also removed explicit wording letting students take part in extracurricular activities, including sports teams, reflecting their gender identity. Premier Blaine Higgs's Progressive Conservative government acted without a legislative vote citing complaints from parents and teachers. Two ministers resigned in protest and two were removed, and eight party members including six cabinet ministers sat out question period in June 2023 over the lack of process, with dissidents calling for a leadership review. About 350 people rallied at the New Brunswick legislature on 14 May 2023 against the review, which Education Minister Bill Hogan confirmed was under way. Pride in Education writer Gail Costello said it saves lives and warned changing or removing it would lose kids. As adopted in 2020 it requires schools to respect chosen names and pronouns and provide gender-neutral bathrooms. The Canadian Civil Liberties Association mounted a constitutional challenge to the 2023 parental-consent rule.

name: Scotland
text: Scotland is a devolved nation of the United Kingdom. The national record for United Kingdom covers the federal layer in detail. A Gender Recognition Reform (Scotland) Bill was introduced in March 2022 and passed in December 2022 by 86 votes to 39, applying only to Scotland. It was blocked under section 35 of the Scotland Act 1998 while awaiting royal assent, the first time that power has been used to overturn Scottish legislation, so the reformed procedure is not in force in Scotland. Hate crime is governed by the Hate Crime and Public Order (Scotland) Act 2021, passed in March 2021 by 82 votes to 32, given royal assent a month later and in force on 1 April 2024, listing gender identity as a protected characteristic. Legislation enacted in 2009 provides penalty enhancements where an offence is motivated by the victim's gender identity. The Crown Office and Procurator Fiscal Service publication 'Hate crime in Scotland, 2025-26', issued 30 June 2026, records 7,115 hate-crime charges in total, up 17% on 2024-25 and the highest since 2003-04. Transgender-identity aggravation accounted for 104 charges, up 21% from 86 the previous year and the highest since the 2021 Act took effect. Sexual-orientation aggravation accounted for 2,062 charges, the second commonest category. Police Scotland recorded 8,538 hate crimes in 2024-25, per the Scottish Government report of 17 February 2026, the first annual report under the 2021 Act. The highest rates per 10,000 residents were in Glasgow City and City of Edinburgh at about 32.25 each. Sixty-two per cent carried a race aggravator and just over a quarter a sexual-orientation aggravator; the report gives no per-resident rate for the transgender-identity category. Police Scotland interim guidance of 25 June 2025 requires searches involving removal of more than a jacket, gloves, headgear or footwear to be on biological sex, in custody and stop-and-search. Where lived gender differs from sex at birth, efforts will be made to provide an officer of that lived gender on request. On 19 June 2026 in For Women Scotland v Scottish Ministers [2026] CSOH 59, Judge Lady Ross of the Outer House, Court of Session, struck down the Scottish Prison Service's non-statutory trans custody guidance as unlawful, holding sex segregation must rest on a lawful basis. It had allowed some trans prisoners to be held in establishments matching gender identity rather than sex at birth. Heard in February 2026, the court was told housing trans prisoners by sex at birth would breach human rights and create unacceptable suicide risk, while government lawyers defended individual risk assessments as flexible; the claimant challenged a policy of holding only biological females in the women's estate. Same-sex marriage has been legal in Scotland since 16 December 2014 under legislation passed by the Scottish Parliament on 4 February 2014 by 108 votes to 15 and given royal assent on 12 March 2014, with first ceremonies on 31 December 2014. No religious organisation or celebrant is obliged to perform such marriages.

name: Michoacan de Ocampo
text: Federal Mexican law applies here. The national record for Mexico covers the federal layer in detail. State law has not typified killing of LGBT people as a hate crime, and most attacks concentrate in Tierra Caliente under armed-group influence. Six LGBT+ homicides were recorded in the first four and a half months of 2026, including Daniela, a trans woman found beaten to death in a drainage channel in Morelia on 2 April 2026, with a suspect arrested in April 2026. The six were in Morelia (three), Uruapan, Ocampo and Maravatío, with at least 56 registered aggressions since 2014. The Observatorio Nacional de Crímenes contra Personas LGBT recorded 46 LGBT+ homicides between 2015 and 2024: Morelia 11, Lázaro Cárdenas 6, Apatzingán and Uruapan 5 each, Zamora 4, with 2015 deadliest at 10 victims. Trans women were most affected at 27 of the 46, and ages 25 to 39 most affected. Thirteen disappearances were reported between 2022 and 2024. These raw counts lack a population denominator, so municipal rankings reflect population size as much as risk. Enforcement is minimal: of 46 cases since 2015 only one was processed for judicialization, the murder of Meredith Escarlet, a trans woman killed in Tarímbaro, and the state prosecutor keeps no disaggregated data.

name: Veracruz de Ignacio de la Llave
text: Federal rules such as passports and executive orders are covered elsewhere; the national record for Mexico covers the federal layer in detail. Veracruz was among the last Mexican states to legislate legal gender recognition. Its Congress reformed the Civil Code in 2025 to create an administrative procedure for legal gender recognition, with no age requirement. Human Rights Watch's state-by-state survey covers Veracruz only in relation to identity documents held by the civil registry; it documents no prison-placement rule for the state and no information on where transgender prisoners are housed. Violence against LGBT+ people is recorded in high raw numbers. Diario de Xalapa reported that Veracruz closed 2025 with 15 recorded hate crimes against the LGBT community. The Letra S annual impunity report published on 7 May 2026 counts six of the 60 LGBT+ murders recorded nationwide in 2025 as occurring in Veracruz, level with Guanajuato and behind Puebla's seven; the same tally includes the November 2025 killing of a trans woman at a motel in Oluta. These are raw counts published without a per-capita denominator, so the state ranking is by raw count only and does not by itself establish that a visitor faces higher risk in Veracruz than in a less populous state. Earlier counts run the same direction. Letra S's 2021 report found that Veracruz led the national count of violent deaths of LGBT+ people for the fourth consecutive year, with 10 recorded cases, ahead of Guanajuato (9), Estado de México (7) and Chihuahua (6); 19 of the 32 states recorded victims that year. The same report documents systematic under-counting: in a third of the 2021 cases no name was published, and in 43 percent the sex was recorded as male with no attention to gender identity. State figures are compiled for the LGBT+ category as a whole, so no trans-specific homicide rate for Veracruz is published. Prosecution is the weak point. The state prosecutor's office holds several open files on LGBT murders, according to the activist Leonardo Ruiz of Orgullo Xalapa, among them the case of Edhibaldo Presa Parra, a Universidad Veracruzana professor found dead on 7 January. Activists argue that hate-crime classification in these cases rests on inference from motive patterns and aggravating circumstances rather than direct evidence, and place responsibility for the absence of outcomes on the FGE. Not every monitoring source points the same way: data from the group Soy Humano put Veracruz's 2024 figures below the national average.

name: Oaxaca
text: Oaxaca stands under Mexico's national framework on legal gender recognition; the national record for Mexico covers the federal layer in detail. Oaxaca created an administrative procedure for legal gender recognition through a 2019 reform to its civil code. A 2021 decree extended the procedure to people aged 12 and over, and a June 2023 Supreme Court ruling reopened access for children under 12, leaving the route open across age groups. Oaxaca's only documented gender-identity legislation governs identity documents. Violence against LGBTIQ+ people and against muxes is documented at state level. Oaxaca's human-rights ombudsperson opened 34 investigations into attacks on LGBTIQ+ people between 2015 and 2022. Muxe teacher Marimar 'Estrellita' Santiago was killed in 2022 on the road to Huilotepec, in the Istmo de Tehuantepec, prompting community demands for justice. A profile published by Trendencias in April 2025 describes Oaxaca as Mexico's fastest-growing tourist destination and, at the same time, the country's most dangerous state for the LGBT+ community. It reports violent incidents under investigation with possible municipal-police involvement in municipalities where armed groups operate, and names two victims: muxe Cristian Hernández Cutino, 31, and stylist Zulma Hernández Mendoza, 43. The ranking is stated without per-capita figures, so it cannot be weighed against the state's general homicide rate. The state's response has concentrated on visitor security rather than institutional reform, according to the same profile.

name: Puebla
text: Mexico's federal framework applies nationwide; the national record for Mexico covers the federal layer in detail. Human Rights Watch's state-by-state review of 11 March 2025 records that the Puebla congress passed a 2021 reform of the state civil code recognising the right to legal gender recognition, accompanied by a corresponding implementing decree. The regime carries a minimum age of 18 years for recognition, a threshold that a court has voided. Quadratin reported on 16 June 2026 that Puebla recorded seven victims in a national tally of murders of LGBT+ people in 2025, the highest raw count of any state. The ranking is by raw count only and is not adjusted for population; the source gives no per-capita figure, so the count does not by itself establish that Puebla is more dangerous per resident than smaller states.

name: Tripura
text: The national record for India covers the federal layer in detail. No Tripura statute, court order or state policy on those questions is recorded. The region's sources document checkpoint and transport-hub enforcement in which gender presentation is treated as a possible concealment method. On 2 August 2024, police at the Panisagar check post in North Tripura district stopped a bus on the Assam-Agartala highway bound for Mumbai via Guwahati and detained seven Bangladeshi nationals, two of them transgender and five described by police as disguised as third gender, with the case registered as fraudulent documents and border crossing. A separate report of the same period records 15 Bangladeshi nationals, seven of them transgender, apprehended in separate incidents within 24 hours, carrying fake Aadhaar and PAN cards. The accounts differ on the Panisagar number and transgender count. On 9 November 2024 a joint 24-hour operation detained 12 Bangladeshi nationals, among them minors and transgender people. Six, including three transgender persons, were held after midnight while travelling to Mumbai, and a second group of six, including three children from Khulna, was held at Udaipur Railway Station. A local facilitator was arrested for moving them. Tripura shares an 856-km border with Bangladesh, with checkpoints on highway and rail routes toward the rest of the country. The operations were immigration enforcement against Bangladeshi nationals, with no record of whether the same scrutiny falls on transgender residents or visitors whose documents and appearance diverge. The figures are raw counts with no denominator.

name: West Bengal
text: West Bengal is a state of India and stands under the national framework on transgender recognition, identity documents and healthcare, which the national record carries. This record covers enforcement, institutions and documented incidents specific to the state. In August 2024 a group of trans women travelling to RG Kar Medical College in Kolkata filed an FIR alleging that a Railway Protection Force constable at Rabindra Sadan metro station groped one of them while checking her gender and made inappropriate remarks. Metro Railway and the RPF denied the allegation and filed a counter-FIR against the group; video footage showed the complainant in tears. The episode records gender-checking conduct by uniformed personnel in the state. West Bengal accounted for three of the seven cases registered nationally under the Transgender Persons Act in 2021, the joint highest count that year alongside Assam and Kerala. The national total is small: 20 cases between 2019 and 2023, which the reporting attributes to police-registration bias rather than to low levels of violence. Official case counts in the state therefore understate what trans people there experience. On border enforcement, South Dinajpur police arrested a transgender woman from Sirajganj district in Bangladesh on allegations of infiltrating India, together with the e-rickshaw driver who had brought her across. The person arrested was a foreign national entering without authorisation, not a visitor on a visa, and the single case does not establish a pattern of targeting trans travellers at the state's land border. West Bengal is among the 12 states and union territories that notified a transgender welfare board. A Right to Information investigation published in November 2024 found the state's board operating without a functioning policy framework, and that most boards nationally have met less than once a year since being constituted, with several lacking a compliance mechanism or any decision-making power.

name: West Bengal
text: West Bengal stands under the national framework on transgender recognition and documents; the national record for India covers the federal layer in detail. In August 2024 a group of trans women travelling to RG Kar Medical College in Kolkata filed an FIR alleging that a Railway Protection Force constable at Rabindra Sadan metro station groped one of them while checking her gender and made inappropriate remarks. Metro Railway and the RPF denied the allegation and filed a counter-FIR against the group; video footage showed the complainant in tears. West Bengal accounted for three of the seven cases registered nationally under the Transgender Persons Act in 2021, the joint highest count that year alongside Assam and Kerala. Official case counts in the state therefore understate what trans people there experience. On border enforcement, South Dinajpur police arrested a transgender woman from Sirajganj district in Bangladesh on allegations of infiltrating India, together with the e-rickshaw driver who had brought her across. The person arrested was a foreign national entering without authorisation, not a visitor on a visa, and the single case does not establish a pattern of targeting trans travellers at the state's land border. West Bengal is among the 12 states and union territories that notified a transgender welfare board. A Right to Information investigation published in November 2024 found the state's board operating without a functioning policy framework.

name: Punjab
text: Punjab has no statute or institution of its own targeting transgender people. A trans visitor stands under India's national framework; the national record for India covers the federal layer in detail. The one region-level event in the source inventory concerns public assembly. Pride Amritsar cancelled its 27 April 2025 parade at the Rose Garden after resistance from Sikh religious organisations, among them the Nihang Singh faction and the Akal Takht; organisers cited religious-group opposition as the reason. The cancellation is the documented Punjab-specific signal on the space available for public LGBT+ events.

name: Tamil Nādu
text: Tamil Nadu stands under India's national framework for legal gender recognition, identity documents and criminal law; the national record for India covers the federal layer in detail. Tamil Nadu was the first Indian state to adopt a transgender welfare policy. Its transgender welfare portal publishes the operative paperwork for changing gender in state records: an affidavit form, a certificate of identity for change of gender, relaxation of membership identification requirements, and user manuals. The thirunangai and thirunambi categories are embedded in state governance rather than sitting outside it. State provision includes free sex-reassignment surgery in government hospitals, and access to housing and citizenship schemes through the state regime. The Madras High Court, in its order of 4 August 2025 in WP 7284 of 2021, recorded that the government had brought the Tamil Nadu State Policy for Transgender Persons 2025 into effect. The court described the policy as a victory for transgender and intersex persons after a long struggle and commended the government for it. Prosecution data place Tamil Nadu ahead of other states in reaching court on transgender offences. A civil-society crime-data analysis published on 30 January 2026 records Tamil Nadu as the only state with a case under the Transgender Persons Act in 2020 (one of one nationally) and in 2022 (one), and as the source of seven of the eleven national cases in 2023. The same analysis warns that registration bias shapes these figures, so the counts measure reporting and prosecution reachability rather than the incidence of violence. The 2023 figure is a share of the national total, not a per-capita rate; no population denominator is given.

name: Assam
text: Assam stands under India's national framework; the national record for India covers the federal layer in detail. No Assam-specific statute on legal gender recognition, criminal law or facilities was identified in the sources reviewed, so the national assessment applies to this state. Complaint machinery under the national Transgender Persons Act has been reachable in Assam. Of the seven cases registered nationally under the Act in 2021, two were registered in Assam; the 2023 national tally recorded none in the state. A Queerbeat crime-data report of 30 January 2026 cautions that these national counts are themselves very small, 20 cases across 2019 to 2023, and attributes the low figures to police-registration bias, so the absence of Assam cases in the 2023 tally does not establish an absence of incidents in the state. State welfare machinery was absent as of the most recent documentation held here. A December 2021 reply to parliament from the Press Information Bureau listed the twelve states and union territories that had constituted Transgender Welfare Boards under the 2019 Rules, and Assam was not among them. No later notification constituting a board for Assam appears in the sources reviewed.

name: Uttar Pradesh
text: Uttar Pradesh falls under India's national framework for transgender people; the national record for India covers the federal layer in detail. No source reviewed here records a state law or enforcement practice restricting transgender visitors beyond that framework; state-level facts concern religious institutions and welfare administration, not criminal law. The Kinnar Akhada, a monastic order of transgender ascetics based in the state, holds rank within the wider monastic order. At the Maha Kumbh in Prayagraj on 12 February 2025, Pavitra Nandagiri, a Mahamandaleshwar of the Akhada, led 15 transgender spiritual leaders in the fair's fourth ceremonial bathing, marching with Naga Sadhus and Aghori ascetics. The fair runs 45 days and is described as the world's largest religious gathering, with transgender monastics appearing at senior rank.

name: Chhattīsgarh
text: Chhattisgarh stands within India's national framework; the national record for India covers the federal layer in detail. One trans-specific killing is documented in Chhattisgarh. On 22 November 2024 a transgender woman, Kajal, known as "Coca Cola", was lured out, stabbed and left in an abandoned quarry at Dhabadih village in Baloda Bazar district. Police described it as a contract killing arranged for 12 lakh rupees by a rival, Tapasya, to prevent Kajal's accession to the head seat (guru gaddi) of the Jora Math community. Five suspects were arrested and 10.5 lakh rupees seized. No general homicide rate for Chhattisgarh was identified, so this single incident cannot be placed against the state's background level of violence; the stated motive was a leadership dispute inside a transgender community rather than an attack on a trans person as such.

name: Ceara
text: Ceará stands under Brazil's national framework; the national record for Brazil covers the federal layer in detail. Ceará recorded 11 killings of trans people in 2024, the highest count of any state in the Northeast and the third highest nationally, according to the ANTRA dossier reported on 28 January 2025. The state has about 9.2 million residents, which the source puts at roughly 0.12 killings per 100,000 residents. Ceará's general homicide rate is not in the source inventory, so the two cannot be compared here, and the national ranking is by raw count, which tracks population size rather than risk. The ninth ANTRA dossier, reported on 26 January 2026, recorded 8 killings in Ceará in 2025, level with Minas Gerais at the top of the state ranking, or about 0.09 per 100,000 residents on the source's own figures. Both counts come from a dossier that compiles media-reported killings. Law No. 17,480, sanctioned by Governor Camilo Santana and published on 19 May 2021, requires public and private establishments in Ceará, from 90 days after publication, to display a notice of at least 50 cm by 50 cm on the exterior or at an entrance stating that discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity is expressly prohibited, and listing the phone number of the Special Coordination for LGBT Public Policies for complaints, clarifications and reports. No enforcement actions, penalties or compliance data under the law are sourced. On 7 March 2013 the state general attorney, Francisco Sales Neto, issued decision 02/2013 obligating all notaries in Ceará to accept same-sex marriages, effective 15 March 2013. For a trans visitor whose relationship or identity documents are read under birth-sex status, that notarial obligation is the operative state-level guarantee; no Ceará-specific rule on how a notary handles a trans partner's documents is sourced. On 22 May 2024 the Court of Justice of Ceará authorized Brune Bonassi to rectify documents to reflect a neutral gender, the first non-binary person in the state to obtain such a rectification. On 29 May 2024 the state was reported to be issuing its first birth certificate recognising a person as non-binary. Whether the two concern the same person is not stated. On 16 November 2006 Governor Lúcio Alcântara signed a law requiring educational material on sexual orientation to be included in the training of Ceará's Civil and Military Police, published in the Official Gazette on 26 November 2006. How the requirement is applied today is not recorded. On 12 December 2017 the Sobral municipal chamber approved Bill No. 2154/17, introduced by Councillor Adauto Izidoro Arruda, prohibiting pedagogical activities that reproduce the concept of "gender ideology" or any discussion of gender diversity in all municipal and private schools in Sobral. It passed by majority with the sole opposing vote from Councillor Maria Socorro Brasileiro Magalhães and was sent to Mayor Ivo Gomes. Whether it was signed or vetoed is not recorded.

name: Rio Granda do Norte
text: Rio Grande do Norte stands under Brazil's national framework on legal gender recognition, anti-discrimination protection and the custody placement of LGBTI detainees; the national record for Brazil covers the federal layer in detail. The sources reviewed record no state statute, state court ruling or state agency policy specific to Rio Grande do Norte on any of those questions, so the national assessment applies here unchanged. Lethal violence against trans women is documented in the state across three consecutive reporting years. The ANTRA dossier for 2024, reported on 27 January 2025, records no trans or travesti killing in Rio Grande do Norte that year. The ninth ANTRA dossier, covering 2025, records four in the state, a figure tied with Paraíba and behind Ceará and Minas Gerais at eight each. Those state figures are drawn from a national total of 80 recorded killings in 2025 and are ranked by raw count alone; these sources give no per-capita denominator and no comparison with the state's general homicide rate, so the ranking does not measure per-head risk. ANTRA states that official bodies do not record LGBTQIA+ victims properly, so its counts are floors rather than complete totals. The sources also carry two irreconcilable figures for the state in 2025: the SBT News report of the ninth dossier lists four killings in Rio Grande do Norte, while a Saiba Mais article from February 2026 reproducing the same dossier records zero registered killings in the state for that year. The discrepancy is unresolved. Naomi, a transgender woman, was found dead inside her own home in Praia da Pipa, in the Tibau do Sul municipality on the state's southern coast, in late February 2026, killed by stab wounds. The Civil Police opened an investigation and the Rio Grande do Norte trans-rights association ATTRANSPARÊNCIA/RN called for justice. No outcome of that investigation appears in these sources. In the early hours of 4 May 2026 Emanuelle Samira Fernandes Neta, a 27-year-old transgender woman, was shot dead inside the rented house where she was sleeping on Rua Vivaldo Dantas in the Dom Jaime Câmara neighbourhood of Mossoró, in western Rio Grande do Norte, after five men broke in. Military police found the body on a routine patrol. One suspect was arrested carrying a pistol and booked for illegal firearms discharge and armed criminal association. ATTRANSPARÊNCIA/RN publicly mourned her as an artist killed by the transphobia she faced. This killing post-dates the state's recorded zero for 2024 and is the most recent documented instance in these sources.

name: Paraiba
text: Federal rules on passports, entry and LGBT prisoner housing apply nationwide; the national record for Brazil covers the federal layer in detail. Paraíba's own documented signal on trans safety consists of lethal attacks recorded by civil-society monitoring. The ANTRA dossier for 2025, reported by SBT News on 26 January 2026, records 4 trans killings in the state that year; CNN Brasil's dossier for 2024 recorded 5. Both are raw counts published without a per-capita denominator, so they do not establish the state's relative risk; the 2025 dossier's national total was 80 killings. No Paraíba-specific implementation, dedicated wing, segregation practice or individual case under the federal housing order is documented.

name: Minas Gerais
text: Minas Gerais stands under Brazil's national framework; the national record for Brazil covers the federal layer in detail. Recorded lethal violence against trans people and travestis places Minas Gerais among the highest-counting states. The 2024 dossier compiled by ANTRA recorded 12 trans killings in Minas Gerais, second nationally behind São Paulo's 16 and ahead of Ceará's 11, with a cumulative total of 100 for the state between 2017 and 2024. The 2025 dossier recorded 8 killings in Minas Gerais, tied with Ceará for the highest count, within a national total of 80. Both sets of figures are raw counts published without a per-capita denominator, so they rank states by volume rather than by rate. A study published on 1 July 2024 by the Federal University of Minas Gerais and the state Public Prosecutor's Office found that 60% of deaths involving trans people and travestis in the state resulted from violence, and that 74% of the victims were Black or Pardo. On 15 July 2026 the Court of Justice of Minas Gerais, working with the National Council of Justice, launched an incident-reporting mechanism for LGBTQ violence in Belo Horizonte. Bathroom access has been fought out in the courts rather than settled by statute. Uberaba's municipal ban on unisex restrooms, approved on 12 September 2022 and enacted on 7 October 2022, was declared unconstitutional by the Court of Justice in 2024, after a 2023 lawsuit by the state Public Defender's Office. A Belo Horizonte law signed on 20 November 2023, which authorised religious institutions to bar transgender people from restrooms matching their gender identity, was suspended by preliminary injunction in August 2025. In August 2026 the Court of Justice ordered a shopping mall in Contagem to pay 2,000 reais in compensation to a trans woman denied access to a women's restroom in a 2019 incident in which a guard demanded proof of "sex change"; the ruling reversed a Contagem court decision that had denied the claim for insufficient evidence. Prison housing for trans people in Minas Gerais is governed by a 2014 federal portaria of the national human-rights secretariat, which applies to the state prison system: transsexual men and women are to be sent to female units, gay and travesti prisoners held in male prisons are to be offered specific conviviality spaces, and LGBT inmates may use their social name, recorded at admission, and choose male or female clothing. The instrument provides no sanctions for non-compliance, and no Minas Gerais-specific implementation, wing, segregation practice or individual case is documented.

name: Bahia
text: Brazil's federal framework applies here; the national record for Brazil covers the federal layer in detail. The ANTRA 2025 dossier records 7 trans killings in Bahia during 2025, placing the state immediately behind the leading states, which recorded 8; a second report identifies those as Ceará and Minas Gerais. Across 1,261 killings recorded nationwide between 2017 and 2025, Bahia ranks third with 97, after São Paulo (151) and Ceará (107). These are raw counts with no per-capita denominator, and Bahia is one of Brazil's most populous states, so the ranking reflects population size as well as incidence and does not establish that the state is more dangerous per resident than smaller ones. The pattern is not new. The ANTRA dossier for 2022 ranked Bahia seventh nationally for killings of trans people, with 7 killings of travestis in the state that year, when Pernambuco led the ranking. On the weekend of 6-7 December 2025, Rhianna, an 18-year-old trans woman, was choked to death in Luís Eduardo Magalhães, in the west of the state. The Civil Police opened a feminicide investigation, treating the killing as gender-based. The suspect, a 19-year-old app driver, drove the victim's body to the police station, confessed and claimed self-defence, and was released. Bahia was the first Brazilian state to enact an anti-discrimination ordinance, in 1997. On 1 June 2022 the Legislative Assembly passed, and on 30 June 2022 Assembly President Adolfo Menezes signed, the Millena Passos Law banning discrimination on grounds of gender identity; a parallel measure covering sexual orientation was signed the same day. Transgender people in Bahia have been able to change their name and legal gender since 2008, with gender self-determination permitted since 2018, and the Bahia Public Defender's Office works with other agencies on joint efforts to facilitate document rectification. A decree signed by Governor Rui Costa on 23 May 2017 gave travesti and transexual people the right to use their social name and have their gender identity recognised across the state's direct and indirect public administration; the social name must appear alongside the legal name on official documents, and minors require guardian authorisation. On 11 May 2022 the Court of Justice of Bahia allowed a third gender option on documents, and on 26 December 2024 Governor Jerônimo Rodrigues sanctioned Law 14,806, exempting the cost of protest certificates so that document rectification is free of charge for transgender people. In 2008 Léo Kret, a travesti club dancer, won a seat on the Salvador city council with 12,861 votes and, on taking office, insisted on a feminine wardrobe and on using the women's restroom. Against these protections, on 17 December 2025 the Salvador City Council approved a bill banning the teaching of gender identity in schools, signed into law on 26 March 2026 by Mayor Bruno Soares Reis.

name: Rio de Jeneiro
text: Brazil's federal framework applies here; the national record for Brazil covers the federal layer in detail. Rio de Janeiro state courts and police have acted in cases involving trans women. In February 2026 the state court (TJ-RJ) ordered preventive detention of a man accused of exploiting trans women in Niterói; the suspect had been a Niterói city-hall employee until January 2026, and pre-trial custody was confirmed in the extortion case. In April 2025 the state tourism police (DEAT) arrested two trans women in flagrante for extorting a Norwegian tourist in Copacabana, in the Zona Sul beach strip. A peer-reviewed census study of travestis and transgender women in the Rio de Janeiro state prison system interviewed 138 self-declared travesti or trans-woman inmates across eleven units classified as masculine in the metropolitan region between April and June 2021, drawing on the state prison administration's own database. It documents that travestis and trans women in that system are housed in units treated as masculine, with some held in so-called neutral or security units, and characterises placement in male units as a double punishment compounded by recurring violations of basic rights. A 2015 Rio de Janeiro state law grants them parity of treatment with cisgender women in women's units, covering hair length, feminine clothing, accessories and cosmetics.

name: Goias
text: Goiás operates inside Brazil's national legal framework; the findings below are those the sources record as specific to the state. The state's own instrument on the subject is Goiás Decree No. 9,755/2020, which sets out guidelines on LGBTphobic violence and defines that violence to include discrimination, bullying and cyberbullying. Access to public facilities is restricted in at least one Goiás municipality. A Novo Gama municipal law, enacted in 2015, bars transgender people from using public restrooms in accordance with their gender identity. After a challenge by the Associação Nacional de Travestis e Transexuais, Supreme Federal Court Justice Cármen Lúcia ordered the municipal government to explain the law and set 11 June 2024 as the deadline for that explanation. Violence data for the state come from a national count. ANTRA's ninth annual dossier, reported on 26 January 2026, records 80 trans and travesti people killed in Brazil during 2025, five of them in Goiás. The dossier publishes no population breakdown for the state-level figure; raw counts of this kind track population size rather than per-resident risk, so five deaths in Goiás does not by itself establish that the state is more or less dangerous per resident than others.

name: Goias
text: Goiás sits within Brazil's federal framework; the national record for Brazil covers the federal layer. Goiás Decree No. 9,755/2020 sets guidelines on LGBTphobic violence, defining it to include discrimination, bullying and cyberbullying. At least one Goiás municipality restricts public facility access: a Novo Gama law of 2015 bars transgender people from using public restrooms matching their gender identity. After a challenge by the Associação Nacional de Travestis e Transexuais, Supreme Federal Court Justice Cármen Lúcia ordered the municipality to explain the law by 11 June 2024. ANTRA's ninth annual dossier, reported on 26 January 2026, records 80 trans and travesti people killed in Brazil in 2025, five in Goiás. The dossier gives no population breakdown; raw counts track population size, not per-resident risk, so five deaths does not by itself show Goiás is more or less dangerous per resident.

name: Maranhao
text: Maranhão sits within Brazil's national framework for LGBTI people; the national record for Brazil covers the federal layer in detail. ANTRA's ninth annual dossier, reported by SBT News on 26 January 2026, records 5 trans and travesti people killed in Maranhão during 2025. The figure is a raw count with no population denominator for the state, so it establishes a number of deaths rather than a rate, and it does not show that Maranhão is more or less dangerous than a state of different size. The national totals and the world-ranking comparison published in the same dossier are not specific to Maranhão.

name: Para
text: Pará stands under Brazil's national framework; the national record for Brazil covers the federal layer in detail. Facilities access is the sharpest state-level change. On 14 July 2026 the governor of Pará signed a state law authorising religious temples and schools to restrict bathroom use on the basis of biological sex. Before enactment the Federal Public Prosecutor's Office recommended a veto, arguing that the measure would violate the rights of transgender people and the principle of secularism. On 15 July 2026 the Socialism and Liberty Party announced it had filed a lawsuit against the law. Documentation. On 21 June 2025 Ember Alves Oliveira became the first person in Pará to obtain a birth certificate carrying an X sex marker, through an action brought by the Public Defender's Office of Pará after the registry office in Ananindeua refused rectification. The registry relied on Provision 73 of the National Council of Justice, which does not provide for a third gender option, and refused a first-name change without stated legal justification. The Public Defender's Office argued that documentation which does not reflect a person's gender identity is a source of suffering and anguish and a violation of human dignity. State law layer. A 2007 amendment to the Constitution of the State of Pará prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, and Decree No. 3831 of 8 April 2024 created a State Council for Sexual Diversity within the State Secretariat for Racial Equality and Human Rights. Violence. The national ANTRA dossier for 2025 records five of that year's killings of trans and travesti people in Pará. The figure is a raw count taken from a national tally and is not accompanied by a state population denominator, so it does not by itself establish the state's rate or rank it against other states.

name: Distrito Federal
text: Distrito Federal sits under Brazil's national framework; the national record for Brazil covers the federal layer in detail. ANTRA's ninth annual dossier, reported in January 2026, attributes two of the 80 trans and travesti people killed nationwide in 2025 to this district. That figure is a raw count: with no population denominator or general homicide rate supplied, it cannot be converted into a per-capita rate, ranked against other units, or measured against the district's background homicide level. It stands as two documented killings and nothing more precise. No district-level variation appears on identity documents, entry, public facilities, gender-affirming care, partner recognition, hate-crime enforcement or police and custody practice. No district court ruling, government measure, police operation or civil-society incident report for this district appears in sources reviewed.

name: Sachsen
text: Sachsen is a state within Germany and stands under the German national framework; the national record for Germany covers the federal layer in detail. On 31 May 2025 thousands marched through Dresden for Christopher Street Day while neo-Nazi counter-demonstrators mounted a protest aimed at disrupting the march; the march went ahead. That far-right attempt to stop Dresden Pride is the documented basis for the elevated risk rating Sachsen carries. Sachsen is a co-sponsor, with Sachsen-Anhalt and Thuringia, of a joint state initiative to tighten the federal Self-Determination Act, launched after the case of Marla-Svenja Liebich and directed at what the sponsoring states describe as misuse of self-identification. The state government is therefore working to narrow the self-identification route at federal level; it cannot amend the national statute alone, and the initiative is a push on the federal legislature.

name: Comunitat Valenciana
text: Spain's national framework on legal gender recognition and federal protections applies here; the national record for Spain covers the federal layer in detail. The Comunitat Valenciana has its own two-statute framework: Ley 8/2017 of 7 April, the integral law on the right to gender identity and expression, and Ley 23/2018 of 29 November on LGTBI equality. Article 1 of Ley 8/2017 sets the law's purpose as guaranteeing an adequate normative framework for gender self-determination for people whose felt gender identity differs from that assigned at birth, and public bodies of the Comunitat Valenciana must treat people according to their felt gender identity. The duty reaches the regional administration, health and education services a visitor may deal with. Ley 23/2018 prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity and expression, provides access and admission rights (article 56), reverses the burden of proof (article 57), and establishes a Title V regime of administrative infringements and sanctions for discrimination against LGTBI people (articles 58 to 66). A complaint about being refused service or admission in the region can shift the evidential burden onto the respondent, and the regional administration can fine discriminators. Regional courts have handled gender-identity-motivated offences. The Audiencia Provincial de Valencia, Section 5, convicted over a June 2022 incident in a Valencia park in Patraix, where an 18-year-old and several minors insulted, chased, filmed and mocked a trans woman solely because of her gender identity. The adult accepted six months' imprisonment, suspended for two years on condition of committing no offence, plus a 720-euro fine and 1,000 euros in moral damages to the victim; two minors had already been sentenced to supervision measures. The specialised hate-crime prosecutor (fiscal coordinadora de delitos de odio) handled the case.

name: Buenos Aires
text: Buenos Aires province operates under Argentina's national framework; the national record for Argentina covers the federal layer in detail. The provincial ombudsman's September 2024 guide sets out steps for rectifying the gender marker of people born in the province, including those now living elsewhere. The ombudsman's Gender Violence Office (Resolución Nº 100/10) submitted evidence to the UN Human Rights Committee for its June and July 2016 review documenting violence, persecution and harassment of trans and travesti people by provincial police and third parties under police cover, including violence by judicial, state and police agents. Research records the criminalisation of trans and travesti women through drug-offence prosecutions under microtrafficking enforcement, concentrated in La Plata's Zona Roja. After the 2012 Gender Identity Law decriminalised trans presence, security-led street-offence policing became the operative instrument of indirect criminalisation, resting on the 2005 transfer of drug sale and possession jurisdiction to the province. No trans-specific placement rule or separate trans housing unit is recorded; placement follows the national prison-housing framework.

name: Subcarpathian Voivodeship
text: Subcarpathian Voivodeship lies within Poland's national framework, which covers entry rules, custody, documents and hate-crime measures; the national record for Poland covers the federal layer in detail. On 20 September 2021 the Podkarpackie voivodeship council repealed its 'LGBT-free' resolution and replaced the ordinance with a generic anti-discrimination statement. The county-level layer ended later: on 27 April 2025 the county of Łańcut, in the voivodeship's southeast, repealed its anti-LGBT resolution at an extraordinary councillors' session, the last local authority in Poland to do so. No region-specific enforcement action, prosecution, healthcare restriction, facility rule or trans-specific incident in Subcarpathian Voivodeship is documented in the available sources. For those matters the national assessment applies.

name: Podlaskie Voivodeship
text: Poland's national framework on entry, documents and protection applies here; see the national record for Poland for the federal layer. The first Białystok Equality March took place on 20 July 2019 with about 1,000 participants. Far-right groups attacked it and tried to block its route; it is described as Poland's most violent assault on a public LGBTQ gathering. Białystok County, the district around the city, was declared an LGBT-free zone in 2019, in a voivodeship that was a stronghold of Law and Justice (PiS). The fourth march, on 28 September 2024, drew about 300 participants and was guarded by around 500 police officers, with counter-demonstrations at several points along the route. Afterwards regional police spokesman Tomasz Krupa said no incidents were recorded and called the event safe. Far-right presence continued; the march passed without reported violence under heavy police cover.

name: Lublin Voivodeship
text: Lublin Voivodeship sits under the Polish national framework; the national record for Poland covers the federal layer in detail. Świdnik, a town in the voivodeship, was the first place in Poland to adopt an "LGBT-free" declaration. Its county council passed the resolution in March 2019, pledging to shield children from "homosexual propaganda" and to refrain from encouraging "tolerance of LGBT people". The text is non-binding and does not restrict a visitor's movement or access to services; it records a local authority's posture, not an enforceable rule. The voivodeship legislature adopted a comparable declaration, kept it on revisit, and repealed it on 20 September 2021 after the European Commission threatened to withhold funding from voivodeships retaining such declarations. Whether county-level declarations, including Świdnik's, were withdrawn is not established.

name: Lesser Poland Voivodeship
text: Poland's national framework covers criminal law, hate-crime provisions, partnership recognition and entry rules; the national record for Poland covers the federal layer in detail. The voivodeship council adopted an 'LGBT-free' resolution and repealed it on 20 September 2021, after threats to European Commission funding. Council leader Jan Duda, father of president Andrzej Duda, had voted only weeks earlier to keep the resolution in place. The repeal removed a formal declaration of exclusion issued by the regional authority. In Kraków, the mayor elected in 2024, Aleksander Miszalski, made attendance at the city's annual LGBT Equality March one of his first decisions, becoming the first Kraków mayor to take part after a predecessor declined. He pledged to hang a rainbow flag at city hall and said he wanted 'a tolerant Kraków, a home for everyone'.

name: Łódź Voivodeship
text: Poland's national framework applies here; the national record for Poland covers the federal layer in detail. Łódź Voivodeship's own anti-LGBT resolution was revoked by the Supreme Administrative Court on 12 October 2023 on equal-treatment grounds under Article 32 of the constitution. Łódź was one of five voivodeships the European Commission wrote to on 2 June 2020, asking governors to withdraw the declarations. The resolution was declaratory rather than penal: no offence, no penalty, no one barred from any place. Its effect was institutional, signalling to bureaucracies and schools which families and identities it considered legitimate. No record specific to Łódź Voivodeship of enforcement, police conduct, prosecution, violence, or facility and healthcare practice was identified. It adds no documented risk beyond the national assessment, which applies here as elsewhere in Poland.

name: Świętokrzyskie Voivodeship
text: Świętokrzyskie Voivodeship is a regional unit of Poland; the national record for Poland covers the federal layer in detail. What is specific to the voivodeship is its own anti-LGBT declaration and its withdrawal. Świętokrzyskie adopted an anti-LGBT resolution during the wave of local declarations that began in 2019. On 2 June 2020 the European Commission wrote to the voivodeship's governor, one of five regional governors asked about such resolutions. The Świętokrzyskie voivodeship council revoked its own resolution on 22 September 2021, and the declaration is no longer in force. The resolution was declaratory rather than criminal. It created no penalties and barred no one physically; its effect was institutional, signalling to local bureaucracies and schools which families and identities the regional leadership treated as legitimate.

name: Masovian Voivodeship
text: Masovian Voivodeship sits within Poland's national framework; the national record for Poland covers the federal layer in detail. On 6 February 2024 the Voivodeship Administrative Court in Warsaw revoked the final document in Poland declaring a locality 'against LGBT ideology', ending the sequence of local anti-LGBT resolutions. The sources do not name the municipality whose document was struck down, so they do not establish whether it sat inside Masovian Voivodeship or elsewhere; what is clear is that the administrative court sitting in Warsaw issued the decision. In March 2019 the Mayor of Warsaw signed a declaration of equality and non-discrimination that includes commitments on responding to hate crime. The declaration stands and the sources record no repeal. It is an instrument of the capital's municipal authorities, not a province-wide provision, and it does not extend to the rest of the voivodeship.

name: Bauchi
text: The national record for Nigeria covers the federal layer in detail. Bauchi's Sharia Penal Code remains in force. The UK Home Office country policy and information note of June 2025 confirms it, and death by stoning is the penalty provided under Section 133 of the Bauchi Sharia Penal Code Law 2001 and Section 134 of the Bauchi State Penal Law of 2001. On 28 June 2022 a Sharia court sitting in Ningi local government area sentenced three men to death by stoning for homosexuality, among them 70-year-old Malam Haruna. The prosecution was brought by members of the Hisbah Vanguard through Adamu Dan Kafi, who told the court the three were arrested at Gwada village, Ningi LGA, on 14 June 2022. Presiding judge Munka'ilu Sabo-Ningi held that they had violated Section 134 of the Bauchi State Penal Law of 2001 and granted a 30-day appeal window. Relatives of the convicted men said the judgment had not been carried out at the time of reporting. Reuters described the sentence as the first time the death penalty had actually been imposed for homosexuality in Nigeria. The UK Home Office note records that the 2022 Bauchi sentence could not be carried out until ratified by the state governor, and that a further report placed a death-by-stoning sentence for homosexuality from a Sharia court in Bauchi in May 2024. Earlier convictions in the state were reversed on appeal. Jubrin Babaji was convicted on 25 September 2003 under Section 133 of the Bauchi Sharia Penal Code Law 2001 and sentenced to death by stoning; the Upper Sharia Court of Bauchi State quashed the sentence for denial of counsel and a defective confession. Yunusa Rafin Chiyawa's conviction was quashed on 14 November 2003. Amnesty International recorded a number of cases in which convictions and sentences to death were quashed on appeal. In 2007 Bauchi state police arrested eighteen men and charged them with sodomy for dressing as women, an offence under the Shari'a penal code. The charges were later reduced to vagrancy, and the men were held in jail for several years awaiting trial; the pre-trial detention dissolved by the end of 2011. Persons perceived as trans-feminine in Bauchi have been arrested and held in custody under Shari'a charges for years.

name: Kano
text: Kano stands under Nigeria's national legal framework; the national record for Nigeria covers the federal layer in detail. Kano operates its own Sharia Penal Code Law 2000, in force since 26 November 2000. Consensual same-sex activity under that code carries 100 lashes and up to one year's imprisonment where the person is unmarried, and stoning to death (rajm) where the person is or has been married. The capital maximum is not confined to men. The UK Home Office note of June 2025 records Kano's maximum penalty for what it terms lesbianism as death, and the Sharia codes as remaining in force. The Prostitution and Immoral Acts (Prohibition) Law criminalises cross-dressing by men, so a trans visitor's appearance is itself legal exposure, distinct from conduct. Eight people convicted of wearing female clothing at a wedding were reportedly flogged in public on hisbah premises in Kano in 2023. The Hisbah, the state religious police, is the most active command among the states examined in the USCIRF 2019 study of Sharia criminal-law implementation, which drew on 173 Sharia-court cases from 2017 in Kano, Sokoto and Zamfara.

name: Sokoto
text: Nigeria's federal framework applies here; the national record for Nigeria covers the federal layer in detail. The Sokoto State Sharia Penal Code Laws took effect across the state on 31 January 2001. Under the code, male same-sex activity is punished by stoning to death where the offender is or has been married, and by 100 lashes where he is not. Sexual acts between women, recorded in the code as wsafa, draw ta'azir punishment of up to 100 lashes and imprisonment. Sokoto's Shari'a criminal code applies to Muslims in the state, one of twelve northern states whose codes carry a maximum penalty of death for men and whipping or imprisonment for women for same-sex acts. Sokoto's Sharia courts apply the code in practice, including its capital provisions. On 9 October 2001 the Upper Sharia Court at Gwadabawa convicted Safiyatu Hussaini Tungar Tudu of zina under sections 128 and 129 of the Sokoto State Sharia Penal Code and sentenced her to death by stoning; the co-accused was discharged and acquitted. She filed an appeal on 26 October 2001, and the Sharia Court of Appeal of Sokoto State quashed the conviction and discharged and acquitted her on 25 March 2002. The conviction was for zina rather than same-sex conduct, but it establishes that the state's religious courts impose the code's capital sentences and that an appellate tier reviews them. An interim committee report was submitted to Sokoto Governor Attahiru Dalhatu Bafarawa on 13 October 1999, and a final report followed on 16 December 1999 with an annexe draft bill to establish Sharia courts applying Sharia law in the state.

name: Zamfara
text: The national record for Nigeria covers the federal layer in detail. Zamfara operates its own Sharia criminal-law layer. Its governor was the first in Nigeria to move, promulgating the Sharia Establishment Law on 27 October 1999, in force 27 January 2000. The Sharia Courts (Administration of Justice and Certain Consequential Changes) Law 1999 was enacted under section 6 of the 1999 Constitution, establishing Sharia courts with criminal jurisdiction and enabling a codified Sharia Penal Code. By 2002 twelve northern states had adopted some form of Sharia into their criminal legislation, and they remain the only Nigerian states where Sharia courts try criminal cases. For a visitor, criminal cases in Zamfara can be heard by Sharia courts applying codified Islamic criminal law, separate from the national statute, and these state courts are where Sharia criminal penalties would be imposed locally.

name: Borno
text: Borno State stands under Nigeria's national framework, and its criminalisation of same-sex conduct rests independently on Borno's own legislation; the national record for Nigeria covers the federal layer in detail. The state's statute on prostitution, homosexuality, brothels and other sexual immoralities was signed by Governor Kachalla on 10 December 2000 and gazetted in Borno State Gazette No. 42 Vol. 26 on 18 October 2001. Section 3 makes engaging in prostitution, lesbianism, a homosexual act or pimping an offence in the state. Section 7 provides that any person who 'engages in sexual intercourse with another person of the same gender shall upon conviction be punished with death'. Section 4 deems all brothels closed on commencement, and Section 9 assigns jurisdiction over the statute's offences to the Upper Sharia Courts, Area Courts and Magistrate Courts. Borno enacted a second, parallel layer of its own. Human Rights Watch's 2004 report lists Borno among the twelve northern Nigerian states that had adopted Shari'a into their criminal legislation by 2002, with Shari'a courts holding criminal jurisdiction over Muslims beyond federal law. The sourcebook of enacted Shari'a Penal Codes records a Borno State Sharia Penal Code Law 2001, signed into law on 3 March 2003, with no operation date or gazette identified; the Borno text was obtained only in May 2006, after the volume's annotation had been completed, which is why Borno is not among the individually annotated codes. The parallel Shari'a layer for Borno therefore rests on a Borno-specific enactment rather than on federal or umbrella coverage. The UK Home Office country-of-origin information note of June 2025 states that Islamic law applies to Muslims in the twelve northern states and criminalises same-sex sexual acts both between men and between women; the maximum penalty for 'sodomy' for men is death in all twelve states, and penalties for 'lesbianism' range from death to flogging and imprisonment. The note carries a dedicated section on enforcement of Shari'a provisions and on the attitude of the hisbah, the morality police. A visitor to Borno therefore faces two state-level regimes, one secular and one Shari'a-based, each of which independently reaches same-sex conduct, and the secular statute's own jurisdiction clause routes those cases to Shari'a and Area Courts as well as to Magistrate Courts.

name: Gombe
text: Gombe State criminalises same-sex conduct under its own Shari'a Penal Code Law 2001, signed into law on 23 November 2001. The enacted statutory text covers conduct by men and women and reaches beyond Nigeria's federal criminal code. Human Rights Watch's 2004 report on Shari'a implementation lists Gombe among the twelve northern states that had adopted Shari'a into criminal legislation by 2002, with Shari'a courts holding criminal jurisdiction over Muslims beyond the federal code. The penalties set by the state statute are severe and gendered. Unmarried men convicted of sodomy face caning of 100 lashes plus one year's imprisonment, and married men face stoning to death (rajm). The lesbianism offence carries up to 50 lashes plus imprisonment of up to six months. Gombe's own formulation defines gross indecency as any sexual offence against the normal or usual standards of behaviour. The UK Home Office country-of-origin information note of June 2025 states that Islamic law applies to Muslims in the twelve northern states, which include Gombe, and criminalises same-sex sexual acts both between men and between women. It records the maximum penalty for 'sodomy' between men as death in all twelve states, with penalties for 'lesbianism' ranging from death to flogging and imprisonment. The note carries a dedicated section on enforcement of Shari'a provisions and on the attitude of the hisbah, the morality police. Enforcement in Gombe is documented through a single mass operation. In October 2023 the Gombe State Command of the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps raided a gathering at Duwa Plaza along the Bauchi-Gombe Expressway that was preparing a same-sex wedding, arresting 76 people. State spokesperson Buhari Sa'ad told reporters that 59 males were detained, 21 of whom wilfully confessed to being homosexuals, and that 17 females were present at the scene; the command stated that the detainees would be charged in court for a crime of social vice in Gombe State. The Guardian of 23 October 2023, byline James Agberebi, independently confirmed the operation from Lagos press, reporting that the arrests followed a tip-off about a same-sex birthday party and planned marriage. Gombe NSCDC Commandant Mohammed Muazu confirmed the arrests; the spokesperson said the remaining males and the 17 females were invited guests and onlookers, and officers voiced concern over the participants' ages. Detention therefore reached people present at a gathering rather than only those alleged to have engaged in conduct. The most recent documented enforcement action in this record is this October 2023 raid; no later instance is documented.

name: Gombe
text: Nigeria's federal framework criminalises same-sex conduct; the national record for Nigeria covers the federal layer. Gombe State criminalises same-sex conduct under its own Shari'a Penal Code Law 2001, signed into law on 23 November 2001. name: Jigawa
text: The national record for Nigeria covers the federal layer in detail. Jigawa State's own criminal layer is the Sharia Penal Code Law 2000, Law No. 12 of 2000, signed 18 December 2000 and brought into operation 27 December 2000 (Jigawa State Gazette Vol. 1 No. 12). It stands under Nigeria's national framework rather than replacing it, and adds offences the national code does not reach, including women's same-sex conduct. The UK Home Office country policy note (June 2025) lists Jigawa in a twelve-state table of Sharia penalties: for male same-sex conduct, married men face death by stoning, while unmarried men face 100 lashes and imprisonment of up to one year; same-sex acts between women carry up to 50 lashes and imprisonment of up to six months. The June 2025 note confirms the Sharia penal layer remains the operative criminal frame for Muslims in Jigawa. The sourcebook places Jigawa among four states, with Gombe, Kano and Zamfara, whose sodomy offence punishes unmarried men with 100 lashes plus one year's imprisonment and married men with stoning to death (rajm); lesbianism carries up to 50 lashes plus up to six months' imprisonment, and Jigawa's code includes the 'unnatural fusion of the female sexual organs' explanation of the offence. By 2002 twelve northern states, Jigawa among them, had adopted some form of Sharia into their criminal legislation, to date the only states where Sharia courts have jurisdiction to try criminal cases.

name: Kaduna
text: Nigeria's federal framework applies alongside Kaduna State's own laws; the national record for Nigeria covers the federal layer in detail. Kaduna separately adopted its own secular Penal Code in 2017, whose Section 259 punishes 'unnatural offences' (sodomy, lesbianism and bestiality) with up to 21 years' imprisonment and a fine, a ceiling above the federal 14-year maximum. Running in parallel, the Kaduna Sharia Penal Code Law 2002 (Law No. 4 of 2002) applies to Muslims. It was signed into law and came into operation on 21 June 2002, published in Kaduna State Gazette No. 17 Vol. 36 of 4 July 2002, and bound with the Sharia Criminal Procedure Code. Human Rights Watch (2004) traces the wave of adoption back to Zamfara's Sharia Establishment Law of 27 October 1999, in force 27 January 2000, after which twelve northern states had adopted some form of Sharia into their criminal legislation by 2002; those twelve remain the only states where Sharia courts hold jurisdiction to try criminal cases, Kaduna among them. The Home Office's June 2025 note carries Kaduna's own row in its twelve-state Sharia penalties table (section 8.4.3, ILGA-derived): death by stoning as the maximum for liwat (sodomy), and same-sex acts between women punishable 'at the discretion of the qadi (Sharia court judge)'. Ostien's annotated volume of Kaduna's enacted text records that Kaduna is one of only three states whose statute states without qualification that 'Whoever commits the offence of sodomy shall be punished with stoning to death (rajm)', with no unmarried/married graduation, while the lesbianism offence is left to ta'azir, discretionary punishment. A trans visitor read as Muslim therefore faces a capital ceiling on men's same-sex acts under Kaduna's own promulgated code, alongside the 21-year secular ceiling that applies regardless of faith.

name: Kebbi
text: Kebbi stands under Nigeria's national framework on sexual-orientation and gender-identity law; the national record for Nigeria covers the federal layer in detail. Kebbi is one of twelve northern Nigerian states that adopted criminal Shari'a during the wave that ran from 1999 to 2002. Human Rights Watch's 2004 report records that by 2002 twelve northern states, Kebbi among them, had Shari'a criminal legislation and Shari'a courts holding criminal jurisdiction over Muslims, the only states in the country with such jurisdiction. Kebbi's own penal layer is the Penal Code (Amendment) Law, Law No. 21 of 2000, signed into law and brought into operation on 1 December 2000 and published in Kebbi State Gazette Vol. 2 No. 1, Supplement, 31 December 2000. The enacted text states that whoever commits the offence of sodomy shall be punished with stoning to death (rajm), a capital ceiling for men's same-sex acts. Kebbi is one of only three states, with Kaduna and Katsina, whose enacted statutory text carries this stoning provision. Women's same-sex conduct is also criminalised under Kebbi's own statute: lesbianism carries 50 lashes and up to six months' imprisonment, the harmonised bloc penalty for women's conduct rather than the Kano/Katsina capital maximum. The UK Home Office's June 2025 country policy and information note carries Kebbi's own row in its twelve-state Shari'a penalties table (section 8.4.3), confirming that Kebbi's Shari'a layer extends criminalisation to acts between women, leaving the state's code broader in scope and harsher than the federal statute for Muslim defendants. Wikipedia's overview of LGBTQ rights in Nigeria places Kebbi inside the northern Shari'a block, where same-sex acts carry penalties ranging from imprisonment to capital punishment and where lesbianism is punishable by imprisonment or caning in most states, with death penalties applied only in Kano and Katsina. On that account Kebbi falls in the lashing and imprisonment tier for women's conduct rather than the capital tier, consistent with Kebbi's own statute, while its sodomy provision for men remains capital. The same source records a cross-dressing layer in the northern block: prison or a fine for men who dress or behave as women, illustrated by a Kano court's 2025 one-year imprisonment sentence. No housing, segregation or placement rule for trans prisoners is documented for Kebbi or elsewhere in Nigeria.

name: Imo
text: Imo is a state in south-eastern Nigeria; the national record for Nigeria covers the federal layer in detail. On 26 April 2018 two men in Imo State were stripped, beaten and paraded through the streets after being accused of gay sex. An inquiry by NoStringsNG found the victims were then arrested by the police and might need legal support. The state detained the people attacked, not the crowd that attacked them. Enforcement continued into 2025. On 19 February the Imo Police Command broke up a party at Graziella Hotels in Orogwe, Owerri West, arrested many present as gay and lesbian suspects, and placed attendees who fled on a search list. Seven years separate the episodes: a street in 2018, a hotel in Owerri West in 2025. Police action is not confined to one locality or to public conduct: a street and a closed private venue both appear, and fleeing did not remove people from the search.

name: Edo
text: Edo State stands under Nigeria's national legal framework; the national record for Nigeria covers the federal layer in detail. Its own documented record is one of mob violence against people accused of same-sex conduct, and it contains no instance in which police protected the person accused. In February 2008, in a remote community in Edo State, police declared Ugbogbo Ovbukhan wanted over 'gay practice' after he and his partner Jerry were found together. A mob beat both men for desecrating the community; Ovbukhan escaped before police arrived and police arrested Jerry for interrogation. The Nigerian Observer reported the wanted declaration on 15 August 2008. On 10 June 2010, The Nigerian Observer reported from Benin City, in Oredo local government area, that Mark Osato Edomwonyi narrowly escaped being killed by a mob after he was found with his partner Paddy in Paddy's rented apartment. A neighbour raised the alarm; Edomwonyi fled through the backyard before the mob arrived, and the crowd then, in the newspaper's words, 'unleashed terror' on Paddy. No police intervention, arrest or prosecution appears in the report, and Edomwonyi's whereabouts were still unknown when it was filed. In May 2018, at Ekpoma, a mob lynched one of two men found together while the other escaped. The report presented the killing as an 'abominable act' against traditional heritage, treating it as community redress. For a visitor, the documented exposure in Edo comes from community perception rather than from a prosecution: in these accounts it is neighbours, not patrols, who raise the alarm, and the single police action documented across the three cases was taken against the couple rather than against those who beat them. The cases reported involve men accused of same-sex conduct, and the inventory holds no Edo case in which a report identifies the victim of violence as a transgender person. Risk to a trans visitor therefore has to be read from the way accusations of sexual and gender nonconformity mobilise a crowd, not from a documented attack on a trans person in the state.

name: Aceh
text: Aceh stands under Indonesia's national legal framework; the national layer is carried by the parent record. The region-specific layer is a provincial sharia criminal code. Special autonomy granted in 2005 authorised the introduction of Islamic criminal law for Muslim residents, and Qanun Aceh Nomor 6 Tahun 2014 tentang Hukum Jinayat, enacted in 2014, has been enforced since 23 October 2015. Aceh is Indonesia's only province that criminalises same-sex relations and enforces Islamic law in addition to the national criminal code. Article 63 of the Qanun defines liwath as sexual acts between males and Article 64 defines musahaqah as sexual acts between females, each determined by sex at birth. Each offence carries up to 100 lashes, up to 100 months' imprisonment, or a fine of up to 1,000 grams of gold. Because the definitions turn on birth sex rather than presentation or legal gender marker, a trans visitor whose documents, presentation or partner's sex are read as same-sex conduct falls within the provision and faces caning, imprisonment or a fine. Public caning is the province's standing punishment for sharia offences. On 23 May 2017 an Islamic court in Banda Aceh applied the 2014 provisions for the first time, ordering two men caned 82 times each before hundreds of spectators outside a mosque; in 2017 two further men, aged 20 and 23, were sentenced to public caning for same-sex relations. The most recent documented enforcement in this record is from 2025. Two men aged 20 and 21 were sentenced on 11 August 2025 to public caning for kissing, after an April 2025 arrest in which police broke into a toilet; CBS News and the Associated Press reported on 26 August 2025 that two men were publicly caned in the province after a sharia court convicted them of hugging and kissing. No later Aceh enforcement incident is documented in this record. Trans people in Aceh have faced targeted enforcement. In January 2018 police in North Aceh arrested twelve transgender women, forcibly cut their hair, compelled them to wear men's clothing and closed their beauty salons. In a separate parlour raid in Aceh in January 2018 police tortured detainees, shaved the heads of transgender women, removed their shirts and bras, and paraded them through the street forcing them to shout that they were to become men.
