name: Lampung
text: Lampung stands under Indonesia's national legal framework; the national record for Indonesia covers the federal layer in detail. The province's own documented record of official conduct toward transgender people is a November 2018 operation in which the Satpol PP, the regional morals-and-order force, raided three trans women, detained them at the Satpol PP office and hosed them down at the firefighter building while an officer recorded the incident. OutRight International's Creeping Criminalisation study names Lampung as one of eight Indonesian provinces whose discriminatory regional regulations it analyses, at both province and district level. Restrictive rules in Lampung therefore operate below the national tier as well as at it, enforced by a regional morals-and-order force rather than solely the national police. For a trans visitor, the documented exposure in Lampung is sub-national.

name: West Papua
text: West Papua adds no provincial or regency-level rules on sexual conduct, gender expression, dress or public morality; the province stands under Indonesia's national framework without local additions. The national record for Indonesia covers the federal layer in detail. Security-force conduct is the defining documented risk. A report published on 22 July 2025 by the Asia-Pacific Solidarity Network recorded 138 acts of torture or other ill-treatment by police and military against people in detention in Maybrat and the Central Highlands through early 2025, with most victims male and under 24, seven female, and seven minors aged 15 to 17; the report's framing is 'impunity, secrecy and silence', indicating a near-total absence of accountability. Any visitor, including a visibly gender-nonconforming one, stands in this environment. The Papua human-rights monitor's Q3 2025 quarterly records a notable increase in military deployments and operations in West Papua's highland regions since August 2025. In Sorong, police arrested over a dozen protest participants in August 2025. On 27 September 2025 a military task force opened fire on civilians in Agats, Asmat Regency, alongside ongoing displacement and racial tension affecting indigenous Papuans. No trans-specific finding accompanies this pattern, but it amplifies exposure for a visibly gender-nonconforming visitor. Provincial document practice follows the national pattern: since June 2021 the Ministry of Home Affairs has conducted outreach to issue transgender Indonesians with Kartu Tanda Penduduk, including residents of Papua, but the card recognises only 'male' and 'female' with no third gender or X designator, and prints gender at birth unless a court recognition is obtained. Families' disapproval can block the process, which officials cite as leaving some residents undocumented and unable to access work or social services.

name: Central Kalimantan
text: Central Kalimantan stands under Indonesia's national framework; the national record for Indonesia covers the federal layer in detail. OutRight Action International's 2022 mapping of Indonesian laws and regional regulations that violate the rights of women and LGBTIQ people lists eight provinces with discriminatory regional regulations; Central Kalimantan is not among them. The province adds no separate criminal or regulatory layer of its own to the exposure a trans visitor already carries under national law. No provincial enforcement action, police operation, prosecution or incident directed at trans or LGBTIQ people in Central Kalimantan appears in the sources reviewed. Absence from a list of discriminatory regulations is a legal finding only. It does not establish how provincial police, local officials or communities treat trans visitors in practice, and nothing in the sources reviewed addresses that question.

name: North Sumatra
text: North Sumatra is part of Indonesia; the national record for Indonesia covers the federal layer. OutRight Action International's mapping covers North Sumatra as one of eight provinces, documenting regional rules imposing dress codes, curfews and restrictions on where transgender people may appear, with significant variation between regions; findings hold beyond the provinces examined directly. Medan, the provincial capital, holds the only documented legal-process case for a transgender person in North Sumatra. Dimas Cahya became the first transgender man in the city to change his name legally; the Medan District Court granted this after a six-week process. The judge warned the change would 'erase my identity' but declined to engage with LGBTI issues; no enforcement action against the couple is recorded. UNAIDS describes Medan as conservative, with LGBTI people regarded locally as 'immoral'.

name: North Sulawesi
text: North Sulawesi stands under Indonesia's national framework; the national record for Indonesia covers the federal layer in detail. The sources reviewed contain no North Sulawesi-specific provincial regulation on gender identity or sexual orientation. OutRight Action International's mapping of Indonesia's national laws and discriminatory regional regulations (Katjasungkana and Wieringa, 2022) examined regional regulations in eight focus provinces: Aceh, DKI Jakarta, East Kalimantan, Lampung, North Sumatra, South Sulawesi, South Sumatra and Yogyakarta. North Sulawesi was not among them. The study documented significant regional variation in dress codes, curfews and restrictions on where transgender people may appear, and states that its findings are valid for regions beyond the focus set, but no such provincial restriction is documented for North Sulawesi itself. Police conduct in Manado is documented through a local account. On 11 June 2016 LGBT groups joined the city's women's movement in a street action against sexual violence at Bundaran Zero Point, running from 08.00 to 10.00 WITA, with SALUT (Sanubari Sulawesi Utara), the local LGBT organisation, taking part. The same reporting records that police raids in Manado have included harassment of LGBT people: SALUT's director Coco Jericho reported that a butch lesbian was groped during a raid. Victims often do not report such conduct because they fear their families will not accept their orientation. No arrests or prosecutions are reported in that account. Public visibility by trans people in the province is documented at official level. On Saturday 10 November 2012 a waria beach-queen pageant was held at Malalayang beach in Manado, organised by Indonesian parliament member Paula Sinjal together with the National Narcotics Agency of North Sulawesi as an outreach event on the dangers of drugs and HIV/AIDS. Sinjal was quoted saying that waria are among local people and deserve attention. No adverse official action is recorded in connection with the event. Media stigma following public visibility is documented in a 2024 Konde.co interview with Alexa, elected Ratu Waria Sulawesi Utara for 2016 to 2018 at the Sahid Kawanua Hotel in Manado. She states that after her title she suffered discrimination from sensationalist media and from the public, with her personal crisis peaking around 25 March 2019. No legal or police action appears anywhere in her account. The most recent incident documented in these sources dates from 2019 and was published in February 2024; no later instance is documented.

name: Southeast Sulawesi
text: Southeast Sulawesi stands under Indonesia's national framework; the national record for Indonesia covers the federal layer in detail. No law, regulation, enforcement action or raid specific to the province appears in the sources reviewed. The OutRight Action International mapping of Indonesia's national laws and regional regulations examines eight focus provinces: Aceh, DKI Jakarta, East Kalimantan, Lampung, North Sumatra, South Sulawesi, South Sumatra and Yogyakarta. Southeast Sulawesi is not among them. The mapping finds substantial overlap between those provinces in the discriminatory regulations they carry, alongside significant variation in dress codes, curfews and restrictions on where transgender people may appear, and its authors state that the findings apply to regions beyond the focus set. No provincial regulation of that kind is documented for Southeast Sulawesi in the source, and the neighbouring province of South Sulawesi was covered while Southeast Sulawesi was not; the province's absence from the mapping reflects the study's scope rather than a documented absence of such rules. Research by Universitas Halu Oleo published in Jurnal Budaya Etnika on 23 December 2024 describes same-sex life in Kendari, the provincial capital. Gay groups there describe same-sex orientation as partly converted into an economically valued 'profession', and men report becoming more introverted and careful about expressing their feelings to others after identifying as gay. Same-sex communities in the city live discreetly. The study reports no enforcement incident, no raid and no local regulation.

name: Special Region of Yogyakarta
text: Indonesia's national framework applies here; the national record for Indonesia covers the federal layer in detail. The Special Region of Yogyakarta carries its own layer of discriminatory regional regulation. A 2022 mapping of Indonesia's national laws and regional regulations that violate the rights of women and LGBTIQ people examined eight focus provinces, Yogyakarta among them, and found substantial overlap alongside significant regional variation. The regulations it documents include dress codes, curfews and restrictions on where transgender people may appear. The mapping states that its findings are valid for regions beyond the eight it examined, so the categories it identifies are not confined to the provinces it names. The most fully documented enforcement action against a trans institution in Yogyakarta is the February 2016 closure of Pondok Pesantren Waria Al-Fatah, a religious school where trans women study Islam. The hardline Front Jihad Islam threatened to seal the school, and on the night of 24 February 2016 a two-hour meeting at the Jagalan ward office in Yogyakarta ended with an agreement to shut it. Those present included ward and residents' officials, the lurah and the local military district commander; an earlier session on 19 February was attended by the Banguntapan camat and the local police sector chief. The district head justified the closure on the grounds that the pesantren lacked a permit, conflicted with Islamic values and had once had alcohol found on site. Its founder, Shinta Ratri, said about 20 waria attended the weekly weekend classes, which taught ordinary Islamic instruction. A waria witness at the meeting said a Front Jihad Islam leader delivered anti-LGBT remarks to shouts of "Allahu Akbar" and vowed the group would keep hunting LGBTI people wherever they gather. The Governor of the Special Region of Yogyakarta, Sultan Hamengku Buwono X, publicly urged restraint on both sides, called LGBT people "sama-sama anak bangsa" (fellow children of the nation) and said the regional government would study the issue. The shutdown concluded on administrative and community grounds; no provincial anti-trans statute was cited. The pesantren and the Yogyakarta waria community were operating again years after the closure, and economic and social marginalisation of trans people in the province persists.

name: KwaZulu-Natal
text: KwaZulu-Natal is a province of South Africa and stands under the national framework; the national record for South Africa covers the federal layer in detail. No provincial law, by-law or provincial institution departing from that layer is documented in the sources. The provincial evidence on violence and victimisation is a 2024 masters thesis in criminology at the University of KwaZulu-Natal in Durban. It interviewed 15 self-identifying queer participants recruited through the Imvelo Yesizwe Organisation in KwaMashu township and reports substantial queerphobic violence and victimisation in that township setting. The study also examines whether the support and interventions available to those residents were adequate, and what safety strategies they used. The study is small and its participants were purposively recruited, so it records the experiences of that group rather than a measured rate of violence. It does not disaggregate transgender participants from other sexual minorities, and no source gives a KwaZulu-Natal figure for violence against transgender people. A trans visitor to the province has no validated local victimisation figure to work from.

name: Nothern Cape
text: The Northern Cape is a province of South Africa; the national record for South Africa covers the federal layer in detail. On the night of 14 May 2024, Jo-Ann Isaks, a 27-year-old transgender woman, was found dead in her burning room in the Paballelo location of Upington. She had multiple stab wounds to the upper body. A family member noticed the fire at about 23:00. Police in the ZF Mgcawu District confirmed a murder case had been opened, described the investigation as at a critical stage and reported no arrests; the same statement identified her publicly by a male name. Jenny Sambok, an LGBTIQ+ leader in the district, said the community in the ZF Mgcawu region had been shaken. Karabelo Pudumo, an 18-year-old transgender Grade 10 learner at Pescodia High School in Kimberley, the provincial capital, was stabbed to death on 1 June 2024. A man she had been drinking with allegedly turned on her after realising she was transgender and stabbed her more than 20 times. A suspect was reportedly arrested, a detail the outlet reporting the case could not confirm with the authorities. More than 300 children and community members attended a memorial service at the school. Her death was the second suspected hate-crime murder of a transgender person in the province in under a month. A third LGBTIQ+ resident, Lazarus Ikaneng Thomas, a 50-year-old gay man, was murdered in September 2024. The three deaths are raw counts for one province in one year, and the sources provide no per-capita or general homicide rate against which to measure them. Organised community presence in the province is recent. The first Northern Cape Pride was held on 30 November 2024 at the Galeshewe Open Air Arena in Kimberley under the theme 'Pride with a Purpose', with a morning parade, speakers and community activities. Pride Committee member Tebogo Makwati called it a historic moment for the province.

name: Mpumalanga
text: Mpumalanga is a province of South Africa and stands under the national framework; the national record for South Africa covers the federal layer in detail. Traditional-authority structures have been openly opposed to legal recognition of same-sex relationships. A published letter of June 2010, issued by the National House of Traditional Leaders together with its provincial houses after a meeting held at Hazyview in Mpumalanga, stated that traditional leaders were disappointed that the Constitutional Court's marriage judgment had given what the letter called an immoral practice a lifeline, declared that they did not support legalisation of same-sex marriage, warned of ostracism and violence, and committed to a five-year campaign against it. The same structure asked Parliament in 2016 to review the constitutional clause protecting people against discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation. Violence against people read as sexuality- or gender-nonconforming has produced both a killing and a mass response inside the province. Portia Mtsweni, a 25-year-old lesbian, was found dead near Zamani Primary School in Tweefontein, in Thembisile Hani Local Municipality, in the early hours of Sunday 29 December 2019; she was half naked and had stab wounds. On 2 January 2020 about 800 people marched in the same municipality in protest, in a demonstration organised by Lasiphumakhona LGBTI, the ANC Women's League and others. Thembisile Hani mayor Nomsa Mtsweni called on parents, leaders and churches to stand united against gender-based violence. Public LGBTIQ+ presence has also drawn official cooperation. Mpumalanga's first Pride march and celebration was held on Saturday 9 August 2014 in the provincial capital, then Nelspruit and now Mbombela, under the theme 'Moving Forward, Proud, Strong & United'. Around 1,000 participants marched from the SABC offices to Nelspruit Plaza, followed by a picnic at Oorwesig Garden Park. The organiser, Joy Kunene, said police were visible and supportive and supplied about 20 police and traffic officers; the event launched the LGBTI Mpumalanga Movement, an umbrella body for the province's LGBTI organisations. Police conduct is the most consistently reported grievance. At a Pride Flag Tour event held at the eMbalenhle Sasol Club on 18 August 2026, LGBTIQ+ community members led by the Rainbow Seed Institute raised concerns about discrimination and stigmatisation at government institutions, particularly police stations. Participants said they were ridiculed, questioned or treated unfairly when seeking assistance, and one member alleged that after she was sexually assaulted in eMbalenhle months earlier, an officer at eMbalenhle Police Station asked why she had not fought back. Attendees said they fear reporting crimes because of stigmatisation. The documented pattern is community-level violence and police mistreatment inside a protective national legal framework. Enforcement appears to turn on the individual station, municipality or venue rather than on any province-wide practice, and the sources identify no Mpumalanga-specific court ruling, provincial policy or facilities rule.

name: Limpopo
text: Limpopo is a province of the Republic of South Africa and stands under the national legal framework. The province-specific material in the source inventory concerns the reach of customary law and traditional authority in the rural districts that formed part of the former Bantustans. Human Rights Watch reported on 29 May 2012 that the Traditional Courts Bill then before parliament would create a parallel customary-law justice system covering people living in the former Bantustan areas, with no provision allowing anyone to opt out of its jurisdiction. The same report states that rural LGBT people already face discrimination, violence and poor police cooperation, and that chiefs' courts punish lesbians in rural areas. Mamba Online reported on 18 April 2012, in a piece by Melanie Judge, that the bill was under debate in provincial public hearings and would re-criminalise gay and lesbian conduct in former-Bantustan areas through a separate customary system. Lesbians were reported punished at chiefs' homesteads and tribal offices, and those able to do so were expected to leave rural areas. Traditional leaders were also reported to have opposed the Civil Union Act of 2006. The most recent documented instance in this record dates from 2012; no later instance is documented.

name: Limpopo
text: South Africa's federal layer — passports, national agencies and federal bans — is covered in the national record for South Africa. Limpopo's own material concerns customary law and traditional authority in rural districts formed from former Bantustans. Human Rights Watch reported on 29 May 2012 that the Traditional Courts Bill then before parliament would create a parallel customary-law justice system covering people in former-Bantustan areas, with no provision to opt out of its jurisdiction. The same report states rural LGBT people already face discrimination, violence and poor police cooperation, and that chiefs' courts punish lesbians in rural areas. Mamba Online reported on 18 April 2012, in a piece by Melanie Judge, that the bill was under debate in provincial public hearings and would re-criminalise gay and lesbian conduct in former-Bantustan areas through a separate customary system. Lesbians were reported punished at chiefs' homesteads and tribal offices, and those able to do so were expected to leave rural areas. Traditional leaders were also reported to have opposed the Civil Union Act of 2006. The most recent documented instance in this record dates from 2012; no later instance is documented.

name: North West
text: North West is a province of South Africa; the national record for South Africa covers the federal layer in detail. The clearest practical obstacle for a trans visitor who depends on prescribed hormone treatment is the provincial health system. No public health facility in North West provides hormone replacement therapy for transgender people, and the North West Department of Health confirmed that position to the South African Human Rights Commission in response to a complaint lodged by Action for Social Justice International. Residents travel sometimes hundreds of kilometres, most often to Soweto in Gauteng, to obtain treatment. A visitor whose supply runs out in the province cannot expect a public clinic or hospital to fill or continue the prescription. Institutional enforcement of gendered appearance is documented in the province. In March 2016 an 18-year-old, Zinzi Manini Molema, was barred from attending school at Maphoitsile village after refusing to wear a skirt; the principal sent her home on the stated ground that she must wear a skirt because she was a girl, and she missed three weeks of classes. The case concerns a pupil rather than a visitor, but it records a North West school applying a dress rule against a gender-nonconforming person rather than accommodating her. The province's quantitative evidence on anti-LGBT discrimination rests on a single survey. Conducted during 2009 and 2010 under the auspices of the UNISA Centre for Applied Psychology with OUT LGBT Well-being, OUT North-West and Gay Umbrella, it surveyed 319 LGBT people, most of them from rural backgrounds in one of the country's poorest and least populated provinces, and asked about openness about same-sex sexuality, how LGBT people perceive their environment, and experiences of sexual abuse and discrimination. Campaign research published in 2016 lists that North West study alongside only two others as the quantitative South African studies of anti-LGBT hate crime conducted up to that point.

name: Eastern Cape
text: Eastern Cape stands under the national framework of South Africa; the national record for South Africa covers the federal layer in detail. Transgender prisoners held in Eastern Cape correctional centres, among them St Albans, Mthatha and East London, are governed by the national placement standard rather than any provincial rule. Under the regulations to the Correctional Services Act on the accommodation of vulnerable inmates, and the Department of Correctional Services' standard operating procedures, inmates are to be housed in cells appropriate to their gender identity where that is feasible and safe, and transgender inmates are to be held in single cells. No Eastern Cape-specific transgender placement case is on record, so the province's custody practice is read entirely from the national instruments. Rural districts under customary jurisdiction carry a risk that does not apply in the metropolitan centres. A bill before the national parliament in 2012 would have created a parallel customary-law justice system covering people in the former Bantustan areas, with no opt-out from customary jurisdiction. Human Rights Watch reported at the time that rural LGBT people already faced discrimination, violence and poor cooperation from police, and that chiefs' courts punished lesbians in rural areas. Gender-affirming care in the province runs through the public hospital system and is documented as slow. In December 2024 LGBT activists in East London delivered a memorandum to Frere Hospital over year-long delays in transgender healthcare. A trans visitor who depends on the public system in the Eastern Cape should plan for waiting times rather than immediate access.

name: Western Cape
text: The Western Cape stands under the national framework of South Africa; the national record for South Africa covers the federal layer in detail. The Western Cape has no provincial law or municipal by-law that bars transgender people from gender-segregated facilities; access is decided venue by venue, by the operator's own rules and by the staff enforcing them. On 19 February 2025 Taswald Ruiters, a transgender woman from Eerste River, was threatened with removal from the Green Point Athletic Stadium in Cape Town after using the women's bathroom. A security guard told her "Look at you, you're a man", directed her to the men's bathroom and said he had the final say. Police were called four times and had not arrived after nearly three hours. The stadium is a public facility operated by the City of Cape Town; on the day it was rented by Western Province Athletics, which was responsible for the security services on site. The incident records a gap between the absence of any provincial restriction on facility access and the response a visibly trans person actually received in the province's best-resourced metro.

name: Île-de-France
text: Île-de-France stands under the French national framework: identity documents, anti-discrimination law, criminal law, care access and marriage are set nationally and apply uniformly across the region, and no separate regional regime governs transgender visitors. What is specific to the region is where recorded anti-LGBT+ offending falls and how the Paris agglomeration's LGBT venues and events are policed. The Interior Ministry's statistics service (SSMSI), in Infraction rapide n°53 of May 2025, records 4,800 anti-LGBT+ offences across France in 2024, up 5% on 2023, with crimes and délits rising 14% per year since 2016. Only about 4% of victims file complaints, so the recorded figure understates incidence. Acts concentrate in urban units of over 200,000 inhabitants, notably Paris, whose rate is 22 per 100,000 against a national rate of 7; the note attributes part of Paris's elevated rate to non-resident victims and commuters. Recorded victims are more than 70% men, so the statistics do not isolate trans victims. Large LGBT events in the Paris agglomeration now carry a documented far-right counter-presence and a heavy security response. The Paris Pride march (Marche des Fiertés) of 28 June 2025 was classed a sensitive event by the Interior Ministry, and CRS police reinforcements were deployed after a far-right homo-patriotes group announced it would join the march; police were framed as separating the opposing groups, with extremists described as the enemy. Paris holds France's densest LGBTQ infrastructure, including France's only officially organised gaybourhoods and the annual Paris Pride parade. As of 2004 the city had 140 LGBT bars, clubs, hotels, restaurants and shops. The city also carries a targeted-violence history: Bertrand Delanoë, who became France's first openly gay mayor of Paris in 2002, was stabbed that same year during the Nuit Blanche festival by an assailant who told police he hated politicians, the Socialist Party and homosexuals. This is the most recent documented anti-LGBT political assault in this record; no later instance is documented here.

name: Provence-Alpes-Côte d'Azur
text: France's national framework applies here; the national record for France covers the federal layer in detail. The region's only documented item bearing on how a visibly non-conforming visitor may be policed in public space is a municipal swimwear order in Fréjus (Var). On 1 August 2023 the town's mayor, of the Rassemblement National, banned "covering and baggy clothing" while swimming from its sea beaches, in force until 17 September 2023, with a €135 fine. The administrative court of Toulon suspended the order's execution on 5 August 2023 and ordered the commune to pay €3,000. In freedom-of-relief order n° 2302537, brought by the Ligue des droits de l'homme, the court held the arrêté to be a grave and manifestly unlawful attack on fundamental freedoms: the manifestation of religious conviction, freedom of movement, and freedom of dress in public space. The mayor's communiqué justified the ban by laïcité while public statements cited safety, and observers read the measure as aimed at religiously marked swimwear. The suspension is interim relief; it prevents enforcement of the order. No other region-specific measure, enforcement practice or incident affecting transgender visitors appears in the inventory.

name: Dagestan
text: Dagestan is a republic within the Russian Federation; the national record for Russia covers the federal layer in detail. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression, version 2.0 of June 2025, names the North Caucasus, Dagestan among them, as an area where LGBT+ people are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution. The note documents systematic campaigns by Chechen and other North Caucasus authorities between 2017 and 2024 involving abduction, torture and extrajudicial killing, and it assesses trans people and visible advocates specifically rather than treating the risk as confined to gay and lesbian residents. Global Affairs Canada advises against all travel to Russia. Its advisory flags frequent terrorist attacks in the republics of Chechnya, Dagestan, Ingushetia and Stavropol Krai, states that entry to certain areas and regions requires special permission from the Ministry of the Interior, and warns of violence targeting 2SLGBTQI+ persons, naming the North Caucasus republics of Chechnya and Dagestan in particular. David Isteev of North Caucasus SOS, who works in exile, told the Human Rights House Foundation that there is no safe life for LGBTIQ+ people in the North Caucasus. The campaigns documented in the Home Office note run from 2017 to 2024; no later incident in Dagestan or the wider North Caucasus is documented in this inventory.

name: Ingushetia
text: Ingushetia is a republic of Russia and stands under the Russian national framework; the national record for Russia covers the federal layer in detail. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) treats the North Caucasus, including Ingushetia, as the exception to its otherwise non-persecutory assessment of Russia, finding that trans people and public LGBT+ advocates in the region are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution. The note documents systematic regional campaigns against LGBT+ people between 2017 and 2024, and states that the November 2023 extremist designation exposes LGBT+ activity in the region to two to six years' imprisonment, rising to six to ten years for organising; the violence associated with these campaigns has spread beyond the region. Global Affairs Canada advises avoid all travel to Russia and lists Ingushetia among the republics with frequent terrorist attacks, alongside Chechnya, Dagestan and Stavropol Krai. The advisory notes surveillance of foreigners and states that 2SLGBTQI+ persons, their allies and their families have been attacked, harassed and abused, that organisations advocating for 2SLGBTQI+ issues are treated as extremist since January 2024, and that the Ministry of Interior requires special permission to enter certain areas. David Isteev of North Caucasus SOS, interviewed by the Human Rights House Foundation, states that there is no safe life for LGBTIQ+ people in the North Caucasus and that even private existence can trigger violence, detention or forced return to families; he attests that conditions in the region have deteriorated year on year.

name: Kabardino-Balkaria
text: Kabardino-Balkaria stands under the national framework of Russia; the national record for Russia covers the federal layer in detail. Within that framework, the North Caucasus, including this republic, is the exception to the UK Home Office's otherwise non-persecutory assessment of Russia: the country policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (version 2.0, June 2025) finds that trans people and public LGBT+ advocates in the region are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution, and documents systematic regional campaigns against them between 2017 and 2024. North Caucasus SOS, an advocacy organisation that works in exile, reports that no safe life exists for LGBTIQ+ people in the region and that even private existence can trigger violence, detention, or forced return to families. The organisation describes conditions worsening year on year. LGBT+ activity in the republic falls under the 2023 extremist designation, which exposes participation to two to six years' imprisonment and organising to six to ten years. The Home Office note records that violence associated with the regional campaigns has spread beyond the North Caucasus.

name: Stavropol Krai
text: Russia's federal LGBT+ propaganda bans and extremist designations apply nationwide, and Global Affairs Canada advises against all travel; the national record for Russia covers the federal layer in detail. The UK Home Office note (June 2025) singles out the North Caucasus, including Stavropol Krai, as the exception to its non-persecutory assessment, finding trans people and public LGBT+ advocates here likely to face persecution. It records systematic campaigns across the North Caucasus between 2017 and 2024, and the 2023 extremist designation attracts two to six years' imprisonment, rising to six to ten years for organising. David Isteev of North Caucasus SOS says there is no safe life for LGBTIQ+ people in the North Caucasus and that even private existence can trigger violence, detention or forced return to families, reporting year-on-year deterioration across the region.

name: Orenburg Oblast
text: Orenburg Oblast lies within Russia's federal framework; the national record for Russia covers the federal layer in detail. Specific to this region is criminal enforcement of the extremism designation against an LGBTQ venue and its staff, the only such prosecution so far. Orenburg's Central District Court registered Russia's first criminal case under the Supreme Court's designation of the "international LGBT movement" as extremist. The file was opened in March 2024 and sent to the court on 9 July 2025, concerning staff of the Pose club in the city of Orenburg. Proceedings concluded in the region in June 2026 with the first known "LGBT extremism" convictions in the country. Pose owner Vyacheslav Khasanov was sentenced to seven years' imprisonment with forfeiture of 1 million rubles, manager Diana Kamilyanova to six years and three months, and art director Alexander Klimov to two years and three months.

name: NCR
text: National law applies here; the national record for Philippines covers the federal layer in detail. Quezon City has enacted an ordinance, sponsored by Councilor Bernard Herrera and colleagues, requiring every city public health facility to provide gender-affirming consultations and counselling, mental health support, and medical guidance and referrals irrespective of a patient's gender identity or expression. Mayor Joy Belmonte said the measure removes longstanding healthcare barriers for gender-diverse and transgender residents. The obligation attaches to city-run facilities, so its reach is municipal, not regional. Trans-specific violence is documented: Shaina Bayabay, 29, was killed in Pasig City on 1 March 2024; the recorded cause is strangulation, and the report states she was killed during a drinking session. The inventory records a single case, with no regional count or rate.

name: Central Visayas
text: Central Visayas stands under the national framework of the Republic of the Philippines; the national record for Philippines covers the federal layer in detail. Within the region, protection against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity is set at the municipal level rather than by a regional instrument. In July 2024 Mandaue City signed the implementing rules and regulations of its Anti-Discrimination Ordinance, at a signing held with the city mayor, the KAABAG LGBT Federation and the United Nations Development Programme. A town in northern Cebu passed a Comprehensive Anti-Discrimination Ordinance days before the end of Pride Month, safeguarding against discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity. The source does not identify the town, the year, or the exact date of passage.

name: Soccsksargen
text: Soccsksargen follows the national framework of the Philippines; the national record for Philippines covers the federal layer in detail. On 23 June 2025 an unidentified gunman shot and killed Ali Macalintal inside an acupuncture clinic in General Santos City. Macalintal was a trans woman, journalist and activist, a former deputy secretary general of Karapatan-Soccsksargen Region and a former anchor-reporter for Radio Philippines Network DXDX-General Santos City. Human Rights Watch described the shooting as an apparent targeted killing, and police examined her activism as a possible motive. The Commission on Human Rights condemned the June 2025 killings of transgender women as marked by cruelty and impunity, naming Macalintal's death among them as part of a disturbing pattern of transfemicide. Bahaghari and other advocates cited the killing in renewed calls for national anti-discrimination and gender-recognition legislation. Commission on Human Rights official Fayda M. Dumarpa pledged the commission's support for the Simplified Legal Gender Recognition Bill during Pride Month. No region-specific rule on identity documents, entry, health care, public facilities, partner recognition or hate-crime protection applies here, and no region-specific protective institution or ordinance.

name: Central Luzon
text: Central Luzon stands under the national framework of the Philippines; the national record for Philippines covers the federal layer in detail. The region enacts no criminal or civil code of its own on gender identity. Bataan is the one province in the region recorded as having a SOGIE anti-discrimination ordinance. The inventory does not record the ordinance's scope, its penalties, or any enforcement action taken under it, so what it changes in practice for a trans visitor or resident in Bataan is unresolved. No trans-specific killing, assault, prosecution, refusal of service or official action in Central Luzon appears in the source inventory. The region's trans-relevant risk therefore rests on the national layer rather than on any documented regional pattern.

name: Calabarzon
text: Calabarzon is a region of the Philippines and stands under the national framework; the national record for Philippines covers the federal layer in detail. Its own legal layer consists of local anti-discrimination ordinances in four units: Batangas province (2015), Cavite (2014 to 2018, later extended to cover gender identity), Batangas City (2016) and Calamba (2017). No regional-level statute is identified. For a trans visitor, protection depends on which city or municipality they are in, and the ordinances are the only region-specific protection mechanism the sources identify. On 13 August 2025 a Philippine daily reported the murder of an LGBTQ pageant winner in Batangas. The victim, crowned in Lipa City days earlier, sustained 13 stab wounds, and police work the case as a homicide. The report states no arrest, no motive and no finding that the killing was bias-related, and does not say whether the victim was transgender. One killing does not establish a rate, and the sources carry no general homicide figure for the region against which it could be compared.

name: Cagayan Valley
text: Cagayan Valley is one of the Philippines' regions. The national legal position on trans identity, identity documents, custody and entry applies here; the national record for Philippines covers the federal layer in detail. Two killings of trans women are documented in the region within a single national monitoring series. On 31 July 2024 a trans person named Cabansag was stabbed to death in Ilagan City, Isabela, after an alleged kidnapping and rape; three suspects were identified. On 23 June 2025 Kierra Apostol, 18, was found dead in a river in Cagayan province. She lived in Zone 7, Centro, Peñablanca, was an incoming first-year Business Management student at Cagayan State University's Caritan campus, and worked as a hair-and-makeup artist on the local pageant circuit. She had been reported missing days earlier; her body was found floating in the river between Amulung and Iguig on the morning of 23 June, and her mother told local media she saw visible signs of physical assault. A criminology student at the University of Cagayan Valley, named online as 'Menco de Guzman' or 'Sherwin Kyqle', surrendered voluntarily at the Peñablanca police station. He admitted picking Kierra up on the Saturday night and denied involvement in her death. No outcome of the case appears in the sources. LGBTQIA+ groups responded with demands for a full investigation and for justice, and renewed their call for the pending SOGIESC Equality Bill. Among those pressing the demand were the Cagayan State University-Andrew campus student organisation CSU Crystal, LGBT Pilipinas Taguig City Inc., and Bahaghari chairperson Reyna Valmores Salinas, who said the killing showed LGBTQ+ people remain unsafe. Both killings are raw counts drawn from a monitoring project's national series. The sources give no homicide rate for Cagayan Valley, so trans-specific violence in the region cannot be compared against its background rate of violence, and the monitoring project's tally is a documented floor rather than a measured magnitude.

name: Western Visayas
text: No law specific to Western Visayas restricting trans visitors appears in the sources. Entry, documentation and criminalisation rules are set nationally; the national record for Philippines covers the federal layer in detail. Region-specific material concerns Capiz State University, whose October 2022 hair-and-uniform directive excluded students perceived as trans women. A legal NGO case study dated December 2025 examines that exclusion and the advocacy campaign that followed. On 7 August 2025 the university's 21st commencement exercises produced its first openly trans woman to graduate summa cum laude: Khaz-JP Padilla, batch valedictorian of the social work class, taking the highest Latin honour, attributed to the 2022 advocacy campaign. Padilla said each haircut felt like losing self-confidence, and said her transition began once pandemic-era online classes removed her from the haircut rule.

name: Ilocos Region
text: The Ilocos Region stands under the national framework of the Philippines; the national record for Philippines covers the federal layer in detail. Bayambang, a municipality in Pangasinan, enforces Municipal Ordinance No. 15, s-2023, which protects lesbians, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer and intersex people in the municipality against discrimination solely on the basis of sexual orientation, gender identity, expression and sex characteristics. The penalty ladder runs from a fine of at least 1,000 pesos or one month's imprisonment for a first offence, to at least 2,000 pesos or between one month and a day and six months for a second, to at least 2,500 pesos or between six months and a day and eight months for a third. A subsequent violation carries one year's imprisonment and a fine of at least 2,500 pesos. Every violator must also complete mandatory human rights education. Complaints are filed through the barangay Katarungang Pambarangay mechanism established by the Local Government Code, Republic Act 7160. A trans visitor discriminated against inside Bayambang therefore has a local complaint route that does not depend on a national anti-discrimination statute. The Sangguniang Panlalawigan of Pangasinan adopted Resolution No. 799-2024 at its session of 19 August 2024 in Lingayen, declaring the Bayambang ordinance conformant with the Bill of Rights and Section 16 of Republic Act 7160. The resolution is a provincial-level endorsement of the municipal instrument; it does not extend the ordinance's protections to other municipalities in Pangasinan. The municipality's official ordinance registry records the instrument as dated 16 October 2023, authored by Coun. Benjamin Francisco S. De Vera, and publishes a certified copy for public view. The ordinance's reach stops at the municipal boundary. The source inventory contains no region-specific legal instrument, enforcement record or incident for Ilocos Norte, Ilocos Sur or La Union, so for those provinces the national assessment applies without local modification.

name: ARMM
text: The Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao stands under the national framework of the Philippines; the national record for Philippines covers the federal layer in detail. Bangsamoro Autonomy Act No. 13, the Bangsamoro Administrative Code, begun 29 March 2019, sets out the region's structures and rules of governance and guarantees religious freedom. Its justice-dispensation clause directs that justice be dispensed "in consonance with the Constitution, Shari'ah, traditional or tribal laws". Nothing in the regional code addresses gender identity or gender non-conformity. A Shari'ah Justice Code proposed in the Bangsamoro Parliament on 14 July 2026 would widen Shari'ah jurisdiction beyond the personal-status field it has occupied since the Code of Muslim Personal Laws (Presidential Decree 1083, 1977), reaching into civil actions, Islamic commercial transactions, ta'tir offences and alternative dispute resolution. The proposal rests on the region's organic-law authority and on the 1977 Code of Personal and Family Relations. For a visitor, the practical consequence is that a dispute can be routed to a Shari'ah forum rather than a civil court, and the applicable law follows the forum. Marriage, divorce, succession and family relations for Muslim residents remain governed by Shari'ah forums, with written opt-in clauses allowing civil entities to take on matters otherwise within that jurisdiction. A visitor married to a Muslim spouse therefore enters a legal-pluralist marriage regime in which the forum that hears a matter determines which body of personal law applies.

name: CAR
text: The national record for Philippines covers the federal layer in detail, including passports, executive orders, federal agencies, national statistics and national bans. No region-specific signal on transgender travel safety was identified for the Cordillera Administrative Region, so the national assessment applies here without local modification.

name: Daegu
text: South Korea's national framework governs criminal law, documents and legal gender recognition; the national record for South Korea covers the federal layer in detail. Daegu's visitor-relevant signal is concentrated in the Daegu Queer Culture Festival, held every June since 2009 without interruption and described as the country's second-largest LGBT event: a pride parade and film festival running a week or two, usually in late June. Opposition is organised, annual and large. A Daegu-Gyeongbuk conservative-Protestant umbrella body convened its 17th annual "National Assembly Against Queer" in response to the festival, gathering roughly 3,500 believers from about 1,600 churches at Banwoldang station and along a 450 m stretch toward Gyesan intersection under anti-homosexuality slogans. An estimated 28 religious and right-wing groups have formed a "gay issue countermeasure committee" in Daegu to block LGBT events, and that opposition has kept the festival off an outdoor stage on a popular central Daegu street. Court bids to stop the festival have failed each year. The Daegu Queer Opposition Countermeasure Committee sought an injunction against the 2025 edition; the court dismissed it, as it had dismissed the bids for 2022, 2023 and 2024. In 2023, under then-Mayor Hong Joon-pyo, municipal officials physically blocked the road. Police again restricted the 2025 march to a single bus-only lane. Organisers framed the event as resistance to "hate and discriminatory politics". The dispute continued into the 2026 edition. The Daegu Queer Opposition Countermeasures Headquarters, made up of the Daegu-Gyeongbuk Parents' Alliance for Protecting the Next Generation, the Daegu Christian Council and the Dongseong-ro Merchants' Association, filed a collective petition with the National Human Rights Commission of Korea demanding a change of venue, arguing the event is likely to infringe public welfare. The group says about 34,000 people signed, which it calls unusually large for a single commission petition. The petition cites the Daegu District Court's dismissal of the festival committee's injunction request, a ruling that found the police notice restricting the event legitimate because Jungang-ro is a key urban traffic artery and one lane must be secured for public welfare. It responds to the festival committee's January petition against the National Police Agency Commissioner General and the National Assembly Speaker over Article 12(1) of the Assembly and Demonstration Act.

name: Daejeon
text: South Korea's national framework governs transgender travellers; the national record for South Korea covers the federal layer in detail. What is documented here runs through a court seated in Daejeon and through a cemetery. On 7 October 2021 the Daejeon District Court ordered the cancellation of the Army's discharge of Staff Sergeant Byun Hee-soo, the first known legal case involving a transgender soldier. The court held that the military should have treated her as female following her legal sex change, that the loss of genitalia was not a valid ground for dismissal, and that a fitness-for-service review must weigh basic rights. The decision upheld the appeal pursued on her behalf after her death. On 24 June 2024 Byun Hee-soo was buried at the National Cemetery in Daejeon; she was Korea's first transgender soldier. Around 60 activists protested at the burial, arguing that it was marred by discriminatory treatment. The ceremony was conducted as an official state honour in the city.

name: North Chungcheong
text: North Chungcheong stands under South Korea's national framework; the national record for South Korea covers the federal layer in detail. The province has no separate law on gender identity or gender expression. Its documented trans-specific event is the death of Byun Hui-su, a 23-year-old transgender woman and the country's first transgender soldier, found dead at her home in Cheongju on 3 March 2021. A counsellor raised the alarm after 28 February. She had been discharged over gender-affirming surgery, and her challenge to that discharge had been rejected in July 2020. The death became the reference point for national debate on the treatment of transgender service members. Public grief and demands for LGBT protections followed. The National Human Rights Commission honoured her, and prosecutors and activists called for an anti-discrimination bill, its eighth introduction since 2007; the June 2020 draft had included gender-identity provisions. A society-wide discourse of responsibility followed. No new provincial law resulted from the incident.

name: Gyeonggi
text: South Korea's national framework governs entry, identity documents, criminal exposure and security screening; the national record for South Korea covers the federal layer in detail. Gyeonggi Province's region-specific record concerns student protections rather than visitor-facing rules. Gyeonggi-do enacted South Korea's first student human rights ordinance in 2010, and the ordinance bars discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity, the clauses that religious groups and parents targeted in the repeal campaign they mounted from August 2022. When the Seoul Metropolitan Council abolished its own ordinance in April 2024, Gyeonggi was one of six regional education offices still enforcing a comparable instrument, together with Gwangju, North Jeolla, South Chungcheong, Incheon and Jeju. A Gyeonggi-based teacher quoted in the coverage argued against wholesale abolition. Gyeonggi and Seoul are the only two jurisdictions whose ordinances include a right not to be discriminated against on the basis of pregnancy. The provincial Superintendent of Public Instruction conducts an annual survey on student human rights, and the province marks a Student Human Rights Day. No Gyeonggi-specific rule on criminal exposure, entry, identity documents, airport or security screening, restroom access or healthcare access was identified.

name: RegiÃ³n del BÃ­o-BÃ­o
text: Región del Bío-Bío stands under Chile's national framework for trans people; the national record for Chile covers the federal layer in detail. Movilh's XXIII annual human rights report, covering 2024 data and published in March 2025, attributes 5.89% of Chile's documented cases of discrimination and violence on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity to Bío-Bío, the third-highest share of any region. Concepción is listed among the cities recording the most documented incidents, with five. That is a raw count: the report ranks cities by number of documented cases, which tracks population size, and publishes no per-capita rate for the region. Regional health services have been the subject of formal complaints. In October 2016 Movilh-Biobío filed a complaint with the Seremi de Salud, naming Mauricio Careaga Lemus, over the treatment of patient Hanna Jiménez Carrasco at the Hospital Traumatológico de Concepción. Jiménez Carrasco was interned from 28 September to 3 October 2016 and was placed and treated as male, despite the legal duty to use a trans patient's chosen name and social sex. The complaint described the staff conduct as brutal and illegal discriminatory acts.

name: RegiÃ³n de TarapacÃ¡
text: Región de Tarapacá stands under Chile's national legal framework; the national record for Chile covers the federal layer in detail. The Court of Appeals of Iquique annulled, in 2023, the trial of Jhonatan Cañón for the 2022 murder of trans woman Yuri Pizarro in Tarapacá. The court held that Chile's femicidio offence covers only a victim who is "biologically female", and that the conviction, framed on that offence, could not stand. The annulment voided the strongest gendered-violence conviction available in the case; the homicide, if pursued again, would rest on a different charge. A trans woman attacked in Tarapacá cannot assume the femicidio framing will attach to her case. Movilh's XXIII annual report, published in March 2025 on 2024 data, attributes to Tarapacá about 2% of nationally documented homophobic and transphobic cases and places the region among those with the fastest year-on-year growth, at +18.18% in its headline figure and +19.51% in its period tables. The two growth figures conflict within the source. The 2% is a share of documented cases rather than a per-capita rate, and the percentages rest on a small number of reports in a region with a small population, so the figures do not establish that Tarapacá is more dangerous than larger regions. The counts combine homophobic and transphobic reports, and no trans-specific breakdown for the region appears in the sources reviewed.

name: RegiÃ³n de La AraucanÃ­a
text: La Araucanía has no legal regime of its own; criminal law, policing, courts and identity documents follow Chile's national framework, and the national record for Chile covers the federal layer in detail. The regional signal is recorded anti-LGBT incidents rather than law. Movilh's XXIV annual human rights report, published March 2026 with 2025 data, names La Araucanía the region where recorded homophobic and transphobic cases and complaints rose most, at 150% year on year; no other region rose more. It holds 1.96% of the national case total, so the rise is on a small base. It ranks first by rate of increase, not volume; no source gives a per-capita rate. The figure aggregates homophobia and transphobia, not disaggregated for trans people, so it sets no trans-specific rate. A trans visitor sees a documented upward trend in complaints, from a low base, with no region-specific rule attached.

name: RegiÃ³n de Magallanes y AntÃ¡rtica Chilena
text: Chile's national framework applies throughout the region; the national record for Chile covers the federal layer in detail. In 2024 a trans woman, Kenia Chacón, was attacked in Punta Arenas. The case was prosecuted as attempted femicide (femicidio frustrado). In April 2026 the court imposed four years' partial internment, short of the five years' total internment sought. SernamEG announced it would appeal the sentence. Chacón's mother stated the attack had been devalued because of her daughter's gender identity. Movilh's XXIII annual report, published March 2025 with 2024 data, records Magallanes at 0.96% of the national case total and among regions with the largest year-on-year increases, at +100%. No absolute case count is published, so the size of that increase cannot be established: a doubling from a small base yields few cases, and the share is under one per cent.

name: RegiÃ³n de Ãuble
text: Chile's national framework sets the entry, document and anti-discrimination rules that apply here; the national record for Chile covers the federal layer in detail. Ñuble has no regional legislation of its own on gender identity, discrimination, healthcare or public facilities, and no Ñuble-specific policing practice, custody rule or facility provision appears in the sources reviewed. Ñuble recorded the sharpest percentage increase in documented homo- and transphobic abuses of any Chilean region in the 2024 reporting year, at +300 per cent, with the region's share of the national total at 1.44 per cent. The figure counts abuses documented by an LGBT rights organisation, not convictions or police-recorded crimes, and a 300 per cent rise on a 1.44 per cent share corresponds to a small number of cases in absolute terms; the ranking is by percentage change rather than per capita, so it does not establish that a visitor meets more hostility in Ñuble than in a larger region. Legal gender recognition is processed through Chile's national system, with no regional count of rectifications published. National reporting on the gender identity law identifies two historic name-and-sex rectification cases in Ñuble, the only regional material in that coverage, which the source treats as evidence of how small a formally recognised trans population the region has.

name: RegiÃ³n de Arica y Parinacota
text: Arica y Parinacota is a region of Chile and stands under the national legal framework; the national record for Chile covers the federal layer in detail. Movilh's XXIII annual human-rights report on sexual and gender diversity, covering 2024 data and published in March 2025, recorded 2,847 cases nationally, a rise of 78.7 per cent, with Arica y Parinacota accounting for 0.84 per cent of the national total, among the lowest shares of any region. Increases were recorded in 11 of the 16 regions. A share that small means a single additional case moves the region's position, and the report itself notes that in regions with such small shares one case can dominate. An earlier Movilh report covering 2021, published in April 2022, recorded national homophobia and transphobia complaints and cases falling 12 per cent, the first decline in eight years, while complaints rose in five regions. Arica y Parinacota was one of them, with reports up around 300 per cent against 2020. The report attributes the national decline to the visibility won by the sexual-diversity movement in the year equal marriage was approved; the region's complaint trajectory ran against that national direction. The 300 per cent figure rests on the region's small complaint base. For a visitor facing discrimination, Fundación Iguales has provided free legal aid in Arica since 14 November 2017, when the city became the fourth location where the foundation offers representation in cases based on sexual orientation or gender identity, through a collaboration agreement with pro bono lawyer Piera Balbontín Nef covering Arica's jurisdiction. The foundation's legal director states that discrimination is greater in regions far from the capital, which is why local legal support matters. The region therefore has an accessible local channel for anti-LGBTI discrimination complaints that does not require travel to Santiago.

name: RegiÃ³n Metropolitana de Santiago
text: The Región Metropolitana de Santiago stands under Chile's national framework; the national record for Chile covers the federal layer in detail. Municipal practice in the region is not uniform. On 15 April 2026 the council of Ñuñoa approved an anti-discrimination ordinance by nine votes to one, the first adopted anywhere in Chile. The ordinance bans hate speech, requires non-discrimination clauses in municipal tenders and contracts, establishes a communal good-practice seal, and requires notices against exclusion in municipal buildings. It was drafted by María Fernanda Ulloa, head of the comuna's Diversity and Non-Discrimination Department, and endorsed by mayor Sebastián Sichel. Elsewhere in the region the posture runs the other way. Vitacura had committed to Movilh to fly the LGBT flag for the 17 May anti-homophobia date, then withdrew under pressure from its councillors and declined to raise it; Santiago and Ñuñoa took part. Movilh records the refusal as a municipal-level retreat in the capital's wealthier comunas. For a trans visitor, official recognition inside the region is set comuna by comuna rather than uniformly. The rights a visitor holds derive from national law; what a municipality does on its own premises and in its own contracts depends on which comuna they are in, and the two documented cases point in opposite directions.

name: Bayern
text: Bayern stands under Germany's national framework on legal gender recognition, identity documents and anti-discrimination; the national record for Germany covers the federal layer in detail. A prohibition on gender-inclusive German took effect in Bavaria on 1 April 2024, barring gender-neutral word forms in schools, universities and all state administration, implementing a government declaration of December 2023 and a cabinet decision amending the language rules for public authorities. Critics dismiss it as symbol politics while noting it reaches every public counter, registry office and classroom in the state. A trans visitor dealing with a Bavarian registry office, town hall or university therefore faces offices operating under an official register excluding gender-neutral wording. Bavaria has co-sponsored a Bundesrat initiative with Sachsen, Thüringen and Sachsen-Anhalt to tighten the federal Self-Determination Act. The Bundesrat's criticism of 20 October 2023 held that the draft allowed parents to decide changes for under-14s "without any counselling, examination and investigation of the child's welfare". The Free State's posture toward self-declaration is openly restrictive, though the procedure itself remains the national one.

name: Berlin
text: Berlin is a Land of Germany; the national record for Germany covers the federal layer in detail. MANEO, Berlin's anti-violence documentation project, recorded 723 LGBTIQ+-hostile incidents in the city in 2025, slightly fewer than the 738 documented in 2024, drawn from 1,014 new reports, which is a new high for incoming reports. The recorded incidents include insults, threats and physical attacks on public transport, in parks and on the street. Schöneberg, Neukölln, Kreuzberg, Friedrichshain and Tiergarten are the most affected districts, and 58 attacks targeted LGBTIQ+ venues, memorials and events. MANEO states that its figures capture only part of what occurs because of a high dark figure, and reports that its own counselling centre was attacked several times in 2025. Neukölln is named among the worst-hit districts. At the 48th Berlin Christopher Street Day, a vehicle was driven into a crowd in the Tiergarten area, killing one woman and injuring several people; the event was cancelled. MANEO offers victim counselling and an anonymous reporting line on 030-2163336, open daily from 17:00 to 19:00. Ahead of the 2025 parade season, Berlin CSD organisers urged vigilance with hundreds of thousands of participants expected. A queer café owner in Berlin-Neukölln reported 45 police complaints over homophobic attacks in 18 months.

name: Brandenburg
text: Brandenburg lies within Germany's federal framework; the national record for Germany covers the federal layer in detail. Region-specific material: two incidents in Cottbus concerning public LGBT life. Lausitzer Rundschau reported a fire at the Regenbogenkombinat, an LGBT venue in Cottbus, shortly before the city's CSD, prompting a Staatsschutz investigation; neither circumstances nor outcome are sourced, and no anti-LGBT motive is reported. Niederlausitz aktuell reported on 26 October 2025 that the CSD parade in Cottbus went ahead under a large police deployment with two counter-demonstrations present. They are the only documented hostility signal in the Land for that period; no arrest figures, injury reports or trans-specific incidents connected with the parade are sourced. No Land legislation on gender recognition, custody, health care or sex-separated facilities is documented.

name: Thüringen
text: Germany's federal framework on identity documents, legal gender recognition and prison placement applies here; the national record for Germany covers the federal layer in detail. Thüringen's own layer is configured by the Landtag elected on 1 September 2024. AfD Thüringen took 32.8% of the vote and is classified by the state's Office for the Protection of the Constitution as right-wing extremist. The CDU followed at 23.4%, the BSW at 15.8% in its first state election, Die Linke at 13.1% and the SPD at 6.1%. The CDU, BSW and SPD formed the state's first Brombeer coalition under minister-president Mario Voigt, a minority cabinet without its own Landtag majority. Formal, multi-layered institutional hostility to gender policy in Thüringen rests on this configuration. Nothing in the sources reviewed documents a trans-specific safety incident, police practice or refusal of service in Thüringen. What is recorded for the state is legislative and party-political, with no state-level enforcement or violence record to assess.

name: Wales
text: Wales sits within the United Kingdom framework for legal gender recognition, equality law and sex-based segregation in custody; the national record for United Kingdom covers the federal layer in detail. The Welsh Government's LGBTQ+ Action Plan for Wales, published in February 2023, states the aim of making Wales the most LGBTQ+ friendly nation in Europe. It commits the devolved administration to pursue a Welsh-specific ban on conversion practices; a Working Group on Banning Conversion Practices was formed in December 2022 and the government published its banning conversion practices document in May 2024. Transgender healthcare in Wales was historically delivered by referral to clinics in London. The first Welsh gender identity clinic opened in September 2019, ending the default referral of Welsh adults outside Wales. The Welsh Government's LGBTQ+ Action Plan document for young people, posted in January 2026, forms part of the standing devolved inclusion programme. The programme's update page addresses the For Women Scotland judgment of 19 December 2025.

name: Northern Ireland
text: Northern Ireland's equality legislation is separate from that of England, Wales and Scotland. The national record for United Kingdom covers the federal layer in detail. As of August 2026 the regional authorities were still assessing how the United Kingdom Supreme Court's ruling on the meaning of sex applies there. The position on single-sex facilities and services should be treated as unsettled rather than as a settled extension of the framework operating elsewhere in the United Kingdom. Legal gender recognition in Northern Ireland runs on the Gender Recognition Act 2004. A May 2021 judgment of the Northern Ireland courts made a binding ruling in the region that gender dysphoria based on an individual's mental dynamic is no longer legally required, following the World Health Organization's 2019 decision to stop treating gender identity disorder as a mental illness or mental disorder. That ruling applies in Northern Ireland only and has not been extended to the rest of the United Kingdom. In December 2025 other executive parties blocked justice minister Naomi Long's plan to add transgender people as a protected characteristic in Northern Ireland's new hate-crime legislation. Long had sought executive approval in early November 2025 with a response deadline in mid-November; the bill had held executive agreement since December 2024. She cited Police Service of Northern Ireland statistics recording close to 100 transgender-identity incidents or hate crimes. That figure is a raw count without a population denominator. In September 2025 guidance supporting transgender pupils was withdrawn from the Northern Ireland Education Authority's website after Education Minister Paul Givan requested its removal, arguing it conflicted with departmental policy and the law in Northern Ireland. The guidance had recommended that trans pupils be allowed to use changing rooms matching their gender identity. Teachers' representatives warned that the removal ignores the practical realities. Same-sex marriage took effect in Northern Ireland on 13 January 2020, under regulations signed on 19 December 2019 after UK Parliament legislation receiving royal assent on 24 July 2019 required extension if the Assembly did not reconvene by 21 October 2019. The first wedding followed on 11 February 2020 after a 28-day notice period, and religious and church same-sex weddings have been permitted since 1 September 2020. Civil partnerships have been available to same-sex couples since 2005 under the Civil Partnership Act 2004.

name: Northern Territory
text: The Northern Territory legislates its own anti-discrimination regime beneath the Australian national framework; the national record for Australia covers the federal layer in detail. The territory's own layer narrowed in 2025. The Anti-Discrimination Amendment Act 2025 (No. 27 of 2025) was assented on 30 October 2025, with Part 3 commencing on 27 July 2026. It removes the civil prohibition on conduct that offends, insults, humiliates or intimidates a person in public because of a protected attribute, gender identity among them. From that commencement date a trans visitor or resident cannot found a vilification complaint on that ground before the Northern Territory Anti-Discrimination Commission. The repeal was announced in March 2025 by the Country Liberal Party government, which framed it as restoring freedom of speech and religious freedom. The government had earlier retreated from scrapping the vilification section outright before the bill passed parliament on 17 October 2025. NT Anti-Discrimination Commissioner Jeswynn Yogaratnam publicly rebuked the change, warning that the government may be opening the doors for a very dangerous stream of hate speech. The territory's hate-crime statute does not list sexual orientation or gender identity among the motives it covers, so coverage of those motives rests on the national layer alone. Territory discrimination protections covering gender identity date from 2022, when the vilification provision was added to the Anti-Discrimination Act; that provision is the one now being removed. Changing the sex marker on a Northern Territory birth certificate has required clinical treatment since 2018. The territory government issued a policy directive in December 2025 banning gender-affirming healthcare for minors. In February 2025 it banned rainbow pride flags in public hospitals. The practical exposure for a trans visitor is a shrinking civil remedy rather than a criminal or entry risk: the conduct that will cease to be actionable from 27 July 2026 is harassment and vilification on the ground of gender identity, and no territory provision replaces it.

name: New South Wales
text: New South Wales issues its own birth certificates and driver licences and runs its own anti-discrimination, conversion-practices and corrections regimes. Marriage and passports are national matters and are carried at the national level. Discrimination on the basis of transgender status has been prohibited in New South Wales since 1996 under the Anti-Discrimination Act 1977, which reaches employment, public education, goods and services, banking, health care, property and nightclubs. Section 16 of the Mental Health Act 2007 states expressly that sexual orientation and gender identity are not mental illnesses. The Act's exemptions remain significant for a trans visitor. Sport and broadly based religious exemptions in non-public schools permit exclusion on sex and gender grounds, including barring transgender people from female sports categories, and religiously run adoption agencies may refuse same-sex couples. Sex designations on New South Wales birth certificates changed on 1 July 2025. Until 30 June 2025 a person had to undergo sexual reassignment surgery and pay $153 to change the sex recorded on a birth certificate; since 1 July 2025 no surgery is required, and the process is an application form, a $73 fee, and a good-faith witness who is an unrelated adult known to the applicant for a year. There is no cap on the number of sex changes, unlike name changes, which are limited to once every 12 months and three in a lifetime; 766 sex changes had been recorded by September 2025. The new certificate does not disclose that a change occurred. Non-binary and unspecified markers are available. In April 2014 the High Court of Australia held that the law permits registration of a change of sex to a non-specific designation, in the case brought by Norrie May-Welby, and since March 2022 rainbow birth certificates listing no gender or sex have been available to people born or adopted in New South Wales. Conversion practices have been a criminal offence in New South Wales since 4 April 2025 under the Conversion Practices Ban Act 2024, passed unamended on 22 March 2024. Practices causing substantial mental or physical harm carry up to five years' imprisonment, and taking a person out of New South Wales for conversion therapy carries up to three years. Anti-Discrimination NSW can investigate complaints from 4 April 2025 with civil referral pathways. The Act carries limited religious and parental exemptions, including an exception for religious sermons. Publicly threatening or inciting violence has been an offence since 13 August 2018 under the Crimes Amendment (Publicly Threatening and Inciting Violence) Act 2018, passed unanimously by both houses in June 2018, with a penalty of up to three years' imprisonment. Documented fatal violence against a trans woman traveller in the state is the 2021 killing of Mhelody Bruno, a 25-year-old transgender woman from the Philippines visiting Australia, in Wagga Wagga. The perpetrator's guilty plea to manslaughter drew a 22-month term. The most recent documented case of this kind in this record is from 2021; no later instance is documented. Corrections practice is governed by New South Wales prisoner protocols and guidelines in place since 1996, which permit transgender people who have had sexual reassignment surgery to be housed in female prisons for protection. An undisclosed New South Wales government settlement was granted to a transgender individual held in a male prison in November 2024. Facilities: Sydney City Council implemented a gender-neutral bathrooms policy in April 2023.

name: Castilla y León
text: Castilla y León follows Spain's national framework on gender recognition and anti-discrimination; the national record for Spain covers the federal layer in detail. Regional protection is unsettled: in December 2024 the PSOE group registered a bill for real and effective equality of LGBTI+ people, one of three it tabled that week, to end LGBTI out-migration; leader Tudanca urged fastest processing. On 11 June 2025 the Cortes took the bill into consideration: 76 articles, meeting long-standing regional LGBTI+ demands; the Partido Popular abstained, Vox against. Debate opens, but advocates fear it could stall in committee. No regional LGBTI equality statute is in force, and no region-specific rules on identity documents, facility access, health care or hate-crime enforcement were found. No documented regional rule departs from the national framework; the pending bill's fate is open.

name: Ciudad Autónoma de Ceuta
text: Ceuta is an autonomous city of Spain with no LGTBI or gender-identity statute of its own; the national record for Spain covers the federal layer in detail. FELGTBI+'s September 2025 report with the Universidad de Salamanca names Asturias, Castilla y León, Ceuta and Melilla as the only Spanish territories still without a specific law on the promotion of LGTBI+ rights. It records legislative progress in Castilla y León and Asturias in June 2025 and no equivalent step for Ceuta or Melilla. A 2020 precedent study placed Ceuta and Melilla at the tail of rankings for recognition and protection of trans students. Europa Press reported on 17 September 2026 that the LGTBI+ association Arcópoli wrote to the Secretary of State for Migration, Pilar Cancela, demanding the urgent transfer to the peninsula of LGTBI+ migrants remaining in Ceuta after thousands entered irregularly on 30 and 31 July. Arcópoli called transfer the only effective measure to guarantee their protection and inclusion, cited the extreme vulnerability of people fleeing criminalisation and persecution in countries including Morocco, and launched a free remote social, psychological and legal support service for those in Ceuta. For a visitor, no regional layer of LGTBI+ policy exists to consult or appeal to: protection operates through the national framework, and the deficit is regional legislation, not a hostile local statute.

name: Ciudad Autónoma de Melilla
text: Spain's national framework governs legal gender recognition, anti-discrimination protection and related guarantees; the national record for Spain covers the federal layer in detail. Melilla has no autonomous LGTBI or gender-identity statute — an index of Spain's regional LGTBI legislation states expressly that Melilla and Ceuta have no laws of this kind and rely instead on the national framework and central-government equality policies. No city-level rule either adds to or subtracts from those national guarantees. The only city-level instrument touching partnership recognition is a registry for unmarried couples, created in Melilla in 2008; comparable registries exist in Ceuta and across the mainland communities, and the benefits they confer are regarded as mainly symbolic. This registry is not an LGTBI or gender-identity statute and does not modify national rules on marriage or adoption, so a trans visitor's recognition as a partner or spouse rests on the national framework rather than on anything the city has enacted.

name: Kelantan
text: Kelantan is a state of Malaysia, and its Syariah criminal jurisdiction operates within the national legal framework; the national record for Malaysia covers the federal layer in detail. The state assembly passed the Syariah Criminal Offences (Kelantan) Bill 2026 on 13 August 2026, legislating decency, the covering of aurat, and gender change as matters of Islamic criminal law.
