The enactment replaces 16 provisions of the Kelantan Syariah Criminal Code Enactment 2019 that the Federal Court struck down in February 2024, so the state's regulation of dress, modesty and gender presentation has been rebuilt on a new statutory basis rather than withdrawn. Clause 15 requires Muslims to safeguard the sanctity and modesty of their private parts in accordance with Islamic law. The state legislature has placed gender change expressly inside the criminal jurisdiction of Islamic law, and the new decency and gender-change provisions are in force and being applied by the Syariah courts from 2026. For a trans visitor in Kelantan, a presentation or a document that raises a gender-change question therefore falls under provisions drafted for that subject, with the operative boundaries set by the state's religious courts rather than by anything the Federal Court's 2024 ruling settled. A February 2026 case, decided before the bill was tabled, was the first Kelantan Syariah Court matter involving gender change. Judicial practice on the question was already running in the state in the months before the replacement enactment came into force.

name: West Java
text: Indonesia's national framework applies here; the national record for Indonesia covers the federal layer in detail. On 22 June 2025 the West Java Regional Police detained 75 people at a privately rented villa in the Puncak area of Bogor Regency, acting on a tip from local residents. Police described the gathering as an LGBT "family gathering" held "to avoid detection". Amnesty International condemned the arrests on 24 June 2025 as a discriminatory raid and "a blatant violation of human rights and privacy", stated that the gathering violated no law, and demanded the release of those held and accountability for the operation. In August 2026 men doused a trans woman with what appeared to be urine on a street in Bogor, one of a wave of attacks on trans women in the province. Activists link that violence to a 2025 presidential regulation classifying the spread of LGBTQ culture as a non-military threat and to discriminatory regional regulations, arguing that official language of this kind legitimises violence against trans women. A trans woman quoted in the reporting said that people who previously appeared in public now live in fear.

name: West Sumatra
text: West Sumatra sits under Indonesia's national legal framework; the national record for Indonesia covers the federal layer. Two local instruments restrict LGBT people. Bukittinggi City's Regional Regulation No. 2 of 2024 on Public Order targets LGBT people, framed as local religious values and Minangkabau customary norms. In Limapuluh Kota regency the legislature finalised a draft anti-LGBT regulation on 13 May 2026, folded into a Public Order and Tranquillity (Trantibum) regulation; the drafting body's chair said finalisation was reached. It provides administrative fines and rehabilitation. Neither carries criminal penalties; sanctions are administrative fines and mandated corrective rehabilitation. Both operate through public-order powers, so reach covers public space in the two named localities. No West Sumatra-specific enforcement action, arrest or prosecution appears in the source inventory.

name: Bali
text: Bali operates under Indonesia's national framework; the national record for Indonesia covers the federal layer in detail. Bali's own social environment differs from the national legal picture. Peer-reviewed ethnographic fieldwork published in 2025, drawing on four case studies in Bali, documents a visible transpuan (trans feminine) community living with precarity, discrimination and informal resistance, challenging narratives of pure victimhood while confirming real material insecurity. Traveller-facing guidance rates Bali 6.3 out of 10 overall but gives it a legal score of 2.0, warning that LGBTQ+ travellers face legal risk under Indonesian law and advising visitors to keep affection quiet despite the island's tolerant reputation. A March 2026 guide describes Bali as broadly welcoming on a 'live and let live' basis, while noting that the new Criminal Code in effect from January 2026 adds complexity to the legal backdrop. Same-sex relationships are not separately criminalised under a Bali-specific provision; the exposure runs through the national code. Seminyak (Eat Street and Batu Belig), Canggu and Ubud are named as the most consistently LGBTQ+-friendly areas with active venues, and public displays of affection warrant discretion across the island.

name: Papua
text: Papua is a province of Indonesia and stands under the national legal framework; the national record for Indonesia covers the federal layer in detail. The sources identify no Papua-specific criminal provision on same-sex conduct, and no Papua-specific enforcement of the national morality provisions is documented. Documented state violence in the province is severe and largely unpunished. A July 2025 briefing by the advocacy group TAPOL records 138 acts of torture or ill-treatment in detention by police and military personnel in Maybrat and the Central Highlands between September 2021 and the first quarter of 2025, with almost no consequences for those responsible. Arrests were largely for alleged links to armed groups or for participation in demonstrations, and deaths during torture were documented in operation areas. The incidents are catalogued on the Papuans Behind Bars database. A quarterly monitoring report covering the third quarter of 2025, published on 31 October 2025, records killings, arbitrary detentions, torture, arrests of protesters and the failure of accountability mechanisms as security forces expand across the region, alongside a healthcare crisis under scrutiny. That report carries no trans or LGBTI findings. For a trans visitor the practical exposure is the generalised impunity of the security forces rather than documented targeting: the abuses on record arise from counter-insurgency operations and protest policing, not from enforcement against trans or gender-nonconforming people. A visitor detained in the province would enter the custody environment those findings describe. No trans-specific violence, hate-crime data or protection measure for Papua appears in the sources.

name: South Sulawesi
text: South Sulawesi is a province of Indonesia and stands under the national legal framework, which applies here in full; the national record for Indonesia covers the federal layer in detail. OutRight Action International's 2022 report Creeping Criminalisation, by Katjasungkana and Wieringa, lists South Sulawesi among the eight Indonesian provinces it covers and records that provincial and city bylaws in these jurisdictions criminalise same-sex conduct and gender nonconformity, adopted under the regional-autonomy powers that let local legislatures pass their own regulations. In Makassar, the mayor reaffirmed in April 2025 a commitment to push an anti-LGBT regional regulation (Perda) after a same-sex act at a night-entertainment venue circulated online. The deputy chair of the city legislature's law-drafting body (Bapemperda) backed the move, saying the regulation was needed to preserve moral and religious norms. The proposal is not new. It entered the 2023 local legislative programme (prolegda) as a priority for discussion, and two city legislature members, including Azwar ST of the PKS faction, said it was modelled on regulations already passed elsewhere, such as Bogor. As of April 2026 the Makassar rule remained a draft (Ranperda) rather than an enacted regulation. Official posture in the city has hardened independently of the draft's status. The Makassar city government's women's-empowerment and child-protection agency (DP3A) is running an LGBT "prevention" programme, and a city legislature member, Muchlis Misbah, backs the pending Ranperda on HIV/AIDS and LGBT as legal reinforcement.

name: South Sumatra
text: Indonesia's national framework applies here; the national record for Indonesia covers the federal layer. South Sumatra is one of two Indonesian provinces that criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women; the Human Dignity Trust country profile records the provincial offence. A trans visitor in such a relationship faces provincial criminal exposure not present across most of the country. Palembang city government is preparing a regulation rejecting LGBT people: Mayor Ratu Dewa announced it on 19 July 2026 in the Grand Mosque courtyard, framing it under the national defence policy listing the spread of LGBTQ culture among non-military threats. No penalty has been specified and no enforcement has been documented. OutRight Action International's mapping of discriminatory regional regulations across eight Indonesian provinces includes South Sumatra.

name: Aguascalientes
text: Aguascalientes stands under Mexico's national framework; the national record for Mexico covers the federal layer in detail. Human Rights Watch's state-by-state survey of 11 March 2025 records that Aguascalientes 'has not reformed its legislation to create a legal gender recognition procedure for transgender people'; its reporting of 31 March 2025 places the state among those that have not legislated such a procedure. The state therefore operates no administrative mechanism of its own for changing name or gender markers on official records. The March 2024 Human Rights Watch report on the cost of absent recognition names Aguascalientes among the non-reforming states whose trans residents have no lawful marker procedure. Its documented consequence is that trans people carry documents contradicting their lived identity, which amplifies discrimination in banking, health care and dealings with police. A court-ordered route now exists. Infobae reported on 9 April 2026 that the Supreme Court, in Amparo en Revisión 430/2025 on a draft by Minister Giovanni Figueroa Mejía, held that the state Civil Code's requirements for changing the gender on a birth certificate, namely judicial or ministerial intervention, civil trials, probative proof of identity and marginal annotations, are discriminatory and violate privacy. The Court ordered the Civil Registry to grant recognition through a simple, confidential administrative procedure honouring self-perception, issuing a new birth certificate with no marginal note revealing a prior gender. The immediate effect is confined to the persons represented by the civil association that brought the case, so the ruling establishes a recognition route in the absence of legislative reform without yet establishing one for the state's trans population generally. No trans-specific homicide offence covers the state. The Guardian reported on 24 July 2024 that Mexico City criminalised transfemicide; Aguascalientes is among the states that have adopted no comparable reform. Violence and coercive practice persist according to local accounts. La Jornada Aguascalientes reported on 23 August 2026 that activists Alicia Cruz, Kevin Cruz and Hened Musalem of Diversx Laboratorio Cultural Disidente say conversion-therapy operations continue in the state under the guise of addiction-treatment annexes despite the legal prohibition, and that a person who escaped one such space reached the group the previous year. The same activists state that trans women continue to suffer prejudice-motivated aggression.

name: Baja California
text: Baja California has legislated an administrative procedure for legal gender recognition. The state congress created it through a 2022 reform to the Civil Code, initially limited to adults. In June 2023 the Supreme Court of Justice of the Nation invalidated the 18-years requirement, holding that the law failed to recognise the rights of transgender children and adolescents, and the state congress responded with a further reform in 2024 establishing a procedure for individuals under 18 and extending legal gender recognition to non-binary people. On the face of the statute the procedure now covers adults, minors and non-binary applicants, which places Baja California among the Mexican states with a legislated administrative route rather than a court-only one. The source inventory records no Baja California-specific evidence on how the procedure is administered in practice: no processing times, no named responsible office, no documented refusals or delays, and no reporting on whether state agencies accept the resulting documents without challenge. No incident of violence against a trans person in Baja California is documented in this record, dated or otherwise, and no figure for trans-specific killings or assaults in the state appears in the inventory. The assessment for a visitor therefore rests on the statutory framework and on the state's documented handling of gender-based lethal violence generally, not on any measured trans-specific risk level. The inventory likewise contains nothing on police treatment of trans people in Baja California, on how the state houses trans prisoners, on outting of patients by healthcare staff in state facilities, or on access to trans-related care. Absence of sourcing on these points is not evidence of either protection or danger.

name: Baja California
text: Mexico's federal framework applies here; the national record for Mexico covers the federal layer in detail. Baja California has legislated an administrative procedure for legal gender recognition. The state congress created it through a 2022 reform to the Civil Code, initially limited to adults. In June 2023 the Supreme Court of Justice of the Nation invalidated the 18-years requirement, holding that the law failed to recognise the rights of transgender children and adolescents, and the state congress responded with a further reform in 2024 establishing a procedure for individuals under 18 and extending legal gender recognition to non-binary people. On the face of the statute the procedure now covers adults, minors and non-binary applicants, which places Baja California among the Mexican states with a legislated administrative route rather than a court-only one. The source inventory records no Baja California-specific evidence on how the procedure is administered in practice: no processing times, no named responsible office, no documented refusals or delays, and no reporting on whether state agencies accept the resulting documents without challenge. No incident of violence against a trans person in Baja California is documented in this record, dated or otherwise, and no figure for trans-specific killings or assaults in the state appears in the inventory. The assessment for a visitor therefore rests on the statutory framework and on the state's documented handling of gender-based lethal violence generally, not on any measured trans-specific risk level. The inventory likewise contains nothing on police treatment of trans people in Baja California, on how the state houses trans prisoners, on outting of patients by healthcare staff in state facilities, or on access to trans-related care. Absence of sourcing on these points is not evidence of either protection or danger.

name: Baja California Sur
text: Mexico's federal framework is covered in detail elsewhere; the national record for Mexico covers the federal layer in detail. Baja California Sur does not criminalise trans people or their presence. The state's elected congress created an administrative procedure for legal gender recognition through a 2021 reform to the state Civil Code, and after the Supreme Court of Mexico ruled in June 2023 that excluding children and adolescents from that procedure was unconstitutional, the congress passed a further Civil Code reform in 2024 extending recognition to children, adolescents and non-binary people. Human Rights Watch's state-by-state tracker of legal gender recognition in Mexico, dated March 2025, records Baja California Sur among the states that have legislated an administrative procedure, and records the 2024 reform as the one that expanded access to minors and non-binary people following the Supreme Court's June 2023 ruling. El Financiero reported on 27 June 2024 that the reform approved by the Baja California Sur congress allows minors to change their gender and chosen name on birth certificates, and that the administrative processes are described as rapid, free and free of prejudice for trans and non-binary children. The XVI Legislature worked the dictamen on the order of the Supreme Court's June 2023 ruling, which had struck down the adult-only limit. For contrast, Human Rights Watch's report of 6 March 2024 on Tabasco, a state with no recognition procedure, documents what the absence of such a procedure produces: institutional mistreatment, the unsolved August 2023 killing of activist Karina Gómez, hate-motivation provisions absent from Tabasco's criminal code, and healthcare staff routinely outting patients by calling legal names. That pattern describes Tabasco, not Baja California Sur, but it indicates what a non-reforming state's trans residents face. Global Affairs Canada advises travellers to exercise a high degree of caution across Mexico because of high levels of criminal activity and kidnapping, with an avoid non-essential travel advisory covering Baja California Sur and the northwestern mainland coast. This is a general-country advisory rather than a trans-specific one.

name: Campeche
text: Campeche stands under Mexico's national framework; the national record for Mexico covers the federal layer in detail. The state has taken its own step on legal gender recognition: Human Rights Rights Watch reported on 31 March 2025 that Campeche's congress passed a 2024 Civil Code reform creating an administrative procedure for recognising a person's gender in official documents. The reform places the procedure in the civil registry rather than requiring a court order. Whether Campeche's procedure is applied without delay or obstruction is not documented in the sources assembled here. No Campeche-specific enforcement practice, refusal rate or processing time appears in the inventory, and no Campeche-specific incident of violence against trans people is recorded in it.

name: Chihuahua
text: Chihuahua stands under Mexico's national framework; the national record for Mexico covers the federal layer. As of March 2025 the state congress had enacted no legislative reform recognising gender identity; the civil registry operates an administrative practice instead. Human Rights Watch's review of 31 March 2025 places Chihuahua among 22 of 32 states whose procedure runs on administrative practice rather than statute, after the 2019 Supreme Court ruling striking down the court-process requirement. A visitor dealing with the registry relies on administrative procedure rather than state-law entitlement, operative as of March 2025. Its criteria, cost, documents and availability to minors are not described in the sourcing. No Chihuahua-specific finding exists on enforcement, trans-specific violence, hate-crime protection, police or custodial treatment, health-care access or facilities.

name: Colima
text: No Colima-specific signal was identified in the sources reviewed, so no local law, incident or enforcement practice is recorded here for trans visitors. The national framework of Mexico applies, and the national record for Mexico covers the federal layer in detail.

name: Durango
text: Durango sits within Mexico's national framework for legal gender recognition and criminal law on violence against trans people; the national record for Mexico covers the federal layer in detail. The source inventory identifies no Durango-specific signal on recognition procedure, enforcement, documentation, facilities, care access or protection machinery, so the national assessment applies here without regional qualification.

name: Guanajuato
text: Guanajuato stands under Mexico's national framework for legal gender recognition; the national record for Mexico covers the federal layer in detail. Human Rights Watch's dispatch of 31 March 2025 records incidents in Guanajuato, named alongside Tabasco, in which trans people without access to a recognition procedure carried identity documents that contradicted their lived identity; the report documents the discrimination that follows in schools, medical clinics and the labour market. No Guanajuato statute, state court ruling or state enforcement action on gender recognition appears in the sources reviewed. For a trans visitor or resident in the state, the operative rules are therefore those of the national framework rather than any locally enacted procedure.

name: Guerrero
text: No Guerrero-specific findings are available on legal gender recognition, enforcement, incidents or protection machinery. Guerrero stands under Mexico's national framework, and the national assessment applies. The national record for Mexico covers the federal layer in detail.

name: Mexico
text: Mexico has no single national procedure for legal gender recognition; the process is set state by state, and the national record for Mexico covers the federal layer in detail. As of March 2025, 22 of the 32 states had legislated an administrative recognition procedure, two more operated one in practice without legislative enactment, and six state legislatures had enacted none. Only seven states extend recognition to children. A trans visitor's document position therefore depends on which state they are in. Several states legislated recognition in their own right. Mexico City's Civil Code amendments allowing transgender people to change gender and name on birth certificates took effect on 13 March 2004. In late August 2008 the Legislative Assembly passed, by 37 to 17, a law formalising the procedure for changing names and obtaining revised birth certificates, replacing a prior process with no specific rules that could take years in court; on 13 November 2014 the Assembly approved a gender identity law making the process much quicker and simpler. The Michoacán Congress approved a gender identity law on 13 July 2017, Nayarit on 20 July 2017, Coahuila on 13 November 2018, Hidalgo on 25 April 2019, and San Luis Potosí began authorizing legal gender changes on 17 May 2019. Where no procedure exists, identity-document mismatch drives discrimination in schools, medical clinics and the labour market, with incidents recorded in Guanajuato and Tabasco. Tabasco had no legal gender-recognition procedure as of a Human Rights Watch and Community Center for Inclusion report dated 6 March 2024. Without identity documents matching a trans person's gender, every document request or appearance scrutiny carries risk of violence, harassment and humiliation, and trans people are excluded from employment, health services, education and financial transactions. The report set those findings against the August 2023 murder of trans woman Karina Gómez in Villahermosa, and against national figures showing that more than 95% of homicides went unpunished in 2022. The report found trans people in Tabasco living without documents that match their gender. Same-sex marriage is legal in every state. Mexico City's law of 21 December 2009 took effect on 4 March 2010 and was upheld 9-2 by the Supreme Court on 5 August 2010. By 31 December 2022 every state had legalized same-sex marriage by legislation, executive order or judicial ruling, though only twenty allowed those couples to adopt children. Civil unions for same-sex and opposite-sex couples are performed in Campeche, Coahuila, Mexico City, Michoacán, Sinaloa, Tlaxcala and Veracruz. A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship can marry in every state; adoption rights vary by state. Mexico City passed an ordinance banning discrimination based on sexual orientation on 2 September 1999, the first of its kind in the country.

name: Morelos
text: Morelos stands under Mexico's national framework on legal gender recognition and on violence against trans people. The sources vetted for this record contain no Morelos-specific enactment, enforcement action, or incident, so the national assessment carried by the Mexico record applies here without local qualification.

name: Morelos
text: Morelos falls under Mexico's federal framework on legal gender recognition and on violence against trans people. No Morelos-specific law, enforcement action or incident was found in the sources vetted for this record, so the national record for Mexico covers the federal layer in detail.

name: Nayarit
text: Nayarit's rules operate within Mexico's national legal framework; the national record for Mexico covers the federal layer in detail. A 2017 reform of the state Civil Code established an administrative procedure for legal gender recognition, allowing adults to change identity documents to match their gender identity. Human Rights Watch's roundup of 31 March 2025 counts Nayarit among the states that have legislated such a procedure. In 2024 Nayarit became the first of Mexico's 32 states to criminalise transfemicide, with a maximum sentence of 60 years. The offence is a distinct category in state law. No Nayarit-specific record of charges, prosecutions or convictions under it is available, so how the statute operates in practice is not established.

name: Queretaro de Arteaga
text: Querétaro de Arteaga is a state of Mexico standing under the national framework; the national record for Mexico covers the federal layer in detail. Querétaro has not reformed its legislation to create a legal gender recognition procedure for transgender people. Human Rights Watch's state-by-state table, current as of March 2025, lists Querétaro among the states that have never legislated any such procedure. A trans visitor has no state administrative route to align identity documents with lived identity, and the papers carried on arrival remain the only identification available. Querétaro's Penal Code prohibits esfuerzos para corregir la orientación sexual y la identidad de género (ECOSIG), the practices commonly called conversion therapies. The reform was published and is in force. It carries a penalty of two to six years in prison, a fine of 20 to 2,000 times the UMA and 50 to 100 hours of community service, and treats the practices as discriminatory and torturous under articles 1 and 6 of the Inter-American Convention to Prevent and Punish Torture. Tribuna de Querétaro reported these terms on 20 September 2023, citing Walter López, spokesman for the Frente Queretano por el Derecho a la No Discriminación.

name: San Luis Potosi
text: The national record for Mexico covers the federal layer in detail. San Luis Potosí began authorising legal gender changes for transgender people on 17 May 2019, and is counted among the states that enacted a gender-identity law that year. Partner recognition is settled at state level: the state Congress voted 14-12 on 16 May 2019 to approve same-sex marriage, effective 21 May 2019, and joint adoption by same-sex couples became legal that month. A trans visitor whose relationship would be read as same-sex under birth-sex status can marry and be treated as a spouse here. The hate-crime statute treats motivation by gender and sexual preference as an aggravating factor, naming gender and sexual preference rather than gender identity. The anti-discrimination law bans discrimination on sexual orientation and gender, but not gender identity, so gender-identity discrimination falls outside it.

name: Sonora
text: Sonora is a state of Mexico under the country's federal framework; the national record for Mexico covers the federal layer in detail. Sonora's Congress approved the Ley de Identidad de Género on 1 October 2020, creating a state procedure for people who identify with the opposite gender to modify their official documentation; Wikipedia lists it among 25 Mexican states with a gender identity law dated to 2020. On 6 December 2022 Sonora's Congress banned conversion therapies (ECOSIG). Sonora's hate-crime legislation treats gender or sexual-preference motivation as an aggravating factor, and the state ratified the 2011 constitutional amendment barring discrimination on sexual orientation. Same-sex marriage is legal in Sonora, so a trans visitor's same-sex relationship is recognised. No source records enforcement in Sonora, and no trans-specific violence or incident data was identified.

name: Tabasco
text: Tabasco is a Mexican state; the national record for Mexico covers the federal layer in detail. Tabasco has not reformed its legislation and operates no legal gender recognition procedure; Human Rights Watch reported on 31 March 2025 that the state is one of eight in Mexico with no such procedure. Without a procedure, a trans person's identity documents never match their gender, and mismatched documents invite police stops and institutional mistreatment. Human Rights Watch's Tabasco-dedicated report, published on 6 March 2024 and produced with a local community centre for inclusion, documents that the documentary mismatch curtails rights across four socio-economic areas. The report sets those findings against the August 2023 murder of Karina Gómez, a trans woman killed in Tabasco.

name: Tlaxcala
text: Tlaxcala lies within Mexico's federal framework, and the national record for Mexico covers the federal layer in detail. The state congress's 2019 reform of the Civil Code (Decree D.113, dated 1 October 2019) created an administrative procedure for legal gender recognition, and the decree text is published on the state congress's own site. The procedure requires no court proceeding, which is the legal basis a trans visitor would rely on to update identity documents in Tlaxcala. The state's civil-union law took effect on 12 January 2017, giving Tlaxcala a state-level partnership status that rests on a separate instrument from the 2019 recognition decree.

name: Yucatan
text: Yucatán is one of Mexico's 32 states; the national record for Mexico covers the federal layer in detail. Legal gender recognition is administrative: a 2024 reform to the Civil Registry Law, published in the Diario Oficial on 26 April 2024, lets transgender people update documents without a court order. Human Rights Watch's 11 March 2025 rundown carries Yucatán on that basis. Same-sex marriage is legal here: the Third District Court of the State of Yucatán ruled for two petitioners on 1 July 2013, and the first same-sex marriage was registered on 8 August 2013. Yucatán's Constitutional Court dismissed a challenge to the Civil Code on 2 March 2015; the federal Supreme Court dismissed the appeal on 31 May 2015. Yucatán's Congress amended the constitution to allow same-sex marriage on 7 September 2021 and secondary legislation on 1 March 2022. Yucatán enacted a conversion-therapy (ECOSIG) ban on 25 August 2021, making it unlawful in the state.

name: Zacatecas
text: Zacatecas is a state of Mexico; the national record for Mexico covers the federal layer in detail. Zacatecas has a legislated administrative procedure for legal gender recognition. Zacatecas is not among the states identified as having no legislated gender-recognition procedure. Deputies of the state's 64th Legislature approved a reform of the Family Code on gender identity on 23 December 2022 by 14 votes to 7, after the Justice Committee issued a positive opinion, allowing a new birth certificate recognising an applicant's gender identity. In 2023 the director of the state Civil Registry issued guidelines giving effect to the law, recorded in Human Rights Watch's March 2025 state-by-state feature. On 25 August 2021 the Congress of Zacatecas approved a prohibition and sanction on conversion therapies (ECOSIG) by adding fraction VI to article 182 Bis of the state Penal Code: inciting hatred or violence on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, or promoting them, faces one to three years' imprisonment or up to 300 days of community work. The same session typified hate crimes motivated by sexual orientation and gender identity in the state Penal Code. A gender-identity initiative debated in that 2021 session failed to obtain enough votes and remained pending; the reform passed in December 2022.

name: Newfoundland and Labrador
text: Newfoundland and Labrador stands under Canada's national framework on gender identity and gender expression; the national record for Canada covers the federal layer in detail. Provincial law has not required sex-reassignment surgery as a condition of changing the gender marker on a birth or marriage registration since an amendment to the Vital Statistics Act, 2009 received Royal Assent on 13 April 2016. The amendment brought the statute into compliance with an order of a Board of Inquiry under the provincial Human Rights Commission, issued in December 2015 on complaints brought by two trans women. Since 23 June 2021, when further amendments to the same act received Royal Assent, a person born outside Newfoundland and Labrador who has lived in the province for at least three months has been able to obtain a change of sex designation there. The change certificate costs $25, counts as official provincial identification, and is described by the government as a document that can be leveraged to update records in other jurisdictions. The amendments align with the earlier addition of a non-binary option on provincial birth certificates; the bill received second reading on 17 June 2021. Under the current application rules, applicants must be 16 or older, or be represented by a parent or legal guardian, with the consent of the other parent or guardian and the written consent of applicants aged 12 to 15. Applicants must be born in the province or have resided there at least three months. The application itself carries no fee; charges apply only to official copies of the updated documents, at $35 for a new birth certificate or $30 online. The province states that it cannot guarantee a birth certificate bearing an 'X' gender marker will be accepted by authorities in other organisations. That is the documented cross-border caveat for carrying provincial records outside Newfoundland and Labrador. Police-reported hate crime in the province was recorded at 5.3 per 100,000 for 2024, the joint-lowest provincial rate in Canada alongside Manitoba. The figure rests on 29 incidents, up from 19 in 2023, which makes the 51 per cent rise statistically fragile at that volume. Police counts capture only incidents reported to and recorded by police. Statistics Canada published the data on 30 March 2026.

name: Prince Edward Island
text: Canada's federal framework applies; the national record for Canada covers the federal layer in detail. Provincial law governs gender-marker changes on provincial documents and driver's licences. In April 2016 the MacLauchlan government tabled a Vital Statistics Act amendment: an Islander may change the gender on provincial documents by declaring the gender they identify with and providing a doctor's letter; sex-reassignment surgery is no longer required. Since 4 December 2018 a driver's licence shows 'gender not listed' as X or 'prefer not to say' as a blank, alongside male and female. The province states this made it the first jurisdiction in Canada to offer the 'prefer not to say' blank; Access PEI photo ID can carry an X or blank. Applicants must be born in Prince Edward Island, resident for at least three months and not in the lawful custody of another person. Forms include a physician statement and the applicant's written statement, signed before a commissioner of oaths at Vital Statistics.

name: Nova Scotia
text: Nova Scotia stands under the Canadian national framework; the national record for Canada covers the federal layer in detail. Within provincial competence, the province operates no restrictive trans-specific legislation and instead maintains an explicit inclusion framework. The Government of Nova Scotia released the province's first 2SLGBTQIA+ Action Plan on 8 January 2026, developed under the Dismantling Racism and Hate Act passed in 2022, described by the province as the first Canadian law of its kind to explicitly acknowledge 2SLGBTQIA+ people. The plan was informed by more than 600 community members through surveys, virtual meetings and consultations, and maps actions to improve programs and policies supporting full inclusion of 2SLGBTQIA+ people. On 10 June 2026 the province announced more than $176,000 through the first round of its 2SLGBTQIA+ Community Impact Grant program, including $12,067 to SeaHorse Sexual Health Centre for queer and trans outreach on the Eastern Shore, $25,000 to LakeCity Works' Queer Careers program in Dartmouth, $25,000 to Pictou County Pride, and $50,000 to Truro Pride to host the province's first provincial 2SLGBTQIA+ conference. Per-project grants are capped at $25,000 from the 2025-26 fiscal year. Discrimination on the basis of gender identity or expression in employment, housing and accommodation is prohibited in Nova Scotia as in all Canadian provinces, territories and the federal government; as of 2017 all Canadian jurisdictions explicitly include gender identity as a prohibited ground in their human rights acts. Transgender people are able to change their legal gender in Nova Scotia under provincial rules. The documented Nova Scotia correctional case concerns a transgender woman from the Halifax region held in a men's prison while serving a two-year robbery sentence. On 18 March 2025 a federal judge granted her more time to file her application for judicial review of that placement, citing a lack of transparency and clear, timely communication in the institutional decision-making and systemic barriers restricting her access to her lawyer. No later instance of this case is documented in the record. Statistics Canada reported on 30 March 2026 that 4,882 police-reported hate crimes were recorded nationally in 2024, a national rate of 12.1 per 100,000, down 2% in 2024 and up 142% since 2018; eight provinces recorded stable or declining rates. The release carries no Nova Scotia-specific rate or incident count. The underlying analysis of sexual-orientation and gender-identity motivations comes from Egale Canada's 2024 hate-crime analysis report. In the 2024 Spartacus Gay Travel Index, Canada including Nova Scotia shared first place with Malta, New Zealand, Spain and Portugal among 213 countries and regions as a travel destination covering lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender and intersex people.

name: Ontario
text: Ontario stands under the national framework of Canada; this assessment covers Ontario's own layer: its human rights code, the commission that administers it, the province's published policy, and Ontario's recorded hate-crime figures. The Ontario Human Rights Commission's policy on gender identity and gender expression states that under the Ontario Human Rights Code people are protected from discrimination and harassment on those grounds in employment, housing, facilities and services, contracts, and membership in unions, trade or professional associations. The policy defines gender identity as a person's internal and individual experience of gender and notes that a chosen name and pronoun are common ways of expressing gender. It is the official provincial statement of the human-rights protections a trans person holds in Ontario's workplaces, housing and services. Statistics Canada reported on 30 March 2026 that police recorded 4,882 hate crimes in Canada in 2024, 1% more than in 2023, at a national rate of 12.1 per 100,000. Ontario recorded the highest provincial rate at 16.0 incidents per 100,000 population. The figure covers all reported motivations and does not isolate gender-identity motivation. Police figures capture only reported incidents, and reporting levels are shaped by awareness and community trust. On 28 August 2023 Ontario education minister Stephen Lecce said parents 'must be fully involved and fully aware' of a child's decision to use a different name or pronoun at school. He said teachers and school boards already weigh 'exceptional circumstances' and potential harm to the child. Ontario had not adopted parental-consent legislation of the kind other provinces were enacting at that time, and no later Ontario legislative instance on this question is documented in this record.

name: Manitoba
text: The national record for Canada covers the federal layer in detail. The Manitoba Human Rights Code prohibits discrimination on the basis of gender identity in employment, housing and accommodation. On 18 March 2025 the provincial government introduced a bill to add gender expression as a protected ground; Justice Minister Matt Wiebe stated the change would bring Manitoba into line with most other provinces and would cover preferred pronouns and outward appearance such as clothing. The bill was before the Legislative Assembly for debate later in 2025, and Trans Manitoba executive director Charlie Eau welcomed it. Statistics Canada reported on 30 March 2026 that police in Canada recorded 4,882 hate crimes in 2024, a 1% increase over 2023, at a national rate of 12.1 per 100,000. Manitoba recorded the joint-lowest provincial rate at 5.3 per 100,000, alongside Newfoundland and Labrador, with no increase in 2024; it was one of eight provinces whose rates were stable or declining. The underlying analysis of sexual-orientation and gender-identity motivations in that data was published by Egale Canada, an LGBTIQ+ organisation. Police-reported figures capture only incidents reported to police. On 30 May 2024 the Manitoba legislature passed a bill recognising 31 March as Two-Spirit and Transgender Day of Visibility, brought forward by Logan Oxenham, a backbench New Democrat MLA for Kirkfield Park who is transgender. Oxenham said the day would show transgender, two-spirit and non-binary Manitobans that they are supported. On 20 November 2023 the province raised the transgender flag in Winnipeg's Memorial Park for the Transgender Day of Remembrance, an observance first marked eight years earlier. The flag was raised by Logan Oxenham, the first openly trans man elected to the Manitoba legislature. Families minister Nahanni Fontaine and health minister Uzoma Asagwara stated that the government supports and upholds the life-saving work of trans, two-spirit and gender-diverse Manitobans. Brandon advocate Anastasia Gibson said the day memorialises people murdered as a result of transphobia, violence she said shows no sign of slowing. Changing the gender marker on vital statistics documents, including birth certificates, falls under provincial jurisdiction in Canada; transgender people are able to change their legal gender in all provinces and territories under varying rules.

name: Northwest Territories
text: The Northwest Territories is a territory of Canada. Criminal law, human rights protections and entry rules are set nationally rather than by the territory; the national record for Canada covers the federal layer in detail. The territory's own legislative activity on transgender issues concerns vital statistics and name change. In June 2026 the Legislative Assembly was taking feedback from police and from the Northern Mosaic Network on proposed amendments to the Vital Statistics Act and the Change of Name Act intended to make the legislation more inclusive for transgender, non-binary, gender-diverse and two-spirit people. The proposals include an option for trans and non-binary people to request that a name change not be published in the NWT Gazette. This is the first on-record territorial legislation in the Northwest Territories specifically addressing transgender and non-binary people. The amendments were under consultation and had not been enacted. The RCMP has taken a position against part of the proposal. Chief Superintendent Dyson Smith asked MLAs to remove or amend the registrar general's option not to notify authorities, arguing that criminal records are tied to a person's legal name and that officers may put themselves in danger if records are not transferred to a new name. Yellowknife North MLA Shauna Morgan pressed the RCMP on how officers would verify legal names without identification. The police service is therefore on record opposing a measure designed to keep a trans person's former name out of public view. Organised community support for trans and Two-Spirit young people is documented in the territory. In June 2023 the Beaufort Delta Education Council bused seventeen regional students into Inuvik for pride events centred on feeling comfortable in one's own gender and sexuality, with workshops led by Two-Spirit Anishinaabe/Metis musician G.R. Gritt, a screening of 'Small Town Pride' and a pride parade. The gathering included a moment of silence at the Inuvik Community Greenhouse for Frank Gruben, an LGBTQ2S community member from Aklavik missing since 2023. Tulita, a small hamlet on the Mackenzie River in the Sahtu region, held its first Pride celebration on 28 June 2025, organised jointly by Chief Albert Wright School, the hamlet administration and the local RCMP detachment. Const. Matt Ryan counted more than 50 attendees and described the day as creating a safe and welcoming space for the 2SLGBTQI+ community. The RCMP covered food and paint while the hamlet and school supplied volunteers, firewood and the venue.

name: Nunavut
text: Nunavut is a territory of Canada and stands under the national human-rights and criminal law framework of the country, supplemented by territorial statute. The Nunavut Human Rights Act prohibits discrimination on the grounds of gender identity and gender expression: members of the Legislative Assembly voted unanimously on third and final reading of Bill 31 on 13 March 2017, and Justice Minister Keith Peterson stated that the amendment would make clear that discrimination against transgender people is prohibited. At the time of that vote Nunavut was the first Canadian territory to list gender identity or expression among the protected grounds in its human-rights law. Nunavut birth certificates carry a third, non-binary sex designation. On 18 September 2025 members of the Legislative Assembly voted 12-8 in committee of the whole to restore that option through amendments to the Vital Statistics Act, after the standing committee had struck it from Health Minister John Main's May 2025 bill, and the bill was then approved on third reading. Bill sponsor Adam Arreak Lightstone said the Government of Nunavut now joins the rest of Canada in recognising non-binary and transgender individuals. The territorial government funds transition-related care for transgender and non-binary residents. Reporting of 22 March 2022 records that the Nunavut Health Department began funding such care, with breast augmentation, chest contouring, hysterectomy and vaginoplasty named among the procedures, under a partnership with the Metropolitan Centre of Surgery in Montreal. The local LGBTQ group Positive Space called the funding overdue while flagging information gaps for residents living outside the capital. No trans-specific violent incident, hate-crime count or victimisation figure for Nunavut itself is documented in this record, and no dated instance of anti-trans violence in the territory appears in it.

name: England
text: England stands under the United Kingdom's national framework; the national record for United Kingdom covers the federal layer in detail. The definitions governing services, searches and detention allocation in England were fixed by the UK Supreme Court's unanimous judgment in For Women Scotland v Scottish Ministers, handed down 16 April 2025. "Woman" and "sex" in the Equality Act 2010 mean biological woman and biological sex, so a gender recognition certificate does not entitle a trans woman to the Act's sex-based protections. Lord Hodge stated that the ruling should not be read as reducing the Act's protection against discrimination for transgender people. The Equality and Human Rights Commission, enforcing the Equality Act 2010 in England and Wales, updated its code of practice on 20 May 2025 in response to that judgment. The code advises that services and businesses may ask a person for a birth certificate where there is "genuine concern" about biological sex, and that trans people may be excluded from single-sex sport "when necessary" for safety. This is the operative guidance a trans visitor encounters at venues, transport and services. Prison and custody decisions in England are governed by the same UK-wide ruling, under which Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights confers no automatic right to accommodation with the opposite biological sex. In argument on 5 February 2026 in a judicial review testing how far that ruling reaches into prison accommodation, government lawyers said a blanket rule housing trans prisoners by sex at birth would breach human rights and create an unacceptable suicide risk, while For Women Scotland called the identity-based policy "Orwellian". The Home Office statistics for England and Wales, published 9 October 2025, record 115,990 police-recorded hate crimes in the year ending March 2025. The transgender strand fell 11% and the sexual-orientation strand 2% against the previous year. The bulletin cautions that recorded figures understate prevalence, giving a Crime Survey estimate of about 176,000 hate-crime incidents a year, and that a February 2024 Metropolitan Police recording-system change means earlier years over-counted.

name: Queensland
text: Queensland is a state of Australia and stands under the national framework; the national record carries the federal law, and this record covers the state layer. Gender identity has been a protected attribute under Queensland's Anti-Discrimination Act since 2002. Amendments that commenced on 29 April 2024 moved serious vilification out of that Act and into the Criminal Code, with a maximum penalty of three years' imprisonment, raised from six months. The same amendments explicitly extend protection to non-binary and gender-diverse people and broaden the definition of gender identity. The Queensland Human Rights Commission described the Anti-Discrimination Bill 2024 as a rewrite that modernised the gender identity attribute and revised the vilification provisions. Queensland was the first Australian state to criminalise conversion practices. The Health Legislation Amendment Bill 2019 passed the parliament on 13 August 2020, making practices including electro-shock, drug and hypnotherapy aimed at changing a person's sexuality or gender identity offences carrying fines and imprisonment for practitioners, with a maximum of 18 months. Survivors report that the ban does not reach conversion practices in informal, non-healthcare settings. Access to gender-affirming care for minors has been restricted since January 2025. The health minister, Tim Nicholls, halted puberty blockers and hormone therapy for new public-system patients under 18 with gender dysphoria, formalised by a Queensland Health directive of 28 January 2025. The restriction remains in force and is legally contested. Patients already enrolled with the Queensland Children's Gender Service are exempt, so the practical effect falls on new patients and their families. Queensland documents have carried an X non-binary option alongside male and female since 1 September 2021, including marriage certificates and official forms. Transgender and intersex residents can update government records and their birth certificate; the requirement to divorce before changing a record was repealed in 2018 and the surgery requirement was repealed in 2024. State law recognises relationships through civil partnership registration or an unregistered de facto relationship, recognised since 2002. A trans visitor whose relationship would be read as same-sex under birth-sex status can register a civil partnership or rely on de facto recognition in the same way as any other couple. The state's criminal-law regime has been progressively liberalised. Private consensual sex between men has been legal since 1991, and lesbian sexual acts were never criminalised. The age of consent was equalised at 16 for all sexual acts in 2016, Queensland being the last Australian jurisdiction to do so; the former section 208 carried up to 14 years' imprisonment for anal sex involving a person under 18. The gay panic defence was abolished from the criminal law in 2017.

name: South Australia
text: South Australia sits within the Australian national framework; the national record for Australia covers the federal layer in detail. State anti-discrimination law protects gender identity and sexual orientation: the Equal Opportunity Act 1984 was amended in 2016 to add both grounds, giving trans residents and visitors a state-level remedy alongside the federal one. Hate-crime sentencing laws explicitly covering sexual orientation, gender identity and intersex characteristics passed and were implemented in November 2021, so offences motivated by a victim's gender identity fall within the state's sentencing aggravation provisions. The gay-panic defence was abolished on 1 December 2020 and ceased to operate on 1 April 2021; a defendant can no longer rely on a claimed non-heterosexual advance by the victim as a partial defence. The Conversion Practices Prohibition Act 2024 is in legal effect from 1 April 2025, prohibiting conversion practices in the state. Birth certificate changes have been available since 23 May 2017 under the Births, Deaths and Marriages Registration (Gender Identity) Amendment Act 2016, which received royal assent on 15 December 2016. A change of sex descriptor requires appropriate clinical treatment but not sex-reassignment surgery, and a marriage does not have to be ended first. Non-binary and indeterminate sex descriptors are also available on state birth certificates. Registered domestic relationships have been available since 1 August 2017. Marriage is recognised under the federal Act that took effect in December 2017; 62.5% of South Australian respondents voted Yes in the 2017 postal survey.

name: Other Territories
text: The national record for Australia covers the federal layer in detail. Norfolk Island, Christmas Island, the Cocos (Keeling) Islands and Jervis Bay Territory have no territory-specific law on gender identity, sexual orientation or intersex status. Norfolk Island was incorporated into New South Wales legislation from 1 July 2016 under the Norfolk Island Legislation Amendment Act 2015 and the Territories Legislation Amendment Act 2016; a visitor there meets New South Wales law rather than a Norfolk Island enactment. Christmas Island and the Cocos (Keeling) Islands, administered together as the Australian Indian Ocean Territories, are jurisdictions in which Western Australian law applies. Jervis Bay Territory is governed directly under Commonwealth law, and the Commonwealth Sex Discrimination Act 1984, as amended in 2013, applies throughout Australia including the external territories governed directly by Commonwealth law. That statute is the anti-discrimination framework a visitor to Jervis Bay stands under. Availability of the 'X' sex descriptor and anti-discrimination protection on the grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity or expression extend across the states and territories alongside concurrent federal protection. No territory-specific provision on markers or on discrimination diverges from that position in the four territories. No territory-specific rule on facilities, care access, entry or screening was located for any of the four, and no territory-specific enforcement action or incident involving a trans visitor was found.

name: Roraima
text: Roraima sits within Brazil's federal framework; the national record for Brazil covers the federal layer in detail. Two instruments specific to this state appear in the sources. State Ordinance No. 1,797/2023 addresses homophobia. On 9 August 2023 a law published in the Official Gazette of Boa Vista, approved by Mayor Genilson Costa of the Solidarity party, prohibited transgender athletes from competing in sports according to their gender identity. No further region-specific signal on policing, custody placement, health-care access or violence against trans people was identified; on those questions the national assessment applies unchanged.

name: Piaui
text: Piauí sits within Brazil's national framework for LGBTI people; the national record for Brazil covers the federal layer in detail. The state's own statutory layer is Ordinary Law No. 5,431, signed by the Governor on 29 December 2004, which bans discrimination based on sexual orientation. The source does not record gender identity among the grounds it covers. Ordinary Law No. 5,916, enacted on 10 November 2009 and published on 12 November 2009, guarantees travestis and transexuais the right to be identified by their social name on registrations, forms, medical records and related documents when using the services of all direct and indirect state public administration bodies. The law defines the social name as the name by which they recognise themselves and are recognised socially, requires it to appear first and prominently with civil identification below, directs the Executive to designate within 60 days the body responsible for registration and issuance of social-name identification, and retains use of the civil name where public interest or third-party rights require. On 20 July 2021 the Piauí judiciary granted civil registration as a non-binary person to a young person, the first recognition of a non-binary gender marker in the state. On 14 December 2012 the Court of Justice of Piauí began granting marriage licences to same-sex couples through all notaries statewide, without the need for a judge's approval; the change was published in the Diário de Justiça on 17 December 2012. In 2012 Judge Maria Luiza de Moura de Melo e Freitas of the 1st Children and Youth Court granted adoption rights to a lesbian couple living together in a stable union since 2007. Teresina restricts facilities. On 17 June 2026 the city council approved by 12 votes to 5, with one abstention, a bill prohibiting transgender women and travestis from using women's public restrooms, and on 30 July 2026 Mayor Sílvio Mendes signed it into law after LGBTQ rights activists protested that it is unconstitutional. The measure governs the capital only; no statewide facilities law is recorded. Violence risk in the state is documented only in aggregate. A 2015 Grupo Gay da Bahia report listed Piauí as the second Brazilian state with the highest risk of LGBTQ people being murdered. That ranking is LGBTQ-wide rather than transgender-specific, and the source supplies no per-capita rate and no transgender-specific breakdown, so it does not establish a separate trans-specific risk level.

name: Rondonia
text: Rondônia is a state of Brazil and stands under the national framework; the national record for Brazil covers the federal layer in detail. The state has no statute of its own prohibiting discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, so protection rests on national law rather than state legislation. An ordinance signed on 28 August 2025 by appellate judge Daniel Ribeiro Lagos guarantees transgender people the use of their social name and the use of bathrooms and locker rooms in accordance with gender identity; it is the clearest region-specific rule on gendered facilities in the state. In 2022 Hanier Miranda became the first person in Rondônia to obtain a birth certificate carrying an X sex marker. The civil registry had refused the entry for lack of a regulated third-gender procedure, and the marker was secured through a year-long lawsuit brought by the Center for Legal Practices, Research and Extensions at the Catholic Faculty of Porto Velho. On 5 May 2025 the state, federal and labour prosecution services, the federal and state public defender's offices jointly recommended that the state security and justice secretariats provide regular training for military police, civil police, firefighters, penitentiary and socio-educational agents on respect for LGBTQIA+ rights. The recommendation set a response deadline of 20 business days and required a training plan within 60 days covering 2025 and later years. It also requires gender identity, sexual orientation and social name to be recorded in police occurrence reports and prison records, with data protection safeguards, so that violence against transsexual women and travestis, including domestic and family violence, can be monitored. Police records in the state logged 240 occurrences of anti-LGBTQIA+ violence across 2020 and 2021.

name: Tocantins
text: Tocantins has no state law prohibiting discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, a gap recorded by the state's own Public Defender's Office. The national record for Brazil covers the federal layer in detail. The state bodies that have acted on trans documentation are the Public Defender's Office of Tocantins (Defensoria Pública do Estado do Tocantins) and the state judicial inspectorate, the Corregedoria-Geral da Justiça. On 29 January 2026 the Public Defender's Office published an article explaining how trans people change names and gender markers on documents. Rectification in Tocantins is administrative and rests on self-declaration. A trans man, trans woman, travesti, non-binary or queer person may apply at the civil registry where the birth was recorded, with effect on the birth certificate and on all official documents, without medical or psychological reports and without proof of surgery or hormone treatment. The service is free where the applicant proves inability to pay, and a court is involved only if the registry refuses the request. The exception is a change to a non-binary or unspecified marker, which the Public Defender's Office states requires a judicial decision. In August 2022 that office asked the Corregedoria-Geral da Justiça to allow "non-binary" entries in civil registry records, and in 2023 the inspectorate published a resolution authorising non-binary individuals to change their documents to include a third gender option. Whether an administrative route to a non-binary marker is open in practice is unresolved.

name: Espirito Santo
text: Espirito Santo sits within Brazil's national framework for LGBTI rights; the national record for Brazil covers the federal layer in detail. Facilities are contested at municipal level. On 6 June 2022 the Vitoria City Council approved a bill banning the installation of unisex restrooms in the city. The source records the council vote but not whether the mayor signed or vetoed the measure, so its current legal force is unresolved. On 14 April 2024 the Legislative Assembly of Espirito Santo approved a bill restricting athletes' participation in competitions according to biological sex. Governor Renato Casagrande vetoed it on 28 April 2024. On 21 June 2025 the Legislative Assembly approved a law allowing parents to prohibit their children from participating in classes dealing with LGBTQ topics. LGBTQ rights organisations challenged it at the Supreme Federal Court, which began hearing the case on 21 November 2025 and struck the law down in May 2026 by 8 votes to 2; Justice Carmen Lucia stated that it violated the Brazilian Constitution. Partner recognition was addressed in Espirito Santo before the national framework was settled. On 3 August 2012 a judge in Colatina authorised registration of the marriage of Ediana Calixto and Kamila Roccon, the first same-sex marriage recognised in the state. The State Public Prosecutor's Office appealed and the recognition was revoked on 15 August; on 20 September the state Court of Justice reversed that decision and authorised recognition. On 15 August 2012 the General Inspectorate of Justice issued a Circular Letter requiring all civil registries to treat same-sex marriages on the same terms as opposite-sex couples, making Espirito Santo the third Brazilian state to address the question statewide. State institutions have also acted on document recognition. On 22 January 2025 the Public Defender's Office of Espirito Santo filed suit to secure name and gender rectification for a non-binary person from Vitoria, and the court granted the request and authorised the rectification. On 27 June 2025 the Legislative Assembly and the Public Defender's Office held a free event to help trans, non-binary and travesti people change their name and gender on official documents.

name: Mato Grosso do Sul
text: Mato Grosso do Sul falls under Brazil's national framework; the national record for Brazil covers the federal layer. Homosexual conduct is not criminalised in the state. The main restriction is municipal, in Campo Grande. In March 2026 the city council approved by 13 votes to 11 a bill banning transgender women from women's public restrooms, and mayor Adriane Lopes of the Progressive Party signed it into law on 22 April 2026. It applies only to the capital, not the rest of the state. It was reported to the state Public Prosecutor's Office on 28 March 2026, and on 29 April 2026 the state Public Defender's Office opened an investigation. On 5 May 2026 Congresswoman Erika Hilton denounced it to the Brazilian Federal Prosecution Office. On 2 April 2013 the Court of Mato Grosso do Sul authorised same-sex marriage in the state, where partners of trans visitors marry before its civil registries.

name: Sao Paulo
text: São Paulo sits under Brazilian federal law; the national record for Brazil covers the federal layer. The 27th Private Chamber of the São Paulo Court of Justice upheld a moral-damages award against a nightclub that refused entry to a trans woman in women's clothing. The first-instance decision, at Barra Bonita, had set compensation at R$4,000. Commercial refusals of service carry documented financial exposure in state courts. The São Paulo Municipal Council's parliamentary inquiry into violence against trans and travesti persons issued a final report with 189 recommendations. An investigation published in May 2024 found that drink-spiking robberies known locally as 'boa noite, Cinderela' were victimising LGBTQIA+ people in São Paulo, as the city prepared for a Pride event drawing thousands of tourists. The reported risk attaches to venues and nightlife rather than to street crime generally.

name: Goa
text: Goa stands under India's national framework on transgender recognition, identity documents and criminal law; the national record for India covers the federal layer in detail. No Goan statute diverging from that national position is on file. Marriage and partnership recognition in Goa is set by the Goa Civil Code, a state-level instrument that defines marriage as between a man and a woman and gives no legal recognition to same-sex marriage or civil union. A trans visitor whose relationship would be read as same-sex under birth-sex status cannot have that relationship recognised in Goa, and the code applies in this state rather than the personal-law system used elsewhere in India. Goa has no state-level anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation. Protection against discrimination on grounds of gender identity in Goa rests on the national Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019, which applies in the state. On 7 May 2025 the state government constituted a 14-member Model Transgender Welfare Board, chaired by the Chief Secretary, under the 2019 Act and the 2020 Rules, with a mandate covering implementation of welfare schemes and safeguarding transgender persons' rights in healthcare, education, employment and housing. Administrative recognition in Goa lags the resident population. The 2011 census recorded 398 transgender people in Goa; by 2024 only 12 transgender people were registered on the state's electoral rolls, the first registrations having taken place in 2022. A trans visitor dealing with state offices should expect registration and documentation processes that have only recently begun to include transgender residents. Harassment of transgender people in Goan institutions is documented. A 2018 study by the Goa Livelihoods Forum found that 87 per cent of transgender respondents had dropped out of school because of harassment. The figure describes the state's social climate for transgender residents rather than a specific risk to short-stay visitors, but it records a local pattern of harassment in schools and comparable settings. No bill on relationship recognition has been introduced in the Goa legislature.
