name: Baden-Württemberg
text: Baden-Württemberg stands under Germany's national framework; the national record for Germany covers the federal layer in detail. Custody placement remains the sharpest documented exposure. Baden-Württemberg's own prison law retains the unrevised 1970s-era placement rules, which operate on a binary men and women housing model. A Verfassungsblog analysis of 18 March 2026 reports that placement rules in most Länder have stood unchanged since the 1970s and are now being revised: since 1 March 2026 a new Art. 17 of Rhineland-Palatinate's prison law is in force, and Bavarian, Saxon and Hamburg rules have also recently entered into force, giving a majority of Länder revised rules. Baden-Württemberg is not named among them. The same analysis argues that no constitutional duty exists to anchor placement to the registered gender entry, since a prisoner self-declaration would intrude less on the right to gender self-determination. Only Bremen's law explicitly references the gender entry; other Länder, implicitly or not at all, do so. How placement is applied in practice has gone both ways. A July 2026 report concerns a convicted far-right extremist holding a legally recognised female gender entry who was transferred from a women's prison to a men's prison after public outcry. The transfer indicates that placement follows the civil-registry entry and that exceptions permitting placement contrary to that entry are invoked inconsistently.

name: Bremen
text: Bremen, as a German city-state, stands under the national framework set by the Self-Determination Act (Selbstbestimmungsgesetz); the national record for Germany covers the federal layer in detail. Bremen has enacted no trans-specific statute of its own and no prison-placement rule of its own. Prison administration and the civil-registry offices are competences of the city-state, so the layer a trans person actually deals with in Bremen is run by Bremen authorities, applying the federal framework without local amendment. Under the Self-Determination Act the legal gender entered in the civil registry is the reference point for prison placement in every Land, and § 6(1) SBGG permits Land law to override that entry. Bremen has not passed such an override. The placement of a trans person held in a Bremen facility therefore turns on the registered entry rather than on a Bremen exception clause; how intake review is conducted in Bremen's prisons is not documented in the available sources. Legal gender changes for Bremen residents are processed through the city-state's own registry offices. Bremen maintains no separate rule on bathrooms, changing or leisure facilities, or identity documents of its own, so a visitor meets the national framework rather than a local variant.

name: Hamburg
text: Prison administration in Germany is a competence of the individual states, and Hamburg is a state as well as a city. Placement decisions for transgender people held in Hamburg's correctional facilities therefore rest with the Hamburg justice administration rather than with a federal authority. No case file, official guidance or enforcement account concerning a transgender prisoner in Hamburg appears in the sources reviewed for this assessment; the longer contest over how a legal gender entry interacts with prison housing is documented nationally and in other German states, and belongs to the parent country assessment. Documentary matters for a trans visitor or resident in Hamburg stand under the national framework of Germany. Legal gender and first-name changes are made by self-declaration at Hamburg's registry offices under the Self-Determination Act, in force since 1 November 2024, with three months' notice and without a psychological evaluation or a court order. Hamburg's own procedural handling of those declarations is not documented in the sources reviewed. Hamburg has a long-established gay commercial quarter in the St. Georg district, where bars, cafés and clubs operate in the streets adjoining the Reeperbahn entertainment area; German-language reference material describes the city as the principal centre of the gay scene in the north of the country. That material records no Hamburg-specific dispute over trans access to those venues.

name: Hamburg
text: The national record for Germany covers the federal layer. Hamburg is both a state and a city; prison administration is a state competence, so placement decisions for transgender people in its correctional facilities rest with the Hamburg justice administration, not a federal authority. No case file, guidance or enforcement account on a transgender prisoner in Hamburg appears in the sources reviewed. Legal gender and first-name changes are made by self-declaration at Hamburg's registry offices under the Self-Determination Act, in force since 1 November 2024, with three months' notice and no psychological evaluation or court order; Hamburg's own procedural handling is not documented. Hamburg has a long-established gay commercial quarter in the St. Georg district, with bars, cafés and clubs adjoining the Reeperbahn entertainment area; reference material describes it as the principal centre of the gay scene in the north of the country and records no Hamburg-specific dispute over trans access to those venues.

name: Mecklenburg-Vorpommern
text: Germany's federal framework, including the Self-Determination Act, applies here; the national record for Germany covers the federal layer in detail. Mecklenburg-Vorpommern has no documented statute, ordinance or placement reform specific to transgender people. The Land is the site of the July 2026 Landgericht Neubrandenburg ruling, which ordered a prisoner held in a men's prison despite a completed legal gender change. That decision is the documented Mecklenburg-Vorpommern flashpoint for how the Self-Determination Act interacts with custodial placement. Placement under the framework analysed by Verfassungsblog on 18 March 2026 follows a prisoner's legal gender entry unless the Land's correctional law provides otherwise. The analysis separates exception clauses written in abstract terms from clauses aimed at trans prisoners specifically, and treats the drafting choice as decisive for the outcome in practice. For a trans visitor, the documented exposure in the Land is custody. A person detained in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern cannot assume that a completed legal gender change will determine where they are held. No Land-level rule on identity documents, facilities access or healthcare specific to trans people is documented.

name: Niedersachsen
text: Germany's federal framework governs identity documents and trans rights; the national record for Germany covers the federal layer in detail. Niedersachsen has no trans-specific statute, ordinance or enforcement series of its own, runs no separate legal gender recognition procedure, and holds no correctional rule of its own on the placement of transgender prisoners, so the position a trans visitor or resident stands under in Lower Saxony is set by federal law. A July 2026 Bundesrat initiative to tighten the federal self-determination law, brought by Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt and Thuringia, would apply in Niedersachsen as in every other Land, but it is a proposed amendment to the federal framework rather than a Niedersachsen measure. No Niedersachsen enforcement action, court ruling or complaint on transgender detention or on transgender visitors is recorded.

name: Nordrhein-Westfalen
text: North Rhine-Westphalia has enacted no trans-specific legislation of its own; the national record for Germany covers the federal layer in detail. The state's correctional law contains no trans-specific placement provision, so a detained trans person in a North Rhine-Westphalia prison is placed under the national default rule that the legal gender entry governs, with no state exception clause to override it. The closest thing to a regional assessment is the study "Queer durch NRW – Lebenslagen und Erfahrungen von LSBTIQ*", published on 25 April 2025, the first comprehensive dataset on the living situations of lesbian, gay, bisexual, trans, inter, queer and non-binary people in the state. It combined quantitative online surveys of more than 5,000 LSBTIQ* respondents, 775 relatives and over 5,000 professionals with qualitative focus groups and expert interviews. Three thematic areas structure it: discrimination, violence and safety; health, care and ageing; and integration, migration and flight. The study was commissioned under a Landtag resolution, Drucksache 18/6360, to give the state's "Aktionsplan für Vielfalt und gegen Homo- und Transfeindlichkeit" a broader data basis. The action plan is a policy programme of the state government rather than a statute, and it creates no rights a visitor can invoke. That discrimination, violence and safety are among the domains the state government measures indicates a recognised problem, but the figures for trans respondents are not in the reviewed sources, so no risk magnitude can be stated for the state.

name: Rheinland-Pfalz
text: Federal law on passports, legal gender recognition and anti-discrimination applies nationwide; the national record for Germany covers the federal layer in detail. Prison placement in Rheinland-Pfalz is set by the state: Section 17 of the Landesjustizvollzugsgesetz Rheinland-Pfalz took effect on 1 March 2026 and anchors inmate placement to the legally recorded gender entry. The accompanying exception clause is drafted in general and abstract terms and is available to all prisoners; it is not written specifically for transgender prisoners. A trans visitor detained in Rheinland-Pfalz therefore has the placement decision taken at intake against the gender entry on their legal record, with the exception clause as the only route away from it. A constitutional-law analysis published on 18 March 2026 reads the Rheinland-Pfalz drafting as the model preferable to the alternative used in other states, where exception clauses are written to target transgender prisoners specifically, and raises constitutional doubts about that alternative approach. The analysis is legal commentary on the statute and on the drafting choice; it is not a record of how the Rheinland-Pfalz clause has been applied.

name: Saarland
text: Germany's federal framework applies here; the national record for Germany covers the federal layer in detail. Saarland has no trans-specific statute of its own. Its state constitution was amended in 2011 so that its anti-discrimination provisions explicitly include sexual orientation and gender identity, one of five Länder constitutions to carry such a clause. Transphobic hate speech is therefore prohibited under Saarland's constitution. Prison placement is governed by the national framework, with the legal gender entry as the default basis. A constitutional-law analysis published on 18 March 2026 cites Saarland's single-cell accommodation with en-suite shower as a positive practice model for trans inmates, but records that constitutional law does not oblige authorities to follow the legal gender entry, so the default in Saarland is a practice rather than an enforceable guarantee.

name: Schleswig-Holstein
text: Schleswig-Holstein stands under the German national framework; the national record for Germany covers the federal layer in detail. The state has enacted no statute or ordinance specific to trans people, and it has no provision of its own governing where a trans prisoner is held. Placement in a Schleswig-Holstein facility therefore follows the national rules, with no state-level variation layered on top of them. No trans-specific exception clause of the kind that has drawn constitutional doubt in other states' prison acts exists in Schleswig-Holstein law. The state's own trans-relevant legislative record is a co-sponsored initiative. Schleswig-Holstein, with Hesse, Berlin, Bremen and Saarland, tabled a joint motion in the Bundesrat for a ban on conversion therapy, presented in plenary on 12 April 2019.

name: Canarias
text: Spain's national framework applies here; the national record for Spain covers the federal layer in detail. Canarias has its own statutory layer: Ley 8/2014 of 28 October 2014, on non-discrimination on grounds of gender identity and recognition of trans persons' rights (BOE-A-2014-11995), gives a trans visitor a region-specific statutory basis against discriminatory treatment. The community has allowed trans people to self-declare their legal gender since 2021, one of 14 autonomous communities to do so before the national statute of 28 February 2023 took effect. Canarias is listed among those that ban conversion therapies, and it created a registry for same-sex couples in 2003, giving partners a regional recognition instrument.

name: La Rioja
text: Spain's national framework applies here; the national record for Spain covers the federal layer in detail. La Rioja passed its own trans-rights law in February 2022, recorded in a national trans federation report dated 18 February 2022, which places La Rioja among the autonomous communities where trans people may self-declare their legal gender. The regional law has applied to trans residents and visitors since 2022 and remains in force alongside the national trans statute of 28 February 2023. La Rioja is listed among the communities that prohibit conversion therapies. The community created a regional registry for same-sex couples in 2010.

name: Comunidad Foral de Navarra
text: Spain's national framework governs gender recognition and LGBTI rights in Navarra; the national record for Spain covers the federal layer in detail. No Navarran statute, court ruling or administrative practice departing from that framework appears in the source material, so visitor-facing practice here matches the national assessment of risk and access. Diario de Navarra reported on 12 May 2026 that Navarra planned to create an observatory against LGBTI-phobia, a measure that remained at the planning stage at that date. No regional equality body of this kind is recorded as operating in Navarra at that point.

name: Región de Murcia
text: Región de Murcia stands under Spain's national framework; the national record for Spain covers the federal layer in detail. The region's own layer is Ley 8/2016 of 27 May 2016 (BOE-A-2016-6170), which prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, and sex characteristics across public and private activity in the region. Within its scope the statute bars any requirement that a person prove a declared gender identity by psychological or medical report, so a regional service, clinic or venue cannot demand documentation of a visitor's gender as a condition of service. Article 5 creates the Observatorio regional contra la discriminación por orientación sexual e identidad de género, a participation and consultation body on which LGTBI entities are represented. Title IV sets the sanctioning ladder. Minor breaches draw a warning or a fine of up to EUR 3,000. Serious breaches run EUR 3,001 to EUR 20,000 and cover degrading remarks or incitement to violence against LGBTI people or their families in the provision of services. Very serious breaches run EUR 20,001 to EUR 45,000, with accessory penalties that include exclusion from regional public aid for up to one year. Multiple discrimination raises the grade of the infraction. Murcia was among eight autonomous regions that approved LGBTI and trans equality laws in the 2010s, and Ley 8/2016 remains the operative regional instrument. Implementation of the national trans-equality law falls to the regional government.

name: Galicia
text: Spain's national framework, including Ley 4/2023 of 28 February 2023 on trans equality and LGBTI rights, applies here; the national record for Spain covers the federal layer in detail. Galicia's courts produced the first application of the discrimination aggravating circumstance for transfobia recorded in the country. In July 2026 the Tribunal de Instancia in Vigo fined the author of WhatsApp messages that threatened a trans woman EUR 300. The conviction was a misdemeanour, and it is the only documented regional enforcement of that aggravating circumstance in the sources reviewed. Nothing in the sources reviewed documents region-specific legislation or practice in Galicia that restricts trans visitors. Recognition, document markers, facility access and healthcare access are governed by the national law, and no Galicia-level measure narrowing them appears.

name: Extremadura
text: Spain's national framework, including Ley 4/2023, applies here; the national record for Spain covers the federal layer in detail. No Extremadura-specific law, enforcement action, incident or institution appears in the available sources. The regional layer that can be documented is administrative: the education-facing and administrative measures of Spain's Ley 4/2023 are implemented by the autonomous communities, and the Extremadura regional government is among the administrations charged with applying them. Visitors should therefore read the regional picture as the national framework in operation, with the regional government responsible for the school and administrative side of it rather than for the recognition procedure itself. Nothing in the sources indicates that Extremadura has legislated independently on gender recognition, hate-crime aggravation, facility access or care provision, in either direction. No regional repeal or restriction of the kind seen elsewhere in Spain is recorded here.

name: Castilla-La Mancha
text: Spain's national framework applies throughout; the national record for Spain covers the federal layer in detail. No source in the inventory identifies a measure, incident, enforcement action or institution specific to Castilla-La Mancha. The single inventoried source is a national statute of uniform application across Spain's autonomous communities and records no provision enacted at regional level for this community.

name: Cantabria
text: Cantabria has no autonomous statute of its own on legal gender recognition, on discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, sexual identity, gender expression or sexual characteristics, or on harassment, so a trans visitor here meets Spain's national framework rather than a Cantabrian variant of it; the national record for Spain covers the federal layer in detail. The one geographic dimension the framework itself carries is a mandate for measures adapted to rural circumstances, the provision most likely to govern how the law reaches Cantabria's inland and thinly populated areas. The source inventory records no Cantabrian enforcement action, incident, prosecution, care restriction or facility dispute, so no region-specific risk picture can be drawn from it.

name: Corrientes
text: Corrientes lies within Argentina's federal framework on gender identity, health care, criminal law, prisons and document recognition; Emergency Decrees 61/2025 and 62/2025 of 5 February 2025 bind every province including Corrientes. The national record for Argentina covers the federal layer in detail. An April 2025 Washington Blade report, datelined Buenos Aires, names Corrientes among the more conservative interior provinces of Argentina where conditions for trans people are worse than in the capital. The characterisation comes from interviews with trans activists rather than from provincial government data, and the report attaches no Corrientes-specific incident, prosecution or policy to the province. The same report records activists' accounts that police violence against trans and travesti sex workers, already present nationally, had worsened and was worst outside Buenos Aires. No figure, date or named case for Corrientes is given.

name: Jujuy
text: Jujuy is a province of Argentina; the national record for Argentina covers the federal layer in detail. No Jujuy-specific statute, provincial court ruling, provincial protection measure or documented enforcement incident was identified in the source inventory. The only Jujuy-specific signal is an April 2025 report datelined Buenos Aires, in which trans activists said police violence against trans and travesti sex workers has worsened and is worst outside the capital, naming Jujuy among the more conservative interior provinces where the situation is "even more so". This is activist characterisation rather than a documented Jujuy incident, with no named Jujuy organisation, victim or case. Jujuy has no local hate-crime reporting infrastructure producing province-level records, so no Jujuy-specific count of anti-trans violence exists. The province sits under the national observatory's aggregate picture, which is not disaggregated by province or by victim group.

name: La Roja
text: La Roja is an Argentine province under the national framework; the national record for Argentina covers the federal layer in detail. No provincial reporting infrastructure generates trans-specific records for La Roja. The only systematic count covering the province is the national hate-crime observatory, which does not disaggregate its 2025 total by province or by victim group, so no published figure describes La Roja on its own. Reporting from April 2025 records that police violence against trans and travesti sex workers has worsened since the change of national government and is worst outside Buenos Aires, in the interior provinces. La Roja is not named in that reporting. The claim describes a regional pattern that includes the province rather than a documented provincial incident, and no provincial source corroborates or quantifies it. A visitor or resident in La Roja therefore meets the national legal protections without a provincial layer of enforcement data behind them: there is no provincial tally of hate-crime investigations, no provincial record of police conduct toward trans people, and no local body publishing either.

name: Mendoza
text: Mendoza is an Argentine province under the national framework; the national record for Argentina covers the federal layer in detail. Mendoza operates no separate gender-recognition regime: legal change of name, image and gender marker proceeds through the national Gender Identity Law 26,743 and the national identity-document system. Mendoza was among the provinces that earlier allowed applicants to leave the sex entry blank on identity documents, a provincial practice predating the current national marker regime. No province-level body in Mendoza monitors hate crimes or publishes a count disaggregated to the province, so the only measure of anti-trans violence covering Mendoza is national and is not broken down by province or victim group. Activists interviewed in April 2025 said police violence against trans and travesti sex workers has become more common, describing the pattern as more pronounced in interior provinces that lack strong reporting infrastructure; Mendoza has no such infrastructure. Mendoza has no local anti-discrimination or harassment coverage on the basis of gender identity or sexual orientation, and no provincial body receives or investigates complaints of that kind. Visitors and residents therefore depend on national provisions, with no dedicated provincial complaints channel.

name: Lower Silesian Voivodeship
text: Poland's national framework applies here; the national record for Poland covers the federal layer in detail. name: Greater Poland Voivodeship

name: Cross River
text: Cross River is not among the twelve northern states where Shari'a provisions carry a death-penalty maximum for same-sex conduct (Bauchi, Borno, Gombe, Jigawa, Kaduna, Kano, Katsina, Kebbi, Niger, Sokoto, Yobe and Zamfara), so a trans visitor here does not face that capital exposure. The federal Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 and Criminal Code apply as they do nationwide; the national record for Nigeria covers the federal layer in detail.

name: Ogun
text: No Ogun-specific law, enforcement action, incident or institutional practice affecting transgender visitors was identified in the sources reviewed, so the national assessment applies; the national record for Nigeria covers the federal layer in detail.

name: Oyo
text: Oyo stands under Nigeria's national framework, including the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014; the national record for Nigeria covers the federal layer in detail. Oyo is a southern state outside the Shari'a regime, and the death-penalty exposure for male same-sex conduct applying in twelve northern states does not reach it. The Criminal Code in force in the state criminalises sex between men with up to 14 years' imprisonment and gross indecency with up to 3 years. No anti-discrimination protection exists for LGBTI people in Oyo. Dating applications carry an entrapment risk not confined to any one city: criminal gangs pose as potential dates, lure men to meetings, film them, then extort, beat or kidnap them; one investigative report interviewed 21 people about being targeted this way. The documented cases and underground scene described are based in Lagos, and the sources extend the same risk to gay and transgender app users in Oyo. Victims seldom report to the police, because making a report carries its own risk of arrest or assault.

name: Lagos
text: No Lagos-specific legal or enforcement signal appears in the material held for this record. The two sources available are national in origin: one is UK travel advice covering Nigeria as a whole, the other reports a killing in Abuja. Neither identifies a Lagos State statute, a Lagos police practice, or a state institution that diverges from the Nigerian national framework, so the national assessment applies in Lagos as it stands. The one region-bounded element in that material is negative: the death-penalty risk recorded under Sharia criminal law is confined to the northern states and does not reach Lagos.

name: Lagos
text: The national record for Nigeria covers the federal layer in detail. No Lagos-specific legal or enforcement signal appears in the material held for this record. The two sources available are national in origin: one is UK travel advice covering Nigeria as a whole, the other reports a killing in Abuja. Neither identifies a Lagos State statute, a Lagos police practice, or a state institution that diverges from the Nigerian national framework, so the national assessment applies in Lagos as it stands. The one region-bounded element in that material is negative: the death-penalty risk recorded under Sharia criminal law is confined to the northern states and does not reach Lagos.

name: Akwa Ibom
text: Akwa Ibom sits within Nigeria's federal framework; the national record for Nigeria covers the federal layer in detail. Akwa Ibom lies outside the twelve northern states whose Shari'a-based criminal codes carry death-penalty provisions for same-sex conduct, so the death penalty does not reach a visitor here. The UK Home Office note on Nigeria (June 2025) confines death-penalty risk to the northern Shari'a states and excludes southern states such as Akwa Ibom, recording no state-specific enforcement divergence. Country coverage of Nigerian LGBT rights puts the maximum in the southern portion, Akwa Ibom included, at 14 years' imprisonment. Neither source describes an Akwa Ibom police command, prosecutor, court or authority acting on same-sex conduct or gender identity, and no Akwa Ibom arrest, charge, conviction or judgment appears. No Akwa Ibom state law or policy is recorded that recognises gender identity, prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, or recognises same-sex relationships. For a trans visitor the result is that the state adds nothing to the national position: no state-level protective instrument to invoke, and no documented state-level escalation beyond the national statute's penalty range.

name: Bayelsa
text: Bayelsa stands under Nigeria's federal framework; the national record for Nigeria covers the federal layer in detail. The maximum penalty a visitor faces in Bayelsa is 14 years' imprisonment, the ceiling in southern Nigeria, covering same-sex sexual activity and same-sex unions alike under the 2014 Act. The death penalty does not reach Bayelsa; it is confined to the twelve northern states with Shari'a-based codes. Bayelsa's framework recognises no gender identity, provides no anti-discrimination protections and recognises no same-sex relationships. A trans visitor therefore has no statutory protection against discrimination on gender identity or sexual orientation, and any union is void under the 2014 Act. No state-specific enforcement divergence is documented for Bayelsa. The UK Home Office note of June 2025 records countrywide arrests, detention and mob violence against LGBT+ people in all states, with no Bayelsa-specific incident.

name: Ondo
text: Ondo is a state in south-western Nigeria and stands under Nigeria's national framework; the national record for Nigeria covers the federal layer in detail. The sources record no Ondo statute, protective measure or enforcement divergence of the state's own, and Wikipedia's overview of LGBT rights in Nigeria does not name Ondo at all. The Shari'a penalty layer does not reach Ondo; as a southern state Ondo stands under the secular framework, where the maximum penalty recorded is a life sentence. The UK Home Office country policy and information note of June 2025 quotes Section 217 of the Criminal Code, under which any male who commits or procures an act of gross indecency with another male, in public or in private, is guilty of a felony liable to three years' imprisonment. That offence applies in southern states such as Ondo. Victor Oluwasina Ayeni, senior lecturer in law at Adekunle Ajasin University in Ondo state, observed in a January 2017 book chapter that the Code fails to define what constitutes an act of gross indecency. The same Home Office note records countrywide harm patterns of arrests, detention and mob violence against LGBT+ people. Wikipedia records no legal recognition of gender identity, no anti-discrimination protections and no recognition of same-sex relationships anywhere in the country, and Ondo supplies none of these itself.

name: Delta
text: Delta State stands under Nigeria's federal framework, which applies nationwide. The national record for Nigeria covers the federal layer in detail. Delta has enacted no protective statute of its own. Section 217 of the Criminal Code applies in the state, making male gross indecency a felony carrying three years' imprisonment; the maximum exposure under the 2014 Act is 14 years. The death penalty attached to same-sex conduct under Shari'a provisions operates only in the twelve northern states and has no application in Delta. Enforcement in Delta has taken the form of raids on private hotel gatherings. In June 2018 police in Asaba arrested more than 100 people attending a party at a hotel on charges that they were gay and lesbian, and by July 2018 the group was facing homosexuality-related charges in court. The Warri raid of 27 August 2023 is the most detailed Delta incident in this inventory. At around 9 pm, officers from the Ekpan Division of the Delta State Police Command raided Teebolus Hotel on Refinery Road, Ekpan, in Uvwie Local Government Area and arrested 67 people at what police described as a same-sex wedding between a 22-year-old groom and a 20-year-old bride. The command spokesman, DSP Bright Edafe, said the operation followed a confession by a male cross-dresser that he belonged to a gay club travelling to a marriage ceremony, that the suspects fled on the officers' arrival, that 67 were chased and arrested, and that drugs and 'gay marriage ceremonial dresses' were recovered. The 67, publicly known as the 'Warri 67', were charged to court, and the spokesman said efforts continued to arrest those who fled. Accounts of that night differ. The USSD 2023 human rights report records that police raided a 'white party' organised by the LGBTQI+ community in Delta State on 27 August 2023 and detained more than 200 individuals, that police alleged the event was a same-sex wedding, and that some civil society representatives disputed that description. One of the 67 arrested at the Warri hotel alleged that he was sexually assaulted by a man at the hotel while intoxicated. Reporting from Delta indicates that the law suppresses complaints as well as enabling arrests. A human rights lawyer based in Warri told the UK Home Office that victims of 'kito' — predatory same-sex assault and extortion — under-report for fear of prosecution under the same statute. A visitor who uses dating or hook-up applications in the state faces the same luring and blackmail pattern documented nationally, in which the threat of disclosure is the leverage.

name: Rivers
text: Nigeria's federal framework applies nationwide; see the national record for Nigeria for the federal layer. The southern criminal code applies in Rivers: sex between men carries up to 14 years' imprisonment and gross indecency up to 3 years. Rivers is not a northern Sharia state, so the death penalty does not arise there. One incident is documented: in January 2015 a 21-year-old man from Lagos travelled to Port Harcourt to meet a Facebook contact and was attacked and sexually abused there; he did not report it to police, and no arrest, charge or official response is recorded. No Rivers prosecution, arrest, police operation, state-government statement or enforcement pattern on same-sex conduct or gender expression is recorded, no Rivers institution appears as hostile or protective, and no trans-specific incident, facility rule or care restriction particular to Rivers is recorded.

name: Kwara
text: Kwara stands under Nigeria's national framework: the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 and the federal criminal law apply in the state, and no Kwara-specific statute on same-sex conduct or gender identity is documented in the sources assembled for this record. In 2022 a court ruled sections 4(1), 5(2) and 5(3) of the act unconstitutional and unenforceable nationwide, and that ruling applies in Kwara. Kwara is not among the twelve states that adopted sharia penal law: Bauchi, Borno, Gombe, Jigawa, Kaduna, Kano, Katsina, Kebbi, Niger, Sokoto, Yobe and Zamfara. No sharia penal application is documented for Ilorin or anywhere else in the state, and the death-penalty exposure under state Zina provisions recorded in those twelve states does not extend to a visitor here. No Kwara-specific arrest, prosecution, raid or act of violence against a trans or gender-nonconforming person appears in the sources covering this state. Human Rights Watch's October 2016 report on the 2014 act, which records mob attacks, arbitrary arrests, extortion and detentions across Nigeria, names no case in Kwara. That silence marks the limit of what these sources cover; it is not evidence that enforcement or violence is absent in the state.

name: Kwara
text: Nigeria's federal framework, including the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014, applies here; the national record for Nigeria covers the federal layer in detail. Kwara has no specific statute on same-sex conduct or gender identity. It is not among the twelve states that adopted sharia penal law, so no sharia penal application or death-penalty exposure under state Zina provisions applies to a visitor here. No Kwara-specific arrest, prosecution, raid or act of violence against a trans or gender-nonconforming person appears in the sources covering this state. Human Rights Watch's October 2016 report on the 2014 act, recording mob attacks, arbitrary arrests, extortion and detentions across Nigeria, names no case in Kwara. That silence marks the limit of what these sources cover; it is not evidence that enforcement or violence is absent in the state.

name: Kogi
text: Under Nigeria's federal framework, the Same Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2013 and the Criminal Code set the penalties (up to 14 years for same-sex marriage or sex between men, 10 years for gay organisations or public shows of same-sex affection, 3 years for gross indecency). The national record for Nigeria covers the federal layer in detail. Kogi is not one of the twelve Nigerian states that administer Shari'a criminal law, so the death-penalty Zina provisions applied in Kano and Katsina do not operate here; exposure in Kogi is imprisonment under secular provisions, not corporal or capital punishment. In 2022 a coalition of Nigerian human rights organisations won a court ruling that Sections 4(1), 5(2) and 5(3) of the 2013 act breached the Constitution and could not be enforced anywhere in the country. Those provisions therefore do not operate in Kogi either, and the ruling effectively allows LGBTQ+ organisations and individuals to exist and organise there. No comparable ruling covers the conduct provisions or the marriage-prohibition provisions, which remain the operative exposure in Kogi. BBC News reported on 9 August 2024 that mass arrests and detention of LGBTQ+ people take place across Nigeria, including in Kogi, and are especially frequent in northern states.

name: Benue
text: Federal law applies; the national record for Nigeria covers the federal layer in detail. Benue State does not administer Shari'a, so the national 14-year maximum is the operative ceiling for same-sex conduct here rather than the harsher penalties, including death, imposed in the twelve Shari'a-administering states. In 2022 a coalition of Nigerian human rights organisations won a court ruling that Sections 4(1), 5(2) and 5(3) of the 2013 Act breached the Constitution and could not be enforced anywhere in the country. That ruling binds in Benue, leaving LGBTQ+ organisations and individuals able to exist and organise under those sections. The entry records no comparable ruling for the conduct and marriage-prohibition provisions, which remain in force in the state. No Benue-specific arrest, prosecution, attack or police incident appears in the inventory. The human rights monitoring source carried no usable finding for the state, so the assessment for Benue rests on the national framework as it applies within the state rather than on documented local enforcement.

name: Anambra
text: Anambra is a state in south-eastern Nigeria, capital Awka, formed in 1976 and Igbo-majority. It sits outside the twelve northern states applying Shari'a criminal law, so the federal statutory penalties apply here in full; the national record for Nigeria covers the federal layer in detail. Same-sex sexual activity in Anambra carries the secular statutory maximum of up to 14 years' imprisonment. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act extends criminalisation to attempted same-sex marriages. In 2022 a court ruled Sections 4(1), 5(2) and 5(3) of the 2013 Act unconstitutional and unenforceable in any part of the country, including Anambra. LGBTQ+ people in Anambra have no legal protections under Nigerian law and face violence; the national record documents police torture, arbitrary arrests, mass arrests at private gatherings and hotels, and unprosecuted killings of transgender women.

name: Nasarawa
text: Nasarawa stands under Nigeria's national framework; the national record for Nigeria covers the federal layer in detail. No Nasarawa-specific law, enforcement action, incident, court ruling or institution is documented in the available sources. The only trans-specific killing recorded occurred on a highway in Abuja in August 2024, outside Nasarawa; no incident within the state itself is recorded, and the absence of a documented case is not evidence of safety.

name: Adamawa
text: Adamawa stands under Nigeria's national framework; the national record for Nigeria covers the federal layer in detail. Two source lists of the twelve northern states where sharia penal codes apply to Muslims — the UK Home Office country policy and information note of June 2025 and Wikipedia's article on LGBT rights in Nigeria — name Bauchi, Borno, Gombe, Jigawa, Kaduna, Kano, Katsina, Kebbi, Niger, Sokoto, Yobe and Zamfara. Adamawa is not among them. On this material the documented death-penalty exposure for male same-sex conduct under state sharia provisions is not recorded as reaching Adamawa; the criminalisation that applies there is the national layer. No enforcement event specific to Adamawa appears in the inventory: no arrest, prosecution, court ruling, state government statement or official action located in the state. The arrests and enforcement actions the inventory records are located in other states or described at national level. The visitor assessment for Adamawa therefore rests on the national layer, with no region-specific signal recorded in either direction.

name: Abia
text: Abia is a state in southern Nigeria standing under the country's national criminal framework; the national record for Nigeria covers the federal layer in detail. Abia is not among the twelve northern states where sharia penal codes apply to Muslims, so that layer does not reach travellers here. Neither source records an Abia-specific prosecution, police operation, venue closure, state government statement or incident, and neither documents a local difference in enforcement or in the treatment of transgender people. What is documented nationally is the operative position for this state.

name: Ekiti
text: Ekiti State operates under Nigeria's national legal framework; the national record for Nigeria covers the federal layer in detail. What is specific to Ekiti is documented enforcement and violence inside the state, concentrated in Ado Ekiti, the capital. On 21 January 2014, days after the SSMPA was passed, Debbie, a 26-year-old transgender woman, was beaten in Ado Ekiti by six men who told her, 'You will get 14 years in prison.' Human Rights Watch's October 2016 report states she was beaten at least twice over the period. Unable to attend the state's health services safely, she travelled three hours each way to Ibadan for HIV treatment, a round trip of roughly six hours. In September 2014 a man was arrested at Faguyi bar in Ado Ekiti, his third arrest, and released after two days in detention after 2,000 naira was paid for him and 10,000 naira for a friend. In a separate 2014 case, a 25-year-old man in Ado Ekiti was extorted by a state investigator. The two documented enforcement cases involve men pursued over same-sex conduct rather than trans identity; the trans-specific incident is the January 2014 assault.

name: Osun
text: The parent country's national framework applies in full; the national record for Nigeria covers the federal layer in detail. No Osun-specific law, enforcement action, incident or institution appears in the source inventory. The one sub-national distinction the material draws is jurisdictional: the death-penalty exposure that foreign travel advice attaches to Sharia penal codes applies to the twelve northern states and not to Osun, which is not among them. UK Foreign Office travel advice dated 19 August 2026 warns LGBT+ travellers to Nigeria of arrest, violence, attacks, blackmail and intimidation, stating that same-sex sexual activity is illegal and can attract up to 14 years' imprisonment, with the law also reaching wedding arrangers and organisers and anyone involved with gay groups. The advisory's Sharia death-penalty warning applies only to northern states and does not apply in Osun; the imprisonment exposure and the warnings about arrest and blackmail apply in Osun in full. BBC reporting of 9 August 2024 on the killing of the 33-year-old Nigerian transgender TikToker known as Abuja Area Mama records that her beaten body was found on the Katampe–Mabushi expressway in Abuja, roughly a year after she had said she feared for her life, and that an investigation was announced. The same report notes that despite constitutional guarantees of non-discrimination and private and family life, mass arrests and detention of LGBTQ+ people are common, especially in northern states. This is national-climate evidence bearing on Osun.

name: Taraba
text: Taraba stands under Nigeria's national criminal framework; the national record for Nigeria covers the federal layer in detail. No Taraba state statute, prosecution or enforcement incident was identified in the sources reviewed for this jurisdiction. The one Taraba-specific legal fact documented is a negative one: the national legal overview lists harsher Sharia-law penalties for same-sex conduct, lashing or caning up to death under state Zina provisions, only for Nigerian states that have adopted Sharia penal codes, and Taraba is not among them. No death-penalty or corporal-punishment exposure under state Zina provisions is documented as applying in Taraba, so a trans visitor's exposure in this state rests on the federal statute rather than on a state Sharia code.

name: Ebonyi
text: Ebonyi State stands within Nigeria's federal legal framework; the national record for Nigeria covers the federal layer in detail. Ebonyi is not among the states that have adopted Sharia criminal law, so the death-penalty provisions that operate in the twelve northern states which have done so do not apply within Ebonyi. A trans visitor's exposure in the state is therefore the federal Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 and its enforcement by the Nigeria Police Force. The source inventory contains no Ebonyi-specific statute, prosecution, arrest, court ruling, incident or state institution bearing on transgender visitors.

name: West Nusa Tenggara
text: West Nusa Tenggara stands under Indonesia's national framework; the national record for Indonesia covers the federal layer in detail. The province comprises the two large islands of Lombok and Sumbawa, with an official mid-2025 population estimate of 5,731,110. Ministry of Religious Affairs data for 2022 records 96.88% of residents as Muslim, and Islam was the official religion of the region's historical kings. The province's recorded character is conservative and religious, and its economy depends on tourism. The majority Sasak people of Lombok maintain strong local traditions, among them Wetu Telu, a form of Islam influenced by local beliefs. No province-specific bylaw, enforcement action, raid, arrest or incident targeting transgender people in West Nusa Tenggara is recorded, and no provincial protective legislation has been enacted.

name: Banten
text: Banten lies within Indonesia's national framework on gender identity and documentation; the national record for Indonesia covers the federal layer in detail. Since June 2021 the Indonesian Ministry of Home Affairs has conducted outreach to issue identity papers, including the electronic identity card (e-KTP), to transgender Indonesians, and Banten is named among the nine provinces where this has operated, alongside West Java, Central Java, East Java, North Sumatra, South Sumatra, South Sulawesi, Lampung and Papua. The stated reasoning was that many transgender people in these provinces were undocumented, particularly where families did not approve of their transition. For a trans visitor in Banten this bears on document status and enrolment: the province is one where identity-document issuance for transgender residents has been carried out since mid-2021.

name: Central Java
text: Central Java is a province of Indonesia and stands under the national framework; the national record for Indonesia covers the federal layer in detail. The source inventory contains no provision, enforcement action, incident or institution specific to Central Java, so no region-specific signal was identified and the national assessment applies.

name: South Kalimantan
text: South Kalimantan stands under Indonesia's national framework; the national record for Indonesia covers the federal layer in detail. The source inventory records no provision specific to the province on gender identity, identity documents, facilities or enforcement, and no documented local divergence from the national position. A visitor's legal exposure here is set by Indonesian national law, and the national assessment applies.

name: West Kalimantan
text: Indonesia's national framework governs what a trans visitor encounters here; the national record for Indonesia covers the federal layer in detail. West Kalimantan has no separate legislation or enforcement record addressing LGBTI people, and no provincial authority has been documented applying distinct rules on sexual orientation or gender identity. No province-specific reporting on policing practice, facilities, care access, document handling or partner recognition in West Kalimantan was identified.

name: Central Sulawesi
text: Central Sulawesi records no provincial legislation or enforcement directed at LGBTI people that operates separately from Indonesia's national framework. No prosecution, local regulation, police operation or institutional practice bearing on trans visitors is documented for the province in the sources reviewed. The province stands under the national framework of Indonesia; the national record for Indonesia covers the federal layer in detail.

name: Gorontalo
text: Gorontalo stands under Indonesia's national framework; the national record for Indonesia covers the federal layer in detail. The source inventory records no ordinance, raid, protection measure, facility or support service specific to Gorontalo, so the national assessment applies.

name: West Sulawesi
text: West Sulawesi stands under Indonesia's national framework; the national record for Indonesia covers the federal layer in detail. No region-specific signal was identified for West Sulawesi: the sources reviewed contain no province-level legal instrument, enforcement incident, or institution for the province, so the national assessment applies to visitors here.

name: Bengkulu
text: Bengkulu is a province of Indonesia, so visitors here fall under the national legal framework; the national record for Indonesia covers the federal layer in detail. No region-specific signal was identified in the sources reviewed: they record no Bengkulu-specific statute, ordinance, protection measure, enforcement action or documented incident bearing on trans people, so the national assessment applies without local modification.

name: Jambi
text: Jambi operates within Indonesia's national framework; the national record for Indonesia covers the federal layer in detail. The source inventory identifies no Jambi-specific finding: no provincial or district-level ordinance addressing same-sex conduct or gender expression, no local anti-discrimination protection, and no documented incident involving a transgender person in the province. A trans visitor to Jambi therefore faces the national assessment without local modification, and no Jambi institution, regulation or enforcement practice altering it was found.

name: Riau
text: Indonesia's national framework on transgender visitors applies here; the national record for Indonesia covers the federal layer in detail. No region-specific signal was identified for Riau in the source inventory. The sources record no Riau-specific law, enforcement action, prosecution, official statement, or incident affecting transgender visitors, and Riau's provincial article records no divergence from the national legal baseline, so the national assessment carried by the parent record applies to a visitor in this province.

name: East Nusa Tenggara
text: East Nusa Tenggara stands under Indonesia's national framework; the national record for Indonesia covers the federal layer in detail. No trans-specific statute, provincial regulation, enforcement action, or service record is documented for the province, and no source reviewed records a local divergence from the national position in either direction. The same absence applies to protective measures: nothing in the sources reviewed documents a provincial non-discrimination provision, a hate-crime provision, or a trans-specific service in East Nusa Tenggara.

name: Maluku
text: No Maluku-specific ordinance, police operation, court ruling, protection scheme or trans-specific incident appears in the sources reviewed for this province. The national record for Indonesia covers the federal layer in detail.

name: North Maluku
text: North Maluku stands under Indonesia's national framework; the national record for Indonesia covers the federal layer in detail. No province-level law, ordinance, enforcement action or institution specific to North Maluku appears in the reporting reviewed, and the province is not among those that criminalise same-sex conduct under provincial religious law. Reported trans-specific violence, police raids and prosecutions in Indonesia are not attributed to North Maluku in the available reporting, and none is documented in the province.

name: East Java
text: Indonesia's national framework on same-sex relations, gender recognition and expression offences applies here unchanged; the national record for Indonesia covers the federal layer in detail. East Java has no provincial carve-out: no bylaw, provincial regulation or gubernatorial instrument creates a separate regime in either direction. The province does not criminalise same-sex conduct on its own authority, nor extend protection beyond national law. No enforcement action, raid, prosecution, custodial death or official statement specific to East Java appears in the source inventory, so no provincial pattern of enforcement or violence can be established. Nothing in East Java civil law barred authorities from placing the trans woman Isa Zega in a women's prison facility by identity, and the province offers no anti-discrimination mechanism through which such a placement could be contested.

name: Bangka-Belitung Islands
text: Bangka-Belitung Islands stands under Indonesia's national framework, assessed as high-risk for trans visitors; the national record for Indonesia covers the federal layer in detail. No deviation from this national position has been documented in Bangka-Belitung Islands.

name: Riau Islands
text: Indonesia's national framework applies here; the national record for Indonesia covers the federal layer in detail. No Riau Islands-specific law, enforcement action, institution or documented incident was identified in the source inventory, and the province shows no divergence from the national framework.

name: East Kalimantan
text: Indonesia's national framework on transgender visitors applies in full to this province; the national record for Indonesia covers the federal layer in detail. No East Kalimantan-specific signal on transgender visitors was identified in the source inventory.

name: North Kalimantan
text: North Kalimantan stands under Indonesia's national framework; the national record for Indonesia covers the federal layer in detail. No trans-specific safety finding is recorded for North Kalimantan, and no region-specific signal for the province was identified in the sources reviewed.

name: Kuala Lumpur
text: Kuala Lumpur is a federal territory of Malaysia; the national record for Malaysia covers the federal layer in detail. Enforcement here is carried out jointly by local agencies. On 28 November 2025 an operation by the Kuala Lumpur police, Kuala Lumpur City Hall and the Federal Territories Islamic Religious Department (Jawi) arrested over 200 people at an all-male health centre in the territory. The Human Dignity Trust country profile for Malaysia, last updated 16 December 2025, records that enforcement since the 2018 election has included arrests, prosecutions and corporal punishment, and that the Federal Court has struck down some state Sharia criminal-code provisions as beyond state power. Human Rights Watch and Justice for Sisters, reporting on 10 August 2022, interviewed 73 LGBT people between 2018 and 2021, including people living in Kuala Lumpur, and documented state-sponsored discrimination against them. The report states that each state and the federal territories of Kuala Lumpur and Putrajaya maintain Sharia codes that typically criminalise same-sex conduct, quotes a Kuala Lumpur activist describing regression as a conservative strand of Islam gains ground, and calls on lawmakers to decriminalise same-sex conduct and gender diversity. The sample was LGBT people broadly rather than trans people specifically, and the interview window closed in 2021.

name: Negeri Sembilan
text: Negeri Sembilan stands under the national framework of Malaysia, which carries the federal Penal Code offences, identity-document rules and entry position; the national record for Malaysia covers the federal layer in detail. The state's own layer is its Sharia criminal law. In November 2014 the Court of Appeal declared section 66 of the Syariah Criminal Enactment 1992 (Negeri Sembilan), which criminalised cross-dressing, unconstitutional for breaching rights guaranteed by the Federal Constitution. The Federal Court has more recently struck down Sharia criminal-code provisions in Selangor and Kelantan on the ground that state legislatures lack criminal-law power; those rulings concern other states, not Negeri Sembilan's section 66. Human Rights Watch and Justice for Sisters, reporting on 10 August 2022, documented state-sponsored discrimination and criminalisation of LGBT people in Malaysia through interviews with 73 people conducted between 2018 and 2021, including people living in Negeri Sembilan. The report states that every state and the federal territories of Kuala Lumpur and Putrajaya maintain Sharia codes that typically criminalise same-sex conduct, and calls on lawmakers to decriminalise same-sex conduct and gender diversity and to abandon 'rehabilitation' programs and rhetoric. Enforcement against trans and gender-nonconforming people in Negeri Sembilan is carried out by the state Islamic religious department under Sharia provisions that apply to Muslims.

name: Sabah
text: Malaysia's federal framework applies nationwide; the national record for Malaysia covers the federal layer in detail. No Sabah-specific signal was identified in the sources reviewed: the Human Dignity Trust Malaysia profile (last updated 16 December 2025) and the Human Rights Watch and Justice for Sisters report of 10 August 2022 document the national framework only, and the national assessment applies to Sabah.

name: Sarawak
text: Sarawak stands under Malaysia's national framework, which sets the criminal offences, the Sharia enforcement machinery and the identity-document rules that apply within the state; that layer is carried by the national assessment and is not restated here. No Sarawak-specific statute, enforcement action, arrest, prosecution, court decision or institutional practice appears in the source inventory reviewed for this record. The national assessment therefore applies to Sarawak without regional modification, and nothing in these sources indicates either a lighter or a heavier local exposure than the national picture describes.

name: Sarawak
text: Sarawak lies within Malaysia's federal framework of criminal offences, Sharia enforcement and identity-document rules; the national record for Malaysia covers the federal layer in detail. No Sarawak-specific statute, enforcement action, arrest, prosecution, court decision or institutional practice appears in the source inventory reviewed for this record, so no regional deviation from the national picture is documented here.

name: Putrajaya
text: Putrajaya is Malaysia's federal territory and seat of the federal administration; the national record for Malaysia covers the federal layer, including the Penal Code offences, in detail. Putrajaya's own layer is its Sharia criminal enactment, the instrument it shares with Kuala Lumpur as a federal territory. Human Rights Watch and Justice for Sisters reported on 10 August 2022 that the Sharia codes of the federal territories of Kuala Lumpur and Putrajaya typically criminalise same-sex activity and gender nonconformity through bans on cross-dressing, and these enactments reach Muslims only. No Putrajaya-specific enforcement case is documented in the sources: the inventory contains no dated arrest, raid, prosecution or court order occurring within Putrajaya itself, so the territory's own enforcement posture is unresolved rather than absent.

name: Pahang
text: Pahang stands under Malaysia's national framework; the national record for Malaysia covers the federal layer in detail. The Human Dignity Trust's Malaysia country profile, last updated 16 December 2025, identifies no arrest, raid or prosecution in Pahang. Pahang's own Sharia enactment allows a court to order a person convicted of cross-dressing or a related offence into counselling or rehabilitation in a religious institution for up to six months (Pahang s.66). Human Rights Watch and Justice for Sisters' report of 10 August 2022, based on interviews with 73 LGBT people across Malaysia from 2018 to 2021, records Pahang among the states where interviewees lived, but documents national-level patterns with no Pahang-specific enforcement case.

name: Perlis
text: No Perlis-specific signal was identified in the source inventory: both sources record findings at national level only, so Perlis stands under Malaysia's federal framework and the national assessment for the country applies. The national record for Malaysia covers the federal layer in detail.

name: Perak
text: The national record for Malaysia covers the federal layer in detail. The source inventory for Perak contains no state-specific law, enforcement action, incident or institution: every documented item is national in scope or located in other Malaysian states, so no region-specific signal was identified and the national assessment applies to Perak without state-level qualification.

name: Penang
text: Penang stands under Malaysia's federal framework; the national record for Malaysia covers the federal layer in detail. A visitor's exposure in Penang is set by that framework together with the state's own Sharia enactment. Penang is one of the Malaysian states whose Sharia enactment criminalises same-sex intimacy and cross-dressing for Muslims only, with penalties of up to three years' imprisonment, a RM5,000 fine and six strokes of the cane. The enactment bars Muslim men from dressing as women; no legal definition of transgender dressing is provided. These provisions reach Muslim residents and visitors, not non-Muslims. No legal gender-recognition procedure is recorded for Malaysia, and the Registration Department routinely rejects gender-marker changes. Discrimination and violence against LGBT people are reported nationally, with transgender people identified as particularly vulnerable. Penang appears in a 2022 Human Rights Watch and Justice for Sisters study as a place where interviewees lived, but the study documents national patterns and records no Penang-specific enforcement case. Days after the 28 November 2025 Chow Kit sauna raid in Kuala Lumpur, police in Penang raided another sauna. No arrests, charges or outcomes from that Penang raid are recorded in this inventory.

name: Labuan
text: Labuan is a federal territory of Malaysia, where the federal Penal Code 1936 applies; the Human Dignity Trust Malaysia profile, last updated 16 December 2025, states that this framework governs what a visitor faces in Labuan, and the national record for Malaysia covers the federal layer in detail. No legal gender-recognition procedure is recorded, and the profile reports discrimination and violence against LGBT people occurring regularly, with transgender people particularly vulnerable. The inventory does not record whether Labuan operates its own Sharia enactment or which provisions apply locally. No arrest, raid, prosecution or act of violence against a transgender person in Labuan is documented in this inventory, and no Labuan-specific enforcement case appears in any source. None of the documented enforcement incidents since the 2018 election — an October 2022 Queer Halloween party raid in Kuala Lumpur with at least 20 LGBT people arrested, an August raid on an LGBT venue with twenty men arrested, a Terengganu Sharia court ordering a lesbian couple caned, and November 2023 Johor conversion-therapy centre plans — occurred in Labuan. The Human Rights Watch and Justice for Sisters report of 10 August 2022, based on interviews with 73 LGBT people across Malaysia from 2018 to 2021, documents federal penal-code penalties of up to 20 years for oral and anal sex and government-run 'rehabilitation' programmes that at least 1,733 people had attended as of June 2021; its federal-territory Sharia-code finding is stated for Kuala Lumpur and Putrajaya and is not extended to Labuan.

name: Sverdlovsk Oblast
text: Sverdlovsk Oblast has no legislation of its own on gender identity or sexual orientation and stands under Russia's national framework; the national record for Russia covers the federal layer in detail. The oblast administration has added no protections of its own. What is documented at regional level is enforcement pressure and violence in Yekaterinburg, the oblast capital. Reporting dated 21 October 2024 records that a gay man in Yekaterinburg was beaten and robbed after being lured into a fake date, and that a Yekaterinburg LGBTQ+ support group shut down after pressure. Together they show targeting in the oblast operating through private violence and through pressure on the organisations that would otherwise provide support.

name: Irkutsk Oblast
text: Irkutsk Oblast stands under the national framework of Russia; the national record for Russia covers the federal layer in detail. Survey data reported in the UK Home Office country policy and information note on Russia place the Siberian Federal District, the district that contains Irkutsk Oblast, at 24% for discrimination from healthcare providers who knew the patient's sexual orientation or gender identity. The same survey found respondents in Siberia more likely to be closeted than the whole-study sample.

The one region-specific finding is survey data showing that respondents in the Volga area were more closeted toward relatives than the whole-study sample, which speaks to the social climate in the region rather than to any legal rule.

The figure is district-wide and cannot be read as an oblast-specific rate.

name: Adygea

Adygea is not named as an exception to that assessment, so a trans visitor to the republic falls within the North Caucasus category rather than the general national one. The note places trans people and the North Caucasus in the same persecution-risk category, and Adygea is not named as an exception to either limb. Nothing in the sources identifies Adygea as safer than the regional baseline. The US State Department travel advisory for Russia covers the North Caucasus republics and interior-permission entry regimes, adding a regional entry layer on top of the national advisory. The sources identify no Adygea-specific protection, enforcement action, or official statement, so the regional picture is set entirely by the national framework and the North Caucasus assessment.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (version 2.0, June 2025) treats Tatarstan as an ordinary region. The note locates its elevated state-persecution exception outside ordinary regions such as Tatarstan; that exception is the category covering trans people, public LGBT+ advocates and North Caucasus residents likely to face treatment amounting to persecution. The note sets an asylum assessment standard for UK claims rather than describing conditions in the republic.

name: Astrakhan Oblast
text: Astrakhan Oblast stands under Russia's national framework, which applies in full across all regions; the national record for Russia covers the federal layer in detail. Penalties applicable in Astrakhan Oblast are substantial. 'Gay propaganda' offences carry fines up to 400,000 roubles (about £3,600) for individuals or up to 15 days' detention, and repeat offences can bring criminal prosecution with up to four years in prison. The November 2023 Supreme Court 'extremist' designation of the international LGBT+ movement makes participation punishable by two to six years and organising by six to ten years. Enforcement volume is documented. Between December 2022 and March 2024 at least 139 people were affected by enforcement of anti-LGBT+ laws. Human Rights Watch reported on 30 June 2025 that Russian courts had issued 101 'extremism'-related convictions tied to the International Public LGBT Movement designation, approximately 98 administrative and three criminal. The Home Office assessment finds that trans people, publicly active LGBT+ advocates and those in the North Caucasus are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution, and affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention. Two foreign-government advisories bear on visitor exposure. The US State Department rates Russia Level 4, Do Not Travel, with warnings directed at LGBT travellers, and states that official support is 'very limited' in parts of the country.

name: Belgorod Oblast
text: Belgorod Oblast sits within Russia's federal framework: same-sex activity is not criminalised, but same-sex marriage, legal gender transition and trans-specific healthcare are banned, and 'gay propaganda' offences carry heavy fines, detention or prison; the national record for Russia covers the federal layer in detail. No source reviewed records any region-specific finding for Belgorod Oblast, and the enforcement climate described nationally applies here as everywhere else in Russia.

name: Novosibirsk Oblast
text: Novosibirsk Oblast sits within Russia's federal framework; the national record for Russia covers the federal layer. A Novosibirsk court fined the Elton John Bar 500,000 rubles (about £4,598) for "promoting LGBTI propaganda" over a rainbow flag, after it appeared in a video by LGBT+ activist blogger Karen Shainyan — the statutes reaching a commercial venue, not only individuals online. Coercive conversion is documented: in summer 2021 relatives lured a transgender woman to a centre near Novosibirsk and held her nine months, forcing testosterone, prayer and labour; she escaped only when police answered a phone she had found. A priest in a village in the Novosibirsk region told The Moscow Times that religion can correct "deviations". Human Rights Watch's tally of 101 extremism-related convictions nationally since November 2023 records no oblast-specific case; absence does not prove none exists.

The sources reviewed for this record contain no oblast-level statute, court ruling, police action, incident or institutional practice bearing on transgender visitors or residents. The national assessment applies in full.

name: Omsk Oblast
text: Omsk Oblast stands under Russia's federal framework, which prohibits legal gender recognition, bans transition-related healthcare and treats the designated "international LGBT movement" as extremist; the national record for Russia covers the federal layer in detail. name: Saint Petersburg
text: Saint Petersburg stands under the Russian national framework; the national record for Russia covers the federal layer in detail. The city's own regional ban on "homosexual propaganda directed toward minors", enacted in 2012, was repealed in 2014, so no separate city-level statute remains in force; the federal statute is the instrument a visitor here is exposed to. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) names Moscow and Saint Petersburg as the large urban centres where survey data suggests LGBT+ people feel more able to be open, and where relocation within Russia may be a reasonable option. A 2023 survey by Coming Out and the Sphere Foundation found 57% of Saint Petersburg respondents out to most friends, 19% out to most relatives and 24% out to classmates or colleagues. An August 2024 study by Citizens' Watch and the Sphere Foundation on enforcement of the propaganda articles drew 13% of its respondents from Saint Petersburg.

name: Sakha Republic
text: The Sakha Republic stands under the national framework of Russia; the national record for Russia covers the federal layer in detail. No Sakha-specific legislation on gender identity or sexual orientation was identified. The one documented Sakha-specific enforcement action is custodial: in November 2024 a court in Yakutsk imposed an additional sentence on a prisoner for allegedly showing the rainbow flag to other prisoners, against a person already in state custody. No Sakha-specific protection machinery was identified: sources record no regional anti-discrimination provision and no regional body that recognises trans identity or registers LGBTQ organisations. A trans visitor should expect the national regime to apply without regional mitigation.

name: Saratov Oblast
text: Saratov Oblast stands under the national framework of the Russian Federation; the national record for Russia covers the federal layer in detail. The sources identify one region-specific enforcement action: in February 2024 a Saratov court fined photographer Inna Mosina 1,500 rubles (about £13.97) for using rainbow-flag imagery in her artwork, recorded as the first criminal prosecution brought under the extremism law. No other Saratov-specific enforcement, custody, healthcare or violence data appears in the source material. A trans visitor's exposure in the oblast is therefore set by the national regime rather than by any documented local practice beyond this single prosecution.

text: Udmurtia is a republic within the Russian Federation, and the sources reviewed identify no regional layer of law, enforcement or practice on top of the federal framework; the national record for Russia covers the federal layer in detail. The only material naming the republic records that the nationwide extremist designation of the "international LGBT public movement" applies within its borders. Nothing in the sources indicates that enforcement, protection or service access in Udmurtia differs from the national picture, so a trans visitor is assessed against that national record, which carries the legal position and the entry warnings.

name: Magadan Oblast
text: Russia's federal framework applies to visitors in Magadan Oblast; the national record for Russia covers the federal layer in detail. No region-specific law, enforcement, incidents or institutions were documented for Magadan Oblast, so no local signal was identified.

name: Ulyanovsk Oblast
text: Ulyanovsk Oblast stands under the Russian national framework, which applies in full with no local deviation or moderation of enforcement; the national record for Russia covers the federal layer in detail. Two prosecutions document how that framework operates locally. In August 2024 Ilya Zhuravlev, former head of the dialysis centre in Inza, was detained on charges of participating in the activities of the designated "international LGBT movement" under Part 2 of Article 282.2, alongside a charge of coercion of a person to act of a sexual nature under Part 1 of Article 133. The case is recorded in an October 2024 OVD-Info report cited in the UK Home Office country policy note (June 2025). In March 2025 a doctor in the region, already facing a maximum of one year's imprisonment over an allegation of sexual coercion, was additionally prosecuted for "involving" another man in the designated movement. He received a three-year sentence, as recorded by Human Rights Watch. The sentence exceeded the maximum available on the original allegation, so the extremism count drove its length. A trans visitor faces the national legal position without local relief, and the documented cases show charges brought against men in professional positions rather than people with any prior profile.

name: Kemerovo Oblast
text: Kemerovo Oblast has no separate legal regime for gender identity; no oblast statute, decree or regional protection appears in the sources, and the national record for Russia covers the federal layer in detail. The only region-specific enforcement event is a penal-system prosecution: in February, a person already serving a prison sentence in Kemerovo region received an additional six-year sentence for participating in the "LGBT movement" and for "involving" other prisoners in its activities. RIA Novosti reported it citing the Federal Security Service; Human Rights Watch recorded it in reporting published on 30 June 2025. The case shows the extremism designation applied by regional courts to conduct in custody, with a sentenced prisoner facing further prosecution for contact with other inmates. For a trans visitor there is no regional variation, and no incident involving a trans traveller in the oblast was identified.

name: Khabarovsk Krai
text: Khabarovsk Krai has no regional law or institution of its own on gender identity or expression, so the national framework applies in full; the national record for Russia covers the federal layer in detail. The region's documented enforcement event concerns a biology and chemistry teacher in Khabarovsk who was forced to resign in September after video of him dancing in high heels surfaced amid public controversy. He filed suit against the Khabarovsk education department in October seeking reinstatement, and the case was still pending when the UK Home Office country policy and information note was published in June 2025. The episode shows that gender-nonconforming presentation can carry employment consequences in the krai, pursued through public controversy and an employer rather than through a criminal charge.

name: Free State
text: South Africa's national framework governs policing, federal agencies and federal bans; the national record for South Africa covers the federal layer in detail. Gender-affirming care in South Africa is concentrated in the major metropolitan centres, and the Free State has no documented concentration of its own. A trans visitor needing hormone therapy or surgery while in the province should expect to travel outside it, paying private prices in the hundreds of thousands of rands or waiting on a long public list. No Free State-specific provider, waiting-time or funding data was identified. No Free State-specific statute, provincial enforcement record, prosecution or documented incident involving a transgender person was identified. Policing, provincial hospitals, municipal facilities and the province's correctional centres operate under the national framework carried by the South Africa record.

name: Normandie
text: France's national framework on transgender rights and detention applies in Normandie without regional modification; the national record for France covers the federal layer in detail. Caen prison is the one institution in Normandie documented in the source inventory as a site of the CGLPL's scrutiny of transgender detainees: the authority carried out an inspection visit there as part of the evidence base for its opinion of 25 May 2021 on the treatment of transgender persons in places of deprivation of liberty. The other visits in that review were at Fleury-Mérogis, Saint-Martin-de-Ré, Toulouse-Seysses prisons and the Toulouse central police station, none of them in Normandie. The published opinion does not separate its findings by establishment, so what inspectors recorded at Caen specifically is not stated; the violations it documents in adult prisons concern the national prison system rather than Normandie. No Normandie-specific law, court ruling, enforcement action, incident, facility policy or regional institution appears in the inventory.
