text: The Zamboanga Peninsula stands under the national framework of the Philippines; the national record for Philippines covers the federal layer in detail. Within the peninsula, the one region-specific protection instrument identified is a SOGIE anti-discrimination ordinance enacted by Zamboanga City, the regional centre, in 2020. It sets the local legal floor for visitors and residents inside the city. The Bureau of Jail Management and Penology in Davao moves LGBT detainees in batches to the City Jail Annex, holding them alongside persons with disabilities, the sick and senior citizens as a stated measure to prevent abuse. The advice the court condemned is a general police practice rather than an incident confined to one city, so the ruling reaches officers in Ulsan, though no comparable Ulsan complaint has been documented. In May 2024 a regional court approved a registered-sex change from male to female for five transgender applicants who had not undergone sex-reassignment surgery. It held that gender change cannot be determined by surgery, that court guidelines requiring surgery are reference material rather than criteria, and that every person has the right to live according to their gender identity. Applications in Ulsan proceed on that footing; the sources record no Ulsan applicant and no Ulsan court ruling on the question.

name: La Libertad
text: La Libertad stands under Peru's national framework, which governs identity documents, facility access and discrimination law; this assessment covers only what is specific to the region. Two documents carry the region-specific record: a national prosecution study that disaggregates homicides of LGTB people by prosecution district, and a 2024 regional ordinance on labour inclusion. Neither establishes a regional anti-discrimination enforcement mechanism, and no region-specific data on policing, restroom-law enforcement or service access appears in the sources. The Public Prosecutor's Office published a study of intentional deaths of LGTB people between 2012 and 2021, drawn from 84 criminal complaints covering 88 victims and 72 identified suspects. Six fiscal districts accounted for 58% of the deaths. La Libertad recorded 10, second only to Lima's 12 and level with Lima Norte, ahead of Lima Este (7), Lima Sur (6) and Callao (6). The ranking is by raw count. La Libertad is one of Peru's more populous regions, and the study supplies no per-capita denominator, so the figure does not by itself show that a trans visitor faces higher risk in La Libertad than in a smaller district. The study was produced with the Justice Ministry's human-rights office and the Cayetano Heredia University LGTB-rights observatory with UNDP support. Ordenanza Regional N.° 009-2024-GRLL-CR, approved in Trujillo on 6 September 2024 and published in El Peruano on 7 November 2024, promotes the labour inclusion of travesti, transsexual and transgender people in La Libertad. It declares their right to formal, dignified and productive work in equitable and satisfactory conditions without discrimination on grounds of gender identity or its expression, and recognises the trans community as a group in a situation of vulnerability in the region. It is a positive-action measure addressed to employment, not a protection a visitor can invoke against police, service providers or private venues, and it specifies no penalty or enforcement body. The ordinance recommends that local governments issue municipal ordinances recognising gender identity and fundamental rights, and orders a working group (mesa de trabajo) to be convened. It cites constitutional equality guarantees and article 323 of the Penal Code on discrimination, and recalls a 2014 regional-council session that set a framework against discrimination on sexual orientation and gender identity. Whether any La Libertad municipality has acted on the recommendation is not documented in the sources.

name: Tacna
text: Tacna stands under Peru's national framework; the national record for Peru covers the federal layer in detail. On 19 April 2025 Marcia Paucara Cora, a 48-year-old trans woman, was found dead in a room of the Los 5 Titos hostel on Arias y Aragüez street in central Tacna. The autopsy recorded death by mechanical asphyxia through compression of the airways. She had entered the hostel with a man who registered under a false identity and who left alone roughly two hours later carrying a white bag. Staff found the body when the rental time expired. Tacna authorities are investigating the death as a possible hate crime, an offence motivated by prejudice and discrimination on grounds of the victim's sexual orientation or gender identity. No suspect had been identified in the reporting of 21 and 27 May 2025. The victim was initially processed as an unidentified body and was named through the hostel's cameras; police were analysing surveillance footage from inside and outside the premises to trace the suspect's escape route. Family members and local LGTBIQ+ collectives held a vigil on Friday 23 May 2025 demanding justice, describing the killing as the reflection of a structural system of violence that silences trans lives. Relatives publicly denounced the killing and pressed for police action.

name: Atlántico
text: Colombia's national framework applies here; the national record for Colombia covers the federal layer in detail. The 2025 report "Un sistema que falla: prejuicio, violencia e impunidad contra personas LGBTIQ+ en Colombia", by Caribe Afirmativo and covered by Publimetro Colombia, counts for Atlántico 54 cases of intrafamily violence, 41 sexual offences, 69 threats, 12 discrimination cases, 8 cases of digital violence, 8 cases of lethal violence, and 2 killings of LGBTIQ+ human-rights defenders during 2025. These are raw departmental totals with no population denominator, so they cannot be read as a ranking against other departments. Barranquilla and Soledad carry a "high" threat level. Violence is expanding into territories with illegal-economy corridors and weak state presence, with the state response judged insufficient. Threat cases show near-total impunity: 99.8% never advance past the investigation stage; whether this figure is departmental or national is not stated. The department's and Barranquilla's development plans commit local authorities to coordinated action with the prosecutor's office, police and judiciary to strengthen reporting, investigation and prosecution of violence against LGBTIQ+ people.

name: Bolívar
text: Bolívar's trans-related law and enforcement sit within Colombia's national framework; the national record for Colombia covers the federal layer in detail. The department's documented record on trans safety centres on the killing of Nawar Jiménez, a trans social leader, in Carmen de Bolívar on 22 May 2025. El Tiempo's data investigation classifies the case as a trans feminicide. Jiménez had campaigned with the 'No Es Hora De Callar' movement and had joined its sixth symbolic return march, which brought together more than 500 survivors of sexual violence. Her friend and fellow social leader Yirley Velasco remembers her as having taken up the fight for trans rights in the municipality. More than 19 days after the killing, the circumstances remained unclear. No arrest, charge or explanation of the death is reported in that period, and the case is the department's documented instance of lethal violence against a trans person. Caribe Afirmativo's 2025 report, 'Un sistema que falla: prejuicio, violencia e impunidad contra personas LGBTIQ+ en Colombia', does not name Bolívar. It documents violence against LGBTIQ+ people expanding toward territories with illegal-economy corridors and weak state presence, and places the department inside the Caribbean-coast cluster flagged for that expansion and for the weakest state response. The department's risk picture therefore rests on cluster-level findings rather than on monitoring specific to Bolívar.

text: Colombia's national framework applies here; the national record for Colombia covers the federal layer in detail. La Guajira's own signal is a campaign of written threats by armed groups. Since March 2024 armed groups have circulated flyers carrying a kill list of named individuals, stating that "all will be military targets" and listing "homosexuals, lesbians, rapists, trans" among those designated. The wording places trans people in a category marked for lethal violence and names individuals rather than a general warning. Exposure therefore tracks where armed-group control is exercised, not the formal legal position, which is protective. The list is written and posted publicly, so visibility to neighbours and to whoever posts it is the operative risk factor; displacement rather than protection is the documented response for those named. La Guajira has no separate legal regime.

name: Caquetá
text: Caquetá is a department of Colombia; the national record for Colombia covers the federal layer in detail. The signal here is organised armed-group targeting, not statute. Reporting dated 30 July 2024 documented armed groups in Caquetá running a 'social cleansing' campaign, distributing flyers on the streets and through WhatsApp naming 'faggots, lesbians and men and women who destroy homes' as legitimate military targets. The campaign has produced displacement. A trans woman who was a local election candidate was told by three armed men she had one week to leave town; she hid for a week and then fled at night. A second trans woman in the department said a friend had been killed. Armed groups here have publicly designated trans people as targets and driven residents out. The flyers name people by perceived sexual orientation and gender expression, not by any official record.

name: Puno
text: No region-specific finding on trans visitor safety was identified for the department of Puno; the national record for Peru covers the federal layer in detail. The sources record no Puno ordinance, exemption, enforcement practice or regional institution of its own on trans matters. As national law, Peru's public-restroom restriction binds Puno: on 2 April 2025 the Peruvian congressional Plenary approved, exempt from a second vote, a bill whose article 5 bars any person from entering or using a public sanitary service that does not correspond to their 'biological sex', with narrow listed exceptions; IDEHPUCP's legal analysis by Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte of 15 April 2025 states this violates the equal-treatment and non-discrimination principle of article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights. The authors argue the law's stated aim of preventing child sexual abuse rests on a stigmatising stereotype presenting trans people as likely restroom harassers, while UN reporting shows trans people are more often victims than aggressors. An earlier committee-stage measure of the same family, reported by Infobae Perú on 20 February 2025, was approved unanimously by the congressional Women and Family Commission as a draft opinion merging bills 6506 and 8457, introduced by congressmen Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Muñante, barring trans people from public restrooms that do not correspond to their birth sex, with exceptions for custody, where medical attention is required, or accompanying an elderly person, a child under 12 or a person with disabilities, plus a ban on 'ambiguous' bathroom signage. The stated trigger was a July 2023 social-media complaint over the Jorge Chávez airport's gendered restroom labels. LGTBIQ activist Gianna Camacho called the measure discriminatory, warning that bathroom access would come to depend on security staff's personal judgment, including ID checks, and noted there is no record of sexual assault by trans women in women's restrooms.

name: Ciudad Autónoma de Buenos Aires
text: Argentina's national framework on legal gender recognition, gender markers, health care and hate-crime law applies here; the national record for Argentina covers the federal layer in detail. The sources assembled for the City record no municipal statute of its own on those matters and no city-level enforcement figure. Activists based in Buenos Aires told the Washington Blade, in reporting published on 10 April 2025, that police violence against trans and travesti sex workers in the city has become more common since the current national government took office, and that harassment and hate speech have risen. The account supplies no incident counts and no dates for individual cases, and no later City-specific instance is documented in these sources. Emergency decree DNU 61/2025, published in February 2025, re-regulates the housing of transgender people deprived of liberty and invites the provinces and the City of Buenos Aires to adhere. It prohibits people who have legally changed gender from being housed in women's prisons when they are detained for sexual offences or violence against women. FALGBT and legal experts describe the decree as illegal and unconstitutional and are seeking judicial intervention. The sources do not record whether the City has adhered or how its prisons have applied the rule.

name: British Columbia
text: British Columbia stands under the national framework of Canada; the national record for Canada covers the federal layer in detail. No statute of the province restricts trans people's access to restrooms or other sex-segregated facilities, to gender-affirming care, or to gender-related name use in schools, and the province has enacted no hostile legislation of its own in these areas. British Columbia's human rights legislation lists gender identity and gender expression as prohibited grounds across employment, housing, and public and private accommodations. Complaints against private businesses proceed under that statute, since Charter equality guarantees do not bind the private sector directly. Section 15 of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms applies in British Columbia. The Supreme Court of Canada has interpreted the concepts of sex and physical disability in section 15 to include transsexuality, and section 15 reaches all laws and government institutions in the province, including law enforcement authorities. Those guarantees remain subject to reasonable limits under section 1 and to the notwithstanding clause in section 33. Vital statistics, including birth certificates and other identity documents, fall under British Columbia's provincial jurisdiction, so a gender-marker change on a provincial birth certificate is governed by the province rather than by Ottawa.

name: RegiÃ³n de ValparaÃ­so
text: Chile's national framework applies here; the national record for Chile covers the federal layer. Region-specific are the distribution of recorded anti-LGBTI discrimination cases and a municipal diversity-office structure. Movilh's XXIV annual human rights report, published in March 2026 and covering 2025, records that Valparaíso concentrated 51.32% of the anti-LGBTI discrimination cases recorded nationally in 2024, an increase of 80.93% on 2023. That is a share of recorded cases, not a per-capita rate, and no population denominator accompanies it; recorded cases reflect where monitoring organisations operate and where victims report, as well as where incidents occur. In 2025 recorded cases fell in Valparaíso and in the Región Metropolitana while every other region rose. Movilh reads the pattern as hostility moving toward regions where LGBTIQ issues have less visibility.

name: Antioquia
text: Colombia's national rules on identity documents, public access and detainees apply here; the national record for Colombia covers the federal layer in detail. Antioquia has no statute or decree of its own. Its record is a killing in Bello, near Medellín: on 5 April 2025 a video circulated showing Sara Millerey González Borja, a 32-year-old trans woman, beaten and thrown into a waterway in daylight while onlookers filmed; her legs, arms and hands were fractured, she could not swim, and she died of cardiac arrest the following afternoon. She was the third LGBTQ person killed in Bello during 2025, the two earlier victims being gay men. A clinic reportedly declined to treat her as an emergency because she had not been shot. Bello city hall was criticised for using her pre-transition name. President Gustavo Petro ordered an urgent investigation, and protests followed in several cities.

Prejudice and discrimination against LGBTI people remain present in a considerable part of the population. For a visibly gender-nonconforming visitor in central Bogotá, that is the social baseline the sources describe, and it sits alongside the capital's visible LGBTI presence. Claudia López Hernández became the first openly gay person to serve as mayor of Bogotá. Pride parades in the city rank among Colombia's large LGBTI events, and a Washington Post report describes thriving gay neighbourhoods in the capital.

text: Madrid stands under Spain's national framework for legal gender recognition; the national record for Spain covers the federal layer in detail. The region was among the first in Spain to pass a gender-identity law, adopting its statute in 2016 alongside the Islas Baleares and the Región de Murcia and after Extremadura in 2015, later amended by Ley 17/2023. After the 2023 regional election, the new government of the Comunidad de Madrid repealed the region's non-discrimination law, repealed the regional ban on conversion therapy as it applies to trans people, removed the penalties that attached to conversion therapy, and repealed several trans legal recognitions. These measures act on the region's own guarantees and leave the national framework in place. Homophobic and transphobic discrimination and violence are described as significant problems in Madrid, and trans people and migrants are reported to face additional barriers within the city's LGBT population. The Chueca district is the centre of the city's LGBT life, and MADO, held annually in late June or early July, is among the largest Pride events in the world and draws millions of attendees. COGAM, founded in 1986, is the city's most influential LGBT organisation; the city government maintains an Oficina de Atención a la Diversidad Sexual y de Género; and Arcopoli works against discrimination and violence.

name: Bourgogne-Franche-Comté
text: France's national framework covers identity documents, criminal law, anti-discrimination protection, legal gender recognition and marriage; the national record for France covers the federal layer in detail. The region's one documented restriction concerns public assembly: the Côte-d'Or prefecture barred the Dijon Pride march from the city centre in June 2025. The Dijon march was not a new event. Pride marches have been held in Dijon, Chalon-sur-Saône and Auxerre since 2013, reported by France 3 Bourgogne, so the ban fell on a gathering with more than a decade of local history rather than a first-time assembly. No region-specific rule on identity documents, entry, healthcare access, facilities or screening was identified in the sources.

name: Occitanie
text: Occitanie stands under the national legal framework of France; the national record for France covers the federal layer in detail. The region-specific record is the opinion issued on 25 May 2021 by the CGLPL, the national inspectorate of places of deprivation of liberty, whose visits covered two facilities in Toulouse: Toulouse-Seysses prison and the Toulouse central police station. The opinion concerns eight transgender women held in those Toulouse facilities. It documents isolation imposed on detainees because of their trans status, and staff who had received no training on trans issues. It further finds that the depathologisation law of 18 November 2016 (n° 2016-1547) was never written into prison rules or into healthcare guidance, so the statutory change of status had no operational effect on how trans detainees were held or treated. The inspectorate's recommendations bearing on the region call for financed research, policies against discrimination, and suitable procedures for searching and for assigning detainees whose civil-status sex does not match the identity they present. For a trans visitor, the operative exposure in Occitanie is custody: police custody at a central station and detention at a prison are the settings where the documented failures occur, and the placement and search practices described apply regardless of how a person presents in ordinary daily life.

name: Jakarta Special Capital Region
text: Jakarta stands under Indonesia's national framework; the national record for Indonesia covers the federal layer in detail. What is specific to the Special Capital Region is a police practice of raiding private LGBT gatherings under pornography and morality provisions rather than under any Jakarta statute naming LGBT people. The raid series runs back a decade. In May 2017 police arrested 141 people at what was described as a gay sex party in Jakarta. On 21 May 2017 officers detained 144 people at the Atlantis Gym sauna, ten of whom were charged. In October 2017 police arrested 51 people at a sauna in Central Jakarta, of whom six were charged. All of these cases were pursued under the pornography law. The pattern continued in 2025. On 1 February 2025 police detained 56 people at a hotel in South Jakarta, described in reporting as a gay party. On 24 May 2025 nine people were detained after a raid on a different hotel in South Jakarta. Offences of this kind can carry up to 15 years' imprisonment. City government, not only the police, has acted against transgender residents. In March 2018 the Jakarta Social Agency declared transgender waria 'socially dysfunctional' and held trans women in city-run rehabilitation centres unless they signed statements promising not to repeat their offence. For a trans visitor the operative exposure in Jakarta is attendance at a private gathering: a hotel party, a sauna, a rented venue. The charges that follow are laid under broad pornography and morality provisions with long sentences available, and the sources record no Jakarta statute creating offences specific to LGBT people.

name: Mahārāshtra
text: The national record for India covers the federal layer in detail. Maharashtra's own inventory contains no state-specific findings on transgender law, enforcement, identity documents, facilities or care access.

name: Delhi
text: Delhi sits within India's national framework on legal recognition, criminal law and identity documents; the national record for India covers the federal layer in detail. The source inventory records no Delhi-specific statute, enforcement action, court ruling or violent incident. The only Delhi-specific signal is a press conference in the city at which the trans activist Grace Banu said the community sought "recognition without invasion" and "rights without humiliation" (BBC). The gathering states the position of advocates in the capital; it does not describe a change in law or policing practice there.

name: Seoul
text: Seoul stands under South Korea's national framework; the national record for South Korea covers the federal layer in detail. On 2 July 2024 the Seoul Central District Court, with presiding judge Chung In-jae, dismissed the government's appeal in a damages action brought by a transgender plaintiff identified as A, and the judgment became final when neither side appealed further. The court awarded 300,000 won (about $240) of the 3 million won claimed. It held that a police officer's advice to an LGBT person in the middle of legal transition to avoid public restrooms for a period infringed personal rights, and that the right to use restrooms comfortably is a fundamental and universal human right. The ruling addresses police conduct rather than venue policy. It establishes that advice of this kind from an officer is unlawful in Seoul. It does not by itself require any particular venue, school or business to admit a trans person to a given restroom.

name: Quintana Roo
text: Quintana Roo stands under the national framework of Mexico; the national record for Mexico covers the federal layer in detail. The state's own law governs legal gender recognition, marriage, adoption, hate-crime liability and the prohibition of conversion practices. Quintana Roo enacted legal gender recognition in 2020. On 15 December 2023 the state congress banned conversion practices, following Morelos. The reform prohibits and sanctions efforts to correct sexual orientation and gender identity, commonly called conversion therapies, with penalties of two to six years in prison and fines of 1,000 to 2,000 times the daily UMA value. It applies across the state, including the tourist corridors of Cancún and the Riviera Maya. The state penal code treats crimes motivated by sexual orientation or gender as hate crimes, and the state ratified the 2011 federal constitutional ban on sexual-orientation discrimination. Marriage in Quintana Roo has been open to couples without regard to gender since 2012. Two marriages were performed in Kantunilkín in November 2011, annulled by the governor in April 2012, and reinstated on 3 May 2012 after the state conceded that its Civil Code sets no gender requirement. That silence in the Civil Code is the operative basis on which a trans visitor's marriage would be recognised in the state. The state congress legalised adoption by same-sex couples in August 2022.

name: Selangor
text: Selangor sits within Malaysia's federal framework; the national record for Malaysia covers the federal layer in detail. Two further layers operate inside the state. The Syariah Criminal Offences Enactment 1995 binds Muslims, and Selangor's Islamic religious department polices appearance and public conduct under it. In February 2021 the Federal Court struck down provisions of the Syariah Criminal Offences Enactment 1995 as exceeding the state's legislative power. The ruling did not decriminalise anything under the federal Penal Code, which continues to apply in Selangor as elsewhere. Selangor's Sharia court has imposed custodial sentences with corporal punishment on same-sex conduct: five men received six to seven months' imprisonment with six strokes of the cane in a case documented by the Human Dignity Trust profile updated 16 December 2025. State authorities in Selangor issued an arrest warrant for a trans businesswoman, Nur Sajat, who failed to appear in court in 2021 to answer charges of "insulting Islam" based on her attire, and announced the deployment of 122 religious-affairs officers to locate her. She subsequently fled to Thailand, was permitted to remain under UNHCR protection, and later settled in Australia. The deployment was cited by Human Rights Watch and Justice for Sisters, in a report released 10 August 2022, as evidence of how far authorities go to enforce rigid gender norms. At least 1,733 people had attended state "rehabilitation programmes" as of June 2021, under a crackdown on the LGBT community that the Human Dignity Trust records as ongoing since the 2018 election. Human Rights Watch and Justice for Sisters found that these state programmes internalise discrimination and foster self-hatred. Investigations into LGBT people documented by Human Rights Watch and Justice for Sisters covered Selangor alongside Kuala Lumpur, Negeri Sembilan, Kelantan, Penang, Pahang and Kedah.

name: Johor
text: Johor is one of thirteen Malaysian state jurisdictions and stands under the national framework: the federal Penal Code applies in full within its borders, and Johor maintains its own Sharia enactment binding on Muslims. The substance of both layers is set out in the national assessment. In November 2023 the Johor state government announced plans to establish conversion-therapy centres to "rehabilitate" LGBT people. The announcement is a formal statement of policy by the state administration rather than a criminal provision, and it is the clearest documented expression of official hostility from this state's government in the record. The conversion-therapy announcement sits within a national pattern of state-conducted "rehabilitation" programmes: at least 1,733 people had attended such programmes as of June 2021, under a crackdown running since the 2018 election. Human Rights Watch and Justice for Sisters' state-conducted investigations, published 10 August 2022, covered Kuala Lumpur, Selangor, Negeri Sembilan, Kelantan, Penang, Pahang and Kedah; Johor was not among the states investigated in that reporting, so no Johor-specific enforcement incident is documented in this record.

name: Johor
text: Johor stands under Malaysia's federal framework, and the national record for Malaysia covers that layer in detail. In November 2023 the Johor state government announced plans to establish conversion-therapy centres to "rehabilitate" LGBT people. The announcement is a formal statement of policy by the state administration rather than a criminal provision, and it is the clearest documented expression of official hostility from this state's government in the record. Human Rights Watch and Justice for Sisters' state-conducted investigations, published 10 August 2022, covered Kuala Lumpur, Selangor, Negeri Sembilan, Kelantan, Penang, Pahang and Kedah; Johor was not among the states investigated in that reporting, so no Johor-specific enforcement incident is documented in this record.

name: Malacca
text: Malacca is one of the thirteen states of Malaysia, standing under the federal Penal Code, the state Sharia enactments and the national enforcement record; the national record for Malaysia covers the federal layer in detail. No Malacca-specific finding was identified in the sources reviewed. The Human Dignity Trust Malaysia country profile (last updated 2024) and the Human Rights Watch report of 10 August 2022, produced with Justice for Sisters, are national in scope and neither disaggregates its material to the state level, so the national assessment applies to a visitor to Malacca.

name: Abuja Federal Capital Territory
text: Abuja Federal Capital Territory stands under Nigeria's national framework, and no territorial variation from it was identified in this inventory: the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 and the criminal provisions it reinforces apply in the capital as they do elsewhere, and the national layer is carried by the parent record. The territory's documented trans-specific killing is that of a 33-year-old transgender TikToker known as Abuja Area Mama. BBC News reported on 9 August 2024 that her beaten and bruised body was found along the Katampe-Mabushi expressway in the Banex/Wuse II area of Abuja on Thursday 8 August 2024, hours after she posted a final video, having previously expressed fear for her life. A police statement described the victim as "a man fully dressed in female clothing with no means of identification". Abuja police chief Benneth Igweh ordered a "thorough and discreet" investigation. The Dial (Issue 25) reports that six months after the killing, no suspects had been charged despite that promised investigation. The same reporting records a petition of nearly 6,000 signatures demanding her murder be investigated as a hate crime. This is the most recent documented trans-specific killing in this record; no later instance is documented for the territory. The legal floor her killers faced, as set out in the same reporting, includes the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 reinforcing colonial-era laws criminalising same-sex activity as "carnal knowledge against the order of nature" punishable by up to 14 years' imprisonment, bans on same-sex marriage and civil unions, gay organisations and public LGBTQ+ expression, no legal route to change gender, and cross-dressing bans under Sharia in the north and in the Nigerian military. The BBC article notes that although Nigerian laws guarantee freedom from discrimination, mass arrests and detention of LGBTQ+ people are common, especially in northern states. UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office travel advice for Nigeria, reported by Sahara Reporters on 19 August 2026, warns LGBT+ travellers of arrest, violence, attacks, blackmail and intimidation. The advisory states same-sex sexual activity is illegal and can attract lengthy prison sentences, that some northern states operating under Sharia law can impose the death penalty, that the law extends to people who help arrange or conduct same-sex marriages and criminalises activities involving gay groups and organisations, and that breaching curfews or movement restrictions could expose travellers to arrest and detention. This advisory is national in scope and carries no Abuja-specific breakdown.

name: Abuja Federal Capital Territory
text: Abuja Federal Capital Territory stands under Nigeria's national framework, with no territorial variation identified. The national record for Nigeria covers the federal layer in detail. The territory's documented trans-specific killing is that of a 33-year-old transgender TikToker known as Abuja Area Mama. BBC News reported on 9 August 2024 that her beaten and bruised body was found along the Katampe-Mabushi expressway in the Banex/Wuse II area of Abuja on Thursday 8 August 2024, hours after she posted a final video, having previously expressed fear for her life. This is the most recent documented trans-specific killing in this record; no later instance is documented for the territory. The reporting sets out the legal floor her killers faced: the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 reinforcing colonial-era laws criminalising same-sex activity as "carnal knowledge against the order of nature" punishable by up to 14 years' imprisonment, bans on same-sex marriage and civil unions, gay organisations and public LGBTQ+ expression, no legal route to change gender, and cross-dressing bans under Sharia in the north and in the Nigerian military. name: Lima
text: Lima stands under the national framework of Peru, and the national assessment carried by the parent record applies here. No separate departmental or municipal regime modifying that framework was identified in the sources. Jorge Chávez international airport in Lima had installed signage reading "for all persons with female identity" and "male identity". The national norm approved in Congress on 2 April 2025 bars such "ambiguous" signage, and article 5 of the fused bills 6505/2023-CR and 8457/2023-CR prohibits entry to and use of public sanitary facilities by any person whose biological sex does not match the sex for which the facility is designated, subject to listed exceptions. The inclusive signs at Lima's international gateway fall inside that prohibition, so a trans visitor should expect facilities across the department to be designated by birth sex rather than by identity. Enforcement of the restriction, as described by LGBTIQ activist Gianna Camacho, would reduce to security staff judging for themselves whether a woman entering a facility is trans and demanding her national identity card (DNI). The sources document no guidance, oversight or complaint route governing that judgement. The human-rights institute IDEHPUCP of the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru, in Lima, reported on 15 April 2025 in an analysis by Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte that the plenary approved the fused bills on Wednesday 2 April 2025, exempt from a second vote. The authors call article 5 direct legislation conditioning basic rights on a "biological sex", a violation of the equality and non-discrimination principle, and note that trans people, though framed as aggressors by the rule, are more often the victims of violence and discrimination. On 12 February 2023 Rubí Torres Silvano, a 31-year-old trans woman and sex worker, was kidnapped from jirón Chancay in central Lima by the "Los Gallegos" extortion gang and killed with roughly 30 gunshots. The most recent documented killing of a trans woman in Lima in this record is that case of 12 February 2023; no later instance is documented. The Agencia Presentes report of 22 July 2024 records state inaction that bears on accountability for that case: no official system records victims' sexual orientation, and hate crimes go unsanctioned. The sources record no outcome in the Rubí Torres Silvano case.

name: Municipalidad Metropolitana de Lima
text: Lima operates under Peru's national framework on gender identity, public facilities, identity documents and hate-crime protection; the national record for Peru covers the federal layer. The bathroom bill approved unanimously by the Congressional Women and Family Commission on 20 February 2025 obliges removal of "ambiguous" signage, and its text names the signage at Jorge Chávez International Airport, reading "for all persons with female identity" and "male identity". That airport is the first site where that removal would apply, and those signs currently direct arriving trans passengers to a facility. Gianna Camacho, a trans human-rights defender, warns enforcement will mean identity-document checks by security staff deciding who may enter a bathroom, a practice she describes as discriminatory and grounded in prejudice; in the capital this discretion sits with staff at municipal buildings, transport terminals and private venues. Violence in the capital is documented. On 12 February 2023 the gang Los Gallegos kidnapped Rubí Torres Silvano, a 31-year-old trans sex worker, from jirón Chancay in the central city and killed her with roughly 30 gunshots. The Observatory report on hate crimes cites the case as an example of the pattern in Lima.

name: Ankara
text: Turkey's national framework applies here; the national record for Turkey covers the federal layer in detail. Ankara's distinct exposure is institutional: the presidency, the Ministry of Family and the drafting machinery for national legislation sit there, so the penal-code package reported by Human Rights Watch on 29 October 2025 is drafted, and would be enforced, through institutions operating in Ankara. The leaked draft, known as the 11th Judicial Package, would amend the penal code to criminalise conduct treated as contrary to biological sex and general morality, punishable by up to three years in prison, and to punish participation in same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies with up to four years. It would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care, surgery included, from 18 to 25, attach mandatory permanent infertility and repeated evaluations at government-approved hospitals, expose health professionals performing such interventions to fines and up to seven years in prison and trans people receiving care the authorities deem illegal to up to three years, and allow courts to order pretrial detention. Fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association opposed the draft, which had not been enacted as of the reporting date. Kaos GL's 2025 annual report concludes that hostility toward LGBTI+ people became explicit state policy, centred on the presidency and implemented through the Ministry of Family, both Ankara institutions. It records censored broadcasts, artistic events cancelled or banned, and an LGBTI+ association closed for the first time in years, with criminal cases opened against 11 of its members. The same report counts six violations of the right to life over the year, three recorded as hate-motivated, with trans people the most affected group, alongside a rise in torture and ill-treatment violations to 89 from 51 the previous year. Turkey compiles no official hate-crime statistics, so these figures rest on the organisation's own monitoring; with no general homicide or violence denominator in the sources, the six deaths cannot be expressed as a rate or compared with the risk borne by the general population.

name: Eskişehir
text: Eskişehir sits within Turkey's national framework; no city-specific statute or local protection body is recorded here, so the national record for Turkey covers the federal layer in detail. The region-specific record concerns public assembly. In June 2021 police blocked Eskişehir's first Pride parade, reaching the area hours before the scheduled meeting time and carrying out identity checks. Organisers were not permitted to hold a press meeting or conduct the parade, and police detained 20 people on the grounds of violating the ban on the march. The ban is the clearest local signal that even in a university city, local authorities have suppressed the local Pride event. For a trans visitor, the documented exposure in Eskişehir is assembly and identity checks at LGBT-related gatherings rather than any city-level criminal provision.

name: Gaziantep
text: Gaziantep shows no divergence from Turkey's national LGBTI+ position; the national record for Turkey covers the federal layer in detail. The province has no criminal provision of its own, no local ordinance and no documented municipal policy bearing on trans residents or visitors, and the exposure a visibly trans visitor meets there is the national one, enforced locally by provincial authorities and courts. The national meeting-and-demonstrations law that monitors record as the basis for detentions and prosecutions of LGBTI+ activists applies within Gaziantep, with no Gaziantep-specific practice mitigating or intensifying that enforcement documented. No Gaziantep case, incident, court ruling or police operation appears in the sources reviewed, so the visitor risk assessment for the province rests on the national position.

name: İstanbul
text: İstanbul stands under the national framework in force across Turkey; the national record for Turkey covers the federal layer in detail. What is specific to the city is the assembly ban and the policing of trans women on its streets. The Governorship of İstanbul has denied permission for and locally banned Pride parades since 2015 on security and public-order grounds, with the 2016 to 2018 bans stated explicitly; one source dates the ban to 2014. Water cannon were used against marchers on 29 June 2015. The 2014 march drew more than 100,000 participants, the largest LGBT event recorded in Turkey. Suppression escalated after the ban. In 2021 police blockaded the route and used tear gas, arresting 25 people. On 26 June 2022 riot police dispersed the march at Taksim Square, blockaded streets in the adjacent Cihangir neighbourhood, shut down public transport to the square and detained 373 people, among them the photojournalist Bülent Kılıç; those held were released after a night in custody. The district governor's offices of Kadıköy and Beyoğlu had banned all Pride Week events for seven days. Arrests continued at 113 in 2023 and 11 in 2024, three of them minors, after organisers moved Pride out of Taksim Square into other public spaces and issued false meeting calls to evade police. Policing extends to trans women going about ordinary business. On 31 July 2025 İstanbul police stopped around 20 trans women in Beyoğlu for identity checks, recorded their names and filmed them; the report describes the operation as profiling.

name: İzmir
text: İzmir lies within Turkey's national legal and security framework; the national record for Turkey covers the federal layer in detail. No İzmir-specific findings on trans legal status, policing, detention, facilities or healthcare access appear in the source inventory. The legislative and enforcement developments documented for 2025 are national in scope or recorded in other Turkish cities, and the national assessment applies to visitors here.

name: American Samoa
text: American Samoa's own criminal code does not punish consensual sodomy. The first sodomy statute, enacted in 1963, covered male homosexual and heterosexual conduct and did not address lesbian conduct; the Fono's 1979 revision, effective in 1980, retained prohibition only for public acts, prostitution, conduct involving minors and conduct with persons unable to consent. The age of consent is 16, regardless of gender or sexual orientation. Same-sex marriage is not licensed. On 20 March 2003 the Senate rejected a bill introduced by Representative Sua Carl Schuster that would have outlawed it, after the House Judiciary Committee recommended the bill be killed; at the committee hearing fa'afafine resident Tifanny Poutasi testified that fa'afafine do not seek marriage with men, describing them as men expressing femininity through dress and speech and citing Christian upbringing. In July 2015 Attorney General Talauega Eleasalo Ale was reviewing whether the United States Supreme Court's 2015 marriage-equality ruling reached the territory and said he did not know, while the Governor stated that it did not apply, citing the territory's preamble, its constitution, Christian values and its unorganised and unincorporated political status. No same-sex couple had filed an application at that point, and a 2026 law-review article by two attorneys practising in American Samoa records that none has applied since. In January 2016 the Senate unanimously confirmed former Attorney General Fiti Alexander Sunia as a District Court judge after he told confirming senators, including retired High Court associate judge Senator Tauolo Manaia Fruean, that he had not read the 2015 ruling, that the district court does not deal with it, and that he would not perform weddings for same-sex couples unless local laws change. In July 2024 an on-island survey by Dr Daniel Hall, a constitutional and comparative law professor at Miami University, tested whether the territory's ban would survive a challenge under the Fourteenth Amendment. As of mid-2024 the ban is treated locally as operative and its constitutional durability as an open question. The 2026 article reaches the opposite conclusion on the law, holding that the 2015 ruling does apply despite those official statements and that the territory would have to issue a marriage certificate to any same-sex couple that applied; it sets out a litigation path through the High Court of American Samoa first, with the Territorial Registrar as defendant, then the United States Department of the Interior. Since 13 December 2022 the territory has been obliged to recognise, though not perform, same-sex marriages performed legally in another jurisdiction, with equal treatment for same-sex and opposite-sex couples. The territory's marriage code does not specify the sex of the parties. It refers to the age of 'the male' and 'the female' on a form in which parties identify as 'son' and as 'daughter'. Gender markers on local documents are changeable within limits. The High Court of American Samoa has held that birth certificates may be altered only to correct information that was erroneous at the time of recordation or to reflect a name change due to adoption, and the Office of Vital Statistics reads that ruling as covering applications from transgender people: it changes the name on a birth certificate when presented with a name change order, and may change the gender marker with medical documentation of the sex change. Documented trans-specific legal matters in the territory concern employment and criminal proceedings. In June 2023 a federal civil action cited a hostile work environment in a transgender woman's lawsuit against the territorial government over her gender identity, and in September 2023 the United States Justice Department secured a settlement with the American Samoa Government resolving an employment-discrimination case involving harassment of a transgender employee. In February 2023 a 51-year-old man was charged with sexual abuse of a 16-year-old transgender teenager; that charge is the most recent documented instance of violence against a trans person in this record, no later instance is documented, and no outcome for the charge is stated. Public climate combines cultural recognition with religious conservatism. Fa'afafine, defined as people born male who embody both male and female traits, are described in Samoan scholarship as a recognised and integral part of traditional Samoan culture, and the Society of Fa'afafine in American Samoa, formed in 2010, campaigns for the community and runs annual events; the first Pride festival was held in August 2016 in Utulei, and beauty pageants among the fa'afafine community draw family support. Society is nonetheless highly religious, conservative attitudes on gender and sexuality dominate, and open displays of affection between couples, same-sex or opposite-sex, may offend. A 2009 travel column described reserved public behaviour as expected of people of all orientations in the territory.

name: Guam
text: Guam's own law governs legal gender recognition, and it requires surgery. The national record for United States covers the federal layer in detail. To amend a birth certificate, a transgender person must give the Office of Vital Statistics a sworn statement from a physician confirming sex reassignment surgery, after which the office amends the certificate. The Motor Vehicle Division Supervisor issues an amended driver's licence on receipt of a sworn physician statement that the applicant's sex has been surgically changed. A 2018 attempt to remove the surgery requirement failed. Senator Fernando Esteves introduced a bill in May 2018 to permit legal gender change on judicial permission with a letter confirming gender identity supported by documentation from a certified psychologist, social worker, therapist or other licensed professional, with no surgery required. The Legislature postponed a vote on 13 December 2018 pending medical and law enforcement process issues, and the bill failed on 17 December 2018 by a 6 to 7 vote. Surgery remains the condition for both documents. Marriage recognition for a trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship rests on the 2015 ruling. Chief judge Frances M Tydingco-Gatewood struck down Guam's prohibition on same-sex marriage in June 2015 after an April 2015 lawsuit by Loretta Pangelinan and Kathleen Aguero, who had been denied a marriage licence. The ruling took effect at 8am on Tuesday 9 June 2015, making Guam the first United States territory to recognise same-sex marriage. Private consensual adult non-commercial sexual conduct has been lawful since the 1978 reform of the Criminal Code; the penal code in force before that, ordained in 1933, had criminalised sodomy, fellatio and cunnilingus with between one and ten years' imprisonment. Guam hosts a large permanent United States military presence, so federal policy on transgender service members bears directly on personnel stationed on the island.

name: United States Virgin Islands
text: The U.S. Virgin Islands is a United States territory; entry, travel documents and airport screening follow United States federal rules — the national record for United States covers the federal layer in detail. The territory's human-rights statute prohibits discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation and gender identity, the protection a trans visitor can invoke. In March 2017 the territory's Attorney General issued an official interpretation holding that the anti-discrimination law applies to transgender students, extending protection into education. In 2015 the Superior Court of the U.S. Virgin Islands struck down refusal of marriage licences to same-sex couples as unconstitutional; later federal recognition settled the question nationwide, and a married trans visitor can rely on their marriage here. The historic sodomy statute, applicable since 1957, has been replaced and is no longer in force.

name: Northern Mariana Islands
text: The Northern Mariana Islands is a US commonwealth. Travel documents, immigration and airport screening are governed by United States national rules rather than by commonwealth law, and the national layer of this assessment sits with the United States record. Consensual same-sex conduct is not criminalised. Marriage between same-sex couples has been recognised in the commonwealth since 2015, and the first such marriage on Saipan was officiated on 27 July 2015. A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship can expect that relationship to be recognised. Adoption has been available to same-sex couples since 2015. Legal gender change is permitted in the Northern Mariana Islands provided the applicant has undergone the specified medical process, so identity documents can be brought into line with presentation, subject to that medical requirement. Commonwealth law provides for enhanced sentencing in hate-motivated crimes. Public Law 22-32, signed in January 2023, amends the Commonwealth Code with criteria covering offences motivated by sexual orientation and gender identity. This is the principal commonwealth-level protection with direct bearing on gender-identity-motivated violence. There is no comprehensive commonwealth nondiscrimination statute covering gender identity. Commonwealth-level protections extend to government employees only, and recourse beyond federal complaint channels is limited. As of 27 September 2026 the Movement Advancement Project scored the territory's sexual orientation policy at 3.5 of 22 and its gender identity policy at minus 2 of 25, an overall rating of 1.5 of 47, classified as Low with a negative gender-identity score.

name: Northern Mariana Islands
text: The Northern Mariana Islands is a US commonwealth; travel documents, immigration and airport screening follow United States national rules, and the national record for United States covers the federal layer in detail. Consensual same-sex conduct is not criminalised. Marriage between same-sex couples has been recognised in the commonwealth since 2015, and the first such marriage on Saipan was officiated on 27 July 2015. A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship can expect that relationship to be recognised. Adoption has been available to same-sex couples since 2015. name: Saudi Arabia
text: Saudi Arabia has no codified penal code. Judges apply an uncodified interpretation of sharia drawn from the Quran and the Sunnah, so penalties for same-sex conduct and gender nonconformity are unpredictable: flogging, fines, lengthy or indeterminate imprisonment, and death in the most severe cases. Same-sex relations are illegal for men and women. Deviation from traditional gender norms is itself treated as a criminal offence, not merely incidental conduct attached to another charge. No legal gender recognition is available, there is no protection from discrimination, and no relationship recognition. LGBTI organisations cannot register anywhere in the country. Enforcement is documented. In October 2021 five Saudi men were arrested in the Northern Borders province after filming themselves in women's clothing and posting the footage on social media. In April 2005, dozens of Saudi men caught dancing and behaving as women at a Jeddah party described as a 'gay wedding' were sentenced in a closed trial without defence lawyers to a total of 14,200 lashes and up to two years' imprisonment. Foreign nationals face deportation as a penalty for homosexuality, and work-visa applicants must pass an HIV test on arrival and before permit renewal, with infected foreigners deported. Entry and exit visa paperwork does not ask about sexual orientation but does ask nationality, sex, religion and marital status. In September 2013 Gulf states discussed a proposal to test and ban gay foreigners, which officials later downplayed as a mere proposal. Enforcement reaches travellers for expression, not only conduct on the ground. Amnesty International documented a business analyst arrested at Riyadh airport on 31 August 2024 as he was returning to the UK with his family, targeted for social media posts published before he arrived in the country. A Pakistani transgender woman, Mohammad Amin, died in Saudi custody after a roundup with 34 others in Azizia prison, Riyadh. Pakistani activists say she was beaten with clubs and hosepipes, aggravating a chronic heart condition; Saudi authorities attributed the death to a heart attack, and the family and trans-rights activists dispute the official account. The most recent documented death in this record is that case; no later instance is documented. Being transgender is not recognised in Saudi Arabia. UK foreign travel advice states that trans travellers could face difficulties with dress codes and access to medical care, and advises couples to avoid public affection. The Saudi Tourism Authority's FAQ page was updated in May 2023 to state that all visitors, including LGBTQ visitors, are welcome, and VisitSaudi states that privacy will be respected; homosexuality nonetheless remains illegal and enforcement is described as not universal. Tourist visas were introduced in 2019 alongside a Public Decency Law fining public displays of affection and immodest clothing. In June 2022 officials in Riyadh seized rainbow-colored products in a crackdown framed as curbing promotion of homosexuality, explicitly targeting 'the young generation' and confiscating children's hair accessories, backpacks, pencil cases and rainbow-striped crayon packs. A3M Global Monitoring's 2024/25 LGBTQ+ Risk Map places Saudi Arabia among the least safe destinations for LGBTQ travellers, in a ranking that also lists Somalia, Yemen, Uganda, Afghanistan, UAE, Tanzania, Malaysia and Pakistan. The ranking is by overall placement, not by a per-capita or incident rate.

name: Ireland
text: Ireland's legal gender recognition framework is the Gender Recognition Act 2015 (No. 25 of 2015), commenced on 4 September 2015 by S.I. 369/2015 and amended by statutory instrument through 2026. Adults change legal gender by self-declaration, with no psychological evaluation and no medical requirement. Ireland is one of only 11 European countries whose law allows gender recognition through self-determination alone. Irish law recognises no nonbinary identity. A visitor travelling on a passport carrying an X marker has no equivalent domestic marker available, and Equaldex records gender change as legal with no restrictions alongside no nonbinary recognition. A November 2019 report by Minister Regina Doherty recommended extending self-declaration recognition to 16- and 17-year-olds with parental consent. The Criminal Justice (Hate Offences) Act 2024 has been in force since 31 December 2024 and explicitly covers sexual orientation, gender identity and sex characteristics; it has been described as the toughest and broadest hate crime legislation in Europe. Gender identity was formally added to the protected grounds of the Prohibition of Incitement to Hatred Act 1989 by the Cabinet in October 2022, and that Act penalises a first offence of incitement to hatred on sexual orientation grounds with a fine of up to €1,000 or six months' imprisonment, rising to €10,000 or two years on indictment. Garda reports of hate crimes rose 15% in 2025, with racism and xenophobia the most common recorded motives. A University College Dublin study reported on 3 July 2025 found that discrimination against sexual and gender minorities in Ireland has increased, documenting a rise in anti-LGBTQ+ prejudice despite the protective statutory framework. Healthcare access is the sharpest documented gap. A Transgender Europe study published in November 2022 put the wait for a first gender-affirming healthcare appointment in Ireland at between 2.5 and 10 years, with a single public trans health provider that was severely understaffed. Patients at that service were reportedly denied care for reasons including receiving social welfare, having an ADHD diagnosis, or not answering "highly sexualized questions" in "the right way", pushing many into the private sector or into self-administered hormone therapy. Reporting in The Journal in April 2025 found that years-long waiting lists for multidisciplinary gender-care assessment were pushing some trans people underground and away from official channels; the HSE defends its comprehensive multidisciplinary model of care. Trans-specific legal exposure in the custodial system is documented in the case of Barbie Kardashian, a trans woman who held a Gender Recognition Certificate and a Department of Social Protection certificate recognising her as female. She was found guilty at Limerick Circuit Court in May 2022 of seven counts of threatening to kill or cause serious harm to her mother, and acquitted in October 2024 of separate alleged threats to a fellow prisoner and a prison officer at Limerick Prison. As of late 2025 a proposed amendment to the Gender Recognition Act 2015 that would limit the effect of a GRC "for the purposes of imprisonment" had passed its first legislative stage; the most recent documented development in this record is that first stage, and no later passage is documented. In Foy's case, Judge McKechnie reproached the government for inaction and said Ireland was "very much isolated" among Council of Europe members on transgender recognition. The historical record includes the 1889 case of John Bradley, assigned female at birth, imprisoned at Grangegorman prison after disclosing. Equaldex records gender-affirming care as legal but restricted for minors, hate-crime protections covering SOGI, employment and housing discrimination protections covering sexual orientation only, intersex infant surgery not banned, and conversion therapy not banned, alongside 61% public support for LGBT openness, ranked #4 of 26 regions. Senator Fintan Warfield's March 2018 bill to ban conversion therapy, which explicitly would not have banned supportive practices for questioning LGBT youth, remained stalled in the Seanad as of April 2022 despite a coalition pledge to ban it. Reporting machinery for a visitor who experiences an incident includes an anonymous online hate-crime reporting form run by Belong To LGBTQ+ Youth Ireland, with rights information and links to Equal Status Acts protections. Open expression is visible: Dublin Pride drew an estimated 60,000 people in 2018, alongside the Dublin Gay Theatre Festival, the GAZE International LGBT Film Festival and gay-friendly venues nationwide. Community facilities include the Outhouse LGBTQ+ Centre and gay and gay-friendly pubs, restaurants, clubs, bars and saunas, with visible LGBT scenes in Dublin, Cork, Galway, Limerick and Waterford. In April 2019 Dún Laoghaire–Rathdown County Council cancelled Glitter Hole's Drag Storytime, first calling it "not age-appropriate" and then citing a high level of homophobic abuse on social media. The Irish state itself was the historical source of hostility: male homosexual acts were criminalised under the Offences Against the Person Act 1861 and Criminal Law Amendment Act 1885 until decriminalisation in 1993, and in Norris v. Attorney General (1983) the Chief Justice invoked the "Christian nature of [the Irish] State" to uphold those laws. On 19 June 2018 Taoiseach Leo Varadkar and Justice Minister Charles Flanagan issued formal public apologies to the LGBT community for state-caused suffering and criminal convictions. A Guardian retrospective on 23 December 2025 marking a decade of the 2015 Act described it as a move away from Ireland's Catholic past, carrying first-person accounts of self-declaration and updated documents alongside renewed calls over remaining gaps in trans rights and healthcare.

name: Switzerland
text: Legal gender recognition in Switzerland runs on self-declaration. Since 1 January 2022 any person registered in a Swiss municipality may change their sex marker, their first name, or both by personal declaration before a civil registrar. No surgery, medical diagnosis or court proceeding is required. About 350 people had used the route in its first months, according to SWI swissinfo reporting of 7 August 2022. Civil marriage has been open to same-sex couples since 1 July 2022 under the Marriage for All reform, which also opened adoption and IVF and passed a referendum with 64.1% approval. A trans visitor whose relationship would be read as same-sex under local birth-sex status can marry in Switzerland and have that marriage recognised on the same terms as any other couple. Federal criminal law has punished public incitement to hatred, denigration or discrimination on sexual-orientation grounds under Article 261bis of the Criminal Code since 1 July 2020. UNHCR's Switzerland guidance records that discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity is prohibited; the criminal provision itself is framed on sexual-orientation grounds. Reported anti-LGBTIQ+ hate crime is rising. SWI swissinfo, citing LGBTIQ Helpline monitoring, gives roughly six reported hate crimes per week and 309 cases in the reference year, with reports up fivefold since 2020. These are raw counts of LGBTIQ+ reports generally rather than trans-specific figures, and the sources supply no population denominator. The OSCE/ODIHR 2024 Hate Crime Report records that Swiss criminal law contains no general hate-crime provision, that such acts are addressed under the anti-discrimination provision, that recording does not sufficiently distinguish hate crimes, and that police do not record bias motivation. The Federal Council adopted Switzerland's first National Action Plan against hate crimes against LGBTIQ persons 2026-2030 on 28 January 2026. Its three pillars are support and protection of victims, prevention of hate crime, and monitoring of violence, with implementation coordinated by the Federal Office for Gender Equality. SWI swissinfo covered the plan's publication in 2026. Placement of trans detainees is governed cantonally. This record documents no federal provision, no Federal Supreme Court case law and no special trans units. The canton of Basel-Stadt inserted an explicit gender-identity clause into its detention law (JVG) adopted by the Grand Council on 13 November 2019: section 2 requires separation of female and male detainees and states that the detained person's gender identity is respected as far as possible, and the prison directorate may deviate from the separation rules in consultation with the referring authority. Conversion therapy remains unregulated at federal level. The National Council adopted a national ban on 12 December 2022 by 143 votes to 37 with 11 abstentions, and the bill is still pending in the Council of States. Cantonal bans are in force in Neuchâtel (2023), Valais and Vaud (2024). The Federal Council states that such therapies are ineffective and cause significant suffering to young people subjected to them and would breach professional duties, and a 2026 report confirms it condemns the practice while leaving further federal regulation open. Support services documented in this record include a helpline launched by Swiss LGBT groups in November 2016, Dialogai (founded 1982) offering helplines and advice, and Transgender Network Switzerland, which advises on legal sex and name changes, the armed forces and asylum.

name: Hungary
text: Hungary's civil regime bars transgender people from correcting their legal gender. Administrative refusal became routine from 2018, and the barrier became explicit law in May 2020, when the government legislated by emergency decree during the COVID-19 pandemic to stop passports and identity cards from reflecting an acquired gender, including for people already legally recognised, while redefining nem (sex) in the civil code as immutable biological sex. Human Rights Watch records the 2020 provision as banning legal gender change for transgender and intersex people. The practical consequence for a visitor is documentation. No domestic administrative route to correcting a gender marker is documented in this record, and a trans visitor should expect to enter, be screened and be recorded under the marker assigned at birth, carrying papers that may not match presentation. Two European Court of Justice rulings bear directly on how a trans person's data is handled in Hungary. In the Deldits judgment of 13 March 2025, on a reference from the Budapest High Court in an immigration case, the Court held that Article 16 GDPR requires the national register authority to rectify recorded gender data where it has changed and no longer complies with the accuracy principle of Article 5(1)(d); this is the operative authority for updating gender markers on official records. In September 2024 the CJEU Advocate General called on Hungarian authorities to correct a transgender refugee's gender marker in national registries. In April 2026 the Court of Justice ruled that Orbán-era anti-LGBTQ laws, including the under-18 gender-change ban argued under child-protection law, breached EU rules on several levels, significantly finding a breach of Article 2 of the EU Treaty, an unprecedented finding against founding values. The ruling came nine days after Hungarians voted in the election that ended Fidesz rule. The political climate has shifted but the legal architecture remains in force. Fidesz lost the 12 April 2026 election, ending 16 years of Viktor Orbán's rule, with the Tisza party taking 138 seats. Budapest Pride spokesperson Johanna Majercsik named restoration of the right to assembly as the most urgent issue and said anti-queer laws can be repealed with a two-thirds majority; the Tisza party's silence on LGBTQ+ rights under Péter Magyar raises questions about the pace of change. An April 2026 analysis characterises the outcome as a return to democratic baseline rather than liberation, detailing a constitutional architecture of erasure that forces trans Hungarians to carry mismatched documents. Public assembly has been the site of documented hostility. In June 2026 Hungary held its first Budapest Pride in the post-Orbán era, with tens of thousands marching in the 31st Budapest Pride against the backdrop of the anti-LGBT laws adopted during Orbán's rule. In 2014 Jobbik displayed a sign reading 'The Parliament Does Not Want Any Deviants' at Budapest Pride and verbally abused attendees. Official hostility is documented in statements and legislative acts. The May 2020 National Assembly resolution rejecting the Istanbul Convention attacked the treaty's measures as promoting 'destructive gender ideologies' and 'illegal migration.' In October 2020 Orbán said 'gays are to leave our children alone.' After a 2021 children's book by the Labrisz Lesbian Association, Fidesz launched a smear campaign confusing homosexuality with pedophilia, and the government-linked media giant Mediaworks published an article calling Labrisz pedophiles without proof; Labrisz won at first instance but the Curia ruled in November 2022 that the article did not violate its right to good reputation, and the case was appealed to the Constitutional Court. In April 2026 the ECJ found that the 2021 child protection law discriminated against and scapegoated LGBTI residents. Same-sex activity has been legal in Hungary since 1961. Unregistered cohabitation has been recognised since 1996 for any couple, including same-sex couples, giving specified rights with inheritance only by testament and a widow's pension after 10 years. Registered partnerships for same-sex couples have been available since 1 July 2009, carrying the same rights as spouses except adoption, assisted reproduction and taking a surname, while same-sex marriage was banned by the 1 January 2012 constitution. Same-sex couples cannot adopt jointly, stepchild adoption is limited to married different-sex couples, and IVF and donor insemination are unavailable to lesbians in a registered partnership. A December 2020 constitutional amendment further banned adoption by same-sex couples and restricted single-parent adoption. In September 2026 Prime Minister Péter Magyar announced intent to repeal the ban on adoption by same-sex couples. In January 2018 the European Court of Justice ruled that asylum seekers may not be subjected by authorities to psychological tests in order to determine their sexual orientation. In 2017 Orbán welcomed the World Congress of Families, a group designated a hate group by the Southern Poverty Law Center, at the National Parliament. A 2025 national report by the Hungarian Helsinki Committee and Háttér Society, part of the EU-funded 'Strengthening the rights of LGBTIQ detainees in the EU' project, documents the situation and rights of LGBTIQ people in Hungarian detention amid the current legal and political climate.

name: Slovenia
text: Slovenia's legal position is favourable for trans visitors. Same-sex relations are lawful nationwide, LGBTIQ organisations can be registered, and legal gender recognition is available. An international LGBTIQ rights organisation's country overview, updated on 12 March 2026, assesses Slovenia as among the most progressive countries in Central and Eastern Europe on LGBTIQ rights, citing comprehensive antidiscrimination legislation enacted from 2016 that expressly covers sexual orientation and gender identity. Antidiscrimination coverage extends beyond the 2016 law. Rules in force since 2003 bar sexual-orientation discrimination in education. A bill approved on 21 April 2016 and promulgated on 9 May 2016 prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity and gender expression. Pride in Ljubljana produced the year's most documented anti-LGBTIQ violence. Roughly 3,500 people marched on 17 June 2023 under the slogan Več skupnosti, en boj, with President Nataša Pirc Musar attending. During and after the march, attendees faced threats, insults, flag burnings and property destruction. Police received a report of an unidentified suspect who physically assaulted two people, causing minor injuries, and investigated attacks, theft and public-order disturbances. A representative of the Pride Parade Association said there had not been such hostility for years. Outside the Pride period, the pattern is under-recorded rather than absent. The US State Department's 2023 human-rights report records no laws criminalising consensual same-sex conduct and no reports of state-condoned violence, but notes that authorities logged violence incidents without tracking case numbers, and that local NGOs describe violence against LGBTQI+ people as prevalent and under-reported. In June 2023 a woman wearing a rainbow flag was assaulted near the Ljubljana Pride route, marchers had eggs thrown at them, and rainbow flags were burned on video. Recorded bias incidents in 2023 appear in the regional LGBTIQ rights review published in 2024: Legebitra documented 17 cases of bias-motivated speech and TransAkcija documented 25 cases of direct bias-motivated incidents. These are raw counts from two organisations, published without a population denominator or a coverage statement, so they describe recorded volume rather than per-capita risk. Support for hate-crime victims runs mainly through civil society. The ENACT national report, published in January 2025 under the EU's CERV-2023 programme, found that civil society provides LGBTI hate-crime victims with counselling, advocacy and safe spaces, while LGBTI people who turn to generic victim-support services meet heteronormative hurdles; it also documents institutional shortcomings in the anti-LGBTI hate-crime framework. Enforcement of the written protections is weak. The 2016 antidiscrimination law and the earlier education rules are described as vague, open to interpretation and very rarely enforced. Partner recognition is the weakest documented area. Reporting from 25 July 2006 records that Slovenia passed a law legalising same-sex marriage but confined the ceremony to the two partners and a local community registration official, excluding friends and relatives; gay and lesbian organisations welcomed it as a concrete step while calling the law insufficient. Parliament adopted a further marriage law in March 2015, and that law was rejected in a referendum later the same year. Four days before the vote, Pope Francis urged Slovenian politicians to support the family. Whether these provisions remain the governing regime is not established by the sources in this record.

name: Estonia
text: Legal gender recognition has been available in Estonia since 1992, when Kristel Regina on 6 April 1992 became the first person in independent Estonia to correct her name and gender on a birth certificate through a medical expert committee. The procedure is currently regulated by the Common Requirements for Medical Operations for Gender Reassignment in force since May 1999 and parts of the Vital Statistics Registration Act in force from January 2014, both originating in a 24 April 1997 decree of Minister of Social Affairs Tiiu Aro. An applicant applies to the Ministry of Social Affairs for a first committee appointment, and hormone replacement therapy requires a ministerial decree to begin. Hormone therapy has not been mandatory since February 2022, genetic testing is no longer required, surgical intervention has not been required since April 1997, and there is no forced sterilisation; minors have access to puberty blockers. A second application, generally a year after the first and not earlier, plus a committee decision submitted in writing to a county town local government, corrects Population Register data; name change is possible earlier under the Names Act, and birth gender can be restored through the same procedure. The recognition committee in place since March 2000 disbanded itself in 2020, leaving no accessible procedure in practice; in July 2021 Minister Tanel Kiik replaced it with a committee relying on self-identification plus mental health diagnosis. Between 1999 and 2021, 186 people began the process (91 trans women, 95 trans men), with around a hundred applicants since the procedure reconvened in early 2022. In May 2023, Minister Signe Riisalo and committee chairman Dr. Kai Haldre stated intent to move to self-identification-based change and correct markers for non-binary people; Equaldex records that legal gender change currently requires medical diagnosis and that there is no nonbinary recognition. Discrimination on the basis of gender identity is implicitly prohibited in all areas under the Gender Equality Act since 1 May 2004, as interpreted to extend to transgender and non-binary individuals, covering less favourable treatment connected to gender and gender-based harassment; employers may not demand gender stereotypes, bar clothes matching gender identity, or treat an applicant unfairly at interview when documents do not match appearance. The F&M Global Barometer of Transgender Rights time series (2011–2024) records that workplace, housing and healthcare anti-discrimination laws include gender identity, while hate speech and hate crime legislation does not include gender identity. Equaldex records no hate-crime protections, employment discrimination prohibited on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity, housing discrimination protections covering sexual orientation only, conversion therapy not banned, and bathroom access protected. The Ministry of the Interior confirmed in December 2021 that legal sex can be changed while remaining married without automatic invalidation if preconditions were met at marriage; annulment requires a court decision on application by a spouse or in the public interest, with the Minister of the Interior holding a discretionary but not obligatory right to apply on public-interest grounds, each case assessed individually. Justice Ministry guidance stated that after societal changes in the previous five to six years, same-sex marriage could no longer be said to be contrary to Estonian public order; fewer than 10 marriages in Estonia had become same-sex marriages as a result of gender reassignment of one spouse by that point.
