A national LGBT+ equal-opportunities action plan was approved in December 2025, developed over about two years by the Equality Policies Department at the Ministry of Economic Affairs and Communications and approved by Economy Minister Erkki Keldo, setting targets across education, healthcare, employment and legal-framework reform, with the legal framework to be updated to support gender identity and expression protections. The ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2026 records that Estonia joined 16 EU states urging Hungary to revise its anti-LGBTI laws, that the Foreign Minister publicly supported Tallinn Pride, and that missions flew rainbow flags. Outright International's country overview (updated 12 March 2026) notes advocacy continues for self-determination-based legal gender recognition and for hate-speech and hate-crime laws covering gender identity. The EU FRA LGBTIQ survey III country sheet for Estonia (2024) reports that 62% of LGBTIQ respondents avoid holding hands with a same-sex partner (EU-27: 53%), 40% avoid certain locations for fear of assault (EU-27: 29%), 38% are open about being LGBTIQ (EU-27: 51%), and work discrimination stands below the EU average (12% vs 19%). Equaldex ranks Estonians first of 30 EU regions for hiding being LGBTIQ at work. A 2023 survey recorded that 61% believed someone assigned male at birth could identify as a woman or vice versa, alongside 75% support for anti-discrimination law, 53% for same-sex marriage and 71% for civil partnerships. Trans-specific lethal violence is documented in the 14 July 2023 sentencing to 12 years of a man who murdered a Jamaican trans woman in a Tallinn Old Town bar in 2022, stabbing her more than 34 times while she tried to flee; the court rejected a provocation claim. The F&M Global Barometer records no known murders of gender-identity minorities in its Estonia time series. The most recent documented trans-specific killing in this record is the 2022 case sentenced in July 2023; no later instance is documented. Transgender people are allowed to serve openly in the Estonian military, though some non-heterosexuals may reportedly be sent for additional medical consultation; Defense Resources Agency head Merle Ulst stated same-sex attraction tendencies are generally not an obstacle to military service unless a mental or behavioural disorder diagnosis connected to homosexuality may become an obstacle. Community infrastructure includes the Estonian Association for Transgender People, founded in 2022 for trans and non-binary people, preceded by Gendy, a support group and helpline founded 8 August 1993, and the Estonian Lesbian Union of 13 October 1990, which accepted transgender people. Estonia became the first Baltic state with marriage equality in June 2023, effective 1 January 2024, allowing same-sex couples to marry and jointly adopt; public support for marriage equality stood at 53% in 2023 (75% among people in their twenties) versus 34% in 2012. All same-sex relations are legal nationwide. LGBTI organisations can register in Estonia. A trans visitor in Estonia would be read under birth-sex status for relationship classification purposes; fewer than 10 marriages had become same-sex marriages through one spouse's legal gender change as of December 2021, and such a marriage remains valid without automatic invalidation. The TGEU/ILGA-Europe 2018 compliance report on Estonia's implementation of Council of Europe Recommendation CM/Rec(2010)5 covers hate crimes and data collection, safety of LGBT people deprived of liberty, hate speech, association, expression, transgender-specific health and private-life issues, employment, education, housing, sports and asylum.

name: Taiwan
text: Legal gender recognition in Taiwan remains gated by a 2008 executive order requiring sex-reassignment surgery before a gender marker can be changed on the national ID. An estimated 90% of trans people are blocked from obtaining a document that matches their presentation, which turns every ID-requiring interaction, including clinic visits and airport security checks, into a potential site of distress and disclosure. The Ministry of Health and Welfare has recognised gender self-determination as a human right since 2013, but the surgical requirement stands. On 19 August 2024 a Taipei court denied a transgender woman's request to change her ID marker without surgery or a psychological evaluation, and the rights group supporting her indicated that an appeal was likely. No later ruling on this question is documented in this record. During 2025 no tangible policy change occurred on abolishing the surgery requirement. Public facilities are a documented friction point. The Ministry of Environment announced in August 2024 an investment of NT$280 million over four years to double gender-neutral public bathrooms nationwide from 623 to 1,246 by 2029; in the same reporting, 17% of trans and gender-neutral survey respondents who reported discrimination said it occurred in public restrooms or changing rooms. In November 2025 an LGBTQ+ rights group found that only 5 of 149 government-listed all-gender toilets met the required standards, including clear all-gender signage. Political climate: anti-gender movement activity has been rising, with organisations backing external anti-trans policy agendas and the Taiwan Solidarity Party calling for a 'two genders' position; pending changes to conscription criteria could actively harm trans people. Public visibility also continues: the 7th annual Taiwan Transgender March in Taipei in November 2025 drew an estimated 3,000 people despite rain, with international participants, calling for an end to discrimination against trans people. Broader protections that a trans visitor may see cited: discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation, gender identity and gender characteristics has been banned in education nationwide since the Gender Equity Education Act of June 2004 (fine of NT$100,000 for schools discriminating in admission, instruction or assessment); employment discrimination based on sexual orientation has been prohibited since the 2007–08 amendments to the Employment Service Act and the Act of Gender Equality in Employment, with fines of NT$300,000 to NT$1,500,000; the Long-Term Care Services Act (January 2017) contains an anti-discrimination clause covering sexual orientation and gender identity; and Judicial Yuan Interpretation No. 748 (24 May 2017) held that the Constitution's Article 7 grounds of discrimination are 'illustrative, rather than exhaustive,' so sexual orientation is protected by the right to equality. Private, consensual same-sex sexual activity between adults is legal, with an age of consent of 16 regardless of sexual orientation or gender identity. Assisted reproduction remains restricted: the Artificial Reproduction Act limits IVF and other assisted reproductive technologies to legally married heterosexual couples, specifically excluding same-sex female couples and single women, and no 2025 policy change on expanding assisted reproduction is documented. Same-sex couples can adopt, with full adoption rights granted since May 2023, replacing the partial stepchild-only rights in place since 2019; Taiwan law also permits single individuals, including individual LGBT people, to adopt depending on circumstances. Youth and education: a November 2018 referendum passed a question to ban LGBT-inclusive sex education in schools (Question 11) and rejected the pro-inclusion Question 15; the Education Minister said LGBT content would be reviewed against the result. Following that referendum, suicide hotlines reported a 40% surge in calls from LGBT individuals, particularly adolescents and young adults. A 22 February 2018 Ministry of Health and Welfare letter effectively banned conversion therapy, with violators liable under the Criminal Code or the Protection of Children and Youths Welfare and Rights Act.

name: Malaysia
text: Malaysia criminalises same-sex conduct and gender nonconformity under federal and state law. Sections 377A and 377B of the federal Penal Code punish "carnal intercourse against the order of nature", covering oral and anal sex, for any person regardless of gender or consent; the maximum penalty is 20 years' imprisonment plus whipping, recorded as mandatory. The offence reaches foreign nationals and tourists, and sodomy was first criminalised in 1871. Section 377D adds "gross indecency", an undefined offence carrying up to two years that remains a discretionary prosecutorial tool. Every state and the federal territories (Kuala Lumpur, Putrajaya) maintain Sharia enactments criminalising same-sex activity and gender nonconformity, including provisions against "a man posing as a woman". These apply only to Muslims, with penalties of up to three years, a RM5,000 fine and six strokes of the cane. Since the 1980s all 13 states have passed Sharia enactments institutionalising discrimination against trans people; all 13 bar Muslim men from "dressing as women" and three also bar "women posing as men", enforced by state Islamic religious departments with no legal definition of transgender dressing. The Selangor and Kelantan codes and the Sharia Criminal Code (I) Enactment 2019 cover "sodomy" and "sexual intercourse against the order of nature". The Federal Court struck down Selangor's section 28 in February 2021 and 16 Kelantan Syariah provisions in February 2024 on federalism grounds, without decriminalising anything under the Penal Code. The High Court separately denied a request to declare the Sharia prohibition on cross-dressing unconstitutional. Enforcement against consenting adults in private is uncommon and tourists are rarely targeted, but raids on queer venues are documented: a Kuala Lumpur gay bar was raided by police and religious enforcement in August 2018, a Halloween party with LGBTQ participants was raided in 2022, and 11 shopping malls were raided in May 2023 over Swatch Pride watches. In November 2024 Kelantan approved amendments to its entertainment law banning activities that promote LGBTQ behaviour. On 28 November 2025 police raided a male-only sauna in Chow Kit, Kuala Lumpur and arrested 208 men under section 377B, the largest such raid since 2022, with media pre-tipped and detainees' faces and personal details leaked; 17 civil servants identified among them were suspended. A magistrate rejected the remand extension as lacking ground under 377B, yet release was delayed, with over 130 held at one point including 31 foreign nationals whose embassies intervened. Justice For Sisters mobilised bailors and legal aid; on 2 December the Home Minister floated revisiting the provisions, and days later police raided another sauna in Penang. State-sanctioned targeting of trans people is documented. In July 2020 Religious Affairs Minister Zulkifli Mohamad Al-Bakri announced he had given the Federal Territories Islamic Religious Department (Jawi) "full licence to carry out its enforcement actions" against transgender persons; the International Commission of Jurists condemned the order and demanded its revocation. In 2021, 122 religious officers were mobilised to hunt Nur Sajat over "insulting Islam" before she fled to Thailand and gained UNHCR protection. Government-funded mukhayyam "rehabilitation" retreats had drawn 1,733 attendees by June 2021, and LGBT events and media content were censored. Violence against trans women is documented: a transgender woman was killed in Klang, a Kuala Lumpur suburb, in a report of 25 June 2019, the third such killing of a trans woman in Malaysia in fewer than two months, alongside police mistreatment and impunity. The most recent documented killing in this record is from 2019; no later instance is documented. The 2014 record documents the 2011 strip-search and sexual assault of Victoria by religious officials, repeated arrests of one woman over 20 times, and the mass arrest of 16 trans women at a wedding on 8 June 2014. Identity documents are a live battleground. In August 2016 the Kuala Lumpur High Court ordered the National Registration Department to update a trans man's identity card with his gender identity and chosen name, reasoning that Article 5(1) of the Federal Constitution guarantees a right to live with dignity as a male, but this judgment was overturned on appeal in 2017. The Registration Department routinely rejects gender-marker changes; the only successful documented change is historical, in 1975. A 1982 National Fatwa Council fatwa holds that sex is determined at birth and remains so after sex reassignment surgery, ending domestic sex-reassignment surgery for Muslims; it was never gazetted and so is not legally binding, but it bars Muslims from the procedure unless intersex. There is no explicit visa rule for transgender visitors; the only entry/deportation policy stated in the sources is a 2001 statement by then-Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad that Malaysia would deport any visiting foreign cabinet minister or diplomat who is gay. Sharia courts may commit women convicted of musahaqah to an approved home for up to six months (Federal Territories s.56, Kedah s.52, Selangor s.54, Sarawak s.53), and may order cross-dressing or other offenders into counselling or rehabilitation in a religious institution: up to six months in Kelantan (s.19-20) and Pahang (s.66), extended to up to one year by Terengganu's 2022 amendment. Trans people face discriminatory denial of health care and employment alongside arbitrary arrest, physical and sexual assault, and imprisonment; prison terms run from four months to three years with male-ward sexual violence. Conversion therapy is practised and openly promoted by politicians and religious leaders. The National Blood Centre of Malaysia prohibits homosexuals and bisexuals from donating blood. There are no Malaysian laws protecting the LGBTQ community against discrimination and hate crimes, and no same-sex marriage or anti-discrimination law. Same-sex couples have no route to recognition; at Cambridge Union in June 2019 Mahathir said Malaysia cannot accept same-sex marriage. The 1982 fatwa additionally ruled that marriages involving transgender people are invalid, though not gazetted; the single exception is the 1975 sharia marriage of transgender woman Sari Kartina in Johor Bahru. Hate speech rules do cover orientation: the Malaysian Communications and Multimedia Content Code 2022, s.6.1(ii), defines hate speech as material that denigrates or devalues a person on grounds including sexual orientation, enforced via s.211 of the Communications and Multimedia Act. In 1994 the government banned anyone homosexual, bisexual or transsexual from state-controlled media. Adoption is orientation-neutral under the Adoption Act 1952 and Registration of Adoption Act 1952, with no restriction on a single person adopting regardless of sexual orientation or gender identity.

name: Iran
text: The Islamic Penal Code criminalises all sexual activity outside heterosexual marriage. Articles 233 to 239 define the offences in anatomical terms and set 100 lashes for the receptive partner in sodomy, 100 lashes for intercrural sex, 31 to 74 lashes for other intimate acts between men, and 100 lashes for tribadism with death on a fourth conviction. The code does not distinguish consensual from non-consensual conduct, and NGOs report that in assault cases both victim and perpetrator are held criminally liable. The UK Home Office country report (CPIN, version 5.0, December 2025) records that the legal framework carries no discrimination protections of any kind and that convictions are frequently brought on the pretext of more severe charges. Outright International confirms that same-sex relations are illegal nationwide for both sexes. Transgender identity is legally recognised only through sex reassignment surgery. Under Article 20, Clause 14 a person who has had surgery may change name and gender on the birth certificate by court order; the CPIN states that recognition follows surgery, sterilisation and a lengthy legal process, and that an LGBT+ person living openly without recognised surgery is likely to face persecution. The state funds gender-reassignment surgery. Since the mid-2000s the government has provided grants of up to 45 million rials (about $1,240) and loans of up to 55 million rials (about $1,500) for the procedure, and the Ministry of Cooperatives, Labor, and Social Welfare required health insurers to cover it. Reporting in 2024 and 2025 describes the same policy as coercive: foreign patients travel for state-subsidised surgery while Iranian trans people face pressure to complete a binary transition or face legal penalty for living outside it. Identity documents can expose holders. New military identity cards have listed the exemption subsection applying to gay men and transgender individuals, who are classified as having mental disorders; 6Rang warned that the disclosure identifies them and puts them at risk of violence and discrimination. Authorities have restricted trans people's presence in public space. Tehran authorities publicly warned transgender people to avoid busy areas, an official advisory limiting where trans residents may be seen. Custodial violence against trans detainees is documented. Ghazal Marzban, an imprisoned trans rights activist, recounted rape in a Ministry of Intelligence detention facility in an open letter published by HRANA. 6Rang has documented forced anal or sodomy tests and degrading treatment of persons charged with homosexual conduct. The enforcement backdrop includes executions and mass arrests. Human Rights Watch recorded two men executed for homosexual conduct on 21 November 2005; records show at least 107 executions on charges related to homosexuality between 1979 and 1990, a raw count over an eleven-year period with no per-capita denominator supplied. Police in Isfahan raided a party in February 2008 and arrested 30 men held indefinitely without a lawyer on suspicion of homosexual activity, and an April 2017 IRGC raid on a private party in Isfahan Province led to 30 arrests, with detainees taken to Dastgerd Prison and told they would be executed. The most recent documented killing in this record is the May 2021 murder of 20-year-old Ali Monfared, allegedly by relatives; no later killing is documented here. Same-sex marriage and civil unions are not legally recognised, so a trans visitor in a relationship that would be locally classed as same-sex has no standing recognition of that partnership. Social treatment differs by direction of transition. Trans men are more visible socially and find acceptance more easily than trans women, who are often misgendered and placed in the same category as gay men. No legislation addresses discrimination or bias-motivated violence on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity. Security forces have harassed, arrested and detained individuals suspected of being gay or transgender, raided houses and monitored internet sites for information on LGBTI persons, and those accused of sodomy often face summary trials.

name: South Africa
text: The Constitution of the Republic of South Africa, 1996, prohibits unfair discrimination on grounds that include sex, gender and sexual orientation. The Promotion of Equality and Prevention of Unfair Discrimination Act of 2000 gives effect to that guarantee through the Equality Court, which hears complaints of unfair discrimination, hate speech and harassment on grounds including gender identity. The Prevention and Combating of Hate Crimes and Hate Speech Act, signed into law in May 2024, places sexual orientation, gender identity and sex characteristics inside a statutory hate-crime and hate-speech regime; its hate-speech offence requires a clear intention to be harmful, to incite harm or to promote hatred. Nothing in South African law criminalises gender identity or consensual adult sexual conduct. The common-law offences of sodomy and unnatural sexual act were struck down by the Constitutional Court in 1998 in National Coalition for Gay and Lesbian Equality v Minister of Justice, applied retroactively to 27 April 1994. A residual statutory inequality kept the age of consent at 19 for homosexual acts against 16 for heterosexual acts until the Criminal Law (Sexual Offences and Related Matters) Amendment Act of 2007 set a gender-neutral 16; the Constitutional Court confirmed the earlier inequality unconstitutional in Geldenhuys v NDPP in 2008, again retroactive to 1994. Legal gender recognition is available under the Alteration of Sex Description and Sex Status Act, in force since 2003, which allows a change of sex status in the population registry and identity documents and passports. The statute requires medical or surgical treatment, including hormone replacement therapy, though surgery is not obligatory; hormone therapy is available from age 16 and surgery from 18, or younger with parental consent. The medical requirement pathologises identity and locks some applicants out, and the binary sex classification excludes non-binary people altogether. Reform toward self-determination is pending but not enacted. Mismatched documents expose trans people to humiliation, denial of service and, in documented accounts, threats of arrest for fraud; a 2024 Gender Dynamix report records a trans woman refused help in filing a domestic-violence case at a police station after showing her identity document, with officers mocking her. In October 2021 the Department of Home Affairs announced plans for gender-neutral identification on South African identity cards, the first such move on the continent, with an identity-management document estimating 530,000 non-binary residents; officials confirmed the change would take a few years as it moved through consultation toward legislation, and no enacted instrument is documented in this record. Detention is governed by a binding precedent. On 14 November 2025 the Gauteng High Court sitting as an Equality Court ruled for transgender inmate Nthabiseng Beverly Mokoena against the Head of Johannesburg Correctional Centre and the Department of Correctional Services (Case 2024/070075), holding that refusing gender-affirming health care prescribed for a transgender inmate falls below the required standard of care and that refusing feminising clothing and accessories is likewise unlawful. The orders compel the department to provide prescribed medical care, including gender-affirming hormone treatment at state expense, to permit clothing and cosmetics expressing her gender identity, and to implement its own standard operating procedures for transgender inmates. The South African Human Rights Commission's National Preventive Mechanism welcomed the ruling the same day. The department has had a standard operating procedure for transgender prisoners in place, but rights organisations have questioned whether it is implemented in practice. Violence against visible trans women is documented. Aobakwe Mahlobo, a 23-year-old trans woman, survived an unprovoked assault at a Tshwane tavern on 26 December 2024, reported on 6 January 2025, leaving her with severe facial injuries and lasting physical and emotional scarring; an arrest was reported. That is the most recent documented attack on a trans person in this record, with no later instance documented. OUT LGBT Well-being's rights watch for December 2024 recorded five LGBTQIA+ murders that month, a raw monthly count with no population denominator, alongside the Tshwane case. Outright International's March 2026 overview reports that violence falls disproportionately on Black lesbian, transgender and gender-nonconforming people in townships. Older documentation alleges negligent police handling of killings of gay men between 2010 and 2013, and activists and ActionAid have condemned impunity around the murder and 'corrective rape' of lesbians, including pupils. Facility access remains contested in law. A 2024 academic analysis examines whether excluding transgender and non-binary people from gender-segregated bathrooms constitutes unfair discrimination under the Promotion of Equality and Prevention of Unfair Discrimination Act read with section 9 of the Constitution, and concludes that trans people do not in practice experience equal protection in facility access. Public opinion is comparatively favourable but uneven: an ILGA survey in 2017 found 67% backing equal rights for gay and lesbian people and 72% for transgender people, while a 2017 ILGA poll found 24% of South Africans still said people in same-sex relationships should be charged as criminals and 57% disagreed.

name: Pakistan
text: Pakistan's Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act 2018 recognises self-perceived gender identity and prohibits discrimination in education, employment, healthcare, housing and access to goods and services. Rules issued under the Act in 2020 introduced a neutral 'X' marker for administrative documents, and a 2010 Supreme Court order had directed free medical and educational facilities, microcredit schemes and job quotas for transgender people. These protections sit under an unresolved constitutional challenge. On 19 May 2023 the Federal Shariat Court, ruling across 12 shariat petitions, held that sections 2(f), 3 and 7 of the Act, covering the definition of gender identity, the right to self-perceived gender identity and inheritance, do not conform with the petitioners' reading of Islamic principles. In its reasoning the court speculated that the Act could facilitate the rape and sexual assault of women by men disguised as transgender women. Amnesty International called the ruling a blow to the rights of an already beleaguered group and had warned the government on 17 May 2023 not to adopt amendments violating human-rights standards. The struck provisions remain in force pending appeals, and the UK Home Office's November 2025 country note records ongoing legal disputes over the Act's status. Lethal violence against transgender women is documented in Karachi with specific dates. In November 2024 gunmen shot three transgender women at close range near Karachi, the second deadly attack on the community there in a week. On 21 September 2025 police found the bullet-riddled bodies of three transgender women shot dead on a roadside highway at Memon Goth, Karachi. A February 2026 report describes a wave of violence that has left Pakistani transgender people afraid to go out, including a night-time Karachi shooting in which activists Zehrish Khanzadi and Bindiya Rana were fired at through a door with three bullets and narrowly escaped. The most recent documented lethal incident in this record is the September 2025 Karachi highway killings; no later killing is documented here. Implementation failure, not absence of law, is the central problem identified by Justice Project Pakistan's policy brief: the 2018 Act's protections have not translated into safeguards against torture and ill-treatment in practice, and the brief makes custody and police-safeguard recommendations. A 21 October 2025 analysis in The News describes trans Pakistanis facing rejection by landlords, dismissal at hospitals and suspicion or ridicule at police stations despite the Act and 2020 Rules. Healthcare access is a documented failure point: in 2016, 23-year-old transgender activist Alisha was shot seven times and left to bleed to death at Lady Reading Hospital in Peshawar while staff argued over whether to take her to the men's or women's ward, and men there taunted her friends. Some transgender women use hormones and silicone under unsupervised conditions because sex-change surgery is rarely available in Pakistan. An active retrograde legislative push is also documented: Senator Mushtaq Ahmad has proposed a government 'gender re-assignment board' that would control transgender people's official gender identity. Consensual same-sex acts remain criminalised under Pakistan Penal Code section 377, carrying two years to life imprisonment, with the definition unclear and, per Human Dignity Trust (December 2024), only men criminalised. The UK Home Office's November 2025 note assesses that LGBT+ people are unlikely to face state persecution, while the US State Department's 2021 Human Rights Report records societal violence and discrimination and notes that transgender persons (khwaja sira) face harassment and violence despite some legal recognition. Same-sex partnership has no legal recognition. The Constitution does not mention sexual orientation or gender identity; Part II section 37 pledges to protect marriage and the family, and Part IX section 227 requires all laws to be compatible with Islam as defined by a government-appointed Islamic council. Article 496 of the Penal Code punishes dishonestly going through a marriage ceremony knowing one is not lawfully married with up to seven years' imprisonment. A small clerical body in Lahore (Tanzeem Ittehad-i-Ummat) declared transgender marriages legal under Islamic law in June 2016, but the Federal Shariat Court's May 2023 ruling on self-perceived gender remains unresolved on appeal. In 2005 a tribal council in the Khyber region ordered a man who married a fellow tribesman to leave the area or face death. Open expression carries personal risk. Pakistani media censors LGBTQ-related news stories: the government blocked Queerpk.com in late 2013, and the Pakistani edition of the International New York Times (Express Tribune) left a blank space where a photo accompanying a same-sex marriage story should have appeared. Penal Code provisions reinforce this: Article 292 bans sale, distribution, exhibition, ownership or importation of 'obscene' books, pamphlets or images; Article 294 prohibits 'obscene' public acts, songs, music or poems; Article 153 penalises inducing students to political activity that disturbs public order with up to two years' imprisonment; and Article 141 designates an assembly of five or more persons an 'unlawful assembly' if its common object is to commit any offence. LGBTQ Pakistanis are generally reluctant to be open about their identity for fear of forced marriage, honour killings, humiliation, blackmail or violence, and a person living openly is likely to face treatment from non-state actors such as Islamist and terrorist groups. A 2016 article by a young Pakistani man in the UK-based Gay Star News had his surname omitted for his security.

name: Uganda
text: The Anti-Homosexuality Act 2023 is in force. It provides the death penalty for "aggravated homosexuality", a category that includes sexual intercourse with a person younger than 18; twenty years' imprisonment for homosexuality or attempted homosexuality; ten years for purporting to contract a same-sex marriage or knowingly attending a purported same-sex marriage ceremony; and three years for a minor convicted of homosexuality. A person convicted of homosexuality or attempted homosexuality cannot be employed in a childcare facility even after release. A provision of the 2023 bill that would have criminalised identifying as gay or non-binary with ten years' imprisonment was proposed but ultimately excluded from the Act. On 4 April 2024 Uganda's Constitutional Court upheld the Act's core provisions, including the death penalty in certain circumstances and penalties of up to 20 years, rejecting public-participation challenges; the same court had voided a similar 2013 law on procedural grounds. Same-sex marriage has been constitutionally prohibited since 29 September 2005, when President Museveni signed a constitutional amendment stating "Marriage between persons of the same sex is prohibited." Enforcement and abuse since the Act: Human Rights Watch's 26 May 2025 report "They're Putting Our Lives at Risk" documents arrests, shelter raids, evictions and public outings unleashed by the Act, with many LGBT people in hiding. In February 2026, Ugandan police arrested two women in Arua after neighbours reported them for allegedly kissing in public, one of the first known arrests under the 2023 Act. In June 2021, a raid on the Happy Family Youth Shelter in Kampala resulted in forty-four arrests, with police claiming an illegal same-sex wedding was being held; several detainees alleged police performed invasive anal examinations. In January 2024 a transgender woman in Kampala was mobbed and beaten into a two-week coma after a false TikTok allegation, sheltering with 20 others at a Kampala safe house. A Reuters report of June 2024 described rights violations against Uganda's LGBTQ community as escalating, according to a pressure group. Document and identity recognition: in October 2021, trans woman Cleopatra Kambugu Kentaro was issued identification documents identifying her as female, the first Ugandan to have a change of gender legally recognised. The source does not address broader document or legal gender recognition processes beyond this case. Digital exposure: Access Now (15 May 2025) reports that digital entrapment via dating and social apps is one of the main tactics authorities use against LGBTQ+ people in Uganda, and that the companies behind popular apps do too little to protect users. Amnesty International's 23 October 2024 report "Everybody Here Is Having Two Lives or Names" documents widespread technology-facilitated gender-based violence including doxxing, impersonation, hacking and disinformation, and finds the AHA 2023 has fostered a climate of impunity forcing people and organisations to alter how they present themselves online. The US State Department's travel advisory for Uganda includes LGBT-specific warnings under its 'Do Not Travel' advisory (the page was not retrievable at research time, HTTP 403). Historical pattern of targeting: in October 2010 the tabloid Rolling Stone published names, addresses, photographs and hangouts of 100 allegedly gay and lesbian Ugandans with a call for their execution; activist David Kato was murdered in 2011 shortly after winning a lawsuit against the paper. Pride Uganda was cancelled in August 2017 after threats of arrest, and in June 2012 the government banned 38 NGOs accused of promoting homosexuality. LGBTQ people in Uganda face severe discrimination actively incited by conservative political, religious and community leaders, with violent attacks and harassment often performed or incited by state officials. The most recent documented killing in this record is from 2011; no later instance is documented here.

name: Kuwait
text: Kuwait's Penal Code Article 198 was amended in 2007 by Article 199 bis, which criminalised an indecent act in a public place or imitating the appearance of a member of the opposite sex, punishable by up to one year in prison or a fine of 1,000 dinars, about US$3,500. The amendment was proposed by MP Waleed Al-Tabtabaei and passed with overwhelming parliamentary support. Human Rights Watch found that the only known targets of the provision were transgender people, who could neither change their legal documents nor obtain protection from the policing it authorised. In February 2022 the Constitutional Court struck down the provision as unconstitutional, after an individual who had been targeted by police challenged it. The ruling removed the criminal exposure the article created; it did not end the dress-code policing that preceded and outlasted it. Human Rights Watch called on parliament to repeal the law outright rather than leave it to judicial invalidation. A Library of Congress entry records the same Constitutional Court ruling against Article 198. Discrimination by officials against transgender people persisted after the 2022 ruling, according to a 2023 assessment one year on. Social and employment discrimination continued, and the ruling was not treated as a step toward recognition of transgender rights. In 2017 Instagram personality King Luxy was arrested in Kuwait for allegedly looking too feminine and held for two weeks before release. Penal Code Article 193 still punishes consensual sexual relations between men by up to seven years, and adultery by up to five years, as recorded in Human Rights Watch's World Report 2024 covering events of 2023. Public morality laws are strictly enforced, with prosecutions of LGBTQ people documented. A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship, or read as such under birth-sex status, faces this exposure regardless of the 2022 Article 198 ruling. Gender segregation and enforced dress codes make transgender people especially vulnerable across the region, per a 2016 overview essay; the film 'The Danish Girl' was banned by censors in Kuwait. In August 2023 Kuwait banned the film 'Barbie', citing promotion of homosexuality. The communications regulator CITRA blocked LGBTQI+ material including advocacy and legal information, per the 2023 US State Department country report, and no candidate ran for National Assembly openly acknowledging LGBTQI+ orientation. In September 2013 it was announced that Gulf Cooperation Council states had agreed to discuss a proposal for some form of 'testing' to detect homosexuality in order to deny entry to gay foreigners; officials later insisted it was only a proposal, with concern over hosting the 2022 FIFA World Cup in Qatar cited as a reason for backtracking. No implemented entry-screening regime is documented in this record. Foreign nationals found to be infected with HIV are deported, whereas Kuwaiti citizens who are infected are entitled to outpatient medical care through a specialised infectious disease hospital. HIV incidence remained under 0.1 percent through 2021 figures, with males aged 25 to 49 accounting for 47 percent of those with HIV; the National Assembly criminalised intentional transmission of HIV in 1992. No known association or charity exists in Kuwait to campaign for LGBTQ rights or organise educational and social events. In 2007 a group of Kuwaitis applied to the Ministry of Labor and Social Affairs to form such an association and never received a formal reply; in July 2019 they announced they would reapply after a Ministry of Commerce crackdown on LGBTQ symbols such as rainbows in shops.

name: Oman
text: Oman criminalises same-sex conduct under the 2018 Penal Law (Royal Decree 7/2018), with penalties of up to three years' imprisonment; the offence applies to both men and women, and prosecution may proceed without a prior complaint where the act causes a public scandal. A trans visitor in a relationship that Omani law would class as same-sex falls within the same exposure. Gender expression itself is an offence target. Article 266 of the Penal Law covers impersonating the opposite sex and entering women-only venues while disguised, carrying 1 month to 1 year's imprisonment, and Article 266(d) is the provision through which gender non-conformity is punished. Article 265 covers public indecency (10 days to 3 months plus a fine of OMR 100 to 300), and Articles 267 and 268 cover producing or sharing content judged to violate public morals, offline and online, with penalties of up to 1 year and 10 days to 1 month respectively. The Cyber Crime Law 2011 (Articles 17 and 31) has also been used against LGBT expression, carrying 1 month to 3 years plus a fine of OMR 100 to 3,000. Enforcement against gender-nonconforming people is documented. In January 2018 the Royal Oman Police arrested a group of men in Salalah for dressing as women after photographs circulated on social media; in September 2018 a Salalah preliminary court sentenced two of them to four years' imprisonment and fined them OMR 3,000 each for cross-dressing and sharing the photos, and two further men to three years with the same fine for appearing in the video. In July 2020 the Royal Oman Police announced arrests of 'men in women's clothing' after Snapchat photographs from a private Salalah party circulated, and separately arrested an Asian expat wearing an abaya and niqab during a women-only park hour at Al Buraimi. Human Rights Watch wrote to Omani authorities on 13 July 2020 about these arrests and convictions under the 'imitating the opposite sex' provision. The most recent documented enforcement instance in this record is from July 2020; no later case is documented here. Border treatment of visibly gender-nonconforming visitors is documented first-hand. On 27 February 2023 a genderqueer/non-binary Indian model-activist arriving at Muscat International Airport on a 10-day tourist visa reported that friends cleared immigration while she was held for a separate examination, made to remove her shirt, and touched inappropriately by officers. Prosecution risk is heightened by digital evidence and surveillance. Article 49 of the Penal Law provides a dual-criminality exception that permits prosecution, and cases are often triggered by digital evidence discovered during unrelated investigations rather than by a family complaint. The state ISP Omantel enables surveillance, and outing carries both social and criminal consequences. Foreign nationals convicted of a felony face mandatory deportation under Article 60 (permanent), with deportation of 3 to 15 years available for misdemeanours. Oman bans legal gender recognition and explicitly bans gender-affirming healthcare, according to a joint stakeholder submission by Cairo 52 and White Tent dated 6 August 2025 to Oman's 4th-cycle Universal Periodic Review. The submission documents systemic legal and institutional discrimination against transgender people, states that recent legislative developments have deepened criminalisation of gender expression, and reports that Oman has ignored earlier UPR recommendations on gender identity, expression and health access. It recommends ending criminalisation, adopting an anti-discrimination law, and permitting legal recognition. Advocacy for LGBT rights is itself a criminal act in Oman, as in other Gulf countries; activists use social media aliases to protect their identities, with rare exceptions. Assembly and advocacy are restricted under the Civil Associations Law. A September 2013 proposal by Gulf Cooperation Council states to devise a test screening out gay foreigners was described by officials as a mere proposal and was not implemented, with concern over hosting the 2022 FIFA World Cup in Qatar cited as a reason for backtracking.

name: Ukraine
text: Being trans is not criminalised in Ukraine. Sexual activity between men was decriminalised in 1991, sexual activity between women was never an offence, and the age of consent is 16 irrespective of gender or sexual orientation. Legal gender recognition exists and does not require surgery. A 2011 Civil Code amendment allowed transgender people who had undergone gender-affirming surgery to change their name, an August 2016 court ruling ordered passport and document changes for two transgender people without requiring sterilisation, and from December 2016 new identity documents are issued before any surgical procedure. Married applicants and those with an underage child may also apply. The gatekeeping attached to that process was removed at the same time: applicants no longer need permission from a Ministry of Healthcare special commission, no longer petition a board of mental health professionals, and no longer spend 30 days in a psychiatric hospital, typically in wards with patients considered mentally ill. Two constraints on the procedure are still stated in the sources: transsexuality is classified as a psychiatric disorder in Ukraine, and sex reassignment surgery is reported as legal only for people over the age of 25. Diagnosis is the pressure point. ZMINA reported on 28 July 2026 that trans women in Ukraine now find it harder to obtain a diagnosis, citing stereotypes, corruption and wartime barriers. A Human Rights Watch essay of 15 May 2024 describes cross-border networks arranging assessments and diagnoses for trans women in Ukraine, including what it calls the often-humiliating confirmation by the Military Medical Commission; a Ukrainian activist quoted there describes commission hours of 8am to 8pm and a gatekeeping logic in which, if a doctor says she is a woman, the state can decline responsibility. Border crossing carries a specific exposure. Since martial law, holders of male gender markers have been stopped at the border by the State Border Guard Service, according to documentation by the Ukrainian NGO Gender Stream, which also assists transgender people with processing or reissuing documents for legal border crossing. Whether being trans grounds an exemption from mobilisation was still an open question at Trans Forum 2026 in Kyiv in early June 2026, and homosexuality is not a legal ground for exemption from military service. Protection machinery is partial. Parliament banned gender identity discrimination at work on 12 November 2015 as a condition of EU visa-free travel, and in December 2022 unanimously passed a media bill banning hate speech and discrimination based on gender identity. The Criminal Code provides harsher penalties only for racial, national or religious intolerance, not gender identity; an April 2020 draft adding gender identity and sexual orientation as hate-crime grounds was withdrawn in September 2020 for lack of those terms in existing legislation. A rule-of-law roadmap approved by the Cabinet on 14 May 2025 scheduled, by the second quarter of 2026, administrative liability for discrimination, gender identity and sexual orientation as criminal aggravating circumstances, criminal liability for public calls for violence, and free secondary legal aid; whether those measures are in force is not resolved in the sources. Family recognition is contested. Article 51 of the 1996 Constitution defines marriage as a voluntary union between a man and a woman, and no registered partnership law is in force despite a 2015 government action plan promising a civil partnership bill by 2017, a Ministry of Justice statement in 2018 that religious pressure blocked it, a civil unions bill introduced in March 2023, and a 14 May 2025 EU accession roadmap setting a third-quarter 2025 deadline. A revised Civil Code draft submitted to Parliament on 22 January 2026 would define family as man-woman cohabitation and automatically annul a marriage if one spouse undergoes legal sex reassignment, a provision aimed squarely at trans people's family status. Against that, the Desnianskyi District Court recognised actual marital relations between two Ukrainian men on 10 June 2025, and the Supreme Court in Kyiv rejected a challenge to a lower-court ruling recognising same-sex couples as de facto family in early 2026. Clause 211 of the Family Code bans same-sex couples from adopting, while single citizens may adopt regardless of sexual orientation. Official hostility and police response remain documented. Amnesty International reported on 16 May 2013 that discrimination and violent attacks on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity operated amid a pervasive climate of homophobia, that lawmakers had been urged to vote down proposals to criminalise, and that attacks were routinely used as a pretext to deny LGBTI people rights of expression and peaceful public events. Sources covering 2011 report harassment and violence against LGBTQ people, a perception that such violence was frequently tolerated by the government, and that police hardly ever detained attackers. The most recent violent incident documented in this record is the 26 June 2012 attack on LGBT activist Taras Karasiichuk near his Kyiv apartment, which left him with a concussion and a broken jaw and drew no immediate police response despite a medical referral; no later violent incident is documented here.

name: Mongolia
text: Consensual same-sex intimacy was criminalised in Mongolia's Criminal Code of 1961 and decriminalised in 1993, when all references were removed. The age of consent is 16 regardless of sexual orientation. Protection against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity is spread across several instruments rather than a single equality statute. Section 14.1.1 of the Penal Code, in force since 1 July 2017, prohibits discrimination on both grounds. Article 6 of the Labour Code, in force since 2022, prohibits discrimination based on sexual orientation, gender identity and gender expression. Article 1.3.2 of the revised Criminal Law adopted on 3 December 2015 bars discrimination in criminalisation and sentencing on grounds including sexual and gender orientation. No comprehensive equality law is in place. Hate-crime and hate-speech provisions cover gender identity. The Criminal Code adopted on 3 December 2015 named gender identity and sexual orientation as protected grounds for hate crimes; the code was scheduled to take effect on 1 September 2016 and was postponed to 1 July 2017. Section 10(1)(2)(14) of the Penal Code aggravates penalties for homicides motivated by hate towards the victim's gender identity or sexual orientation, and hate speech on the basis of gender identity is outlawed. Article 16(11) of the Constitution defines marriage as based on the equality and mutual consent of a man and a woman who have reached the age determined by law, with State protection for family, motherhood and child. Same-sex relationships are not recognised, and same-sex couple households are ineligible for the protections available to opposite-sex couples. No union recognition of any kind is available. LGBT groups can register. A June 2009 amendment to Article 20(1) of the Civil Registration Law allows transgender people to change their legal gender on birth certificates or citizen identification cards following sex reassignment surgery. Enforcement of the hate-crime provisions remains weak. As of August 2018 the LGBT Centre had trained more than 300 police officers, prosecutors and judges on handling hate crimes, and reporting from October 2019 puts the figure at over 500 trained after an officer assaulted a detained transgender woman. The police force now has guidelines requiring officers to address transgender detainees by their identified gender regardless of identity documents. Despite this training, local reports and activists say police continue to disregard or not take seriously complaints of hate crimes against LGBT people, and attacks often result in no punishment. Documented violence against transgender people includes a September 2009 incident in which a hyper-nationalist group kidnapped three transgender women in broad daylight at a promenade in Ulaanbaatar, drove them to a cemetery on the city outskirts, and beat, sexually assaulted and forced them to perform sexual acts on the perpetrators as a warning. The attack was not reported to police. Other documented attacks include the 2001 rape, abduction and stabbing of a lesbian woman by two men and a February 2014 sexual assault on a gay man by a neo-Nazi group; such violence is often not reported to police for fear of victimisation and reprisal. The most recent documented attack in this record is from February 2014; no later incident is recorded. Survey data on the climate facing LGBT people in Mongolia is dated. A 2012 National Human Rights Commission survey of LGBT people found that almost 80% had experienced broadly categorised 'human-rights abuse' during the preceding three years, and almost three-quarters had considered suicide because of intolerance; the survey window closed in 2012. A 2019 report found 79% of LGBT-identified young people had experienced bullying, discrimination or ostracism. A 2013 report found over 73% of LGBT Mongolians had considered suicide due to social non-acceptance and intolerance. Mongolian culture is and has remained strongly heteronormative, and ostracism, harassment and violence persist socially and systemically despite the 2017 protections. In June 2014 the law provided no additional penalty for bias-motivated violence and no requirement for law enforcement to record a suspected bias motive. A January 2014 working-group draft that would have added hate-bias motive as an aggravating factor, with penalties, reparations and police training, was replaced in late May 2014 by generalised discrimination references. In May 2014 the Government announced it would consider anti-discrimination legislation following public outcry. Sexual orientation and gender identity are discussed in the sex education curriculum introduced in 1998, though teachers may choose whether to cover these topics.

name: Ecuador
text: Article 11 of the 2008 Constitution binds the state to respect differences of ethnicity, nationality, social and generational standing and gender, expressly including sexual orientation and gender identity, within a secular, multinational order. Same-sex sexual activity has been legal since 1997, when Constitutional Tribunal Case No. 111-97-TC struck Article 516 of the Penal Code, and the 1998 Constitution made Ecuador the first country in the Americas to bar discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation. The age of consent is 14 regardless of gender or sexual orientation. Legal gender recognition rests on self-determination. The 2016 Gender Identity Law allows a change of legal gender and birth name on identity documents without surgery or medical diagnosis. The National Assembly's reforms of 12 December 2023 to the Organic Law on Identity Management and Civil Data were followed by the reglamento that President Noboa issued on 11 June 2024, which streamlines the civil-registry procedure through which marker changes are carried out. Rulings reported by AP in April 2026 let trans adolescents change name and sex on official records, in a case described as opening a path for others seeking legal recognition. Outright International's country overview, updated 12 March 2026, states that legal gender recognition is not available to people under 18, so the reach of the April 2026 rulings for minors is not settled in this record. Same-sex marriage has been legal since 2019. Adoption is limited to different-sex couples under Article 68 of the Constitution, and on 14 August 2026 new adoption legislation passed 118-0 explicitly prohibiting single and same-sex couples from adopting. In May 2018 the Constitutional Court ordered the Civil Registry to register the daughter of the same-sex couple Helen Bicknell and Nicola Rothon, the child Satya Amani Bicknell Rothon, by 5-3 with one abstention; lawyer Jose Luis Guerra said the refusal had violated the child's rights. A trans visitor whose relationship would be classed locally as same-sex can marry, and faces the same adoption bar as any locally same-sex couple. Conversion practices are criminalised. Article 151 of the Penal Code, added in 2014, treats conversion therapy as equivalent to torture and carries 7 to 10 years' imprisonment, and Outright International records that conversion practices involving torture are explicitly criminalised. As of 2023, hundreds of clinics were still promoting the practice. Los Angeles Blade reported in January 2024 that violence against LGBTQ Ecuadorians is increasing amid the country's internal armed conflict. The U.S. State Department's 2011 Human Rights Report recorded discrimination based on sexual orientation among societal problems, found that gay, lesbian and transgender people suffered discrimination from public and private bodies, found that the right to equal access to formal education was frequently violated, and reported LGBT groups' claims that police and prosecutors did not thoroughly investigate deaths of LGBT individuals. The most recent official country report in this record dates from 2011. Detention carries a specific and documented exposure. Trans women are held in Ecuador's almost universally male prisons, in male spaces, and Silueta X's PrisioTrans documentation covering 2011 to 2026 records gender-identity discrimination, unsafe placement, sexual violence, forced suppression of gender expression and barriers to health care. Trans woman Helen Maldonado died during the November 2021 massacre at Penitenciaria del Litoral while held in a male prison space; a 2022 complaint alleged cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment of trans women in Lago Agrio; 2024 allegations concerned forced head-shaving, beatings and violence targeting breast and body implants; and the 2026 death in State custody of a 23-year-old trans woman at the El Encuentro maximum-security prison drew calls for an independent investigation.

name: Tanzania
text: Tanzania criminalises same-sex sexual conduct. The Penal Code as revised by the Sexual Offences (Special Provisions) Act 1998 provides a maximum penalty of life imprisonment for same-sex acts between men; section 138A treats "gross indecency" as an offence carrying one to five years' imprisonment or a fine of TSh 100,000 to 300,000. Heterosexual oral and anal sex are also offences under the same framework. The semi-autonomous jurisdiction of Zanzibar, governed by its own House of Representatives, runs a separate criminal statute. The Penal Decree Act No. 6 of 2004 defines "gross indecency" broadly as any sexual act falling short of intercourse, sets sexual-offence age thresholds (absolute below 12, with under-18 and marriage distinctions) and provides penalties including three years' imprisonment. Zanzibar's Penal Code of 1934, as amended in 2004, outlaws sex between women with up to five years' imprisonment or a TSh 500,000 fine. Same-sex couples have no legal recognition anywhere in Tanzania, so no partner can be sponsored, inherited from, or recognised as next of kin through relationship status. Adoption requires a married couple, so a same-sex couple cannot adopt jointly. Documented violence against LGBT people includes a June 2024 attack on Tanzanian transgender activist Mauzinde of Rahaleo, abducted by 12 men and found beaten in a forest with her ears cut; the UN Human Rights Office condemned the attack as "horrendous" and flagged possible violations of ICCPR Article 20 and Tanzania's Constitution Article 13 equality guarantees, calling for bold action to combat discrimination against LGBTIQ people. Amnesty International's January 2024 report "We Are Facing Extinction" documents escalating anti-LGBTI sentiment and the weaponisation of law against LGBTI people in Tanzania, with legislation on same-sex relations deferred after protests, in a documented climate of discrimination limiting rights enjoyment. An OONI report from 2024 documents state-directed blocking of LGBTIQ websites and social networks in Tanzania, constraining LGBT access to information online. A 2013 Human Rights Watch and Wake Up and Step Forward Coalition report documented torture of LGBT people in police custody, including a 19-year-old gay man arrested after leaving a nightclub in Mbeya who said police raped him and beat the soles of his feet with canes, electric wires and water pipes. In October 2017 the government deported staff of several HIV/AIDS groups on the basis of "promoting homosexuality", directly disrupting services. In 2018 a "witch hunt" against gay people was declared in Dar es Salaam, where gay men were forced to undergo anal examinations and torture; also in 2018 Paul Makonda, the Dar es Salaam Regional Commissioner, announced a 17-strong committee of police, lawyers and doctors to identify and punish homosexuals, scouring the internet for videos of supposedly LGBTQ people; the Foreign Ministry said the crackdown lacked government support and Denmark withheld 65 million kr (about US$9.8 million) in aid. The most recent documented incident in this record is from June 2024; no later instance is documented. Government respect for freedom of speech and freedom of assembly is described as declining, and UN human rights defenders in Tanzania may not make public statements supporting tolerance for fear of reprisals. The 2018 broadcast content regulations bar inciting hatred on grounds of sexual preference; the online content regulations issued the same year banned such hate speech but were completely repealed by the 2020 online content regulations. The Media Council of Tanzania's 2020 Code of Ethics for Media Professionals still bars hate speech, stereotypes and discrimination based on sexual orientation. On the policy side, the 2013 National Family Planning Guidelines and Standards commit to services "regardless of age, parity, marital status, creed, race, color, or sexual preference", counselling "any woman, man, couple, or young person regardless of age"; the Nursing and Midwifery (practice) Regulations 2010 bar withholding nursing care based on sexual orientation; and the 2017 National Guidelines for Respectful and Compassionate Nursing and Midwifery Care require non-discriminatory care. No youth-specific healthcare provision beyond the age-inclusive family planning counselling language is stated. There are no gay bars in Tanzania, although some places exist where gay men meet, and lesbians are less visible than gay men. Tanzania has a high HIV/AIDS rate with reportedly one million people infected. The US State Department 2013 Human Rights Report for Tanzania identified the three most widespread problems as security-force excessive force, gender-based violence including FGM/C, and lack of access to justice, alongside discrimination based on sexual orientation and societal violence against persons with albinism; the same report details police custody abuse and describes Tanzania's human rights record as poor. An interview with three pseudonymised Tanzanian LGBT activists from September 2020 documents substantial prejudice, discrimination and violence against LGBT people in Tanzania and denial of basic rights, with homophobia and transphobia driving the urgency of rights advocacy. Activists Maria Sarungi Tsehai, Fatma Karume, Mwanahamisi Singano, Carol Ndosi, Zara Kay, Khalifa Said and Goodluck Haule have openly backed LGBTQ rights against officials such as Magufuli, Paul Makonda, Ally Hapi and Hamisi Kigwangalla, who pushed persecution.

name: Guatemala
text: Consensual, private, non-commercial same-sex sexual activity between adults has been lawful in Guatemala since 1871, following earlier Spanish colonial punishment of sodomy. Guatemala provides no legal gender recognition. Since 2016 a person may change a legal name to match gender identity only with judicial permission; legal gender cannot be changed, and a person cannot self-report gender for official documents, which must show the sex and name assigned at birth. The resulting mismatch between presentation and identity documents exposes a trans visitor to scrutiny during identity checks. Guatemala is bound by the Inter-American Court of Human Rights advisory opinion OC-24/17 of 9 January 2018, which holds recognition of gender identity on official documents to be a human right under the American Convention on Human Rights and requires states parties to grant same-sex couples access to all existing domestic family registration systems, including marriage with all rights deriving from marriage. Guatemala's compliance with the opinion is not recorded in these sources. A December 2017 bill to recognise the right to gender identity and allow transgender people to change name and gender on birth certificates was rejected in August 2018 by both the Legislative and Constitutional Points Commission and the Women's Commission; a later legislative proposal for a gender identity law has been advocated without enactment. Legislative action has moved in the opposite direction. Initiative No. 5940, received by the Legislative Directorate on 12 July 2021 and presented to the plenary on 13 September 2021, proposed a law to guarantee the integral protection of children and adolescents against "gender identity disorders". Bill 5490 advanced in December 2021 to remove education regarding transgender individuals in schools on grounds of protecting children and adolescents, and to require censorship of media featuring transgender individuals; it was unanimously approved by the Congress education committee and moved for full congress review. Human Rights Watch reported in January 2022 that bills before the Congress would erase gender-identity protections and restrict legal recognition. Guatemalan law does not prohibit discrimination on the basis of gender identity in employment, education, housing, health care, banking or public accommodations such as cafes, restaurants, nightclubs and cinemas. A May 2017 bill proposing to add gender identity to Criminal Code articles 27 and 202 as a protected category remains unadopted, and no convictions for discrimination on sexual-orientation or gender-identity grounds are recorded through 2021. Bias-motivated crimes on the basis of gender identity are reported to be tolerated by the government, especially where harassment or violence is directed at transgender people, with the absence of hate-crime protection attributed to prevailing attitudes about sexual identity and gender roles. Central American governments have long excluded trans women from femicide protections, and Guatemalan officials have justified this exclusion by stating that transgender women are not "biological women". The exclusion is official and underpins the documented violence context. Prison placement follows birth sex. A 2020 Human Rights Watch report documents trans women held in men's prisons in Guatemala, facilitating anti-trans violence and exposing them to sexual assault. Bárbara Herrarte, a trans activist with the trans-led organisation Redmmutrans, described her time in a men's prison: "Always, at night, someone got in my bed and forced me to have sex with him." The report records no gender-identity-based placement policy, no trans-specific unit or segregation practice, and no court ruling on trans custody. Conversion practices are documented as continuing. Evangelical-funded conversion therapy centres, mainly in rural areas, subject persons to electroshock therapy, "corrective" rape prosecuted only as rape and not as a hate crime, forced marriage and coerced sex; conversion practices, including by mental health professionals, remain normalised. There is no legal recognition for same-sex couples as marriage, civil unions or domestic partnerships. A civil unions bill introduced in December 2016 by Deputy Sandra Morán has not been debated since. The Law for the Protection of Life and Family, approved by Congress on 8 March 2022 with a renewed congressional approval recorded on 9 March, would have expressly prohibited same-sex marriage in the Civil Code and required schools to teach heterosexuality as the norm; after President Alejandro Giammattei announced a veto on grounds it violated the Constitution and international agreements, Congress archived and discarded the law on 15 March 2022 with 119 votes, leaving those prohibitions without effect. United Nations and NGO reports from the late 1990s documented systematic targeting of LGBT people for death as part of a social cleansing campaign, including the 1997 gunning down in Guatemala City of transgender AIDS activist Luis Palencia. The most recent documented fatal case against a trans person in this record is that 1997 killing; no later fatal case is documented. The most recent documented instance of trans-specific violence of any kind in this record is the 2020 prison sexual assault described above. Official hostility is current. In August 2025 the Guatemalan Congress hosted the Meeting for Religious Freedom, Life and Family to advance an anti-LGBTIQ agenda. Despite the election of a more progressive government in 2024, Congress remained predominantly conservative with no significant pro-LGBTIQ initiatives.

name: Uzbekistan
text: Article 120 of Uzbekistan's 1994 Criminal Code criminalises consensual sexual conduct between men and provides for up to three years' imprisonment. Human Dignity Trust's country profile, Human Rights Watch's World Report 2024 (covering events of 2023) and the UK Home Office's country-policy and information note of July 2024 all record the offence as in force. The Home Office documents cases prosecuted under Article 120 between 2009 and 2023, so the provision is applied rather than dormant; 2023 is the most recent documented case in this record. Human Rights Watch reports that police target gay and bisexual men and trans women with arbitrary detention, prosecution and imprisonment. The same report records that forced examinations carried out in these cases amount to torture under WHO definition, and that impunity for police ill-treatment persists. The Home Office describes police intimidation, violence and exploitation of gay men and trans people as routine. The US State Department's 2023 human-rights report records that LGBTQI+ people are arrested and then released, or threatened with arrest unless they pay bribes, and that police coerce LGBTQI+ people into informing on others under threat of prison. Its 2021 report, covering an earlier period, records torture and ill-treatment and arbitrary detention in custody alongside social stigma and violence against LGBT people under the criminalised framework. Human Rights Watch reported in March 2021 that gay and bisexual men face discrimination, violence, blackmail and extortion from both state and non-state actors with almost no legal protection. Official hostility is on the record. In April 2023 Uzbekistan's constitution was adopted with sexual orientation deliberately omitted from the list of protected characteristics, which did include gender, race, religion and nationality. In November 2024 the leader of the Milliy Tiklanish party announced he was drafting a law banning discussion of LGBTQ people, stating that it was inspired by statements made by Ivanka Trump about "LGBT propaganda" in schools. LGBTI organisations cannot register in Uzbekistan and operate unofficially, according to the July 2024 Home Office note, which also reports that a rural taboo drives discrimination. The US State Department's 2023 report records continuing societal harassment.

name: Tajikistan
text: Consensual same-sex relations have been legal in Tajikistan since May 1998, sex between women was never criminalised, and the age of consent is 16 regardless of gender or sexual orientation. That legality carries no protective apparatus. No law prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity: the country's first anti-discrimination statute, adopted in July 2022, dropped both grounds and retains only "sex", and a monitoring review covering 2024 finds it only partially aligned with international standards. Police maintain a register of LGBTIQ people introduced in 2016, and a separate account dates a government registry of "proven" LGBT persons to 2017. The 2024 review records police luring LGBT people into fake meetings in order to register them in a database, harvesting their social-media contacts and extorting money, with more than ten such cases documented in Sughd province. Raids in 2022 and 2023 brought forced HIV testing and arbitrary criminal charges, and ill-treatment, sexual abuse and extortion by officers are documented. ECOM recorded 27 human-rights violation cases against LGBT people in Tajikistan during 2024, involving arbitrary police arrest, blackmail and extortion. That is a raw count of recorded cases with no population denominator, so it measures what was reported and recorded rather than per-capita exposure. The 2024 review separately documents forced or sham marriages imposed on LGBT people with police declining to intervene. For a trans visitor the document environment is restrictive. Tajik law permits gender reassignment on some documents, but medical institutions issue no official documents for that purpose. A diagnosis of transsexualism is required, surgery is required for transgender women but not men, and evaluation is by a commission of three psychiatrists on an unregulated case-by-case basis in which activists say bribes are often necessary. Only three to six people are recorded as having changed legal gender. Gender-affirming medical services are not available in the country, trans people must go abroad to transition medically, and most doctors have no expertise in the treatments trans people need. LGBTQ patients report disrespectful treatment by medical staff, and some psychologists and doctors offer pseudoscientific "cure methods" that treat homosexuality as an addiction comparable to alcoholism or drug dependence. A trans-focused non-governmental organisation has drafted a hormone-replacement-therapy protocol used to educate endocrinologists. No relationship-recognition framework exists: same-sex couples are not eligible for the legal protections available to married heterosexual couples, so a trans visitor in a relationship read as same-sex under birth-sex status has no recognition to rely on. Public expression of support for LGBTQ people is effectively suppressed and public attitudes have been described as "entirely negative", with homophobic and transphobic remarks from politicians forming part of everyday politics. The Supreme Mufti, Saidmukarram Abdulkodirzoda, has called same-sex relations a "disaster", condemned countries legalising same-sex marriage and spoken against human-rights activists and anti-discrimination laws. LGBTQ groups operate anonymously, one focused solely on trans issues and one on general LGBTQ issues, and activists have no access to the Ministry of Health or other state authorities, which makes state-level advocacy impossible. A legislative analysis built from questionnaires completed by local partners records barriers and gaps for gay men, men who have sex with men and trans people, including situations where the written law protects but practice does not. The most recent documented incidents in this record are from 2024; no later instance is recorded. An account from January 2013 describes people who disclose their orientation becoming targets of physical and psychological abuse including from police, and characterises the community as one of the most closed in society.

name: Syria
text: Syria's Penal Code criminalises the conduct a trans visitor may be read as engaging in. Article 520 of the 1949 code prohibits "carnal relations against the order of nature" and carries up to three years' imprisonment; Article 517 covers public indecency. Outright International's country overview, updated 12 March 2026, records that both provisions reach men and women alike, so a trans visitor is reachable under the same articles irrespective of legal sex marker or presentation. Legal gender recognition is not available in Syria, LGBTI organisations cannot register, and no anti-discrimination protection exists in any field. The state's response to same-sex conduct is criminalisation, which removes the complaint route a visitor would otherwise have after an assault, a refusal of service or a document dispute. Enforcement has fallen on private gatherings. In June 2010 Syrian authorities raided several private parties over preceding weeks, arresting more than 25 men, most charged with "homosexual acts" and others with drug offences; the same crackdown included charges of encouraging homosexual behaviour and organising obscene parties. Syria Direct reported on 11 October 2020 that homosexuality and public-decency offences remain illegal in Damascus, where a resident described meeting friends in gay-friendly cafes "only in whispers." Violence against LGBT Syrians has also come from non-state armed actors. A Human Rights Watch report of 16 April 2018 (updated 30 August 2021) tallied at least 16 killings claimed by ISIS in Syria for alleged sodomy as of June 2016, and reported that the Islamic State said it executed at least 30 people for "sodomy" in areas under its control, an issue raised at the UN Security Council in August 2015 in the Council's first-ever discussion of LGBTQ concerns. Beatings and torture of LGBTQ people by Hay'at Tahrir al-Sham and the Islamic State are documented in the same record. Political actors have endorsed harsher treatment: Free Syrian Army member Nasradeen Ahme stated he would enforce tougher laws and would not object to stoning homosexuals, while secular leader Miral Bioredda said Syrian society would say "no way" to gays claiming rights. Public cultural expression has been squeezed since the civil war. The region's only gay tour, covering Damascus and Aleppo, stopped operating; the underground LGBTQ hubs of Damascus have been eradicated; and the hammams of Aleppo and Damascus that served as the tour's main venues no longer function in that role. Digital expression persists anonymously: the "One of you" movement began on Facebook in March 2020 and moved to Twitter, with participants using fake accounts for fear of identification, and it faded amid COVID-19. Health care access is shaped by official stigma. In 2005 the Deputy Minister of Religious Endowments publicly called HIV/AIDS "divine punishment" for fornication and homosexuality, while the Health Ministry claimed only 369 people were infected, a figure NGOs estimated at least five times too low, and the UN chastised the government for ineffective prevention. The state runs voluntary HIV testing clinics and offers a limited HIV/AIDS educational program in secondary schooling, but comprehensive public education for LGBTQ people does not exist. Prevalence was under 2 per 100,000 in the general population and under 1% among most-at-risk populations in 2018, with 1,013 reported cases through Q3 2019 since the first reported infections in 1987. A GEM (Guardians of the Gem) report of April 2025, working through an on-the-ground reporter network, investigated and found inaccurate a report claiming LGBTQIA+ individuals were being hunted and targeted in Homs, debunking it to avoid stirring incitement against the community. The most recent enforcement incident in this record remains the 2010 party raids; no later state raid is documented here.

name: Mauritius
text: Mauritius decriminalised same-sex conduct on 4 October 2023, when the Supreme Court struck down Section 250 of the Criminal Code of 1838 as unconstitutional, ruling that it must be read to exclude consensual acts. The provision had carried penal servitude of up to five years. Prosecutions were rare: the US State Department's 2016 country report found that sodomy references arose overwhelmingly in heterosexual divorce proceedings as an aggravating factor, although a same-sex couple was arrested in 2015 on suspicion of practising sodomy. In October 2019 a group of young people filed a constitutional challenge to Section 250, supported by the Young Queer Alliance and the Love Honor Cherish Foundation, alongside activist Abdool Ridwan Firaas Ah Seek, 29, backed by Collectif Arc-En-Ciel. Legal gender recognition is not available in Mauritius. The Civil Status Act of 1981 and the Central Population Database form the framework under which trans Mauritians are denied recognition, according to an AfricLaw analysis of 23 August 2024. The Young Queer Alliance's July 2021 policy brief on administrative recognition of trans people argued for legal gender recognition and noted that the WHO's ICD-11 removed trans categories from mental disorders in 2019, calling on Mauritius to join countries recognising gender identity in law. Outright International's country overview, last updated 12 March 2026, records that legal gender recognition remains not possible and that progress for trans and intersex people has been 'less evident' than advances for lesbian, gay and bisexual people since the 2023 repeal. No same-sex marriage or civil union is recognised. The Equal Opportunities Act 2008 and the Workers' Rights Act 2019 protect against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation.
