Under the 2021 Civil Status Act, intersex newborns may be registered as 'undetermined', but nonconsensual intersex medical procedures are not banned. LGBTI organisations cannot register. Visibility carries documented risk. During the 2024 national elections, a parliamentary candidate branded sexual and gender diversity a 'Western deviation' and other candidates used anti-LGBTIQ hate speech. Pride has been held since 2005 with counter-protesters present; in 2018 the Pride march was annulled after hundreds of death threats believed to come from religious extremists, and a counter-protest was organised by Javed Meetoo, an Islamic extremist under state surveillance. Earlier in 2018 a strong police force had been deployed to protect marchers, and an LGBTQ sit-in at the Caudan Waterfront followed with the Prime Minister's support. Collectif Arc-En-Ciel, founded in 2005, organised the country's first Pride and has done so for fifteen years, drawing more than 1,200 participants in 2016 when the march moved from Rose-Hill to Port Louis. The US State Department's 2016 report documented LGBTI victims of family verbal abuse or violence reporting to local NGOs including Collectif Arc-en-Ciel and Young Queer Alliance, and recorded harassment of a transgender person for wearing women's clothing; no later trans-specific incident is documented in this record. The 2024 AfricLaw analysis describes pervasive stigmatisation alongside the participation of Jeanny Michelle Karla Fanfan, the first transgender woman in Miss Universe Mauritius 2024, and concludes that legal recognition and protection for trans Mauritians remain inadequate despite the visibility milestone. Access to care is uneven. According to the government, hormone therapy for transgender people is provided in public hospitals, but gender-affirming care is available only in limited form, and LGBTQ people may face discrimination notably in public hospitals. In 2014 the Ministry of Health amended blood donation policy to allow men who have sex with men to donate, although anecdotally LGBTQI persons have still been prevented from donating on occasion. Conservative attitudes remain commonplace. AfriGay reports that gay life is fairly quiet, existing mainly online, in private and at occasional parties, though resorts are welcoming and non-discriminatory and no problems with LGBTQ couples sharing hotel rooms have been recorded. LGBTQ people may face bullying in schools, while acceptance is growing particularly among the younger generation, with polls indicating Mauritius is one of Africa's most LGBTQ-friendly countries; a 2016 poll found 49% of Mauritians would like or not mind having an LGBTQ neighbour. State and religious actors have also shown support: Cardinal Maurice Piat and other religious leaders condemned the anti-LGBTQ protest and called for tolerance, and the Opposition stated that sexual orientation should not be an obstacle to equal rights.

name: Somalia
text: Somalia criminalises same-sex sexual activity, and the sources give irreconcilable penalties. The Human Dignity Trust country profile records a maximum of life imprisonment under a penal code it dates to 1964, together with the death penalty under sharia in some regions. The US State Department's 2021 human rights report gives up to three years, while its 2022 report gives three months to three years for "carnal intercourse with a person of the same sex", with no official reports of enforcement available for that year. Article 409 of the penal code, dated to 1973, sets three months to three years for sexual intercourse with a person of the same sex and two months to two years for an "act of lust" other than intercourse. Article 410 permits an additional security measure, usually police surveillance, intended to prevent re-offending. Under local interpretations of sharia, homosexuality is punishable by death. The 2022 State Department report states that no known state-conducted executions of that kind were reported and that impunity generally remained the norm, while the same report and an encyclopaedia entry record capital punishment being imposed for consensual same-sex sexual activity in areas under insurgent control and in Jubaland, at a judge's discretion. The 2021 report separately records that the insurgent group al-Shabaab enforces strict sharia in which death is a possible punishment. An international LGBT rights organisation reports killings by al-Shabaab or other non-state armed groups of people alleged to have engaged in homosexual activity: two male teenagers aged 15 and 18 together with a man aged 20 in 2017, a young man in 2018, and two men executed by al-Shabaab in 2024. The 2024 case is the most recent documented instance in this record; no later instance is documented. The sources give no denominator and no per-capita comparison, so these raw counts cannot be ranked against other jurisdictions or read against the country's general conflict death rate. In government-controlled areas, civil law specifies prison sentences of up to three years and LGBTQ people are regularly prosecuted. The law does not prohibit discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, as the US Department of State reported in 2022. The Marriage Law of 1974 defines marriage as "a contract between a man and a woman having equal rights and duties with the object of creating a family", which excludes same-sex unions from legal recognition. Sexual orientation is a taboo subject with no public discussion in any region of the country, per US Department of State reports from 2010 and 2022, and severe societal stigma prevented LGBTQI+ individuals from making their sexual orientation or gender identity known publicly as of 2022. Stigmatisation and criminalisation operate in a country where 99% of the population follows Islam amid decades of civil war and unstable government. Family planning services and factual information on human sexuality are hard to access, and Islamic social mores often make it difficult to discuss HIV transmission publicly. Since 1999, much AIDS/HIV education and care has come from international organisations such as the United Nations; Somalia has one of the lowest HIV infection rates on the continent, with adult prevalence estimated at 0.5% in 2007.

name: Eritrea
text: Article 310(1) of Eritrea's penal code criminalises "homosexual conduct" and carries a maximum sentence of seven years' imprisonment. The provision descends from the 1957 Ethiopian penal code, which Eritrea retained at independence and carried into its first post-independence penal code, adopted in 2015, with an enhanced sentence. The 2023 US State Department country report records the criminalisation alongside societal discrimination against LGBTQI+ persons and a separate law making no gender distinction for assault. The prohibition is applied to foreign nationals as well as residents. In 2013 Paolo Mannina, an Italian citizen teaching literature at a technical school in Asmara, was dismissed and deported; the government described him as a "dangerous individual who is potentially destabilizing to the moral order and public of the country" and justified the expulsion under Article 7 of the Agreement on Italian Technical Schools, which requires compliance with local law including the penal code's prohibition. In 2004 three hotel workers from Western countries were expelled for homosexual activity, at least one of them openly gay; Eritrea's ambassador to Italy stated that any foreigner must respect local customs and the provisions of law prohibiting homosexual relations, and Italian diplomats condemned the action. The most recent documented expulsion in this record is from 2013; no later instance is documented. Detention is used against people suspected of same-sex conduct. In 2003 six gay men arrested in a public bathroom in Asmara were transferred to the Adi Abeyto prison facility, which is known for housing political prisoners and journalists. The most recent documented arrest of this kind in this record is from 2003; no later instance is documented. Reporting on those facilities records abuse, torture and beating of prisoners as commonplace and some illegal executions, although the UK Foreign and Commonwealth Office reported that the death penalty was not used in 2013. Openly LGBTQI+ persons risked imprisonment and, on that basis, did not participate in the political process, according to the 2023 US State Department report. That report found no public LGBTQ organisations and tight restrictions on expression of sexual orientation and gender identity, so LGBTQI+ people cannot assemble, associate or express themselves publicly for fear of identification, arrest, discrimination or violence. State censorship is compounded by social stigma; in the early 2000s state-run radio and television aired programmes detailing the alleged dangers of homosexuality. The government labels disloyal individuals "gay, traitors, rapists, pedophiles", a practice recorded in the 2011 US State Department report. Criminalisation undermines health and care access. ILGA and some HIV/AIDS prevention groups have condemned the law, arguing that it makes prevention programmes directed at men who have sex with men extremely difficult, and the US State Department lists societal discrimination against people with HIV/AIDS as an area of concern. There is no law banning conversion therapy; OutRight Action International found that conversion therapy and attempts to forcibly change sexual orientation or gender identity are widespread due to social stigma, and LGBTQ people have reportedly been offered conversion therapy in lieu of jail time. Same-sex couples have no legal recognition in Eritrea and cannot adopt. There is no protection against discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity, and no anti-discrimination legislation protects lesbian, gay, bisexual or transgender people; the UK Foreign Office recorded raising these concerns bilaterally and through the EU. The government rejected a UN Human Rights Council Universal Periodic Review recommendation to legalise same-sex sexual activity as "in direct contradiction with the values and traditions of the Eritrean people", with no major efforts to change or rescind the existing law, and in 2010 Eritrea joined other African states in rejecting the Yogyakarta Principles.

name: Barbados
text: Same-sex conduct between men was decriminalised in Barbados in December 2022, on the outcome of a constitutional challenge filed in June 2018 with trans activist Alexa Hoffmann as claimant, supported by the Canadian HIV/AIDS Legal Network and the University of Toronto's international human-rights programme. A High Court ruling on sodomy, published in May 2023, found discrimination based on sexual orientation unconstitutional. Barbados does not screen or protect LGBT travellers as a distinct category, and the state has questioned the legitimacy of LGBT migration. In 2011 the government said it was investigating claims that gay Barbadians were seeking refugee status in Canada. In 2016 Foreign Minister Maxine McClean expressed concern that such applications were an attempt to abuse the Canadian refugee system, noting that two of nine Canadian applications had been denied, and a Guyanese newspaper reported over 300 LGBT members in Barbados seeking asylum in Canada, the United Kingdom and the United States; UGLAAB said it would investigate the same allegations. Employment protection stops short of trans people. The Employment (Prevention of Discrimination) Act, 2020, passed by Parliament in August 2020, bars employment discrimination on grounds including sex, sexual orientation and domestic partnership status, but trans activist Alexa D.V. Hoffmann argues that it excludes trans workers because gender identity and gender expression are not listed as protected grounds. Violence against trans people has produced a documented impunity outcome. In February 2018 Hoffmann was attacked with a meat cleaver by Brandon Coward and suffered serious injuries including to her throat. Coward was convicted in April 2019 and ordered to pay Hoffmann BDS$460 (US$230) or serve three months in prison; no jail time was imposed. The most recent documented case in this record is from 2018, with sentencing in 2019; no later instance is documented. No same-sex relationship or union is recognised in Barbados. In June 2016 the government ruled out changing the law to allow same-sex marriage, and in September 2020 it announced only a plan to recognise "some form" of civil union followed by a referendum on gay marriage. Critics said the civil union proposal was unnecessarily vague and that the referendum was likely to fail, and as of the source's account neither had been enacted. Entry rules for the "Welcome Stamp" remote-work visa introduced in July 2020 initially allowed foreign workers to bring only an opposite-sex spouse, and were changed to permit same-sex spouses. Regional protection machinery is unresolved in the record. In 2018 activists filed a case with the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights challenging the Sexual Offences Act (Ch.154, ss.9 and 12), and the Commission gave the government three months to respond in late July 2019; failure to repeal could send the matter to the Inter-American Court of Human Rights for a binding decision. The record does not resolve what became of that case after the December 2022 decriminalisation.

name: Bahamas
text: Consensual sexual conduct between adults was decriminalised on 16 May 1991 under the Sexual Offences and Domestic Violence Act, and no source records a prosecution risk for a visitor on that basis. The criminal law retains an unequal age of consent: 16 years for opposite-sex acts and 18 years for same-sex acts, so a trans visitor in a relationship that local law reads as same-sex falls under the higher threshold. Gender identity appears in no anti-discrimination or anti-harassment statute in the Bahamas. Discrimination on the basis of gender identity in employment, education, housing, healthcare, banking and public businesses is not illegal, and the same gap applies to sexual orientation. The Constitution's prohibition on discrimination covers neither characteristic. The 2006 Constitutional Reform Commission did not regard sexual orientation as deserving protection, and efforts to include it in a proposed Constitution were blocked by members citing religious opposition. There are no national hate-crime laws to prevent or punish violence directed at LGBT people. A 2001 Employment Bill clause banning sexual-orientation workplace discrimination was removed shortly after passage. The Data Protection (Privacy of Personal Information) Act 2003 lists "sexual life" as sensitive personal data, which is the narrowest statutory protection recorded. Marriage and partnership recognition is closed: the Marriage Act defines marriage as between a man and a woman, same-sex households are denied the rights given to opposite-sex married couples, and maritime marriage law states a marriage is void if between male-male or female-female. In 2011 former Minister of State Zhivargo Laing stated a marriage is void if between persons of the same sex, calling this a community standard. The 2016 referendum bills were not inclusive of transgender or intersex people, and marriage eligibility was framed as between a man and a woman with male and female determined at birth. Official hostility toward trans people is documented at the political level. Government member Leslie Miller publicly called for the "Exile of Transgender out of the Bahamas," urging financial contributions to relocate transgender people to a private island so "they stay out of the way" and pledging $1,000 toward it. Former Prime Minister Perry Christie stated in 2013 he did not believe in same-sex marriage and in 2016 said a referendum would not legalise it, defining marriage as between male and female determined at birth. Bahamas Transgender, Intersex United launched the 'Bahamian Trans Lives Matter' campaign on 27 April 2016, stressing that no laws protect transgender and intersex Bahamians; member Torri Culmer advocates against job termination for trans and intersex workers. This is organised advocacy in the face of a documented absence of trans-specific legal protection. Violent targeting of a gay visitor during a major tourist event is documented: on 8 May 2017 Adrian Brown, 24, Jamaica-born and US-resident, was treated at Doctors Hospital for a head laceration after being targeted and beaten because he is gay at Bahamas Junkanoo Carnival, and he wants charges laid. There are no national hate-crime laws under which such an attack would be charged as a bias crime. Juries have acquitted or leniently sentenced killers invoking gay-panic defences, including a 2009 acquittal for the murder of a homosexual HIV-positive man and a 10 June 2010 case in which the Court of Appeal president stated "One is entitled to use whatever force is necessary to prevent one's self-being the victim of a homosexual act." Nine murders of gay men between 2001 and 2015 remain unsolved, including an accused in the 2007 Harl Taylor slaying found not guilty. The most recent documented case in this record is from 2017; no later instance is documented. Social conditions constrain visibility. Many Bahamians belong to conservative Christian denominations treating homosexuality and cross-dressing as decadence, and politicians have been leery of publicly supporting LGBT-rights legislation. Surveys record 85.5% strongly disapproving of same-sex marriage in 2015 with 10.6% approving, and over 84% strongly disapproving of a gay or lesbian politician in 2013 with 12% positive; these figures measure attitudes toward sexual orientation, not gender identity specifically. Due to lack of confidence in the judicial system, legal inequalities and homophobia, many LGBT people keep sexual orientation or gender identity private, and LGBT groups are often pressured to keep social events hidden. No exclusively gay bars or clubs exist; the Nassau scene is underground. Police raided a gay party in downtown Nassau on 6 October 2007 with no arrests, and the Ministry of Tourism later apologised. Groups of LGBT tourists have been protested, including church group opposition to Rosie O'Donnell's 2004 cruise and a 1998 protest against a lesbian cruise; in September 2007 the Bahamas Christian Council formed an anti-gay committee over a request to a local cable company to carry the LGBTQ channel Logo. The Plays and Films Control Board banned Brokeback Mountain in March 2006 and attempted to block a public-square screening of Children of God on 24 June 2011, though the government overruled it. In May 1998 National Security Minister and Deputy Prime Minister Frank Watson announced the military, prison service and police do not discriminate on the basis of sexual orientation, and LGBT citizens face no prohibition on serving in those forces. The Communications Act 2009 empowers URCA to issue codes of practice against content likely to incite hatred or vilify persons on the basis of sexual preference. In 2005 an 18-year-old beauty queen had her crown stripped after confirming she was a lesbian. In 2016 the Canadian government issued travel advice warning gay couples about the risk of homophobia in the Bahamas. No HIV-specific or trans-specific care provisions are recorded.

name: Haiti
text: Haiti has not criminalised same-sex conduct since 1791. Its legal framework provides no recognition of gender identity, no anti-discrimination protection covering gender identity or sexual orientation, and no hate-crime enhancement, and the judiciary does not function in practice as a protection avenue. A trans visitor therefore has no statutory remedy to invoke and no aggravated-penalty framework standing behind a complaint. Two Senate measures would tighten the regime. In August 2017 the Senate passed a bill banning same-sex marriage and public LGBT advocacy, carrying up to three years' imprisonment and a fine of about US$8,000 for the parties. A June 2017 bill would allow denial of the Certificat de Bonne Vie et Mœurs, the good-conduct certificate that employers and universities require, on grounds of homosexuality. Both awaited a vote in the Chamber of Deputies as of November 2017, and this record documents no later legislative outcome. A 2018 US State Department report found that attitudes in Haiti remained hostile toward LGBTI people who were public and visible about their sexual orientation or gender identity and expression, particularly in Port-au-Prince. The report is the most recent official climate assessment carried in this record, and no later assessment is sourced here. Charlot Jeudy, president of Kouraj, Haiti's national LGBTQ advocacy organisation, was found dead at his home in Port-au-Prince on 25 November 2019. An LGBTQ news outlet reported that he may have been poisoned, a finding it could not confirm, and ILGALAC issued a mourning statement. The most recent documented death of this kind in this record is dated 2019; no later instance is documented. Transgender people face documented harassment in the displacement camps that followed the 2010 earthquake. No later instance of camp-based harassment appears in this record, and no prevalence figure is sourced for it. Constitutional guarantees of health care, housing, education, food and social security extend to citizens, so a trans visitor cannot invoke them. After the 2010 earthquake, gay and bisexual men reported adopting a more masculine demeanor to avoid harassment and to reduce the chance of being denied emergency housing, healthcare and food-for-work programs; no later disaster-response evidence appears in this record.

name: Fiji
text: Private, adult, consensual conduct between men and between women has been lawful in Fiji since 1 February 2010, when the Crimes Decree 2009, cited as the Crimes Act 2010, took effect and repealed the colonial Penal Code offence at Article 175, which had carried a maximum of fourteen years' imprisonment. Enforcement had already stopped: in July 2006 Fiji's High Commissioner in New Zealand confirmed an official policy that men engaging in consensual gay sex would no longer be arrested. The enforcement era produced prosecutions. In April 2005 an Australian tourist, Thomas McCosker, and a Fijian man, Dhirendra Nadan, received two-year sentences under Article 175, and the trial judge described the acts as 'so disgusting... any decent person vomit'. Those convictions were overturned in August 2005 by Fiji's highest court as violations of the constitution then in force. Days after the sentences were passed, Prime Minister Laisenia Qarase rejected international pressure to legalise gay sex, calling homosexuality a sin in what he described as the conservative Christian nation. The 1997 Constitution explicitly prohibited government discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation; Human Rights Watch stated in April 2005 that this made Fiji one of the first two countries worldwide to do so, alongside South Africa. That constitution was abolished in 2009. The Constitution promulgated in September 2013 prohibits unfair direct or indirect discrimination on grounds including sex, gender, sexual orientation, and gender identity and expression under Article 26(3), and in 2013 the government included sexual orientation and gender identity in anti-hate-speech law and in law dealing with discrimination in certain businesses. The constitutional guarantee has no implementing route for gender markers. Legislative and policy frameworks permit no change of gender marker and do not recognise traditional third-gender identities, a gap the Asia Pacific Alliance described in 2023 as producing documented marginalisation and discrimination for trans people despite what it called a constitution unique worldwide in its protection of gender identity and expression. Fiji has no legal gender recognition process. The traditional third-gender population known as vaka sa lewa lewa, assigned male at birth but who dress, act and behave as female, have traditionally been accepted by Fijian society, but that cultural standing carries no legal status. No relationship recognition is available. The Marriage Act 2002 limits marriage to one man and one woman, Fiji family law provides no recognition of same-sex marriage or civil unions, and prime ministerial opposition to such recognition was reaffirmed on 26 March 2013, in January 2016 and in 2019. On care, the Mental Health Decree 2010 provides that persons are not mentally ill if they refuse or fail to express a particular sexual orientation and prohibits conversion therapy by registered mental health professionals, and health professionals are barred from trying to change sexual orientation. Intersex bodily autonomy is unprotected under Fiji law. On violence, a young transgender woman was brutally murdered in Suva in May 2018. No later anti-trans killing is documented in the sources assembled for this assessment. Reporting of anti-gay violence and hateful discrimination is discouraged by lack of trust in police, attributed to possible harassment, and activist accounts describe physical violence and domestic abuse operating as familial conversion therapy for LGBTQ+ people. Social climate is shaped by majority Methodist and Catholic denominations and by a Muslim minority of about 6%, which tend to view transgender identities negatively or cross-dressing as sinful behaviour to be corrected. Public displays of affection are not illegal but are generally considered offensive. Reports of societal discrimination and bullying are documented, and social mores regarding sexual orientation and gender identity are described as conservative with little public support for LGBTQ rights.

name: Tuvalu
text: Sections 153, 154 and 155 of Tuvalu's Penal Code criminalise male homosexual intercourse, attempts to commit it, and gross indecency between males. All three are felonies, carrying maximum sentences of 14, 7 and 5 years' imprisonment respectively. The provisions date to the colonial period, and ILGA World's jurisdiction database records them as still in force. The exposure is defined by sex. Because the offences apply to male persons, a transgender woman whom police read as male falls within their scope; what matters at charge or in custody is the classification officers apply, not how she identifies. For a trans visitor who has sex with a man in Tuvalu, the statute creates a felony exposure in principle regardless of how rarely it is used. The male homosexual provisions also carry heavier penalties than other sexual conduct. The age of consent is 15 for heterosexual vaginal sex and for lesbian sex, while the Penal Code's male homosexual provisions carry separate felony penalties of 14, 7 and 5 years. This asymmetry falls on young men who have sex with men; a 2005 study found about 14% of young Tuvaluan men aged 15 to 24 had had sex with a male partner at some point in their lives. Enforcement is documented as absent rather than merely rare. The US Department of State's 2013 Human Rights Report for Tuvalu noted no prosecutions of consenting adults under these provisions, and reported no government abuses. The most recent enforcement statement in this record is from 2013; no later prosecution data is documented here, and an undocumented present is not a safe one. Discrimination protection is partial and does not reach gender identity. The Labour and Employment Relations Act 2017 bans workplace discrimination on sexual orientation and on a list of protected grounds including gender, sex, pregnancy, marital status, HIV/AIDS status and disability. Constitutional protection is narrower: section 27 of the Constitution, as amended in 2023, lists sex among protected attributes but does not refer to sexual orientation. No gender-identity or gender-expression protection appears anywhere in the record. Same-sex relationships have no legal recognition. Tuvalu does not recognise same-sex marriage or civil unions; the 2023 constitutional amendments banned same-sex marriage, and section 43(2)(b) of the Charter of Duties and Responsibilities defines a family unit as "a marriage as between a man and a woman to the exclusion of all others." The Marriage Act (Cap 29) does not expressly prohibit recognition of same-sex unions but assumes the parties are male and female, and same-sex marriages do not appear in its restrictions-on-marriage section. No partner-visa, next-of-kin or foreign-union recognition provisions are discussed in the source. The record contains no hate-crime incidents, hate-crime statistics or hate-crime legislation for Tuvalu, and no detention-conditions, strip-search or custody-treatment findings for transgender detainees. The US State Department's 2013 report described traditional customs as perpetuating religious and social discrimination including against women, while recording no government abuses. Diplomatically, Tuvalu was among roughly 80 signatory states of the UN joint statement on human rights, sexual orientation and gender identity in 2011, and in 2011 signed the UN joint statement on ending acts of violence and related human rights violations based on sexual orientation and gender identity. The 2017 Ministry of Health Global AIDS Progress Report sets out a national HIV response drawing on the Pacific Multi-Country Mapping and Behavioural Study on HIV and STI risk vulnerability among key populations, including MSM and transgender Tuvaluans; 2017 UNAIDS estimates put the population at about 300 MSM and about 40 pinapinaaine nationwide.

name: Nauru
text: Nauru repealed the criminal-code provisions that prohibited consensual same-sex conduct in 2016, a change reported on 29 May 2016. The sections struck out belonged to a criminal code inherited from Queensland in 1899, and the same repeal covered the attempted-suicide offences that sat alongside them. Consensual same-sex intimacy between adults is not a prosecutable offence under Nauruan law, and a visitor should not expect prosecution on that basis. Marriage and union recognition is a separate matter. Same-sex marriages and unions remain illegal in Nauru, and there is no recognition route for a trans visitor whose relationship would be locally classed as same-sex. Kaleidoscope Trust's country assessment records that intersex and transgender people in Nauru have no explicit legal recognition or protection, and that lesbian, bisexual, trans and intersex people have no employment-discrimination protection. Nauru's most recent CEDAW state report, submitted in 2016, contained no LBTI-specific information, so the official reporting machinery carries no account of trans people's situation in the country. One detention-specific protection is documented. The Nauru Regional Processing Centre Rules 2014, made under the Asylum Seekers (Regional Processing Centre) Act 2012, prohibit discrimination against any person on the basis of sex or gender, sexual preference or gender identity inside the regional processing centre. This instrument governs immigration detention rather than Nauru's criminal-justice prison system, and it addresses non-discrimination rather than placement by birth sex versus identity, special units or solitary-confinement practice. No documented data was found on where transgender prisoners are housed in Nauru's corrections system, and no trans-prisoner case or ruling is recorded.

name: Benin
text: Consensual sexual acts between adults are legal in Benin. Article 545 of the Penal Code, in force since 2018, sets an equal age of consent regardless of sex, while keeping heavier penalties for an indecent or unnatural act with a minor of the same sex. Legality is not the same as protection: the general indecency provision has been used to prosecute same-sex conduct, and no criminal ruling on the same-sex provisions had ever been rendered as of Benin's statement to the 2008 review, on the government's account because families would not allow children to be brought to court. No law prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression or sex characteristics, and there is no protection on grounds of gender identity at all. Legal gender recognition is impossible. A trans visitor has no recognition pathway to rely on and no statutory protection against discrimination in employment, services, or public life. Service denial is documented and specific. LGBTQI+ persons are routinely refused medical care, including hormone treatment, as well as social services; healthcare providers regularly refuse gender-affirming hormone therapy and also deny general care such as malaria treatment. Employers often will not hire people known to be LGBTQ, with transgender and intersex people singled out. The US State Department's 2023 report records hostility toward the community especially outside major urban areas, an urban/rural split a visitor should weigh. Violence risk is real and largely unpunished. Anti-gay lynchings are described as commonplace in Benin in an April 2024 report; violence and lynchings are mostly committed by civilians rather than state authorities, and police rarely pursue perpetrators. Those who report violence or discrimination to police conceal their sexual orientation or gender identity out of fear of mistreatment. The most recent documented public event in this record is a 17 May 2013 International Day Against Homophobia, Biphobia and Transphobia gathering in Cotonou drawing 200 people; no later incident is documented here. Small survivor-support infrastructure exists. The Hirondelles Club at the Rehoboth Friendship Centre has housed LGBT+ youth since about 2020, a 20-place temporary accommodation centre through which almost 380 young people from Benin and the sub-region have passed; a separate account describes 20 shelters run between 2020 and 2024 housing 380 LGBTQ people. These are the only documented support structures in this inventory. Religion is a significant source of hostility. Catholic churches bury LGBTQ people in separate cemeteries, priests are documented calling transgender people demons, and imams, priests and traditional healers perform conversion therapy often coerced by families. Evangelical temples and Muslim mosques participate in homophobic preaching. A 2015 account describes LGBT Catholics in Benin, Ghana, Togo and Nigeria facing discrimination from both churches and governments; that account is dated 2015 and is context rather than current-state evidence. Same-sex couples and families are not recognised by the government, though it grants diplomatic visas and immunity to same-sex partners of foreign diplomats. Article 104(d) of the Children's Code (Law 2015-08) bars foreign homosexual couples from international adoption. Limited protections exist on paper: Article 394 of the Digital Code (Law 2017-20) prohibits processing personal data revealing sex life or sexual orientation, Article 6 of the 2009 Personal Data Protection Law prohibits collection without consent, Article 23 of Law 2011-26 requires business leaders to prevent sexual harassment, and Article 552 of Law 2017-20 punishes incitement to discrimination or hatred on grounds of sexual orientation by electronic network with one year imprisonment and a five million CFA francs fine, in force since 2018. LGBTI organisations cannot register. Benin rejected states' recommendations to improve the situation for LGBTQ persons in the 2012 Universal Periodic Review, with a 4 March 2013 meeting noting that certain things would be rectified. Of fifteen 2023 UPR recommendations, the government accepted two: one to investigate and prosecute violence against LGBTQ people, and one to combat stigma against HIV. Decree No. 1999-639 imposes no specific blood-donation restrictions for LGBT people.

name: Togo
text: Togo criminalises consensual same-sex sexual activity between men and between women. Human Dignity Trust's country profile records a maximum penalty of three years' imprisonment plus a fine. The 2015 Penal Code defines the offence in Article 393 as an indecent or unnatural act committed with a person of the same sex, punishable by one to three years' imprisonment and a fine of one to three million CFA francs. The Penal Code of 13 August 1980 imposed the same custodial range with a lower fine of 100,000 to 500,000 CFA francs, and the prohibition dates to 1884, when it was introduced under the German Togoland protectorate. Advocacy is separately criminalised. Article 392 of the 2015 Penal Code punishes LGBTQ advocacy expressed through spoken words, writing or images deemed to violate public decency. The United States Department of State's 2023 human rights report reads the statutory ban on "promotion of same-sex conduct" as reaching advocacy and gender identity expression, and records that the law was enforced. Violence and threats targeting LGBTTQI persons are listed among significant human-rights issues in that department's 2022 and 2023 reports on Togo. There is no legal route to change the gender marker on government documents in Togo. No statute prohibits discrimination on the basis of gender identity, and none prohibits it on the basis of sexual orientation. No law explicitly bans cross-dressing, yet presentation-based arrests of transgender people are documented. A transgender person was arrested in March 2018 for supposed cross-dressing. In 2023 Bobo Períta, a TikTok influencer known for cross-dressing, was arrested for violating public decency, convicted on 1 June 2023 and sentenced to civil prison in Lomé. In November 2019 police followed a transgender person to her home and refused to let her leave until she had sex with them. The sexual assault was prevented only by the presence of the victim's mother. That 2019 case is the most recent instance of trans-specific police violence documented in this record; no later instance is documented. Enforcement also runs through neutral offences. Arbitrary arrests and a disproportionate use of loitering and immorality provisions against LGBTQ people are recorded, including the January 2021 arrest and imprisonment of a gay man and his partner until Afrique Arc-En-Ciel paid for their release. A Washington Blade feature published on 31 August 2015, based on interviews conducted in March 2015 and a return visit to Lomé, describes the capital's police as "particularly merciless when dealing with LGBT locals and tourists" and records a 2008 attack on the author at a site he revisited. It is the only on-the-ground account of tourist exposure to Lomé policing in this record, and it is a decade old. Custody and care carry documented risks. Prison chaplains have refused communion to LGBTQ prisoners who have not repented for homosexuality, and LGBTQ prisoners are denied HIV/AIDS treatment and condoms. Providers at HIV and STD treatment centres discriminate against LGBTQ patients, and the resulting avoidance of care is documented. The 2022 US State Department report separately lists cruel treatment, harsh prison conditions, arbitrary detention and criminal libel enforcement among significant human-rights issues. Protection machinery is limited. Article 5 of the Press and Communications Code Law 2020-001 prohibits dissemination of defamatory comments, including homophobic defamation. Decree No. 2023-116/PR, at Articles 17, 27 and 39, requires passenger screening by the Passenger Information Unit to be non-discriminatory and not based on sexual life or sexual orientation, and protects sexual orientation in data processing. Neither provision is stated to extend to gender identity. Impunity is documented. The US State Department's 2011 human rights report for Togo records security-force torture and impunity alongside official and societal discrimination against members of the LGBT community. Mistreatment by civilians or state authorities tends to go unpunished, and stigma together with the risk of legal consequences from the criminalisation of same-sex conduct and LGBTQ advocacy deters victims from reporting.

name: Gabon
text: Same-sex sexual activity between consenting adults is lawful in Gabon. The offence created in 2019 was repealed in 2020 and no provision criminalising same-sex conduct is in force. Gabon became independent in 1960 without inheriting a colonial sodomy statute, and same-sex conduct was lawful before July 2019. Law No. 042/2018, the penal code that entered into force on 5 July 2019, created the offence: Article 402 filed 'les relations sexuelles entre personnes de même sexe' under 'atteintes aux mœurs' without using the term homosexuality. Conviction carried up to six months' imprisonment and a fine of up to five million CFA francs, reported at about US$8,500 to US$8,561. The repeal followed a recorded legislative sequence. The National Assembly voted on 23 June 2020 by 48 in favour, 24 against and 25 abstentions to remove the punishment; the Senate approved on 29 June 2020 and the president signed on 7 July 2020, restoring the pre-2019 position. The 2019 provision was applied while it stood. Two men were arrested under it within months of entry into force and were released only after paying bribes to police. Police had also arrested two men alleged to be a couple in December 2013 and released them, before any same-sex offence existed on the statute book. The constitution adopted by referendum on 16 November 2024, with more than 90 per cent voting yes on roughly 55 per cent turnout, rejected civil-society demands to re-criminalise homosexuality and added privacy protections in Article 18. The same document defines marriage in Article 16 as a union between two people of opposite sex, entrenched as unamendable and reported as effective from 12 April 2025, so a visitor whose relationship would be read locally as same-sex has no route to recognition. The constitution was drafted under the military regime that took power in the August 2023 coup ending 56 years of Bongo-family rule. There is no legal gender recognition in Gabon, and no legal protection against discrimination based on gender identity. The criminal provisions on the books concern same-sex sexual activity rather than gender identity. The limited statutory protection that exists covers sexual orientation and sexual life as data: Law No. 025/2023 of 9 July 2023 amended Law No. 001/2011 of 25 September 2011 to treat them as sensitive personal data. Police are reported to make occasional use of 'breaches of modesty' charges against people with non-gender-conforming presentations and against same-sex couples; the source describing this states that such misuse of neutral laws is not widespread and that state-sponsored harassment of LGBTQ+ people as a group is not present, while harassment by individuals is described as common. The most recent documented enforcement of a same-sex offence in this record dates from 2019 and the repeal from 2020; no later prosecution is documented.

name: Burundi
text: Article 567 of Burundi's Penal Code criminalises sexual relations between people of the same sex, and applies to conduct by both men and women. The provision was passed on 22 November 2008 and took effect on 22 April 2009; such conduct was not an offence before that date. Conviction carries three months to two years of imprisonment and a fine of 50,000 to 100,000 Burundian francs. OutRight International's March 2026 country entry cites Article 250 of the Penal Code for the same offence, with up to two years in prison and a fine. The sources do not reconcile the two article numbers. Burundi provides no legal gender recognition as of March 2026. A visitor cannot obtain local documents or identity markers matching their gender, and LGBTIQ organisations cannot register as associations. Article 29 of the Constitution bans same-sex marriage. Same-sex marriage and civil unions are not recognised. Documented enforcement starts on 1 July 2009, when a man in Bujumbura was arrested for being gay and police offered release in exchange for money; he was freed after advocacy intervened. Two women were briefly arrested in 2012 and released. In September 2014 a case in Karuzi Province involving a foreign company employee and a Burundian man was dropped after three days for lack of evidence. On 2 November 2016 the High Court of Cibitoke Province sentenced a 15-year-old boy, who had admitted raping a seven-year-old boy, to one year in prison on charges of rape of a minor and homosexuality. The US State Department's reporting for 2016 states that no prosecutions for consensual same-sex conduct were reported that year, and that LGBT people faced societal discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity with no government protection from it. Enforcement intensified in 2023. In March 2023, 24 people were arrested on same-sex conduct charges; that charge was dropped after one accused person died in detention, but seven defendants were convicted of inciting debauchery. In August 2023 seven people were sentenced to one to two years in prison for engaging in homosexual acts. In December 2023 President Évariste Ndayishimiye said gay sex was like choosing Satan and that people found engaging in it should be taken to stadiums and stoned, and he rejected development aid conditioned on respecting LGBT rights. Human Rights Watch reported the remarks in January 2024. SOS Médias Burundi reported that LGBTQ Burundians described terror in their wake; the Iteka League, operating in exile, called the remarks a call for the lynching of LGBTQ people, and two members of LGBTQ associations speaking anonymously described them as a real license to kill us. US State Department human rights reporting for 2009, 2010, 2012 and 2015 documents discrimination against gays and lesbians and, for 2015, arrests and harassment of LGBT persons. The 2015 report sets these findings within a documented national crisis that included extrajudicial killings, arbitrary detention and media shutdowns. OutRight International's March 2026 entry reports harassment, discrimination, family rejection and stigmatisation of LGBTIQ people, in a setting it describes as including extrajudicial killings, enforced disappearances, arbitrary arrests, torture and sexual and gender-based violence, with no meaningful legal reform. The most recent documented incident in this record is the January 2024 reporting on the president's December 2023 remarks; no later enforcement case or official statement is documented here.

name: Madagascar
text: Same-sex conduct between adults is lawful in Madagascar only from age 21. Article 331 of the Penal Code treats same-sex acts involving a person under 21 as indecent assault, with a reported penalty band of five to ten years' imprisonment; the record also carries a two-to-five-year penalty for "indecent or against nature" acts. The age of consent is unequal, so a trans visitor whose partner or counterparty is under 21 carries a criminal exposure that a heterosexual visitor does not. Marriage is closed to same-sex couples, and no recognition of civil unions is provided. Article 2 of Law No. 2007-022 on Marriage and Matrimonial Regimes prohibits marriage between two persons of the same sex whether before the Civil Registrar or under traditional ceremonies. Article 39 of the same law names "gender identity" as a cause for absolute nullity of marriage, a direct legal exposure for a trans person whose marriage is challenged. In a 2020 case a 33-year-old woman was arrested for the statutory rape of a 19-year-old woman after the younger woman's mother filed a complaint; the mother was allegedly acting to cover an incest and rape accusation against the father. Religious leaders offered the younger woman conversion therapy during the proceedings. Public expression is constrained. In early July 2021 the Malagasy government cancelled an LGBTQ party held at a bar in Antananarivo on the grounds of "incitement to debauchery". A France 24 report of August 2024 found that although homosexuality is not illegal, it is socially unacceptable to a degree that many LGBT people hide their sexuality to keep their jobs and live in peace, developing their own networks and coded language. The most recent documented finding of violence against gender-nonconforming people in this record is the 2011 US State Department Human Rights Report, which recorded public attitudes ranging from tacit acceptance to violent rejection, particularly of transgender sex workers, who were frequent targets of verbal abuse, stone throwing and even murder. That report covered a post-coup period in which it also documented unlawful killings and societal discrimination and violence against the LGBT community. No later instance of anti-trans violence is documented in this record. One further incident is undated in the source: supporters of a same-sex couple were subjected to insults and death threats on social media, and religious leaders publicly accused them of "promising homosexuality". At Madagascar's fourth Universal Periodic Review in January 2025, out of 235 recommendations, the government rejected UN recommendations to combat anti-LGBT violence and hate speech and to equalise the age of consent. Six Malagasy organisations, Queer Place, Mifoha Olo Mazoto, Divers' Unité, Justice Égalitaire, Men Engage and Madagascar LGBT+, responded that "Refusing to act is to endorse impunity and condone violence." Health protection is framed through HIV policy rather than trans-specific care. Act No. 2005-040 on the Fight against HIV/AIDS requires information, education and communication programs adapted to the sexual orientation of target groups, and Article 26 mandates special provisions to protect vulnerable groups, expressly including young people, sex workers, men who have sex with men and mobile populations, against HIV transmission. Two statutes limit disclosure of a visitor's status. Law No. 2014-038 on the Protection of Personal Data, Article 18, bars processing of sensitive data including data on health or sexual life, and Law No. 2017-045 on Credit Information Bureaus, Article 2, likewise protects sexual orientation as sensitive data.

name: Comoros
text: Same-sex sexual activity is criminal in Comoros. Article 300 of the 2020 Penal Code punishes any act of a sexual nature contrary to morality or unnatural, and the sources in this record disagree on the penalty. Outright International, and the text of Article 300 as quoted in reference material, give six months to two years imprisonment plus a fine of 100,000 to 300,000 francs, about US$240 to US$720. An archived copy of the 2020 Penal Code specifies two to five years and a fine of 50,000 to 1,000,000 francs. Human Dignity Trust records a maximum of three years. A December 2024 press report on the Comoros court cites Article 318 as the operative provision, carrying up to five years. The 1982 Penal Code that preceded the current statute punished the same conduct with up to five years imprisonment and a fine of 50,000 to 1,000,000 francs. Enforcement is documented. In 2022 a man was prosecuted after a sexual video of him with another man was leaked online, recorded as the first prosecution of consensual adult same-sex activity under the 2020 Penal Code. In June 2024 two women were arrested after asking an imam to marry them; the request was not proven in court, but the women stated they had previously had sexual relations. They were detained from June until December 2024, convicted of homosexuality on 12 December 2024, and sentenced to five and six months respectively, then released because the terms were shorter than the time already served. Reuters and the Washington Blade both reported the December 2024 ruling, and Human Dignity Trust called the conviction a human-rights violation. The most recent documented enforcement case in this record is the December 2024 conviction; no later instance is documented. The US State Department's 2023 human rights report on Comoros states that authorities reported no arrests or prosecutions for same-sex conduct during 2023 and did not actively enforce the criminalising law that year. The same report records that police stated they did not incite or tolerate violence against LGBTQI+ persons and that none was reported in 2023, while listing widespread impunity among the country's major human-rights problems. No non-discrimination law exists. Legal gender recognition is unavailable: transgender people are not permitted to change their gender markers, and no law prohibits discrimination based on gender identity. The 2012 Labor Code provides no protection for LGBTQ people. There is no recognition of legal rights for couples read as same-sex. The Family Code defines marriage as the union of a man and a woman. The government has repeatedly declined to decriminalise homosexuality when recommended by United Nations bodies. No LGBTIQ organisation is known to operate in the country; Article 5 of Law No. 86-006/AF of 1986 prohibits organisations founded on an unlawful cause or for an unlawful purpose contrary to the law or public morals, which reference material identifies as chilling registration of such groups.

name: Equatorial Guinea
text: The Penal Code in force since 15 November 2022, a revision of the Spanish Criminal Code dating to the Francoist era, does not explicitly criminalise same-sex intimacy or gender diversity. Same-sex sexual activity is lawful and the age of consent is 18 regardless of gender or sexual orientation. Article 364(2) bars employment discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation, the first provision in Equatoguinean law explicitly protecting lesbian, gay and bisexual people, and Law 1/2016 on the Protection of Personal Data (Articles 10 and 41) protects personal data on "sexual life" where it entails discrimination. Enforcement does not follow the statute. Authorities continue to apply the 1954 Law on Vagrants and Criminals, which classifies homosexuality as an illness and normalises conversion practices. A 2020 Draft Law "Regulating Prostitution and the Rights of Homosexuals" would effectively criminalise same-sex conduct; its status is unresolved in the most recent source, an Outright International profile updated March 2026. Three further instruments institutionalise discrimination: the Military Justice Code, a ministerial order concerning "immoral" activities, and a provincial regulation. Couples whose relationship the law reads as same-sex have no legal recognition and are not eligible for the protections available to opposite-sex couples. Police and military personnel intervene in the spaces of assembly, expression and residence of lesbian women. In Bata, police have detained known lesbians collectively, on the stated ground that "lesbians are members of a sect", and have imposed collective punishment when a single lesbian is sought. The Synergía IHR report documenting these practices was published in 2024 and does not date the raids. Transgender women have reported harassment and sexual violence while in police custody, and security forces have subjected LGBTQ+ people to sexual violence and discrimination in the military, jails and prison. School officials have reportedly denied transgender students access to some facilities, teachers have reportedly discriminated against and excluded LGBTQ+ girls, and academics and government employees can be ousted if perceived as not heterosexual. LGBTQ+ children are reported to be driven from their homes, with school dropout as a consequence. Documented incidents include the 2014 detention of four men over a video found on a phone, after which they were made to explain their actions on national television; a lesbian couple in Añisok tied up at the police station, paraded through town with banners calling them witchcraft-practicing lesbians, photographed and shamed; and the August 2023 illegal detention by police of Trifonia Melibea Obono, founder of Somos Parte del Mundo, after her group submitted a report on torture and ill-treatment of LGBTQI+ people to the EU headquarters in Madrid, after which arrests and restrictions rose significantly. The most recent dated incident in this record is August 2023; no later dated instance is documented. ILGA reports that state intimidation of sexually diverse individuals persists, and that LGBTQ+ people are still detained and punished through public shaming despite the absence of an explicit prohibition. The record documents rape used as a form of conversion practice, and the forcible impregnation of queer women in an attempt to make them heterosexual. LGBTQ+ women and transgender men are described as vulnerable to sexual violence in the military and from family members. Laws against rape are not effectively enforced: the source states that the crime is rarely reported, and that police and judicial officials may decline to act where the perpetrator has political connections or is a member of the police or military. A local NGO identifies transgender children as especially vulnerable to commercial sexual exploitation, and minors generally are sexually exploited for commercial sex. The US State Department's 2021 human-rights report found that same-sex conduct was not specifically criminalised, that LGBT persons faced societal stigma, and that no anti-discrimination protections existed. That snapshot predates the 2022 Penal Code and its employment provision.

name: Eswatini
text: Same-sex relations are criminalised in Eswatini for men and women throughout the country, as of 12 March 2026. No legal gender recognition is available, so a trans visitor's passport and other identity documents are read exactly as issued, with no administrative route to align them with lived gender. Eswatini recognises no same-sex relationships. A trans visitor travelling in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship falls under the criminal law. In June 2012 Prime Minister Barnabas Sibusiso Dlamini said that people of the same sex could not even go to regional offices to get married and that the country was not ready to consider the question; in 2014 press secretary Percy Simelane said the government was monitoring the situation with a view to taking a legal position. No registered national advocacy body exists to turn to for help. The registrar of companies refused in June 2019 to register Eswatini Sexual and Gender Minorities on grounds of morality, and refused a further LGBTI group in July 2019. In April 2022 the High Court upheld the refusal to register ESGM while accepting that the constitution protects LGBTQ persons' rights to freedom of association, privacy and expression. Outright International reports that LGBTI organisations cannot register as of 12 March 2026. There are no broad legal protections against discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity in areas such as education, health, housing and employment. Rock of Hope states that with no legislation recognising LGBTIs or protecting gender identity, LGBTQ people cannot be open about their orientation or gender identity for fear of rejection and discrimination, and most choose to remain in the closet or move to South Africa. Access to care carries a documented risk of refusal. A 2019 survey found 59% of LGBTQ Swazis had been discriminated against or treated disrespectfully at public health facilities, and 30% denied healthcare services. Policy runs the other way: section 4.3 of the 2013 National Policy on Sexual and Reproductive Health requires the Ministry of Health to make family planning information and services available regardless of sex, gender, age, status, sexual orientation and religion, and in February 2012 public health officials ran a Valentine's Day campaign urging gay people to test for HIV, with Deputy Director of Health Simon Zwane saying the Health Ministry was extending HIV counselling and testing to same-sex couples. Targeted violence is documented with dates. In March 2015 a 26-year-old lesbian woman from Nhlangano was murdered by a man who did not want to be in the presence of lesbians, and a few months earlier a gay man was murdered in the same town. The most recent documented case in this record is from 2015; no later instance is documented. Official hostility is on the record. The US State Department's 2021 report noted that some traditional, religious and government officials criticised same-sex sexual conduct as neither morally Swati nor Christian. In 2012 former Foreign Affairs Minister Mgwagwa Gamedze rejected a UN working group call for an LGBTQ protection law, saying so few gays lived in Eswatini that drafting one was not worth the effort; in May 2017 the UN Human Rights Committee pressed the government on measures to protect people from discrimination and violence based on sexual orientation and gender identity. The National Guidelines for Adolescent Sexual and Reproductive Health (2021) state that the right to equality includes freedom from discrimination because of one's sex or sexual orientation, define gender-based violence to include violence directed at a person based on gender identity or perceived adherence to norms of masculinity and femininity, and name LGBT people as a key population at higher risk of gender-based violence. These policy instruments sit beneath a criminal law that has not changed.

name: Lesotho
text: Lesotho does not criminalise consensual same-sex conduct. The common-law offence of sodomy was struck down in 2012, and male same-sex sexual activity has been lawful since; sexual activity between women was never criminalised. A joint stakeholder submission to the Universal Periodic Review filed in October 2024 by The Advocates for Human Rights, the Master of Healing Foundation and the Rainbow Alliance of Lesotho records same-sex conduct as lawful while documenting the absence of protections. No general anti-discrimination statute protects LGBTIQ+ people. The Labour Act 2024, the current statutory framework for workplace rights, bans employment discrimination on the ground of sexual orientation and defines workplace gender-based violence and harassment as violence and harassment, including sexual harassment, directed at workers, trainees, probationers, applicants, managers, supervisors, customers, clients, suppliers or contractors because of sex, gender or gender identity, or affecting persons of a particular sex, gender or gender identity disproportionately. The Act operates in the employment sphere only. No law in Lesotho permits a change of legal gender marker on documents. A 2017 constitutional analysis by the Southern African Litigation Centre argues that section 4(1) of the Constitution, in its references to sex and other status, should be read to include gender identity in line with the UN Human Rights Committee, and warns that a transgender person travelling on a passport whose gender marker does not match their presentation could face charges. A October 2020 briefing by the Southern African Litigation Centre, the People's Matrix Association and the Women in Law Southern Africa Lesotho office benchmarks Lesotho's law and policy against international best practice and identifies the Matrix as the only known LGBTI organisation in the country. The October 2024 joint stakeholder submission documents discrimination, rape and assaults against LGBT people, barriers to health and education services, and SOGIESC discrimination at community level. A November 2024 submission by the International Commission of Jurists to the same review places LGBTIQ+ persons' rights to equality and non-discrimination among three key concerns, alongside inclusive education for children with disabilities and the revocation of practising certificates held by NGO lawyers. On partner recognition, the Marriage Act No. 10 of 1974 and customary law permit marriage only between opposite-sex couples, and same-sex marriages and civil unions are not recognised. A trans visitor whose relationship would be classed as same-sex under the sex recorded at their birth has no recognised union in Lesotho. On enforcement, the 2016 United States Department of State human rights report for Lesotho stated that LGBTI persons faced societal discrimination and official insensitivity, that same-sex relationships were taboo and not openly discussed, and that no assaults were reported because incidents often went unreported for fear of stigma. The same report recorded that the Matrix Support Group operated freely in all ten districts with a good working relationship with the Lesotho Mounted Police Service, including police intervention in December 2015 to enable a lesbian forced from home by her brothers to return, and a supportive police escort for a march of approximately 200 people in Maseru on 21 May 2016. The most recent documented instance of violence against LGBT people in this record is the October 2024 Universal Periodic Review submission, which records rape and assault; no later instance is documented. Support structures exist. The Matrix Support Group was established in 2009 and fully registered in 2010 as an LGBTI organisation including transgender and intersex people, working principally through engagement with partner organisations on gender-based violence. It organised the first gay pride march on 18 May 2013 in central Maseru with supportive authorities providing an escort, and pride marches have been held annually since, attracting a few hundred people.

name: Cabo Verde
text: Cabo Verde does not criminalise consensual same-sex conduct. Article 71 of the 1886 Penal Code prohibited unnatural acts; a 2004 amendment removed all provisions relating to consensual homosexual sex, making Cabo Verde the second country in Africa to decriminalise after South Africa. The age of consent stood at 16 at decriminalisation, the same as for consensual heterosexual acts; a source covering 2015 records it as 14. No legal gender recognition framework is on record. Civil law blocked the change to a female legal name sought by Tchinda Andrade, the first publicly self-outed transgender woman in Cabo Verde, who came out in 1997 at age 19 and in a local newspaper in 1998; a 22 June 2016 interview records that refusal, and the sources contain no later statute or administrative procedure permitting a legal gender change. A visitor whose passport marker differs from presentation should expect no local precedent for documentary flexibility. Workplace protection stops short of gender identity. Since 2008, articles 45(2) and 406(3) of the Labour Code have barred discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation, with a fine set case by case, and article 406(3) applies the same penalty to unlawful dismissal on racial, ethnic, religious or sexual-orientation grounds. The sources record no equivalent statutory protection covering gender identity, and Cabo Verde is one of few African countries with any such workplace protection. No same-sex union is recognised. On 11 July 2017 Prime Minister Ulisses Correia e Silva stated that legalising same-sex marriage was not on the government's agenda, following demands from the LGBT community for civil unions and marriage. Trans-specific violence in this record is limited to one account. In the 2016 interview Tchinda Andrade reported verbal violence and two physical attacks in Cabo Verde, which the source does not date; no later trans-specific attack or killing is documented here. The state's external posture is protective. Cabo Verde joined 65 other states on 18 December 2008 in a UN General Assembly statement affirming that human rights apply regardless of sexual orientation and gender identity and urging an end to criminal penalties on that basis; it signed UN documents in 2011 condemning violence and discrimination against LGBT people; it made anti-discrimination commitments in its 2024 Universal Periodic Review; and on 28 June 2025 it was the only African country to sign a 15-state foreign-ministers declaration rejecting criminalisation and stigmatisation, backing the eradication of transphobic harassment and socio-labour inclusion especially for trans persons, and calling for an end to conversion practices and to prosecution carrying imprisonment or death. Cabo Verde is one of two African members of the UN LGBTI Core Group. Public-attitude data does not measure transgender acceptance. Polling records 82% of respondents in 2019–21 saying they would accept a 'homosexual' neighbour, and an Afrobarometer poll published in May 2020 found 80% of Cabo Verdeans would welcome or not be bothered by a homosexual neighbour, one of only four African countries polled with a majority in favour. Every tolerance finding in the sources is framed around gays, lesbians or homosexual neighbours, with none specific to transgender people. A 2010 US State Department Human Rights Report found that societal discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity continued to be a problem despite the legal provisions protecting homosexual conduct.

name: Maldives
text: The Maldives criminalises same-sex conduct and same-sex marriage under its Penal Code, whose amended provisions took effect in 2015. Section 131 defines criminal sexual contact as sexual contact without a reason permitted under Islamic law, and section 411(2) names same-sex intercourse as an offence under section 411(f). Section 410(a)(8), in force since 16 July 2015, criminalises marriage between two persons of the same sex. Penalties run to one year for unlawful marriage under section 410(a)(8), up to eight years for the conduct covered by sections 411(a)(2) and 411(d) with a supplementary 100 lashes available under Sharia, and up to four years for unlawful sexual conduct under section 412. The 2014 code extended the offence beyond Muslims to all persons. Capital punishment is not available for these offences. The record states that homosexual acts cannot be punished with death under Maldivian law, that executions have been suspended since 1953, and that under sections 92(k) and 1205 death is reserved for egregious purposeful killing; plans to restart executions were later abandoned. No transgender-specific criminal provision, document rule, screening procedure, facility rule, custody rule or care restriction appears anywhere in this record. Every codified offence and penalty described concerns same-sex sexual activity and same-sex marriage. There is no legal protection against discrimination based on gender identity, and none based on sexual orientation. The provisions are framed by sex, and the record contains no guidance on how a trans person's gender would be classified under them. The only enforcement action documented in this record is the arrest of two men, aged 56 and 27, on Dhaandhoo island on 29 August 2015 for homosexual activity in their private home following a public complaint. No later instance is documented. A 2020 foreign government country report found no reports of officials complicit in abuses against LGBTI persons, while noting that societal stigma likely discouraged reporting. Documented violence against LGBT people in the record consists of the 2013 neck stabbing of gay blogger Hilath Rasheed in Male. The United Nations Population Fund reported that people perceived as homosexual or transgender in the Maldives were the target of hate crimes and other human rights violations and recommended law reform to protect LGBTQ individuals; the government noted those recommendations without accepting them. In 2014 New Zealand granted asylum to gay Maldivian Abraham Naim on the basis that he was at risk of serious harm from state agents, after a President's Office spokesman commented that people seeking asylum over sexual-orientation discrimination would face prosecution on return. Official posture at the United Nations is restrictive. The Maldives rejected 60 Universal Periodic Review recommendations covering matters said to contradict the Islamic faith and the Constitution, including matters relating to lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender and non-traditional forms of the family. It rejected the 2011 and September 2014 United Nations resolutions on sexual orientation and gender identity, signed a 2008 document opposing decriminalisation, and noted but did not accept 2015 recommendations to decriminalise consenting adult same-sex relations. The Human Rights Committee recommended anti-discrimination legislation covering sexual orientation and action against stigmatisation of homosexuals. Travel guidance in the record reports that LGBTQ tourists are generally welcome at most private tourist islands, resorts and hotels, which are usually isolated from civilian population centres and are described as not subject to Islamic law, with alcohol sales offered as evidence; guides advise caution about displays of affection outside tourist areas. A local advocacy group warned in 2015 that tourists could face threats similar to those faced by residents. The record contains no documented statement about societal tolerance of transgender people as a distinct group. Every description of tolerance or hostility in it refers to LGBTQ people generally, to homosexuality, or to homophobia.

name: North Korea
text: The DPRK Criminal Code of 1950, revised in 2009, appears to contain no penalty for consensual same-sex acts. Two provisions nonetheless leave enforcement to official discretion: Article 193 bans the import, keeping and distribution of "decadent culture", including sexual recordings, and Article 262 bans collective "obscene activities". Neither is defined in terms that constrain how it is applied. The US State Department's 2022 human rights report reaches the same conclusion, that no specific law criminalises same-sex conduct, and adds that the regime's total control leaves no space for LGBT life. The same department's 2020 report states that no reliable information on LGBT persons exists and that the repression of all civil society is the dominant human-rights reality. Changing the sex marker on a birth certificate or citizen card is technically possible under "unavoidable circumstances": an application to the People's Security Agency together with a state forensic medical evaluation, with surgical intervention required in practice. No law explicitly bans gender-affirming care, but the under-resourced health system makes hormones and surgery effectively inaccessible. Article 8 of the Family Law states that marriage may be done only between one man and one woman; as of 2026 no North Korean law recognises same-sex marriage, civil unions or domestic partnerships. Same-sex couples could not legally adopt children as of the 2020 State Department report. The Constitution, last revised 2024, does not address discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, and no provisions exist in North Korean law prohibiting such discrimination. Official hostility is documented. A 2014 KCNA commentary rejected the UN Commission of Inquiry's report as a political fabrication and attacked commissioner Michael Kirby with a homophobic slur, evidence of hostility toward homosexuality even while the state denies its existence. A 2014 KCNA statement denied homosexuality's existence outright. Violence records are sparse and dated. A 2023 South Korean Ministry of Unification report cites defector testimony that at least one male detainee in a detention camp was secretly executed for homosexuality in 2014. A 2011 Korea Times report, sourced to Free North Korea Radio, claimed the execution of a lesbian couple, a North Korean woman and a Japanese woman, for capitalist influence and corruption of public morals. No documented state or non-state violence against LGBTIQ people is recorded by Outright International beyond these accounts; the most recent documented case in this record is from 2014, with no later instance documented. Defector accounts indicate a climate of forced concealment. Jang Young-jin, a novelist who defected in the late 1990s, was forcibly outed and is the first publicly known gay defector; an openly gay defector published an autobiography in 2017. The BBC's 2024 feature documents how a collective-over-individual regime forces DPRK sexual minorities into silent self-suppression. New laws, including the Pyongyang Cultural Protection Act, tighten control as of that reporting. No registration route for LGBTI organisations exists.

name: Isle of Man
text: The Isle of Man is a self-legislating Crown Dependency of the United Kingdom. Tynwald enacts its own statutes on gender recognition, equality and criminal law, and United Kingdom legislation reaches the island only when extended by Order in Council rather than automatically. The Gender Recognition Act 2009 (c.11) allows transgender people to change their legal gender and to have the new gender recognised. The Equality Act 2017, granted royal assent on 18 July 2017 and largely in force from 1 January 2019, lists gender reassignment as a protected characteristic and as a ground on which discrimination is prohibited. A ban on conversion therapy covering sexual orientation and gender identity was passed in 2020 as an amendment to the sexual offences bill in the Legislative Council and took effect in 2024. In 2024 the Isle of Man became the first British territory, and the first part of the British Isles, to prohibit the practice. In July 2022 community consultation progressed on a hate crime bill that would explicitly include gender reassignment alongside sexual orientation and marital or civil partnership status. The bill's status after that consultation is not sourced. Sexual offences law applies gender-neutrally. Private consensual male homosexual acts were decriminalised in September 1992 with an age of consent of twenty-one, lowered to eighteen by the Criminal Justice Act 2001 (c.4), then lowered to sixteen and made gender-neutral for all sexual conduct regardless of gender and sexual orientation by the Sexual Offences (Amendment) Act 2006 (c.3). Until 2021, Section 9 of the Sexual Offences Act 1992 retained offences of buggery and gross indecency between men if under sixteen or committed elsewhere than in private; in 2021 the more-than-two-persons specification was deleted and language on indecent exposure and sexual activity in a public place was made gender-neutral under the Sexual Offences and Obscene Publications Act 2021, which received royal assent in July 2021 and took effect on 1 July 2022 by proclamation. On partner recognition, same-sex couples have held civil partnerships since 6 April 2011 under the Civil Partnership Act 2011 (c.2), and marriage has been available since 22 July 2016 following royal assent on 19 July 2016. Existing civil partnerships could be converted without a second ceremony, and the first conversion was completed within days of entry into force. A trans visitor in a relationship that would be locally classed as same-sex enters a jurisdiction that recognises the union. Family law has not kept pace with that recognition. Under the Civil Partnership Act 2011, same-sex couples have had equal access to full joint or stepchild adoption since 6 April 2011 and lesbian couples have access to artificial insemination, but as of an August 2023 consultation same-sex couples are not recognised as parents on birth certificates in cases of IVF and surrogacy, and no law on the island acknowledges surrogacy.

name: Guadeloupe
text: Guadeloupe is a French overseas department. Criminal law, identity-document rules, custodial conditions and the national preventive mechanism are set at the national level and carried by the parent record; this assessment covers what is specific to the island. Guadeloupe's first LGBT+ centre, the Maison des Diversités et de l'Inclusion, opened on 24 April 2024, run by a federation of Guadeloupean associations.
