It offers reception, support and orientation for people of diverse identity, sexual, bodily and gender diversities. The opening was attended by the visiting national minister Aurore Bergé, who announced measures to strengthen the fight against gender-based violence and discrimination in Guadeloupe, with structures adapted for the overseas territories. The centre's opening was presented as a concrete step toward inclusion and safety. Community organisations Secret's Out, Queer Gang and Lovo Nova partnered on a year of LGBT-friendly social events across Guadeloupe in 2025, described locally as a potential 'annus mirabilis' for the island's community. A September 2023 interview with Leïla of Secret's Out reported that community members increasingly reconcile their lives with their orientation, and described activism on the island as advancing after neighbouring Martinique; the interview also featured Prisca Melyon-Reinette of Amalgame Humani's.

name: Aruba
text: Aruba is a constituent territory within the Kingdom of the Netherlands and stands under that framework; the island's own Criminal Code (Wetboek van Strafrecht / Kódigo Penal), enacted in 2012, carries the anti-discrimination provisions in force here. Article 1:221 defines discrimination as any form of discrimination, exclusion, restriction or preference that has the purpose or effect of affecting the recognition, enjoyment or exercise of human rights and fundamental liberties in political, economic, social or cultural fields or in other areas of social life, and Articles 2:61 and 2:62 set penalties ranging from fines to one year of imprisonment. The enumerated grounds cover heterosexual or homosexual orientation only. Gender identity and gender expression are not addressed, and no transgender-specific provision is cited in the sources. Same-sex sexual activity is legal for both male and female forms, and the age of consent is 16, equal for heterosexual and homosexual intercourse. This is the only youth-specific legal threshold in the record; no findings on education, schools, or minors' access to services or documentation appear in the sources. Partner recognition is established at two levels. On 8 September 2016 the Aruban Parliament voted 11 to 5, with four abstentions per the Associated Press account of 9 September 2016, to extend civil-code marriage articles to registered partnerships open to both opposite-sex and same-sex couples, granting spousal pension and emergency medical decision rights. Same-sex marriage has been legal since 12 July 2024, when the Supreme Court of the Netherlands upheld the Appeals Court decision barring discrimination based on sexual orientation in the ruling that made same-sex marriage legal in Aruba. Since the Dutch Supreme Court ruling of 13 April 2007, Aruba must recognize same-sex marriages registered in the Netherlands and in Bonaire, Sint Eustatius and Saba. A same-sex marriage bill introduced in June 2022 was rejected after tied parliamentary votes in May and June 2024, immediately before the July 2024 ruling. A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship is dealing with a regime whose protections are written in terms of sexual orientation alone. On 22 April 2015 representatives of all Kingdom governments endorsed prompt equal rights for LGBT persons expressly including transgender persons on Aruba, Curaçao and Sint Maarten. Aruba's own representation at that meeting acknowledged that strict conservative norms made coming out difficult for LGBT youth on the island, who were stigmatized as disordered. Harassment has been documented. Charlene and Esther Oduber-Lamer reported frequent harassment and having rocks thrown at them during their court challenge (2004–2007) that forced Aruba and the other Dutch Caribbean islands to recognize same-sex marriage. The Aruban government was particularly vocal in opposing same-sex marriage during that court challenge, and the Roman Catholic Church, the island's largest denomination, contributed to mainstream societal opposition to LGBT rights. The most recent documented incident of anti-LGBT harassment in this record is from that 2004–2007 period; no later instance is documented. Several specific gay bars and clubs operate in the capital city of Oranjestad, and various venues, hotels and restaurants cater to or advertise as 'LGBT-friendly'. Numerous LGBT associations operate, including Equality Aruba (Igualdad Aruba), Equal Rights Aruba and Alternative Lifestyle Federation Aruba. The last is quoted: 'Aruba has always been accepting, as long as it's not in their face. People are out, but discreetly out. There has never been anything official.'

name: Faroe Islands
text: The anti-discrimination provision in force since 1 January 2007 makes anyone who publicly makes a statement threatening, insulting or degrading a group on account of race, colour, national or ethnic origin, religion or sexual orientation liable to a fine or up to two years' imprisonment. Gender identity is not among the listed grounds. On the sourced account this made the Faroe Islands the last Northern European jurisdiction to prohibit discrimination and harassment on grounds of sexual orientation. Before that provision took effect, homophobic conduct was legally unaddressed. In 2006 the openly gay singer, songwriter and radio host Rasmus Rasmussen was severely beaten by five men in Tórshavn and hospitalised shortly after coming out; he and his family then received threatening telephone calls, and police refused to handle the case because no Faroese law banned discrimination against sexual minorities at the time. He was later moved to a psychiatric hospital with severe depression exacerbated by the beating, never recovered, and died by suicide in 2012. The most recent documented assault in this record is that 2006 attack; no later instance is documented. A second documented attack dates from 2005, when the Norwegian drag group Great Garlic Girls had to run from a gang of young men intent on physically assaulting them in Tórshavn; the group was not attacked anywhere else on its tour. Hostility from elected office is documented across a decade. In September 2010 Centre Party leader Jenis av Rana refused to attend a state banquet for the visiting Icelandic prime minister and her partner, citing his religion. In June 2015 Løgting Speaker Jógvan á Lakjuni published a letter attacking the national broadcaster Kringvarp Føroya for the space it gave LGBT Føroyar and condemning a drag show at the Nordic House as 'non-culture', asking whether 'these people do not feel any shame'. The same year av Rana demanded that Pride be banned and repeatedly compared LGBT Føroyar to Sea Shepherd whale-hunting protesters, and his party remains formally opposed to homosexuality. Singer Eivor Pálsdóttir publicly urged people to ignore him, documenting organised public pushback alongside the hostility. Public expression has been contested since the first gay pride march in 2005, which provoked substantial controversy; in 2015 av Rana also suggested the Tórshavn pride parade be moved out of the city centre. Partner recognition is unresolved in this record. In 2006 LGBT activists gathered around 20,000 online signatures demanding an end to sexual-orientation discrimination and a registered-partnership law aligned with the rest of the Nordics; at that point the Faroe Islands, with a population of about 47,000, had neither protection nor partnership recognition. No later sourced statement establishes the current status of partnership or marriage registration here.

name: American Samoa
text: American Samoa's own criminal code does not punish consensual sodomy. The first sodomy statute, enacted in 1963, covered male homosexual and heterosexual conduct and did not address lesbian conduct; the Fono's 1979 revision, effective in 1980, retained prohibition only for public acts, prostitution, conduct involving minors and conduct with persons unable to consent. The age of consent is 16, regardless of gender or sexual orientation. Same-sex marriage is not licensed. On 20 March 2003 the Senate rejected a bill introduced by Representative Sua Carl Schuster that would have outlawed it, after the House Judiciary Committee recommended the bill be killed; at the committee hearing fa'afafine resident Tifanny Poutasi testified that fa'afafine do not seek marriage with men, describing them as men expressing femininity through dress and speech and citing Christian upbringing. In July 2015 Attorney General Talauega Eleasalo Ale was reviewing whether the United States Supreme Court's 2015 marriage-equality ruling reached the territory and said he did not know, while the Governor stated that it did not apply, citing the territory's preamble, its constitution, Christian values and its unorganised and unincorporated political status. No same-sex couple had filed an application at that point, and a 2026 law-review article by two attorneys practising in American Samoa records that none has applied since. In January 2016 the Senate unanimously confirmed former Attorney General Fiti Alexander Sunia as a District Court judge after he told confirming senators, including retired High Court associate judge Senator Tauolo Manaia Fruean, that he had not read the 2015 ruling, that the district court does not deal with it, and that he would not perform weddings for same-sex couples unless local laws change. In July 2024 an on-island survey by Dr Daniel Hall, a constitutional and comparative law professor at Miami University, tested whether the territory's ban would survive a challenge under the Fourteenth Amendment. As of mid-2024 the ban is treated locally as operative and its constitutional durability as an open question. The 2026 article reaches the opposite conclusion on the law, holding that the 2015 ruling does apply despite those official statements and that the territory would have to issue a marriage certificate to any same-sex couple that applied; it sets out a litigation path through the High Court of American Samoa first, with the Territorial Registrar as defendant, then the United States Department of the Interior. Since 13 December 2022 the territory has been obliged to recognise, though not perform, same-sex marriages performed legally in another jurisdiction, with equal treatment for same-sex and opposite-sex couples. The territory's marriage code does not specify the sex of the parties. It refers to the age of 'the male' and 'the female' on a form in which parties identify as 'son' and as 'daughter'. Gender markers on local documents are changeable within limits. The High Court of American Samoa has held that birth certificates may be altered only to correct information that was erroneous at the time of recordation or to reflect a name change due to adoption, and the Office of Vital Statistics reads that ruling as covering applications from transgender people: it changes the name on a birth certificate when presented with a name change order, and may change the gender marker with medical documentation of the sex change. Documented trans-specific legal matters in the territory concern employment and criminal proceedings. In June 2023 a federal civil action cited a hostile work environment in a transgender woman's lawsuit against the territorial government over her gender identity, and in September 2023 the United States Justice Department secured a settlement with the American Samoa Government resolving an employment-discrimination case involving harassment of a transgender employee. In February 2023 a 51-year-old man was charged with sexual abuse of a 16-year-old transgender teenager; that charge is the most recent documented instance of violence against a trans person in this record, no later instance is documented, and no outcome for the charge is stated. Public climate combines cultural recognition with religious conservatism. Fa'afafine, defined as people born male who embody both male and female traits, are described in Samoan scholarship as a recognised and integral part of traditional Samoan culture, and the Society of Fa'afafine in American Samoa, formed in 2010, campaigns for the community and runs annual events; the first Pride festival was held in August 2016 in Utulei, and beauty pageants among the fa'afafine community draw family support. Society is nonetheless highly religious, conservative attitudes on gender and sexuality dominate, and open displays of affection between couples, same-sex or opposite-sex, may offend. A 2009 travel column described reserved public behaviour as expected of people of all orientations in the territory.

name: Northern Mariana Islands
text: The Northern Mariana Islands is a US commonwealth. Travel documents, immigration and airport screening are governed by United States national rules rather than by commonwealth law, and the national layer of this assessment sits with the United States record. Consensual same-sex conduct is not criminalised. Marriage between same-sex couples has been recognised in the commonwealth since 2015, and the first such marriage on Saipan was officiated on 27 July 2015. A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship can expect that relationship to be recognised. Adoption has been available to same-sex couples since 2015. Legal gender change is permitted in the Northern Mariana Islands provided the applicant has undergone the specified medical process, so identity documents can be brought into line with presentation, subject to that medical requirement. Commonwealth law provides for enhanced sentencing in hate-motivated crimes. Public Law 22-32, signed in January 2023, amends the Commonwealth Code with criteria covering offences motivated by sexual orientation and gender identity. This is the principal commonwealth-level protection with direct bearing on gender-identity-motivated violence. There is no comprehensive commonwealth nondiscrimination statute covering gender identity. Commonwealth-level protections extend to government employees only, and recourse beyond federal complaint channels is limited. As of 27 September 2026 the Movement Advancement Project scored the territory's sexual orientation policy at 3.5 of 22 and its gender identity policy at minus 2 of 25, an overall rating of 1.5 of 47, classified as Low with a negative gender-identity score.
